INTRO - 02-02-2024:
Given all the sad news of licenses expiring (probably of the licensed music in the game for songs from Alice in Chains & Jimi Hendrix, for starters) and this game (Spec Ops: The Line) being pulled from digital stores (Xbox Store, GOG, Steam, etc.), I'm going to do a retrospective & re-review (on a replay) of the outstanding military-style third-person shooter (TPS) by Yager, which certainly is one of the most memorable of these type of Gears of War-like cover shooters ever made.

CROSS(-ING) THE LINE.
In this game, you play Walker from the military, a soldier who has a squad that goes into Dubai for a recon mission. That doesn't say much and I'm not going to go too much further into that, as that's the set-up and you're likely better off not knowing much going in here. That is just the start of the game's descent into brutality & madness, in which this game eventually becomes something else entirely in so many ways, without going into spoiler turf here.

This is not an easy game for many people to stomach, given its commentary here & also the grisly and brutality of the content in this game & some of its scenes. This game's well known for some players not finishing the game at a certain common "quitting point" in the game, due to its nature - but for those that can see it through even after that point, that quitting point (QP) is not just the only brutal part of this game; it still gets brutal in other ways here after that QP, too. The game is both a physical and mental tour de force here, for both gamers & the characters in this game, without spoiling anything here.

Basically, Spec Ops: TL is gaming's Heart of Darkness & Apocalypse Now (for all you movie and book buffs here), without really heading into spoiler turf here, as it has so much to say about its subject matters - i.e. military, war, violence, morality, Gov't agencies, patriotism, and more.

GAMEPLAY.
The set pieces and shoot-outs here are outstanding, along w/ the licensed soundtrack & voice-acting. The combat's intense and really good, if you love those Gears of War type of TPS's, but instead it's more realistic than that. The script's a total cinematic & gaming masterpiece, all rolled into one here. If you like military games and Gears of War type of TPS cover-shooters, you're going to really like the combat & gameplay here, as it certainly does its thing & plays very well. Just, you know...don't expect to battle bugs and robots here, as this is not a sci-fi game; this is a military game aiming for realism.

On a replay here at 1080p and maxed-out on my 6gb VRAM RTX 3060 laptop here - in which that laptop's loaded with also R5 5600H, 16gb RAM, 1 TB SSD, W11 - this game has no problem running on modern systems here for me. Runs super-smooth and very rarely goes under 60fps, which is great. Amazingly, the game still looks great & that stuff still holds up to very well to this day, due to also the game's art direction and also the number of details in the game-world. I also shouldn't forget this game's own immersion factor here, with the way it depicts Dubai, war, and others things here - and not to forget the outstanding soundtrack of licensed music, too.

LICENSE TO REMOVE, FIX, OR SOMETHING.
This is the point where I state this about licenses in games: I wish" forever-licenses" existed for games so games can be sold w/ their original & proper vision w/ key songs intact (same could go for cars in racing games, too). But, this is how musicians and/or the music industry makes money, where companies need to re-license a track so it keeps getting sold.

So, as much as I hate to say this: I wish more games pulled a Hi-Fi Rush, having a back-up plan in place so streamers can stream the game without NDA strikes & without licensing music playing, instead using generic and/or music from the studio - which also seems like a great back-up for plan for the sad moment when key songs for the game sadly might need to get pulled b/c it's still being sold on a digital service & b/c said publisher don't want to pay for the license anymore.

It's sad to see Michael Jackson tunes removed from classic GTA's and all of the great tunes from Mafia 1 (original) have to get pulled; and/or sad to see games like Specs Ops: The Line & Alpha Protocol disappear from purchasing b/c of this madness. At least w/ Mafia 1 (on Steam and GOG), that game is still being sold, even if it's sadly without its OG licensed tunes. I'll be sad for the day all the great licensed tunes from Vampire: Bloodlines need to get pulled, too.

OUTRO, FOR NOW.
It's a shame to see such a great TPS game with tons to say & still very relevant - and it probably always will be, TBH - get pulled from digital stores. Though I do see Xbox 360 & PS3 copies from retail on EBay now going for over $70-150. So, yeah - "Wow! Just wow!" It's not a long single-player campaign, which can go for around 8 hours or so - but with multiple difficulties here & it's an extremely well-executed and also feels right & perfect in length, it rocks. It never lets go of the player in so many ways & is definitely being thought-provoking from start to finish.

For those that can stomach it, this really should not be missed; this descent into its theme of War is that place below us here is just gripping, brutal, and loaded with tons to say.

One thing that stood out to me more than most shooters for Spec Ops is the gradual realization that Captain Walker is an unreliable perspective. As you progress throughout the game, Walker insists he is dutifully "completing the mission" and bringing a rogue colonel to justice. However, his justifications ring increasingly hollow. The game shifts perspectives - the supposed "villain" is revealed to have understandable motivations, while the supposed "hero's" motivations become irrational and selfish. It uses this distorted viewpoint to suggest that the "mission above all else" mentality typical in military shooters calls for it to be examined. We see Captain Walker so committed to his mission that he can no longer comprehend morality or recognize his deteriorating state of mind. Through this distorted lens, Spec Ops leaves the choices up to the players to re-evaluate the "win at all costs" design imperative that propels and excuses the unrelenting violence in these games. 

Overall, Spec Ops was something new that I had not planned for, and I loved every minute; I really enjoyed the different perspectives and messages of these genres.

Bloody hell, how intense and brutal can a game get? I'm not very good at third-person shooters, so you can imagine I found this game remarkably tough, especially towards the end. To be honest, I thought I knew Spec Ops wasn't going to be a run-of-the-mill jingoistic military shooter as soon as the menu screen loaded up, and was greeted by a mournful piece of guitar music that less screamed "War!" and more like "This is sad". 

The story of The Line is an uncomfortable character study, and one which presents you with several moral choices that hit you like a ton of bricks when their consequences play out: this is the opposite of a feel-good game. I cared about the protagonist and his relationships with his two squad mates, and genuinely wanted them to come through despite everything that was happening around them.

The gameplay holds up equally well for the most part. You can carry two weapons plus grenades at a time, and all the guns feel different. You take cover, which is mostly reliable, and can vault over walls to escape or to perform takedowns in certain situations. The firefights with enemy turrets in the field were monstrously tough-going. The game doesn't have many bullet-sponge enemies: most soldiers go down quickly in a few successful shots, but the equivalent to this is that you, too, are very vulnerable. Keep your head down! Also, you will be called on to heal your mates in the battlefield if they stray too far from cover and lose too much health. This part of the game is real risk-assessment and you have to be very quick doing it as you'll inevitably be in the line of fire. 

The low point: sometimes the game saves BEFORE the cutscene and not AFTER, and the checkpoint system sometimes is very harsh around this. There was one section which took about 7 attempts, forcing me to replay a 3-minute long cutscene over and over. No game should do this.

Not exactly fun, but mightily effective.

We need more story-based shooters like this. Spec ops: The Line is a thousand times better than any campaign from Call of Duty. Essentially, it's Apocalypse Now if it was a video game. Everything that occurs in this game will stick with you forever. Spec Ops: The Line is a masterpiece in story-based gaming that has no limits when showing gamers the true horrors of war. 10/10.

This game, from the very beggining, takes heavy inspiration from the legendary 'Apocalypse Now' movie and the classical 'Heart of Darkness' book. I must say, this is probably one of - if not the - best adaption of a book/movie I've ever seen in the form of a videogame. As I said in the title: this game belongs to a now-extint species. Playing this felt like playing Dead Space 2 or Halo: Reach for the very first time. Today, it's rare to see a game so condensed with quality - a game that doesn't do absolutely anything to waste the player's time. Yes, it's short. Yes, the gameplay is janky. And yes, the game was terribly ported to PC. 
But, despite all these flaws, this game is a hidden and underrated gem. Maybe not a masterpiece overall, but close. It saddens me that these kind of experiences are gone now, games like this aren't made anymore. It all turned into endless, bland and boring "RPGs" (that aren't RPGs down to the core). Spec Ops: The Line is a  must-play - a cult classic.

Very War-On-Terror era game about 'the horrors of war' from the jingoistic Support Our Troops era of American politics.  The plot and narrative are nonsense that makes no logical sense, but the gameplay ironically is what holds up the best, despite being considered generic and by-the-numbers at the time.  Does some interesting things with squad tactics and contextual elements (you can shoot out windows to drown the Americans you're killing in sand, grenades can kick up dust that blinds your enemies).  Has some Silent Hill esque hallucinations that are nice to see, including missable sequences if you die at certain moments.

The most interesting thing about the characters is how everyone goes through the *opposite* of character development; Walker starts as a bog-standard late 2000s-early 2010s shooter protag and ends a psychotic delusional murderhobo, blaming everyone else for his own mistakes (I can see why this is Nolan North's favorite videogame role, he does a great job).  Lugo, the comic relief and Adams the no-nonsense operator, becomes a cold emotionless killer and a bloodthirsty maniac.  All the characters you meet along the way used to be better people, based on left-behind audio logs.   Just by playing through the game, you see the entirety of the games cast turn into monsters and die pointlessly, either thru suicide or murder, its great, and the best part of the games story.  

All and all, expect a subversive period piece from back when critiquing the US Military wasn't mainstream, and "realistic"  brown cover-based shooters were the only games on the market.

Spec Ops: The Line is a thrilling third person shooter. Dubai has been blasted by worse and worse sand storms, and many civilians have become trapped inside Dubai. Dubai is also surrounded in a "storm shield", which conveniently blocks radio communications in and out. You and your squad are tasked with entering Dubai, searching for survivors, and then leaving the storm shield to call for reinforcements.

[b]Gameplay - 7.3/10[/b]

The game is pretty good. I played it on Suicide Mission, and that is definitely the difficulty it was meant to be played on. You die very quickly so you spend 90% of the time in cover, and 5% of the time switching cover. There is a large variety of weapons, and a decent variety of enemies. It was very fun to slowly get better and better weapons, to slowly fight tougher and tougher enemies. The game intercuts between cover-to-cover gun fights and some other cool set pieces, like shooting with a minigun out of a helicopter as it circles a city.
The gameplay never got boring or repetitive or stale, however at times it did feel unbalanced ESPECIALLY on the highest difficulty (FUBAR). The game is so obviously not balanced around FUBAR. Heavies kill you so quickly you can't even throw a grenade out of cover if they are targeting you. There are also many points in the game that become extremely difficult or almost impossible. Those times mainly revolving around when the game doesn't let you take cover (i.e. [spoiler]when you are being chased by that helicopter or when you are on the side of the truck with a rocket launcher[/spoiler]). In these situations, you have to play extremely well and have incredible RNG to pass. However, I never felt like they were extreme roadblocks if you just persevered.
One large problem the game had is that the friendly AI is a bit stupid. Mainly pushing forward when I wasn't, reloading out in the open, etc. When they weren't in cover though they were fine, even on FUBAR difficulty.
Overall, the gameplay remains fun and engaging and reminds me a lot of Left 4 Dead 2's gameplay in a way.

[b]Story, World and Characters - 7.7/10[/b]

The story is great. The game forces you to make moral choices, and forces you to question the ethics of war. How much is too much? Is collateral acceptable if it doesn't outway the reward? If so, how much does a human life cost? Etc. There are a few moments where you are probably supposed to feel bad for things you've done (most notably the [spoiler]white phosphorus[/spoiler] part), but for the most part I am desensitised to this ♥♥♥♥.
Despite that it was still a great story. The characters are interesting, and I like how they slowly start to resent you more and more. You can see it in their voices and in the way they act. There are voice logs and notes found in appropriate places to enhance the world, however I feel like the world aspect did suffer a bit. I would feel like some characters would just appear out of thin air, like they never existed before the story showed them to me directly. (Mainly Riggs, who even was that guy???)

[b]Graphics and Audio - 8/10[/b]

The game looks good considering it was made in 2012, and at no point did I find myself complaining about the graphics at all... Okay, maybe the water at the start of the game looks a little ♥♥♥♥. However, that doesn't matter I promise. 
The music fits well, for the most part it hides in the backgrounds but at moments (especially when the music does something unique) it becomes noticeable. The music does a good job at adding tension to the game.
The sound effects do a good job, though explosives should probably be a bit louder. I also like how the enemies and the players communicate to each. The enemies will scream at each other, and so will you to your AI. It's great.

[b]Replayability, Value for Money and Extra Content - 6.2/10[/b]
There is no replayability or side content outside of the achievements. Of the achievements, despite there being 50 of them, I got 40-45 of them without trying in the first 6 hours by just playing through the game.
The only actual difficult achievement is completing the game on FUBAR difficulty, but that only took me about 6-8 hours to do. The rest of the achievements are easy to get simply due to the fact you can reload chapters, and you don't need to get all the collectibles in the same playthrough. You can load up a specific chapter, and only need to collect them once. Talking about collectibles, there are a maximum of 2 per mission and each of them give you an audio log to listen to as a reward for finding them. This is how collectibles should be done, easy to find and rewarding for getting.

~Spec Ops: The Line~ plunges players into a harrowing narrative that serves as a heartbreaking examination of the human psyche amidst the horrors of war. 

As Captain Martin Walker says, the descent into the unforgiving sand covered ruins of Dubai mirrors the erosion of morality and sanity. 

The game's desolate setting, coupled with haunting visuals and a sombre soundtrack, creates an atmosphere saturated with sorrow.

What sets ~Spec Ops: The Line~ apart is its unflinching portrayal of the emotional toll of war. 

Choices made in the heat of battle ripple through the storyline, revealing the consequences of morally ambiguous decisions. 

The characters, once heroes, become vessels of tragedy, and the unravelling narrative leaves players grappling with a sense of inevitability and despair.

The game's masterful storytelling navigates the complexities of guilt, responsibility, and the devastating impact of conflict on the human spirit. 

It is not a traditional war game; it's a heartbreaking exploration of the toll violence takes on the soul. 

~Spec Ops: The Line~ stands as a testament to the emotional weight that video games can carry, leaving players with a lingering sense of sadness and contemplation about the true cost of war. 

In the end, ~Spec Ops: The Line~ stands as a sombre testament to the human cost of war. It's a game that doesn't just tug at heartstrings, it wrenches them, leaving players with a profound sadness that lingers long after the final credits.

Well it seems Spec Ops The Line threw out that philosophy and made the corniest and least fun game they could make. It seems they wanted to subvert the genre by having this """brutal""" war game with terrible controls but also the goofiest writing and the least subtle messaging that "WAR IS BAD AND STOP HAVING FUN IN THIS UNFUN GENRE", and it just makes for such a pretentious, laughable, and borderline pathetic experience.

If they wanted to make a commentary on how Modern Military Shooters from the time were slipping into nihilistic military propaganda, all they had to do is just basically make a game like the original Call of Duty; something so simple and understandable that people would've realized that the genre was slipping into ridiculous and nihilistic depths. But no, they wanted their cake and to eat it to, and it just comes off as spineless and fraudulent.

The fact Yahtzee chose this as his game of the year is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ crazy. And you wonder why there are still modern military games to this day.

It's easy to make something un-subtle, over the top and in your face. It's harder to make something dead simple and understandable to all.

"Spec Ops: The Line" is a third-person shooter that stands out in the crowded military shooter genre for its narrative depth, moral complexity, and psychological intensity. Here's an extensive review of why this game is considered a dark gem and why players should engage with its haunting journey.

Narrative and Themes:
The narrative of "Spec Ops: The Line" is its most striking feature. Unlike typical war games that glorify combat, this game delves into the psychological trauma of warfare. Players take on the role of Captain Martin Walker as he leads his squad into a sandstorm-ravaged Dubai to locate a missing U.S. Army battalion. The story is heavily inspired by Joseph Conrad's "Heart of Darkness," which is itself a profound study of the human psyche. The game's portrayal of the horrors of war and the decline into madness is both compelling and disturbing, offering a commentary on the genre as a whole.

Moral Choices:
Throughout the game, players are faced with difficult moral decisions that have significant consequences. These choices are far from black-and-white, often presenting dilemmas without clear right or wrong answers. The weight of these decisions impacts not only the narrative outcome but also the mental state of the protagonist, which is a rare exploration in gaming.

Environmental Storytelling:
"Spec Ops: The Line" uses the environment of a shattered Dubai as a narrative device. The opulent city now buried in sand serves as a metaphor for the façade of civilization and the underlying brutality of human nature. The game's setting is both a battleground and a character in its own right, with the shifting sands acting as an unpredictable element in gameplay and story.

Combat and Gameplay Mechanics:
While the gameplay adopts standard third-person shooter mechanics, it serves the narrative rather than acting as the main attraction. Tactical squad commands, cover-based shooting, and the harsh environmental conditions of sandstorms create challenging combat scenarios. The game doesn't shy away from showing the brutality of the player's actions, with graphic consequences that serve to unsettle rather than entertain.

Psychological Impact:
"Spec Ops: The Line" is designed to make players question their actions and the typical heroism associated with military shooters. As the mental state of Captain Walker deteriorates, players are forced to confront the unsettling reality of their in-game choices. This psychological journey is one of the game's most potent aspects, often leaving a lasting impression on players.

Visual and Audio Presentation:
The game's visuals effectively convey the luxurious decay of Dubai, with striking contrasts between the remnants of opulence and the desolation of the sand-covered ruins. The audio design, including voice acting, gunfire, and the haunting soundtrack, contributes significantly to the immersive and distressing atmosphere.

Critical Acclaim:
Upon release, "Spec Ops: The Line" received critical acclaim for its daring narrative and thematic depth. It has since been studied for its storytelling techniques and themes, earning a place as a subject of video game analysis and academic discussion.

Impact on Players:
"Spec Ops: The Line" is not a game that's easily forgotten. Its impact on players can be profound, prompting reflection on the nature of war, violence in video games, and the psychological cost of combat. It challenges players to think beyond the controller in their hands and consider the moral implications of their virtual actions.

In conclusion, "Spec Ops: The Line" is a game that defies genre expectations to deliver a harrowing and thought-provoking experience. It is a testament to the power of video games as a medium for storytelling and moral examination. For those seeking more than just action-packed gameplay, who are interested in the narrative potential of video games and the exploration of complex themes, "Spec Ops: The Line" is a compelling and essential play.

In one of my earlier reviews based off the game Homefront, I described a scene in the game where you are pinned down in a house while being constantly bombarded with enemy forces. These enemy forces would pelt you with bullets while also charging through windows and the front door. All this would be happening while you're trying to protect a mother and her screaming child, creating a situation where there is so much audio clutter from the child screaming, soldiers shooting, teammates calling commands, and everything else around that I became overwhelmed playing. This feeling, while never fully reached during Spec Ops: The Line, is a central idea that is strongly routed throughout the game and even expanded on in new ways to truly show the horrors and reality of military combat.
For this review, the multiplayer and cooperative modes were not touched but solely the campaign. If anything, I feel like playing those modes would ruin the overall message that the developers are pushing in the campaign, so I recommend staying away from them if you want the true experience. Also, this game is over 10 years old so even trying to find servers or players for this would be very unlikely. But that message that is prevalent throughout the entirety of the campaign raises an interesting question as part of what made this experience so memorable is going through it blind. I'd probably started watching three to four videos on this game and just never bothered to finish watching them and that was probably the best accident I made as it would've ruined it completely. So I'll try my best to tip toe around certain key elements and story beats so that even after reading this review you'll still be left wondering what happens. The reason I never finished those YouTube videos is I just thought this was another third person shooter from the Xbox 360 era, and in certain cases that is true, but the story is where this game shines as it paints an accurate portrayal of the horrors of war and the emotional and physical toll it has on it's participants. It doesn't pull any punches and is constantly shoving into your face the reality of what war truly is, without appearing all edgy. The issue is the game play doesn't accurate reflect this tone as it wants to be a fun shooter yet tell this griping story and it can't have the best of both worlds.
Looking exclusively at game play, there are some fun ideas present that helps it stand above the crowd just a little. Setting your story in a post-apocalyptic Dubai makes for some really interesting and fun environments, making all your combat encounters have memorable locations. I typically hate desert areas in video games, but this game truly transforms the desert into being way more than just sand and nothing. There are huge buildings to scale, ruins to traverse, and even though a majority of it is sand, there are moments where the environment takes a complete shift whether it be an aquarium or the tops of skyscrapers. I was so intrigued I was excited to keep seeing what new location would pop up next. I can't really say the same for combat encounters as while I never hated them, I never truly enjoyed them. There's a variety of guns to use and there are loads of different enemy types, but the actual shooting just feels off in a way I don't know how to describe. Maybe it was a sensitivity option but I could never get proper precise aiming and it was always a smidgen off. Even trying to readjust was a hassle as I would constantly move the cursor too far or too little that it became really annoying on higher difficulties. Speaking of difficulties, I beat the game on the two highest difficulties and while I didn't think they were too bad, there are certain areas with huge difficulty spikes that borderline become unfair, these got to the point where I would constantly have to just reload the checkpoint and hope I get decent RNG in enemy placement or bullet spray that I would come out successful. The entirety of the game you also have two AI allies and while they can be helpful, on higher difficulties they would die so fast that they would instead become a burden rather than a useful tool. Then AI would also constantly bug out too and they would either get stuck or wouldn't follow orders. I started to dread having them with me and would constantly have to go out of my way to revive them, with some of them even getting me killed. In all of these moments, it became apparent how rough some of the animations are, and it's especially noticeable in some scripted moments. Everything kind of has a little jank to it that it takes away from the realism that the game is trying to portray. The one benefit I will give to this game is that I really enjoyed the incorporation of environmental destruction and weather effects. You could occasionally break a wall to have sand pour on enemies or a sandstorm would come in and cause everyone to be blind. The only other thing I wish is that these sandstorms were random instead of being scripted moments.
However, all these negatives pertaining to the game play pails in comparison to just how intriguing the story is. As mentioned earlier, I'm not going to go too far into detail to try and avoid spoilers, so the most basic story synopsis I'll give is that three soldiers go into a ruined Dubai in order to rescue civilians, but get more than they bargain for. This premise leads way for some of the most brutal and visceral moments I've seen, as it doesn't shy away from showing what war can cause. The toll of having to take so many lives while also constantly making decisions where one way or another someone will get hurt is constantly prevalent in our main character that we get to witness firsthand his descent into madness. There is one certain moment that appears about halfway through the game that acts as a catalyst for our main character and his team's demise that I wasn't expecting at all. My basic description doesn't do it justice as you should just really play it for yourself, if not then at least watch a video on it as it is really that good. There are certain twists and turns you will never see coming and the realistic approach to war that so many other games gloss over and glamorize is extremely refreshing. There are even certain moments where the game breaks the fourth wall whether that be in actual game play/cut scenes or even in the loading screens; the game is constantly adverting your expectations. The only negative I'd say is that there is a radio host within the story who plays classic rock music during some fire fights and it feels really jarring. The game is trying to make you feel badass and cool slaughtering all these men but it also wants you to really consider what you're doing and it just doesn't work. There's an argument to make that this is the point of the radio host but I'd say it doesn't properly accomplish that and instead feels like a major tonal shift. 
I feel like that tonal shift, which was also mentioned at the beginning of this review, is the main issue with this. The game wants to have it's cake and eat it too and it just doesn't work. You can't make this story focusing on the toll of violence and war then try and make a fun shooter, it almost hearkens to the Last of Us 2 situation where the game play didn't match the story. I will say though this is a situation where the story overpowers that middling game play and is worth playing for the story alone.

Spec Ops: The Line is not your typical military shooter; it's a gripping and thought-provoking journey that takes you deep into the heart of darkness. This game is a remarkable departure from the standard shooter fare, and it stands as a testament to the power of storytelling in gaming.

The narrative in Spec Ops: The Line is the driving force behind its success. It delves into the psychological and moral aspects of warfare, forcing players to confront the consequences of their actions. As Captain Martin Walker, players must make decisions that challenge their moral compass, and these choices have a profound impact on the game's branching storyline. It's a haunting exploration of the human psyche, and it keeps you engaged from start to finish.

The game's setting, a post-apocalyptic Dubai buried under sand, is a breathtaking and unique backdrop for the action. The level design is top-notch, and the sandstorms that sweep through the city add an element of unpredictability and chaos to the gameplay. It's not just a backdrop; it's a character in its own right.

The character development in Spec Ops: The Line is outstanding. The well-written dialogue and exceptional voice acting breathe life into the characters, making them feel real and relatable. Captain Walker's descent into moral ambiguity is a journey that is both harrowing and captivating.

The combat mechanics are solid, offering a satisfying blend of cover-based shooting and tactical gameplay. The AI of both enemies and allies is well-executed, making for intense and challenging firefights. The game's realistic damage system and weapon variety add depth to the combat experience.

What sets Spec Ops: The Line apart is its willingness to tackle mature and thought-provoking themes. It's a game that doesn't shy away from exploring the horrors of war and the moral dilemmas faced by soldiers in combat. It challenges players to consider the consequences of their actions, making it a deeply immersive experience.

The music and sound design further enhance the game's atmosphere, creating a haunting and evocative auditory experience that complements the gritty narrative perfectly.

In summary, Spec Ops: The Line is a dark, compelling, and unforgettable journey through the complexities of war and human nature. It's a game that not only entertains but also challenges your thinking and emotions. If you're looking for a shooter with a rich and engaging story, this is a must-play. Spec Ops: The Line is a true gem that proves that video games can be a powerful medium for storytelling and reflection. It's a title that will stay with you long after you've put down the controller.

There was a time where grey & brown shooters were the norm. It was expected to have very few differences between them and the scenerarios were similar. But then, among them, there was Spec Ops The Line, a game that could be thrown to the very same bucket of that era but fortunately it stood out for being raw, anti-hero and less about winning or loosing but instead to make you wonder about the non-victory of war.

It's one of the few third person shooters were I actually replayed, on different platforms and it still made me feel uneasy about certain actions. Speaking of actions, you will face choices during the game. Some minor, others more impactful. In the end it will not make a huge mistake on the narrative but it makes you thing that not everything is what it seems to be but also, sometimes there's no right choice and no wrong decision. It just... an action or lack of it. At some point, you would wish said options of choice could be more frequent but the game makes sure to point what you may choose and what you must endure weather you like it or not.

You can't expect a mix of different scenarios. The game will happen in one country and that is all you are going to see so I hope you enjoy the desert. Everything goes wrong and as you go further into the mission you understand the mission itself become very blurry. Your team mates will question and judge your actions and you will see from the early stage of the game that you, the main characther is not ok. Sometimes if you down an enemy he may not be down for good which means you will have to kill him for good. The way you finish him it's proof of how unstable the main character is and will become. Spec Ops The Line doesn't try to sugar coat war. Sometimes a bad decision is just that, without a happy ending or a honorable mean to a cause. Sometimes is just an action to keep going and even keep going will be questionable later on. You will catch a glimpse of hard sentences even on the loading screen during missions where you will find things such "dying was the best part for someone because at least he's not suffering from PTSD". This is, if you allow, as dark as it gets. Stating death is a better end scenario from someone and that PTSD would be a worse ending for a soldier.
 
Gameplay wise there's not much in the creative way. It's a TPS where you point and shoot, take cover, provide supressing fire, give orders to your team members and that is pretty much when it comes to point and shoot mechanics. Speaking of shooting, there will be a lot of dead bodies to pile on your mind hence some decisions will give a more heavier feeling depending on how much you let the mood of the game get under your skin.

This is a title I've heard about for years, via various video essayists or in discussing video games with memorable stories - while the gameplay experience itself lies within the homologous (and ultimately mediocre) realm of derivative 7th-gen over-the-shoulder cover shooters, the story does serve as a reasonably interesting take on storytelling within the shooter genre, as well as provides a moderately surrealistic commentary on processing the horrors and trauma of war.

Having only played/experienced the game in current day, it's quite apparent how it has aged across the board, and falls flat compared to the quality of both gameplay and storytelling of video games in current day. It's worth playing through (on an easier difficulty), and nothing really overstayed its welcome in the ~5 hours it took for me to beat, even if a substantial portion of the characters and sequences feel largely unimportant to the central conflict of the game. 

 I can't imagine I'll ever look to play this title again - the gameplay experience offers very little to return to, and a large amount of the net enjoyment I got out of the game was the catharsis of finally experiencing a story I had heard about for over a decade, which ultimately landed in a satisfactory but relatively lackluster zone. While it certainly stood out at the time of release, I'd place the current-day experience of playing the title at around 6/10: worthwhile for those interested but ultimately watered down by age.

[spoiler]The 33rd were in Dubai to oversee the evacuation. ♥♥♥♥ goes sideways, everyone is trapped in Dubai. No one can leave. Since the 33rd are the only form of authority in the city, they take over. This doesn't go well. They enforce martial law. People die.

The CIA goes to Dubai to basically kill the 33rd. They go about doing this by inciting a rebellion against the 33rd. In the same way the MACV-SOG were used in 'Nam to train insurgent forces to fight the north Vietnamese. The CIA has to kill the 33rd because if word ever gets out that America came in and took over Dubai it could start a serious war between the Middle-East and the US. So the CIA's goal is basically kill everyone and erase all the evidence.

The Civilians are under the protection of the 33rd whether they like it or not. The 33rd are still trying to save everyone from an admittingly hopeless situation.

It's unclear whether or not the insurgents existed before the CIA arrived and stoke the flames. But in any case, the Insurgents want the Americans out. They see this as another case of classic American interventionism in a country they don't belong in. Vietnam, Afghanistan, Iraq, you name it. They want them out. This is their home and they will fight them to do it. The 33rd's violence against civilians during riots and martial law only fan the flames.

Ok so that is all before Delta shows up. This is where things get complicated.

Delta arrives and runs into rebel forces. They attempt to have a conversation. Interestingly enough in Dubai, the local population speaks Arabic, Lugo talks to them in Farsi. In any case, they try to talk, Walkers and Adams discuss how to kill the rebels in case things go bad. The rebels notice them talking and say "they're plotting to kill us". And they're right, technically. The rebels shoot at you because they think you're the 33rd coming to take them back to the Nest. So you start killing them because you think they're bad guys.

Then you get to the plane and shoot at more rebels who're fighting the 33rd. The 33rd, at this point, are actually fighting against the CIA trying to prevent the cover-up/destruction of Dubai.

You run off to rescue the soldier taken by the rebels, and find out it's the CIA running the rebels. You now think well if the CIA is fighting the 33rd, the 33rd must be the bad guys, right? Why would the US Government fight the 33rd unless they went off the reservation and turned traitor? So now you side with the CIA against the traitorous 33rd. The first sequence where you shoot Americans is more or less started by you. If you let the soldier go, he warns his friends some CIA goons are coming. You're met with resistance and you shoot. You kill because you think you know what you're doing. Similarly, in the market where the 33rd are shooting at civilians? They're not shooting at them. They're trying to evacuate the civilians and take them back to the Nest.

By the time you figure out that the CIA is just trying to kill everyone, it's too late. You've already massacred freedom fighters, civilians, and American troops. You've already doomed everyone.

The 33rd keep fighting you because they have to. You're killing them! Walker and Delta are like a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ meat grinder, everything they run into is reduced to quivering slabs of meat. The 33rd also think you're part of the CIA, at least initially. But the most telling scene is near the end when you make your run at the tower. Even after everything you've done, after all the soldiers you've slaughtered, even after the white phosphorus attack... the 33rd have you surrounded and they ask you to surrender. The 33rd are willing to let you give up! They weren't trying to kill you, they were defending themselves!

Delta constantly thinks they're the good guys, but they're not. They make decisions when they think they have all the facts, but they only ever know a fraction of the story. They have good intentions, but it leads to death, destruction, and despair at every turn.

The story is unclear because it has to be. Walker has to make his decisions with partial facts and half-truths. If you know more than Walker, the effect is lost. You have to be just as blind as Walker for the story to have any impact.

And none of this touches on Walker's hallucinations and madness. That's another discussion. As are the messages of the game. I'll plug two great discussions on Spec Ops: The Line. First is the Errant Signal episode where he discusses the themes and tropes the game tackles. The second is a great bit of game journalism, a critical reading of the game by Brendon Keogh called Killing Is Harmless. [/spoiler]

At this point, Spec Ops: The Line is widely recognized for its deconstruction of war shooters in its narrative. Whenever you hear the name of this game, you recognize it as, "Oh, the 'war bad' game." And, yes, that is exactly what the game is. Inspired by the novella "Heart of Darkness," and the film inspired by it, "Apocalypse Now," Spec Ops: The Line tells a narrative about war far, far removed from any concept of "good and evil." And it will stick with me as one of the most poignant narratives I've ever experienced for the rest of my life.

I don't want to spoil anything major that happens as it is much better to experience this game for myself, but I will admit that this game shook me to my core several times. It sent chills down my spine, made me feel depressed, and nearly made me sick. 

The only thing lacking in Spec Ops: The Line is subpar gameplay, but it is easily made worthwhile with the incredible voice acting done by the cast (especially Nolan North) and a story that will stick with you for a very long time.

EDITED Review:
After playing for another 19 hours, trying every possible outcomes, and toying with mods like "Gears of Spec Ops Assault Recon", I can see a good game being here, but it was stillborn. Everything has just been executed poorly. There are many nuances you wouldn't know if you're new to shooters, carried over from other games of the genre. For instance, every weapon has a hidden class category with different movement speeds. There isn't anything innovative, and many things here are not intuitive. The amount of times I've killed myself by aiming out of cover too fast with a grenade launcher is unacceptable. If you aim too fast, your character will still be aiming at the ground before readying his weapon, but you wouldn't notice that in a firefight, when the cursor readies itself, your body is completely out of cover, and the enemy starts firing at you. I even killed myself by blind-firing a grenade in cover a couple times, recreating a gag from Red vs Blue, in a very real sense. 
Some scenes feel very RNG to survive, due to there being very specific triggers that make little sense. Too many. It doesn't feel gamey. It just feels broken.
I don't know how people can recommend this, and I've had my fill. I've played this plenty more than I should have, honestly. 
Do I regret playing it? No. Do I recommend it? No.
And I wish it was never recommended to me.
I don't regret playing it. I regret buying it.

Even after all this negatives mentioned, this game is still in my opinion a masterpiece. Why? Because of the story it tells. 

It is hard (for me at least) to say why is this story so awesome without spoiling too much, so all you can do is buy this game and see it for yourself. Its that type of game where its best to go in without looking anything online, and game that will affect you in some way for sure. Game is short (around 3-4 hours) and replay value is there. 

Overall, when looking from tehnical point, this game is a mess, not going to lie. But, if you can survive all that and play it for a story, you are really in for a treat.

Oh boy, where do I even begin with Spec Ops: The Line? This game takes you on a wild ride through a post-apocalyptic Dubai, where sandstorms are as common as tourists getting lost in the desert.

First things first, let's talk about the protagonist. Captain Walker, the game's main character, is like your typical action hero, except he's got a serious case of "why me?" syndrome. I mean, seriously, every time something goes wrong, he's just like, "Why is this happening to me? Why can't I just have a nice vacation in Dubai?"

Speaking of Dubai, let's not forget the city itself. Sure, it may be buried in sand and chaos, but boy, does it look pretty. The developers really went all out on the sand physics, making you feel like you're playing a game of "The Floor is Lava" except with sand instead. Who knew sinking in sand could be so much fun?

Now, let's move on to the story. Spec Ops: The Line tries to be all deep and philosophical, questioning the nature of war and all that jazz. But let's be honest, most players are just there for the explosions and shooting bad guys. Who has time for introspection when you've got an assault rifle in your hand?

But don't worry, the game has got you covered on the action front. The gunfights are intense, and the enemies just keep coming like they've got an unlimited supply of bad guys hidden in the sand dunes. It's like they took a page out of the "Enemy Respawn for Dummies" playbook.

And let's not forget the moral choices in the game. They're supposed to make you question your own morality and all that, but let's be real, most players just want to see what happens if they choose the most messed-up option available. Sorry, not sorry, virtual civilians of Dubai.

In the end, Spec Ops: The Line is a wild, sand-filled adventure that will leave you questioning your life choices and the nature of war. Or, you know, it'll just be a fun distraction where you get to shoot things and make questionable decisions. Either way, it's a good time in a sandy, post-apocalyptic kind of way.

Pros: - One of the most poignant soundtracks ever for a game. Practically dripping with a twisted irony, and used to perfectly accentuate both story and gameplay moments (and I'm not supposed to say this but the songs themselves are good too).
- This game has fantastic art direction, and because of that still holds up visually over a decade later. "Welcome to Dubai, gentlemen".
- Gameplay is generic but works solidly and will keep you on your toes, especially at higher difficulties. The inclusion of some light tactical elements is very welcome, and despite being simple add some extra strategy and variety to the combat. Enemy variety is also much better than I initially expected.
- While the gameplay might be generic, it is placed within some phenomenal level design that is easy to follow, dramatic, dynamic, and can even be related back to the story with its masterful use of verticality.
- One of the best narratives to a video game that I've experienced. I wont say too much as this game is best experienced blind. It has a strong anti-war message, and this works perfectly in the medium of video games. This is the only game that has actually made me disgusted with my actions. You will be floored.

Cons: - The main downside to this game is that the gameplay itself can get somewhat repetitive. This is for two reasons: the gameplay does not evolve much over the course of the campaign, and the gameplay is not super innovative to begin with (basic third-person cover shooter with some light tactical mechanics). At the same time, there is an argument to be made that the themes and narrative of the game are strengthened by this at a meta level. The game is also not long enough to get too repetitive in the first place (6-8 hours), so even this main gripe is not a huge one.
- The cover system is also a bit odd and sticky, but it gets the job done once you're used to it. I found this game to be much more enjoyable with a controller rather than keyboard and mouse, mainly because of the cover mechanics.

"Home? We can't go home. There's a line men like us have to cross. If we're lucky, we do what's necessary, then we die. No, all I really want, Captain, is peace."

Hung corpses, lynched comrades, valleys of stripped and meatily rendered dead men. The sands of Dubai are marked with the worst of humanity - the ever looming shadow of death that radiates like a mirage's aura from a lost horizon. In this "post apocalypstick" setting of a Dubai completely sanded over by a historic storm, terror is delivered to the surviving populous -  brought forth by the hand of once courageous men who are now out of chances, out of hope, nearly out of supplies and water... but some of them are simply out of their minds. While others, are merely there to make sure no one learns the truth of what happened here.

This is Spec Ops the Line.

One of the most harrowing games of all time, this game had absolutely captivated a niche audience back in the day, even gaining the approval of some of the most jaded and cynical of gamers. Usually the people who got filtered by this game or believe it overhyped (admittingly, many of its great aspects were lovingly exaggerated by enthusiastic fans, but that shows just how cherished it is) are actually NPCs who only see game stories in shades of narrative tropes or 'sins'. I think these people have completely lost touch with gaming as a narrative, interactive story telling medium and they have completely lost the ability, ironically through the overindulgence in more "polished" games, to empathize with the human aspects of fictional characters.

When games take an anti-war stance, they often go the "war is hell" route, but the smart games go the Blood Meridian/Heart of Darkness route. Spec Ops the Line is certainly that, but it does so while making an extremely solid and fun to play game. Mechanically, the game did nothing new, but it looks spectacular and only suffers from some brief control jank that dominated its genre. 

This game came out in an oversaturated market of shooters with this colour palette (and that being said, very few of its contemporaries manage to have the same soul as its presentation) and that makes this game's "genericness" its best subversion. I had a colleague in I knew from school and I recommended this game. He merely played the first level, returned my physical copy to me and simply gave me an unconvincing "7/10!" and a thumbs up. From there, I knew he was an NPC and the rest of his life proved to be further proof of this.

But that is what is great about this game, it effectively gatekept the very players it critiqued from the game itself. Why? Because they are the gamers that don't play for narratives that are creative, but merely narratives that are trope hook after trope hooks to justify a multiplayer setting, if at all. The game rather coldly critiqued the military industrial complex's place in its propaganda-laden support for certain games as mini-recruitment campaigns and at the same time, the game also compliments its medium as one that allows for a type of critique that will reach more young people than say, a modern book may. After all, video games are the most profitable and enjoyed entertainment medium out there and there is perhaps, not a single other form of entertainment, that will benefit younger audiences as video games in many ways.

The gameplay is solid enough, but most people are no doubt attracted to this game for its message and its presentations. The protagonists become shells of themselves in both psyche and appearance. The level of detail and focus on highlighting the real impact of battle on their bodies is not only fantastic and immersive, but completely plays well into its narrative. 

By now, everyone knows the twist of this game and it becomes rather apparent early on. However, the game did not need to be subtle, in fact, its esoteric moments can be mistakenly considered to be spoonfed by the end. But this game is not about tricking you, but forcing you, the player - as the commanding force behind Captain Walker, to confront his sins.

The game really has more guts than any of its brothers, taking place after a hypothetical and disastrous withdrawal from Afghanistan, Captain Walker is a man already once broken, having survived what was apparently a vicious battle in Kabul - who must confront the man who once saved him.

Konrad was a hero to Walker and many others, but he was not a hero to himself. Devastated with the lost mission in Afghanistan, he wanted to truly regain the dignity of his men, of the mission - only to lose control entirely. The side intel the game paints is a vivid and interesting picture of the Damned 33rd: a seemingly competent if not entirely remarkable battalion of US Army soldiers, who have been pushed to the brink by necessity and paranoia and inner factionalism, falling into direct antagonistic relations with their former nation and the CIA. 

One remarkable thing I noticed on my most recent playthrough, via one of the intel pieces, we find out that Konrad burned the stars off of an American flag - which inspired the initial mutiny of his top command, that you find dead later on in the game. The intel tells us more than what the characters assumed and actually helps us understand the story behind Konrad that actually isn't explored as much as one would think in the gameplay and active plot itself. Konrad was a man who loved his country unconditionally and yet, in his dismay, in a misguided attempt to build a new symbol, he blackened and charred out the blue and white stars on the flag. The stars obviously representing the unity of the American states, but the blue represented the values of vigilance, perseverance and justice. What remained, was the original frontier - the thirteen stripes that represented the original colonies of America, finding themselves in a new nation with a "hostile" native population at their mercy and vice versa. But not only that, Konrad's flag still carried the red and the white. The red representing hardiness and valor, while the white symbolizes purity and innocence. Much like Walker in the game, Konrad believed himself the hero and had lost his sense of integrity, his idea of justice and upholding himself to a higher standard. Believing blood and hardiness, "survival" alone would justify his actions. Its a small tidbit of information in a game with a lot of depth, but this alone reminds me why this game has one of the best narratives for a third person linear shooter while also one of the best ambient-stories having gone on in its immediate background. 

I played this game many times before, just not on Steam. I will note that the PC version is superior in every way, with 33rd gear having custom markings on their weapons and entire sections being a tad longer, as well as some different choice real-time cutscene shot renders and some slightly dialogue during these same scenes.

This game is an enduring, perfect mix of hyper violence, superb graphics for its time, remarkably inspired locations in the atypical Dubai setting (which in itself, is a city of luxury painted over with sand, perhaps a jab at how Americans have begun to view the "world over" in the Middle East and Gulf as merely a sandbox) provide strong contrasts and styles. This game was certainly built in a certain era, as the soldiers wear UCP camo with a variety of National Guard-esque gear, perfect given the 33rd were there originally as a humanitarian force and not the occupiers they became and their special forces, as brief as they appear, almost resemble the Helghast from Killzone. Some characters resemble Travis Bickle from Taxi Driver, as well, rather intentional most likely.

There is something so grounded about this game, simply because it was written by one man with a very inspired, motivation mission and not a board of people who wanted to make a game that was inoffensive in its critiques.

A very decent military third person shooter. However, it seems to have been trapped between two extremes: on one side, the devs, aching to tell a story about the horrors of war, and on the opposite, 2K trying to squeeze every penny out of gamers by forcing the developers to add meaningless fluff, such as multiplayer and DLC. As a result, the game is clearly broken. It pretends to be a by-the-numbers action romp, whilst it tries to subvert one's expecations by throwing little "sanity effects", narrative twists and dire decisions after facing gauntlets of enemies. In terms of gameplay, the game does not impress or revolutionize the genre. Mass Effect, XCOM Declassified, Vanquish, Binary Domain, and many others do cover based team shooters better. Your two partners, Lugo and Adams, don't have much to offer. You simply hold down RB, highlight an enemy, and hope they don't run to their deaths. Since there's no power wheel, or tactics of any kind (no squad directives, no AI styles, no directions to give outside of focusing fire on a target), every fight blends with the rest. However, every once in a while you will get a massive prompt to have Adams flashbang a mob, or to tell the guy who's not bleeding out to pick up the one that is, but that is it. Thankfully, there's a decent array of weaponry and most of them feel good to use. Sadly, you can only have two at a time (shocker, I know!)

I played this on suicide mission, and the game can get pretty tough, with enemies instantly gibbing you the moment you peek thru cover to try and aim your reticle. Some segments can be grueling, since giving instructions end with your teammates bleeding out in the middle of the battlefield, making it impossible to rez them, and sometimes I felt like the game didn't stop spawning enemies until I moved up to a certain location to trigger an event. It was fun, but very restrictive since the game lacks tactics and directives for the AI to help you in those situations, at least, the usual kind found in other games I've played.

The music is pretty decent, and was chosen to remind you of movies that treat this kind of topic, such as Fullmetal Jacket. Off-putting and unnerving, so as to make you question what's really going on. Graphics-wise, this is an UE3-looking ass game, extremely generic, saved only by the setting: Dubai in the middle of a severe sandstorm. As for MP, who cares? Honestly, I don't know if there's any replay value to be had here. Clearly there are a few decisions that matter, sprinkled between its 15 chapters, and various endings, but the whole point is to live with the consequences of your actions. You might squeeze in a second playthrough, since the game is short, but all of its shock value would be lost.

Spec Ops is a good game, but not superlative or awe inspiring as reviews would lead you to believe. If you enjoy third person cover shooters, like I do, it's worth experiencing, but more for its narrative than its gameplay, which pales in comparison to more than a few other examples of the genre.

[h1]Introduction[/h1]
"It's only a war crime if you end up losing". Not a quote extracted from this title, but it most certainly fits the bill and there will be plenty of similar adages taking you on a veritable guilt trip. Spec Ops: The Line is without the shadow of doubt the main anti-war video game within a special niche that is drizzled in irony, since this is a third person shooter as well.

Believe it or not, this is the final entry in a series that has been mostly console exclusive (5th generation). Not to mention that the predecessors were conventional in terms of approaching modern warfare, no underlying messages and just a straightforward narrative. Simpler times, eh? Co-publishers 2K and Missing Link took a one-time gamble by reviving Spec Ops and I'm almost certain it wasn't a financial success. Such a pity.

A sleeper hit it was not, yet I still consider The Line to be developer's YAGER finest creation and it pains me that they have shifted their focus on F2P detritus in the eleven years since Spec Ops (re)launched. Yes, it was a 2012 project which treated very serious topics with social commentary rarely seen before or after in its genre. And it is most importantly, an experience you can enjoy in single player. No bros needed, imagine that!

[h1]Story[/h1]
The 1899 novella "Heart of Darkness" by Joeseph Conrad served as inspiration to both this game and to the cinematic masterpiece known as Francis Ford Coppola's "Apocalypse Now" from 1979. It goes without saying that you should read the source material and watch that movie as soon as you can, if the hardly digestible topics in Spec Ops: The Line have piqued your interest. 

It cannot be boiled down to just the human condition being heavily influenced by the horrors of war. “Good. Bad. I'm the guy with the gun” as Ash Williams from Army of Darkness so eloquently puts it. You probably knew war is hell even with all the constant propaganda being shoveled daily by all forms of media. But you are rarely shown just how easy it is for seemingly good-natured individuals to cross the titular line towards irrational violence.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=782360075

Is it the separation between good and evil? Is such a distinction even possible when we're talking about horrendous acts commited with the excuse of self-preservation? I'm not here to judge you, but Spec Ops most certainly will. In such a subtle manner that you won't even understand the implications of your actions until you're halfway through the story.

A rescue mission gone wrong. A city buried under constant sandstorms. Anarchy reigns supreme and what follows can only be summarized as steep descent into madness. You still won't be prepared for the final twist. And if you weren't already acquainted with the devastating effects of white phosporus, Spec Ops shall indulge that morbid curiosity as well. Overall, this is a tale you will remember for all the right reasons. The are lessons to be learned.

 [h1]Graphics[/h1] 
Among the first Steam titles to "nurture" my predilection for screenshots, I wasn't yet disabling HUDs in 2016. Alas, Spec Ops has aged like fine wine, testament to the prowess of Unreal Engine 3 even on its final legs. There are so many epic set pieces in this title. Numerous occasions to just stop and stare after the guns have gone deathly silent. 

Attention to detail is quite obvious, from clever stencils and grafitti and down to the ever-changing Main Menu showcasing to some extent, your in-game actions. Few games go that extra mile, especially ones which can be pretty much spedrun in a single sitting, if you're commited to the story. I took my sweet time to explore, so my initial 10 hours from start to finish don't reflect average playthroughs. There's no reason to rush it, let it all sink in.

It ran maxed out in 4K back when that resolution was mostly a pipe dream in terms of PC gaming (circa 2016). No technical issues to report, it was a smooth ride though the topics themselves made it stand out and ended up playing in short sessions. Not the sort of "bro shooter" where you can turn off your brain for some mindless fun. Do no mistake Spec Ops: The Line for a Gears of War clone, to keep its subgenre intact or far worse, compare it to some Call of Duty strain.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=782360439

[h1]Audio[/h1]
No guilt trip would be complete without some very eloquent voice actors. Of course there's Nolan North in the cast. It was either hiring him or Troy Baker when you wanted a solid lead for your upcoming video game. No complaints from me. The soundtrack features some true rock classics which are put to good use during specific scenes, amplifying their impact. In a contemporary music world relying on autotuned covers from sheer lack of creativity, it's far better to return to the originals instead.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
Cover-based shooting against waves upon waves of nondescript foes. Tango down, mission accomplished. It's not that simple after you take a few good looks at the carnage you leave behind in a quicker or slower succession of levels. The game railroads most of your choices, perhaps trying to mock the illusion of choice to some extent. "I was just a soldier following orders, I am not to blame". You still had a choice, but disobeying your superiors in a combat scenario has very finite consequences, right?

Self-preservation works both ways. Perhaps that's a lesson best learned while you're mowing down those desperate people trying to survive. How you justify that in the end, Spec Ops: The Line leaves at least that small amount of ambiguity up to the players. The core gameplay follows a familiar path, yet its the narrative structure that shall put the former element in a difficult spot. It most certainly wasn't the constant need to shoot from one safe spot to another, the memorable aspect to this otherwise fascinating journey. Willie Pete below.

https://www.youtube.com/shorts/LK82rjh8E80

Come to think of it, the gunplay was passable and yet I was always more interested in the scripted sequences between those literal shooting galleries. Playing The Line for the first time and going in  without any expectations at all, is probably the best way to approach it. Let it slowly punch you in the gut. Then press on, towards the inevitable conclusion. A lingering objective since level one still needs to be crossed off your to-do list. Will it bring closure?

[h1]Verdict[/h1]
Only one way to find out. Sadly, there's little replay value here for me, I'm obviously not interested in that dead in the water MP mode that's void of the SP's defining substance. Still a haunting adventure. I'd say it's a mandatory task for hardcore fans of military shooters. Might not open your eyes, you might not even like it and yet war has to be examined from all angles until you're free from its carefully tailored image by state media and various mouthpieces on a payroll.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=821336400

The time for my second playthrough, draws ever near. As for the story, it was not a popular opinion but it stands unique through its indirect preaching. Spec Ops: The Line has no direct competitors and we are living in an age in which World Peace is still an unachievable goal. I was never optimistic enough to believe in it though. Humanity will always find a pretext for War. Casus belli. It's hardcoded in our very nature. You can't truly fight that.

Worth a buy on a discount just for the experience. If you're half-decent at shooters you'll be done with it in about 4-6 hours. There is very, very little replay value beyond getting a couple of achievements you might've missed.
I'll elaborate a bit more on each aspect below.

[b]Gameplay:[/b] 
I can't stress enough - the gameplay is generic in every sense of the word. There's not really anything it does that hasn't been done better by other games in the genre. Nonetheless, it works, and for the most part it isn't frustrating to play. Although moving around cover has been fatally clunky on more than one occasion.

[b]Story:[/b]
The narrative itself is interesting; enough to keep me wanting to see how it ends at the very least. However it falls victim to the time-old ludo-narrative dissonance as [spoiler] you're not really given any choice. After you're forced to kill the civilians you kinda take a backseat perspective on the whole thing rather than feeling like "your choices caused this". Nonetheless, the climax left me feeling satisfied. [/spoiler]

[b]Visuals:[/b]
Sand and ruined skyscrapers encompass about 70% of the game's locations, which makes sense given that it takes place in a sandstorm and war-torn ruined Dubai. There's some truly impressive views to be had at points, and despite how same-y it starts to feel as it drags on, they do experiment with colours and lighting a fair bit.
One key problem I had however was readability. Every entity just kinda blurs together and it's difficult to tell what kind of enemy you're shooting at in a lot of situations - or even if you're shooting an enemy at all.

[b]Replay Value:[/b]
Beating the game on the third difficult unlocks the fourth difficulty, which further ramps up the damage you take as well as the aggressiveness of enemies. Beating the game on this unlocks an achievement.
There's also a few pieces of "intel" hidden around the levels which are just little pieces of lore and whatnot that you can read.
As I said - very little replay value.

The sand thing is also used in some combat encounters either as a scripted event or an environmental hazard. Mechanics are about what you can expect from games in the genre, use cover to avoid enemy fire, take advantage of regenerating health, fight through waves of enemies, use turrets from time to time, enjoy the occasional setpiece. It's decent fun, and some weapons can be especially fun to use, though you might find yourself switching since ammo in the game is a little scarce. Also has lightweight squad mechanics, you can use them as much or as little as you want.

Really the star here is the narrative, and you either know all about it or are lucky enough to be going in blind, and if you're in the latter category I will keep it short and say that it's an interesting and darker take on the kind of story you would expect from this sort of modern military shooter, and if that interests you or you do not mind another typical game of this genre then I'd recommend this.

There's been a lot of ink spilled over this game, for good reason, so I'll try not to be redundant. No matter how much of this game you may have been spoiled on, no matter how "overrated" people have told you it is, play it. No story spoiler can capture every surprising moment or perfectly miserable and desolate tonal piece. Also, the degree to which people describe this game as "do this thing, oh no you did the thing you're so evil" is really disingenuous, and seems to be driven by people who either didn't play the game or did and felt called out. The method it actually tends to use is more tricking you into doing something you'll regret but not knowing at the time [spoiler]white phosphorous scene[/spoiler], giving you a false choice [spoiler]saving Gould vs saving the civilians[/spoiler], or giving you an actual choice that is in fact respected [spoiler]shooting above the civilians who killed Lugo to disperse them, rather than shooting them[/spoiler]. 

Two things I will actually critique. First of all, I've never been a fan of the idea that a game actively playing worse adds anything to it artistically, even if the point of the art is "what you're doing shouldn't be fun." The fact is that if you're going to make an interactive piece than the interaction should be as painless as possible. And the fact is that the awkward controls, the tendency to move in and out of cover in unpredictable ways, the clumsy button assignment in the PC port that the player can't really fix, reduce engagement with the core of the game. I'm not thinking about the horrors of war when I'm trying to steer Walker's lumbering ass around without him ducking against some random pile of garbage.

Secondly, I do actually disagree with one component of the story. [spoiler] I don't think it was the right choice to make Konrad and his orders entirely a hallucination on Walker's part. I feel like "ur crazy lol" actually removes some of the ideological critique by implying a non-crazy officer in his position wouldn't have been led down the same path.[/spoiler]

Overall,  it's still a meaningful game even years later, and everyone needs to experience it at least once.

It's easy looking back to see why a lot of folks might've overlooked Spec Ops: The Line when it first came out in 2012. Modern military games, along with both third and first person shooters all trying to be Gears of War and CoD respectively left the market saturated with cheap imitations that mostly weren't worth our time. At first glance, Spec Ops might seem like just another also-ran that happened to get some top tier voice talent like Nolan North, Bruce Boxleitner, Omid Abtahi, and Jake Busey. Just a few levels into its all too brief campaign though, it shows its true colors with a thought provoking narrative to keep you moving through beautifully designed maps showcasing a ruined Dubai and all the opulence it was home to. 

Following Walker and his squad and seeing how the characters develop was absolutely a highlight of the game, with subtle and not so subtle changes in their behavior and dialogue as their mental state deteriorates letting the player know just how awful war can be. Speaking of your squad, they actually listen to commands and can legitimately aid you against the enemy in battle besides just being bullet sponges. Weapons are relatively standard but multiple of them have some sort of alternate fire like a suppressor, under sling grenade launcher, zoom, or just switching from burst to full auto. They were all pretty fun to shoot and I had fun experimenting with different combos to see what worked best for me: I usually would keep an assault rifle and shotgun, unless a sequence called for a sniper rifle. 

While I wish the game was longer, its fast pace meant things never got boring, and choices you can make throughout had me eager to go back and try different ones to see what would change in the story. There is a multiplayer mode, or at least there was when the game launched. I didn't even attempt to load in to see if anyone is still playing or if it even works still at all however, so I can't speak to this part of the game. Even if the multiplayer does work I can't imagine there's too many people ever online so this is one you'd buy now purely for the campaign experience. 

If this is on sale and you like shooters or even just games with great acting and an interesting story that makes you think, definitely pick this one up. If shooters aren't your thing, just turn the difficulty down to easy and enjoy the ride. This is one of those games that will stick with me forever thanks to its memorable story and engaging characters. I would definitely play it again one day to try a higher difficulty or go back and make some different choices. In the now modern era of always-online live service games that never end and launch broken and unfinished, there's something to be said about a game that's less than 10 hours but still feels complete and leaves you feeling very satisfied with the time you spent on it.

Spec Ops: The Line is a game that needs no introduction. It's a game that was released during a period where it was forced to compete against a myriad of other similar military-type shooters in a market that was already started to get heavily oversaturated with them. The fact that it's name could be found under the dictionary definition of the word 'generic' likely also didn't help. However, what set it apart from the rest of the flock was its violence - namely its approach to violence.

Spec Ops: The Line is a game that forces you to contend with and confront the many grim and gruesome realities of war and its impacts on the human psyche, the lives of civilians, and the very battlefields on which it's fought. The game has no qualms about showing you uncomfortable and disturbing scenes of violence; it's almost the game's bread and butter in how its victims are often killed in brutal and dehumanizing ways - often those befitting a wartime setting. It's one of the most striking ways the game sets itself apart from its contemporaries: it pulls no punches in its approach to showing you just what war does to everything it touches. Mass graves, slaughtered civilians, broken cities; it's all here and it's all ugly.

One of Spec Ops: The Line's greatest strengths is its unique setting: a war-torn and sand-scarred Dubai. The Middle East is a common enough locale for many post-CoD4 military-style shooters, but to see one of the richest and most glamorous cities on the planet reduced to rubble, and then having that rubble be buried under almost literal mountains of sand, is quite the spectacle. You'll often find yourself traversing and shooting through buildings covered in sand, as constant sandstorms have ravaged the city and left it looking apocalyptic. One of the game's more interesting features is using sand as a weapon, either by shooting out windows holding back walls of sand to bury your enemies, or shooting the ground around them to kick up sand and blinding them for an easy (and gory) kill.

The game's mechanics are suited well-enough for a shooter, but at times can feel clunky. There's a squad mechanic in place where you can give orders to your two other squad-mates and it functions appropriately enough. Your AI companions are capable of following and executing orders quite well, even if the game never goes out of its way to shove this mechanic in your face. The cover system is also certainly useful (this is a post-Gears of War TPS, after all) but can sometimes be a bit rough around the edges when it doesn't understand that you'd like to take cover from an angle as opposed to straight-on. Overall, it serves as a decent foundation for the rest of the game to be built upon. There's a good variety of standard weapons to choose from including pistols, shotguns, and assault rifles along with heavier weapons like grenade launchers and sniper rifles.

Spec Ops: The Line is a game that every fan of military-style shooters should play. Its unassuming (and fairly generic-sounding) name might promise one experience, but from the moment you start the game and glimpse its very-telling main menu you know you're in for something different. The content of this game is not for the faint of heart and I'm glad that it chose not to pull any punches - in an industry that seems to glorify digitized violence, it's good to see a game like this where the curtain is ripped back to reveal the ugly truth that's always there, bubbling and lurking underneath it all.
