Some thoughts on this game from a player in 2021 (during the US withdrawal from Afghanistan!).

I will only comment on the story. There’s not much to say about the gameplay: it’s a standard third-person duck-and-cover shooter with a nice variety of weapons and team tactics. It’s fast-paced, challenging, and fun.

OK, the story. Wow. It’s good. A US Army battalion (the 33rd) goes rogue trying to help evacuate Dubai, after it had been hit by severe sandstorms. “The evacuation was a complete failure,” Colonel Konrad states in a radio transmission. You’re the leader of a Delta force team (Captain Walker) who is sent to investigate. Walker discovers that the CIA are there leading Emirati rebels against the 33rd. He also discovers that the 33rd enacted Martial Law in order to survive the besieged city. [spoiler]They rounded up the local populace and executed people for petty crimes, so the CIA wants to eliminate them to cover up their deeds.[/spoiler] 

However, Walker remembers Colonel Konrad from a previous mission and believes him to be a good man. Convinced that there must be more to the story, he makes it their mission to find Konrad and defies his orders. He and his team (Adams and Lugo) fight through the whole 33rd to see this through. This leads Walker to make a number of horrific decisions, including [spoiler]bombing a heavily defended part of the city called The Gate with white phosphorus, which scorches a large number of soldiers and a group of Emirati refugees that the 33rd were sheltering from the storms.[/spoiler] Walker blames this atrocity on Konrad and the 33rd, and stubbornly proceeds with his mission.

The story centers largely on these themes: that war is horrific, brutal, and ugly, that war is psychologically damaging, that in war there are never “good” choices, and that war turns good, heroic people into brutal killers. (“I didn’t want to hurt anybody,” Walker says to his rescuers at the end). 

What’s so chilling about this is how well the game succeeds at making you identify with Walker. Walker is likeable! He’s a smart, decent soldier. His thought process is understandable. When the Delta team survive the first attack by the 33rd, Walker points out to his teammates that they had to act in self-defense. Even though Walker becomes obsessed with finding Konrad and battling the 33rd, this basic point remains a fact throughout the game.

This leads me to some of the problems I had with the story. The story is so critical of war that it paints Walker as a bad guy (this is clear by the parallel the story makes between him and Konrad). After all, can we really root for someone who [spoiler] accidentally kills 47 innocent people?[/spoiler] No. The problem though is that the whole situation is created by the 33rd! If Walker hadn’t fought them, someone would have (like the Emiratis). They might have caused collateral damage too. Such is the nature of war. It’s ridiculous to suggest that, because war causes both sides to make brutal decisions, there is *no* moral difference between good guys and bad guys. As a rule, war should always be avoided, but the ones defending themselves do have the moral high ground. 

This ties into another problem with the game: the meta aspect. I will be a minority on this, but I found the meta commentary idiotic. The game is well-known for implicating the player in the decisions of Walker. You’re the one making some of these hard moral choices. You’re the one playing the game and enjoying the brutal combat and modern military experience. The game speaks directly to the player in the loading screens: “The United States Army does not condone the killing of unarmed combatants. But this isn't real, so why should you care?” All this is to suggest that you, the player, have something in common with Walker. Like Walker, you could’ve stopped. But you didn’t stop playing after [spoiler] the white phosphorus mission. [/spoiler] You didn’t make your own choice to turn the console off. However, this is not deep commentary. It's a game. The only way to see what happens next is to progress through the story and make all the decisions that [b] the game [/b] has set for you. Trying to suggest that you might be a morally defective person for advancing through a video game is absurd and on par with the 90s moral panic around video games causing violence. I’m surprised that this wasn’t called out more.

That being said, the game succeeds as an immersive experience, with a compelling and thought-provoking story. I was so fascinated by the story that, upon completing my first playthrough, I immediately started a new game and ran through it again. I wanted to better understand what had happened and try the other choices and ending. I also enjoyed the combat and wanted to fight the 33rd at the highest difficulty. This is probably the best way to play Spec Ops: The Line. By the time I was two-thirds through the second playthrough, I felt like Walker: exhausted and beaten-up, but obsessed with seeing it through. It’s around this time that Walker becomes more brutal in his utterances to his teammates. “Heavy is f**king dead!” The downbeat rock song “Welcome to Hell” kicks on, and you start feeling the same hatred that Walker has for the 33rd (especially if you die a lot like I did). 

If you play the game like this and you choose the ending in which Walker is rescued, something very chilling happens. When the soldier asks you to drop your weapon, it’s… hard to let go. The game presents the situation like every ordeal you just faced. There are a bunch of armed solders in front of you, and you automatically assess the threats and scan for cover. Bizarrely, it [b] makes sense [/b] to keep fighting, even though Walker would be wrong to do so (these soldiers aren’t the 33rd).

This is where the game captures something of what it must be like to suffer from PTSD or psychosis. I’ve never played a game before that convincingly evoked an experience like that in the player. That’s why this is one of the best games I’ve ever played.

I've played a lot of shooters over the years.  Halo, Call of Duty, Titanfall 2, Battlefront, Battlefront 2 and too many others to list.  That being said, Spec Ops The Line is the most unique and the most brutal shooter I've ever played.  In most shooters, you play the hero who fights the terrorists, the nazi's or the big bad guy who overcomes all odds and wins.  Most of the time not giving any regards to the guys you are fighting.

Spec Ops The Line strays so far from the Generic shooter.  Sure it has some of the same generic things as other shooters:  Turret sections, obvious bad guy spawn points, run for your life sections.  (Thank God it doesn't have a "Escort VIP"), and many other things you would normally see in a generic shooter.  Gunplay is good, if a little outdated, (that's a good thing).

What does Spec Ops The Line set apart from other shooters you might ask?

Story:  It's brutal, it doesn't pull any punches, it doesn't care about you being the hero.  The game makes you think of war in a different way.  The truth about war, is that war is not some glorious thing, not some fun thing that you can go off and do.  War is brutal, war is dirty, war is not fun.  

Gameplay:  While generic and outdated for it's time.  The gameplay and the setting work flawlessly to put you into a world where you try and piece together what happened before you got here.  Gunplay is great, and there are lots of weapons to choose from, your teammates do well for themselves, and you have many ways to choose how you want to go about a situation.  Oh and the AI is great, hands down the hardest AI I've ever fought.

Difficulty:  On easy it's a walk in the park, on FUBAR however, your in for the fight of your life.  They don't care about how good you are, they can fight back just as hard as you can.  Most enemies die in a few hits, on FUBAR, so do you.  It can get a little unfair at times, but hey, that's fine by me.  War isn't fair.

Conclusion:  You don't play Spec Ops The Line do be a hero, you play Spec Ops The Line to experience a once in a life time opportunity of what someone thought to take a shooter in a different direction.  This game has a story that is worth experiencing just once, no spoiler here.  

Thank you for reading my review.  Shalom, and good luck.  You'll need it.

[h1]Overreaching[/h1]
[b][I]Spec Ops: The Line[/i][/b] is a decently-directed third-person modern-military cover-based shooter which does everything acceptably but misses a single spec of zest at its core - the gameplay.

Throughout the story, all you do is the run-of-the-mill duck-and-cover and shooting some intellectually severed enemies with the limited selection of armaments that sadly lack any punch. 
The gamepad layout is weirdly designed and not the most comfortable one (for example, to vault, you have to press the [b]B[/b] button on the [b]Xbox 360[/b] gamepad, whilst a double [b]A[/b]-tap would suffice).

The amount of environmental interactable props is underwhelming. It is ultimately disappointing as the game could have potentially provided for quite a few amusing situations involving destroying the enemies with sand traps - sadly, such prospects do only occur twice or maybe thrice throughout the whole campaign. The classic environmental hazards are scarce too (explosive crates, etc.).

The graphics are moderately enjoyable and there are a few astonishing shots of the devastated city here and there.

Whilst the plot unwinds steadily from the direction point-of-view (the voice acting and sound design (including the OST) are immaculate), the whole premise just does not hold up: [spoiler]why would a measly White Phosphorus incident have such an excruciating effect on the main character's (a battle-hardened Delta operator) psyche is inexplicable; additionally, it is completely unrealistic that a slow-burning conflict between some-1000 US soldiers and maybe a few thousand rebels would be overlooked by all the other military personnel in the immediate area (i.e. the whole region), regardless of the weather situation[/spoiler].

Verdict: [I]a botched attempt at a unique game that did not age well.[/i]

Overall, Spec Ops: The Line is a must-play for anyone who enjoys third-person shooters or thought-provoking stories. There are two incredibly smart aspects to this game. The first is how liberally it uses from the contemporary shooter campaign, everything from the language to the general aesthetic. Despite the game's age, its relevance as a piece of meta-narrative on the industry's fascination with shooting nameless people remains strong, as is its highlighting of the atrocities of war/conflict. The second aspect is that the writing and delivery is top notch. Loading screen tips becoming a lot more directed and your squad's lines getting more unhinged, aggressive and desperate as you progress sell you on the immersion of this beautifully ruined environment. Browns are almost boundless thanks to the desert setting, but the moments of bold colours emphasise what this area used to be like before the reality of war made itself home.

All of this is talking around what the game actually is, which is a rather perfunctory third person cover shooter. That is sort of the point, though. The hyper-linear levels can feel frustratingly restrictive at times, but it does help drive home the narrative. A suite of weapons let you mow down wave after wave of enemies covering all the staples. It is, however, what the game doesn't present to you that makes the mechanism of play so thoughtfully developed. Prompts will guide you when to do what action, but actually listening to your squad and taking a second to appreciate the scenario can open up other options for you to take, options completely unmentioned. The game gives you every tool to kill, but you do not need to take every single one.

I found a defining part of absorbing what the game has to say in how you can react to dying enemies and a good example of finding the third option. As they struggle desperately to move despite bleeding out, or begin gurgling thanks to drowning in their own blood, you're invited to perform executions. These are your typical canned animations showing brutal finishers on helpless targets. Executions aren't required though as downed enemies won't get back up to fight you, so you only really serve to put yourself at risk performing them. Instead you can simply let them wrestle with their last few seconds of living before an unceremonious death. Hearing their death cries becomes rather unsettling quite quickly though, especially as panicked enemy chatter cries out. So instead of executing them or letting them succumb, I found shooting them once more finishes them off. To me that's a far more charitable act, but regardless of what you choose the game doesn't punish nor reward you for whatever action you take. It's war, you have to kill or be killed. 

The game isn't without its flaws and whilst it'd be easy to dismiss them as being part of the whole narrative, I think that can only go so far. Getting in and out of cover can be deadly frustrating and combat arenas are clearly discernible based on how much chest-high cover there is. Similarly, difficulty spikes come too frequently in the back half and can bring the pacing to a crawl, mitigated if you happen to have a good set of weapons for the type of combat being asked of you. By this point though I never found these to be a serious road-block to wanting to see the story out.

These minor concerns aside, what Spec Ops: The Line offers is a taut, thoughtful narrative supported by solid gameplay mechanisms that encourage you to think a little for yourself whilst playing and to think critically of the genre as a whole when you're not. For that reason, it's hard to see this game stop being relevant.

Sand, blood and lead can drive a man crazy. Spec Ops: The Line tells a highly action packed story of a team of soldiers trying to save Dubai from a tyrant. During your adventure, you will be accompanied by two other fighters, whom you can command to help you along your way.  Let me tell you, that this is no cake walk from point A to point B.

Adversity awaits around every corner from swarms of soldiers toting heavy firepower. Not only does everyone pursue you for blood, but the land is ruthless. From piles of sand covering buildings you're not even aware you're walking on to blinding sandstorms, the world is constantly changing as you move.

Not only is the land and enemy harsh, but choices can be sometimes too. Don't let it get to you, they are just orders... right? Right? If you're the type of player that enjoys a game with a bit more than just simple gun blazing combat, jump in and go down the crazy ride that is Spec Ops. It is worthy of your time.

Spec Ops: The Line is essentially Apocalypse Now the Game, taking heavy inspiration for its plot. I think the best way to describe it is that it's one of those games where you play it to get the next story beat. That doesn't mean shooting isn't fun, but towards the end combat starts to drag a bit, particularly with higher health enemies and on Hard which is the difficulty I played on. There's a lot more to say about SOTL, but as a TL;DR on whether to buy it or not, it's a Story-based 3rd person shooter that's definitely a relic of its time, early 2010s cover-based shooter + set-pieces, with questions about morality in warfare. SOTL is one of those games that has reached cult-classic status, and I think it's worth picking it up if any of this interests you; however, you might want to wait for a sale due to the $30 price tag if $/hour is your main concern.

Also, in order to change some settings like mouse sens. or acceleration, you need to download a decrypter to edit the files, rather than just being able to edit the local files from the get-go. Since the initial settings are so high, and since accuracy is important on higher difficulties, you might have to spend several minutes to do this, just as a disclaimer here.

That said, my description of SOTL isn't 100% accurate, as it is a weird amalgamation of so many different sub-genres and tones. There's a lot of fantastical realism: the setting, Dubai, is a real place, but the circumstances involving it is extremely fantastical; dialogue between the characters at the start (and with some of the characters later on) feels a bit off if you were to gauge it as being realistic, but combat dialogue between the first insurgents you meet (and all the enemies pretty much for that matter) sounds really close to actual combat. There's many questions on what the right call is to do, which is a realistic aspect of being in Spec Ops. For instance, you can survive a 50 floor fall in an Uncharted-esque set-piece, after seeing a realistic depiction of corpses of people that were executed.

In terms of gameplay, there's a similar mix of casual and tactical. As much as the later part drags on, I think you get the most mileage playing on Hard as the game surprisingly holds well under a lower TTK. This is because a lot of the level design, though linear, highly encourages the use of concealment to mitigate damage, as well as having a low TTK for enemies. In most cases, enemies only take a couple of shots to down with most weapons, and doing short, accurate bursts seems to be way more effective than running and gunning. Enemies will try to flank you, and on Hard, one continuous burst from the enemy is enough to down you; that said, the checkpoint system is generally well-placed and you don't have to end up replaying too much of what you already did. However there's a lot of casual elements as there is a regenerating health system, and you're often taking out entire platoons of bad guys at a time. 

SOTL is a product of its time and it shows, being a mix of Uncharted and other early 2010s 3rd person shooter elements. I really think that SOTL would've benefited if it came out after the wave of set-pieces and generic PS3/360-era shooters, and maybe emulated something similar to The Last of Us, which came out towards the end of this cycle and was more narrative-based, though still had the general skeleton of something like Uncharted. I actually think SOTL would benefit from less combat and more environmental story-telling and navigation, as the story is undoubtedly the best part and center-focus, and plus the combat can get a bit stale towards to end, especially with higher health enemies. I think part of its charm of it coming out in 2012 was that it subverted the casual 3rd person shooter with its depiction of warfare at the time. 

Even still, SOTL is a good game to this day with realistic story themes that haven't really been replicated since, and there's nothing quite like it in that regard.

After years of hearing this game hyped up, I finally gave it a shot. I'm not sure I'm all that impressed.

The game itself isn't all that fun. It's a cover based military shooter where you'll die in just a few seconds if you stand out in the open. Since you'll be spending so much time in cover, you would think the cover system would be well polished and functional. It's not. The game clearly wants you to hop between cover and advance so that the AI doesn't overwhelm you, but utilizing the cover system is not very fluid. It always felt risky to change cover, so I found myself hunkering down behind a singular piece of cover for most firefights. I found myself sometimes unable to leave cover or, if I managed to leave cover and sprint towards another one, my character would randomly stop running. You can't rotate to another side of cover without completely leaving the cover then re-entering, again opening yourself up. Did a grenade land right next to you? Good luck fighting the controls to change cover before you eat shrapnel. Multiple times I shouted "I HATE THIS GAME" because of the clunky controls mixed with quick deaths.

The game mechanically doesn't really try to innovate either. Early on, the game introduces the ability to give your squadmates commands. This mechanic is quickly forgotten because it seems pointless or random. You can ask them to target specific enemies, but there never really seemed to be much of a point behind this. You can also ask them to throw flashbangs, but what triggers this is a mystery to me. You can't do it on command, only when the seemingly random popup appears.

Speaking of squadmate AI, they will frequently rush behind enemy lines. This leads to confusion because you think if your teammates are pushing forward then it must be clear until you get blindsided by enemy bullets. Many times my teammates would pop out where the enemy was occupying and I'd shoot at them thinking they were an enemy. Why are they even there? It doesn't help that your teammates can get downed, requiring you to pick them up before a meter fills up. They are fairly tanky, so it didn't occur too often, but your teammates are definitely overly gung-ho and lead to confusion in battle.

One thing I did like was how limited ammo is. This requires you to constantly be picking up and trying new weapons. I found this refreshing compared to a lot of generic FPS where you pick your standard setup and stick with it for most of the game.

But if you've already read other reviews, you know this game isn't praised for its gameplay but for its story. 

While I applaud the devs for doing something other than your typical military bro, America is always the hero type story, I don't think it was very successful to me. You'll see this compared to Apocalypse Now, and that's a very apt comparison.

The story can be confusing, perhaps intentionally so. When it comes down to it, it's the motivations behind the characters that I don't quite understand. It feels contrived. The game will also frequently have you make choices, but for most of them I never felt compelled one way or another nor did I care about the consequence. I also never really felt very impacted by my decision nor did the characters. I think this is where games have a hard time also being art. On one hand, you want to tell a serious and interesting story. On the other, you have to make a game fun to play. I think the story gets hidden and even muted by all the constant, and frankly, boring shooting gameplay. 

This is also a short game. It took me 5 hours to complete. I suggest buying on a deep sale. It's not worth the full price. Even though I'm not recommending it, I would still urge you to give it a try if you can pick it up for cheap. Maybe the game will impact you more than it did me. It clearly has a following, but I feel like if you've seen or read the multitude of movies, books, and television shows that highlight the atrocities of war, you're not going to get much from this game. A step in the right direction for video game storytelling, but far from a home run.

[h1]Where the Line Disappears[/h1]

After grappling with the enemies here in Dubai, my soldiers urged me not to deploy the mortars—those loaded with white phosphorus. Yet blinded by chaos, and by the exhaustion of waiting, that relentless impulse to push forward whispered: do it.

I did.

I committed the gravest error of my life.

One that left me in tears, unable to touch the computer for some time. Then the truth of my mistake revealed itself: a scorched mother, her children cradled in her arms. They were gone.

I was lost. I did not know what to do. I felt utterly shattered—devastated. And it was not born of haste or impatience. I despise haste. I take my time. I linger. I stood there, weighing obedience against refusal, believing I still possessed a choice.

I… I broke that time.

Forgive me.

When a game commands do it, I always question the act. Always. And in that moment—faced with the image of that mother and her children—I would have endured anything instead: shrapnel, bullets, punishment, death itself. Anything but this cruelty. Spec Ops: The Line wields a harrowing mastery of realism.

At first, the game extends a sense of welcome—but it is a hollow illusion. We are so accustomed to other games, where bullets are tools, instruments of advantage. Dubai dismantles that false heroism, especially within a war that seems to belong more to itself than to the people trapped inside it.

But when everything begins to unravel, in that singular moment, a soldier’s instinct to survive becomes a betrayal. One breaks—as I did—in countless ways. The body bears wounds, yes, but so does the soul. And the trauma remains: shrapnel marks etched by the most inhuman act I have ever committed.

White phosphorus.

This review is less a critique than a confession, written through tears. And yet it grants me the space to say this: even in fiction, war is pure, disembodied dehumanisation—utterly soulless. The pain becomes so unbearable that the boundary between body and soul dissolves, just as the line vanishes between soldier and victim.

I played this game 3 times on my Xbox back in 2012 and until now I didn't know that Walker and his team died in the helicopter crash and everything after that is Walker's purgatory. To extend this I think that he is stuck in a loop, there are a few minor clues that seem to confirm this such as before the white phosphorus mortar strike when Lugo says "There's always a choice" and Walker responds with, "There's really not." This implies to me that Walker has no control over his actions, he is being forced to relive the personal hell of his final moments over and over. Later when you reach the stage of the escape from Radioman's HQ in the helicopter which was also featured at the beginning of the game Walker bizarrely states, "Wait, this isn't right, we've done this already!" Which again implies that Walker has done this before, maybe hundreds of times, and is only faintly aware of it. Then we reach the end where he confronts Konrad and is offered the option to kill himself, thus taking responsibility for his actions and breaking the cycle of his personal hell or continuing to delude himself and blaming Konrad, continuing with the cycle indefinitely.

Walker is a ticking time bomb from the start, despite clear orders to locate survivors and leave he insists on rescuing the locals and finding Konrad, it is implied that when Konrad rescued him in Kabul they suffered horrific circumstances which left both men with PTSD that ultimately affected their judgment later on and Walker now has a strange obsession with Konrad which makes him see visions of his face on billboards, something we don't realize on our first playthrough as we don't know what Konrad looks like. The white phosphorus incident seems to have been the trigger that snapped Walker's mind completely however, after this he began hallucinating vividly and regularly, both visually and audibly and he made Konrad a scapegoat for his own mistakes. This rubs off on his squadmates who while terrified of the circumstances they find themselves in are even more terrified of Walker who insists on pushing forward with psychotic single-mindedness despite their reservations about his sanity. I think it's interesting that they didn't try to kill him, maybe out of fear they would take the blame for his actions? That they wouldn't survive without his leadership? Or out of simple, misguided loyalty? Who really knows?

Of course, the game can also be taken entirely at face value, that this is Walker's one and only time through Dubai and the deja vu in the chopper is simply part of the mental degradation he is suffering. The different available interpretations are what makes this game so great. I especially love the ending, so original and the voice actors deserve enormous credit for the effort they put into bringing these characters to life.

War also breeds hate. Doesn't matter which side you're on, aggressor or defender it always leads to hate. First maybe to increased patriotism (which is isn't bad), then nationalism and in the end both sides including regular citizens just hate each other and wish all the worst for opposing faction's citizens.
Wars are caused by governments in most cases so hating the whole nation only worsens the situation. In short – war is bad, there are no winners. Although my cynical side must say a word too. Big wars like WW2 also unite people when the war ends and sometimes humans need it. Or a pandemic. Or any other global disaster so people would understand how important friendship and unity is.

Ok, I talked enough about war, lets talk about the game. Too bad there's not much to talk about. You play as an American soldier in Dubai after it was devastated. You basically run to the objective and shoot people. Gameplay is nothing special, shooting mechanics are pretty basic and sometimes clunky. It's not a realistic game, there's no tactical gameplay or anything like that, you just shoot enemies running at you while hiding behind the cover.

The best part of the game is showing the horrors of war. I'm used to violence and I love violent games but seeing all those images war caused was really disturbing.

Graphically it's average at best. It has that annoying filter from ~2008 wave of games. I'm so glad it's gone and we rarely see it anymore. Level design again is nothing special. At times the game could look good but for the most of the time it feels like an indie game. 2K published this, they could've invested more into studio which made this. And yes I know it's an old game but I felt that way years ago when I played it.

Sounds are pretty nice. There's some nice music playing while you're in combat and of course the usual gunshot sounds. The most terrifying sounds are screams of dying people which again just like some cut-scenes makes the game very disturbing.

It's a good game if you play for the story but if you're looking for good gameplay or graphics it's not for you. So if you want to see what war does to people then just buy it, it cost pennies on sale.

This is an amazing game. Yes, it can be extremely annoying at times. But through the uninspired gameplay shines a story that you won't find in any other FPS. And as you get lost in that story, you'll find yourself forgetting about the mechanics. Even if you don't like narrative shooters, I can almost guarantee you'll like this one. 

Play this game. Play it for the story. That's what Spec Ops is all about.

That said, the gameplay has some issues. Enemy AI is extremely predictable in every way EXCEPT the amount of damage they deal, which ranges from a light scratch to sudden death. Hiding behind objects doesn't guarantee safety, as for some reason the player character doesn't seem to grasp the concept of ducking his head. It's very hard to tell teammates and AI apart, and your teammates will often do stupid things that will leave you scrambling to rescue them. Vault and melee buttons are combined, and it's far from intuitive what you can and can't vault over, so you may find yourself about to make a brilliant leap, and frantically punching the air. The graphics are ... acceptable. Mine were pretty much constantly blurry, for reasons I never discovered. There's no way to manually save, so if you die ... well, let's just say that's why I have 9.1 hours invested in a very short game.

Again, I can almost promise you'll forget about all of that fifteen minutes in. But it's worth knowing beforehand so you can adjust your play style to suit the story. I would suggest playing on an easier mode than you usually would, so that you can experience the story's strongest points without suffering from irritating mechanical problems.

**EDIT** I don't know if anyone else is having this problem, but I thought I'd point it out because it caused me a good half hour of headache before I could play. When you launch Spec Ops for the first time, your keyboard may SOMEHOW be switched to function mode. In order to do anything in the game, you'll need to switch it back. The directions for doing this vary by model - the only surefire way is to restart your PC and then relaunch the game, at which point it will work fine.

This is not just another generic shooter, even if it might look like this, especially by judging its cover art. Well, maybe from gameplay perspective it is, as it's pretty standard cover-based third-person shooter from Xbox 360/PS3 era. However, what heavily distinguishes it from many other similar games is its plot. It is heavily based on Heart of Darkness novel and Apocalypse Now movie. Actually, in this case it's better to know about the story as less, as possible. So, if you still considering buying it, I suggest you to go and play the game, and once you finish it, go back to this review and finish the reading. So... Still here? Or have you already returned? Anyway, I warned you. So, when I was first playing this game in the early 2010s (if I am not mistaken, if was pretty soon after it came out), I did not know much about plot as well. And at the first sight the game looked pretty close to other shooters released prior it. It was a massive trend of military shooters back then, where player was offered to beat a standard campaign with killing bunch of enemies and ultimately saving the day in the end. I think, it all started pretty much with Call of Duty 4. The videogames were becoming more and more mainstream in that time and, of course, it was raising the questions about how violent they can be. And some people who were complaining about it had their point, as story-wise it sometimes really looked kinda strange. The player was supposed to be a good guy who was basically killing hundreds of enemies. Of course, it's just a game, but still such story looked often biased. It's now when this review is written this is pretty obvious and the topic was raised countless times, but back then it was different. So, when first playing "Spec Ops: The Line" I was expecting it to be a typical story where I had to save everyone by its end and killing bunch of enemies in the game was justified. They were supposed to be bad guys after all. Or they weren't?.. Well, at some point of the story I began questioning actions of my protagonist, captain Walker, as well as his sanity. He and his squad mates, Lugo and Adams, came to Dubai which was devastated by terrible sandstorm (the game's setting is indeed amazing by the way) to save everyone, isn't it? But wait, they were supposed to be just on recon mission. Why in the middle of the story they got involved in a war between CIA and remnants of the "Damned 33rd" Infantry Battalion?? Martin Walker was making right decisions all this time, correct? But then how on Earth he along with Lugo and Adams eventually committed those terrible war crimes, killing many civilians with white phosphorus, along with soldiers protecting them? How that did even happen? I was obviously shocked by this moment in the game's plot. And this is ultimate point of the game, in my opinion. Because even after this tragic event Walker still says that it's a John Conrad's fault, who is pulling the string from behind controlling the remnants of 33th, while reality is, it's all the fault of Walker himself, in his selfish attempt to become a hero (this role of Nolan North is indeed one of his best, by the way). Because at least before blaming Conrad for his own terrible actions Walker saw him as a hero and a role model for himself. But Conrad tried to save people in Dubai just for the sake of his career and when evacuation attempt has failed and so many people died because of him, he committed suicide to escape shameful and devastating end of his career. The game has multiple endings and player can choose how this story will eventually end but the truth is, there is no good ending at all. The only best way for achieving a "good ending" here would be to simply stop playing. But if you will still decide to finish the game, I guess at some point you will realise that this is not another biased story about saving the day by killing all the enemies. Of course, not everyone will understand it fast. The game itself even will be making fun of a player by different means. For example, by its loading screen, where instead of typical game hints you will see "Feel like a hero yet?" at some point. And as Walker will be falling deeper into his insanity, as more violent this story will be becoming. And here I need to say that I am extremely grateful to Yager Development for making this game and to 2K for publishing it. We do need such anti-militarist and deep story-telling in our mass-culture and videogames, especially now in 2023, when there is full-scale war going on in Europe, and it will never be too much of it. So, concluding this review I want also note that apart from so good plot this game has awesome instrumental soundtrack and very stylish graphic design. All this together makes it an ultimate atmospheric experience and by moment when this review is written it really did age as a good wine.

The title may suggest that this is just an another TPS where you run around and shoot people in flashy, "overly romanticized" gameplay. But that is far from the truth. But I guess, if you're here, reading reviews of a 2012 game, you probably know what to expect in terms of the game's story (it's main differentiator from generic shooters). And let me tell you, the rumors about this game are true. So instead, I'll just mention some technicalities and gameplay experiences instead:

The game ran very well on my GTX 1060 (6G), in 1440p, over 60FPS, at very high settings. The gunplay feels good, aiming isn't wonky, gameplay-wise nothing feels rushed. The only technical problem I had was that if you died, existing bodies and their weapon drops disappeared upon reloading the checkpoint. 

On Suicide Mission difficulty, you'll probably not spend much time in the open. Actually, on this difficulty, the gameplay to me suffered a bit towards the end of the game. Not because of dying mind you, but because, it just came down to taking cover, shooting a few times, waiting for your health to recharge, then repeat. Since there was no room for error, I was more-or-less forced into this "pattern", because any other tactic would have resulted in instant death. (note: I'm not extremely experienced in shooters) I can't speak for the other difficulty levels. I also haven't tried the multiplayer (does it even exist at this point?), in my opinion the value of Spec Ops: The Line resides in it's campaign, and that I can recommend for anyone who's up for a game that's a bit more difficult to digest.

the story is what you're here for. it's fantastic and holds up amazingly nearly a decade later. that being said, there are a couple of minor cons:

-it's a great story locked behind a generic brown military FPS. it's still worth playing if, like myself, generic military FPS games aren't normally your cup of tea.
-the controls are extremely clunky. i've died more than once because of how awkward it was trying to control the main character.

it's still a wonderful experience and can be found dirt cheap during a sale. it's not too long—i completed the campaign in about 4 and a half hours—so i don't recommend it at full price.

Playing this for the parts that critique military shooters is like sitting thru Adam Sandler's Jack and Jill because you wanna watch an Al Pacino movie. 

First of all, can we all just agree that Cover Shooters are just the f**king worst? That they're just boring shooting galleries that encourage no experimentation from the player? Yes? Great. 

Secondly, can we agree that Cover Shooters which have some kind of system where you attach yourself to a surface with a button press are the f*cking buggy, broken nadir of an already terrible subgenre? Oh I'm so glad we're on the same page about these things.

Yeah Spec Ops is a whole lot of cover shootin' for not a lot of reward. It reminds of Doki Doki Literature Club in that it spends way too much time presenting itself as the genre its trying to deconstruct before it gets to the interesting stuff. Except 1. Doki Doki, is a way shorter experience and 2. I suspect it's a much better visual novel than Spec Ops is a shooter (can't say for sure though because I'm not a weeb).

I get why Yaeger wouldn't have wanted to necessarily make the game more "fun" to play, considering its a critique of an entire genre, but faaaaaackin hell, could they have found some way to make the game less tedious?  There's some interesting environmental kills you can do with sand avalanches (a mechanic that's woefully underused) and ocassional attempts at surrealism but overall it's a deconstruction of bad military shooters that's... predominantly a bad military shooter?

But worst of all, is that all of the things it wants to say about Military Shooters are barely threaded into the game, but used as a "twist", something that only becomes apparent in the final hours of the game. There's subverting our expectations and then there's just making us suffer thru mediocrity only to realize at the end There Was Something Afoot The Whole Time.

Honestly, unless you have a particular affinity for this kind of game, just watch a lets play of the key moments.

Playing this game now it really hasn't aged well. I can appreciate the motions it took to try and put a spin on the typical shooter based in the middle-east, but its probably a game you can digest better by watching segmented clips on YouTube that represent what your choices mean in an overall arc without the action nonsense on top of it.

The gameplay is downright clunky and felt worse than most third person shooters in terms of gunplay and movement. Perhaps it was me playing on mouse and keyboard when it was intended for controller?

Another caveat is that you can't pick the hardest difficulty off the bat (have to beat on 2nd hardest first) which I understand: you want people to replay the game and experience the different choices but honestly when the choices are binary (and rather forced on you) its kind of pointless. Had the game had splintered endings or different endings I probably would have found it much more appreciable. 

It had a lot to say about war but ultimately I think there are many ways it could have done it in a better way while also staying grounded to real post-war consequences as described by veterans that live to experience it. At the end it felt too much in the scheme of trying to reach the levels of Call of Duty: Modern Warfare in telling a war story while also subverting the player's expectations.

Spec Ops: The Line is a horror game disguised in a modern military shooter. When I first watched the gameplay trailers years ago on Xbox, I thought it would essentially be a third person Call of Duty. ♥♥♥♥ me, was I wrong.

Functionally, the game is exactly what you would expect from a third person shooter. Cover based mechanics, hordes of enemies, a couple of AI support characters to aid you along the way, the whole shebang. Where the game shines is in its storytelling. The voice acting is excellent and the plot drags you further into madness with the characters portrayed. Similar to what Yahtzee said he felt in his Zero Punctuation review, this game caused me to feel genuinely sick, something that cannot be said for most horror games I've played.

This game is worth purchasing at full price, even better if you can grab it on sale. Easily, it's one of the best military shooters I've played, if not the best. Again, gameplay is pretty cut and paste, but the game thrives from its horrific and disturbing narrative.

This game is an absolute work of art.

From Post-apocalyptic Dubai being one of the most beautiful FPS worlds ever created, with its terrifying sandstorms, the bloody highways and underpasses and collapsing malls filled with enemies of uncertain faction and loyalties to its brilliant commentary of CoD-like shooters that were popular at the time. The gameplay however isn't something special and borderline bad at times with its Difficulty spikes. Oh, and the voice acting is Bloody amazing.

I would recommend it more than any CoD, but this little indie Publishing firm 2K or something pulled it from the steam store, and you can only get it by buying a key or sailing the sea.

If you can get a copy, I strongly recommend Spec Ops: The Line
best single player TPS i've ever played and finished, i wish theres going to be a sequel to this game because this game is 9 years old for now, going to replay it on ps now and xbox one.

This is my *SPOILER FREE* review of the game. Spec Ops: The Line is one of the most underrated game that I've ever played. Heck, even the name makes it sound like a generic shooter with a shi**y story line, non-relatable characters, grindy...you get the idea. But infact, this is one of the most traumatizing games I've played in a long time. 

A little bit about the story, *spoiler free*: The game starts off as any game would. You play as the hero, complete a mission, get praised...blah blah blah. You play as a Captain Martin Walker of the Delta force, looking for US Army, the 33rd Battalion's survivors after a massive sandstorm hit Dubai. However, sh*t gets fu**ed up real quick. "You become the very thing you swore to destroy".

The game is based on the psychological horrors of war. What war can do to your brain, what it can do to your life, how it can turn your life around in an instant. Martin Walker, an average guy, "hero" if you will. An identifiable main character who was sent to war to complete a mission, similar to other shooters, like COD or Battlefield. And you, the player, are at the center of it all. The game makes you question, do you like killing because the game tells you to or for your own pleasure and narcissistic need to play the "hero" ?

In conclusion, (if you haven't figured it out already) I highly recommend this game. Although, the campaign is short, about 7-ish hours, it is well worth $30 in my opinion. I've beat the game twice already, and I can see myself playing it again a few more times.

This is another one of those old games that is difficult to rate in the present day.  On one hand the story is gripping and possesses a certain depth not found in many generic shooters.  On the other hand, the graphics and mechanics are quite dated which leads to a very dull gameplay experience.

This is a short title and to be honest, it was a drag to get through. However I'll give it a thumbs up on an objective rating system - that's to say I didn't have a great time playing through Spec Ops but I do think it's a "good" game overall.  The shooter mechanics may have been fairly on par back in 2012 but they fall very short nearly 10 years later.  On top of that there are next-to-no interesting game mechanics to keep the player engaged.  This game relies on a good story to keep the player hooked whilst running through linear missions and blasting through cannon fodder AI.  The one thing that drew me to Spec Ops was the "choices matter" aspect of the game but that was severely lacking in practicality.  Over the ~5 hours of gameplay, I counted only 4 total choices to make which doesn't offer much variety.  The redeeming quality here is that the game's atmosphere and dialogue are very fleshed out and this creates a dynamic world that forces you to revel in the (very few) choices that you will make.

Overall it's a good game.  It was fairly difficult on the higher difficulty settings but the gameplay is ultimately stale.  As with many older games, the game settings are fairly lackluster - in particular the insanely high look sensitivity that I ultimately had to edit via .ini files.  If you want a good war story, this one is worth a play.  Just don't expect anything revolutionary.

Did you rescue them and want to make it back? Too bad, you can either walk back while being shot or attempt to run and deal with a autoslide that you can't turn off. When you are "in cover" like this, you have to either press your sprint key again to get out of cover or manually back up. Don't press and hold though, because you'll *instead* flip into other nearby cover. 

Another fun one is when you clear an area out, then move back through it and watch the enemies respawn again in front of your face, so have fun dying and reloading whatever progress you might have made.

In Spec Ops the Line you play as Captain Martin Walker leading a 3 man team through a sandstorm covered Dubai. Events unfold and soon Walker and his team find themselves in a desperate and impossible situation one they cannot seem to find a way out of. Walker eventually pushing through the campaign gets multiple people killed including unarmed civilians, this breaks Walker and sends him over the edge, he cant handle the fact that his orders killed 47 innocent people. The colonel that Walker has been trying to find and help also turns out to be the main villain or at least thats what we want to believe. You destroy the last of the water kill more people and as you go along Walkers sanity begins to slip. He begins seeing things and even dying at certain points in the game Walker gets visions (i.e. Konrad standing above him and the civilians hes killed). His squad members in the last few chapters also end up getting killed due to his actions and its awful. Sgt. John Lugo ends up being lynched by the same civilians you were supposed to save and Lt. Alphonso Adams commits assisted suicide. After everything Walker makes it to the tower that Konrad is in and confronts him. This is when the game goes from having unique elements to being a story that completely turns yours and Walkers beliefs that you're still the good guy on its head. Konrad is dead, he always was, and he explains everything. Walker pushed into the city against orders, if he had just stopped none of the death and killing would've continued. Walker and possibly the player are still in denial but Konrad is dead, you've killed everyone and Konrad at least the one in your head gives you to the count of five before he pulls the trigger. There are technically 5 endings 2 are basically the same. Letting Konrad shoot you which is actually you shooting yourself as Walker turns the gun on himself means and the ending where Walker straight up shoots himself both end up the same. Walker dies and the transmission at the beginning of the game replays overlooking the dead city. The other 3 endings are when Walker shoots Konrad and the epilogue plays out. You can either kill all the soldiers and Walker turns into the Konrad that he saw as the villain, Die trying to kill the soldiers and an ending transmission different from the ending where Konrad/Walker kills himself plays out where Konrad explains that theres a line men like them have to cross and then hopefully they die, that he only wants peace. Finally the last ending Walker hands over his weapons and finally gets to go home. When asked by a soldier how he survived the events of Dubai Walker doesn't really answer only saying "who says I did." which I personally love. We were taught to question everything Walker saw and if it was real and even at the end Walker and the player cant even be sure if he did survive the game...

The character development as the main trio slowly lose their mind is superbly written, animated and voice-acted. I didn't expect the narrative to be this good in a shooter. It's a relatively simple concept but perfectly executed, with the gameplay itself reinforcing the themes of the story and maintaining a consistent tone until the very end.

It is a game that makes you think about what you are willing to compromise morally and ultimately where you draw THE LINE.

Disclaimer: Review from a guy who was a hardcore Hatred fan.

TL;DR - A case of good intentions, but sub-par execution.
Overall: 6 out of 11; pun intended.
I respect that devs were brave enough to actually make and release this but it is kinda hard to enjoy the gameplay.

Long version:

First of all, none of that is truly ""shocking"", if you enjoyed playing violent games in that past. But I can understand that the world was not ready for something like Hatred back then, and/or the game would simply not sell at all.

Still, the gameplay could have been better. For instance, you can execute downed enemies in return for ammo, but this opportunity is so rare - you get shot from quite a few directions already, so risking my life for a couple of bullets and putting myself in front of other enemies is just not worth it - that it becomes non-existent. Other than executions, I haven't found even a single feature, which makes the game pretty generic.

Controls are clunky, feels like a direct port from consoles. Single key to run and take cover is bs. It just doesn't feel natural, often I leave the cover instead of running, or vice versa.

Difficulty is fair but again, controls are screwing it all up.

On the plus side, the setting is interesting and map design is neat. Graphics are decent, considering the release date. Wish there was some "HD textures" mod.

PS: Don't ask me to make FPS mod for it lol.

Spec Ops: The Line is a third-person shooter with an incredible story. Storytelling is wonderful. Presentation of the story is spectacular. Spec Ops makes you question your morals. Game presents you moral choices, but these aren’t your typical video game morality choices. Morality in games usually means there’s a fork in the road, carefully presented to make the players feel as though they’ve some sort of power over the narrative, some semblance of control. Instead, Spec Ops’s choices serve to shape what shade of monster Walker will turn out to be in the eyes of the people forcing him to make the choices to begin with. Graphics are really good for 2012 and I think it still looks beautiful. Voice acting is excellent. Gameplay is pretty generic but when you progress through the game and get to the juicy parts of the story, you won't mind the gameplay. This game tells a dark and brutal story. Ending and the last one hour of the game is unforgettable. I can easily say this is one of the best TPS I have ever played. From start to finish it is an unforgettable experience. I want to finish this review with a great quote from the game.
"It takes a strong man to deny what's right in front of him"

Game mechanics are...look, it's a 3rd person cover shooter. I don't think I've ever seen a 3rd person cover shooter where I enjoyed the shooting or taking cover, and this game is no exception. The cover system is a little clumsy, and the shooting is just shooting: you point your gun at the enemy and fire, they die, you get a little dopamine, whee. Nothing about it really interested me though, and it was mostly 'stand somewhere, shoot the enemies when you can see them, duck when you're close to dying, repeat until no more enemies, then advance'. And that's pretty much the entire game in terms of mechanics

Full disclosure I played on the easiest difficulty, for 2 reasons:
     After playing on 2nd easiest difficulty I realized that the only difference higher difficulties are going to make for me are more time sitting in cover waiting for health to regen, having to micro-manage my NPC allies(a pet peeve of mine), and having to restart a lot after dying
     Having died once or twice because of scripted ♥♥♥♥ that I couldn't have known about, I decided that I didn't want to EVER have to replay a section if I could help it. This is where having fun mechanics would have made a difference; once you take out the novelty of a slightly new area, you're pretty much just repeating the same fights you've been doing since the beginning of the game



If you want a story that's dark and gripping or w/e, then I've certainly never heard of a game being more recommended than this one, but if fun gameplay is a must for you than I would look elsewhere

Spec Ops: The Line se na první pohled tváří jako generická střílečka z třetí osoby z přelomu dekády, která efektivně poškrábě jakékoliv svědění po military shooteru z této doby. Opak je však pravdou. Pod povrchem se skrývá kriminálně přehlížený klenot, který je nejen ukázkou skvěle budovaného příběhu, temné atmosféry a vývoje postav, ale také demonstrací odvrácené tváře válečného konfliktu. Hra mne dokonce natolik nadchla, že po letech jsem nucen napsat na Steamu krátkou recenzi, kde sepíšu své dojmy z tohoto herního skvostu...

V této hře jste postaveni do bot kapitána Walkera, který se se svým týmem vydává do písečnou bouří zdecimované a pískem pohřbené Dubaje, aby zde zjistil, co se stalo s 33. plukem, který byl zodpovědný za neúspěšnou evakuaci města. Jak však postup zbytky zničeného města pokračuje, saturuje jak brutalita a surovost, tak i temný a děsivý ráz celého příběhu. Současně s ním degraduje i mentální stav hlavních protagonistů, jak si na nich prožité události vybírají svou dan. To vše končí překvapivým finálem, ve kterém vykrystalizují myšlenky týkající se hlavně podlomené psychiky a traumat vojáků působících ve válečných konfliktech. Celá hra tak nese navzdory přemíře násilí, které je zde vyhnáno do extrému, zcela jasné protiválečné poselství.

Spec Ops: The Line is modern re-telling of Joseph Conrad's 'Heart of Darkness', or perhaps more appropriately, an echo of the 1979 'Apocalypse Now', which is itself a retelling of Conrad's story. Although, SO:TL is not completely derivative, as the narrative is shifted from an anti-imperialist motif to one of anti-war.

I'm unsure whether or not your stock-standard 3rd person shooter is the appropriate medium for an anti-war story, but there's something to be said about an anti-war game centralising on mindlessly killing hundreds of soulless enemy soldiers as it's core gameplay. 

With gameplay in mind, It has to be said that it's completely ♥♥♥♥. It's a subpar 3rd person shooter at the best of times, a clunky mess at it's worst. The game is a shooter, it's nothing but that, and it does a poor job of it. No redeeming qualities. Additionally, the level design is samey and becomes boring quickly. Maybe that's the natural outcome of setting a game in an destroyed city in the middle of a barren desert, but it is what it is.

The only reason to play this game is the story, and in my opinion, it's pretty take it or leave it.

The game ditches it's sources narrative of imperialism, which is a shame, as US ventures into the middle east would serve as a prime canvas. Alternatively, it prioritises an anti-war narrative by highlighting the atrocities all participants face;  war crimes, PTSD, etc. It's a little too on the nose and simplistic for me, take the main menu as an example...

A shot of a ruined middle eastern city with a tattered US flag waving in the foreground, with Jimi Hendrix's sounds-of-war infused rendition of the US national anthem playing from a distant loudspeaker. Could the message be clearer?

A brief music-related tangent, the game blares 60's rock music throughout combat, which is definitely a highlight and a little comically ironic.

Another perspective would be that the story is "easily digestible", which is perhaps appropriate for the crowd which might be attracted to this game by it's surface appearance. It's a subversive narrative, and perhaps a breath of fresh air for the genre. I respect SO:TL for that. 

I appreciate what SO:TL tried, and I like the source material, but save yourself a few hours and just watch 'Apocalypse Now'.

[h1] Spec Ops: The Line [/h1]

[b] Plot: [/b]
6 months ago, a sandstorm ravaged the city of Dubai and in an attempt to evacuate the remaining forces of the 33rd Battalion stayed within the city, ultimately becoming trapped. You play as Captain Walker, a US Army Delta Force Operator alongside his two squadmates, Lieutenant Adams and Sergeant Lugo. Sent on a mission to infiltrate Dubai and find out if there are any survivors within the city. Things quickly get out of hand as you are thrust into a civil war between the remnants of the 33rd "Damned" Battalion and the local population. Your mission remains however, find Colonel Konrad and find out what happened.

[b] Gameplay: [/b]
It's your generic 3rd person cover based shooter with light (and I mean light, most you can do is mark targets and occasionally order them to throw a flashbang) squad tactics. There is a semi-decent amount of weapons but I found myself sticking to the same 3 or 4 the entire time cause there wasn't really enough differences between them. In terms of enemy types, you only have a few and again most of them are essentially the same with different weapons. Recommend starting on the harder difficulties as you will easily blaze through the game on normal and lower.

[b] Graphics: [/b]
They're meh for a game from 2012 but they work.

[b] Sound: [/b]
Same as graphics. Voice acting from the main two antagonists and cutscene lines from Captain Walker are good but the rest are just ok, not good but not terrible. Very generic gunfire and explosions that lack a punch.

[b] Replay Value: [/b]
Low. Only reason to really replay the game is to see the alternate endings (there are 4 of them) but I would just recommend watching them through Youtube.

[b] Fun: [/b]
Kindof. It's mundane but not awful.

[h1] Do I recommend the game? [/h1]
Yes, but only on sale. The best part of the game is the story by far which is why I feel like this would work better as a movie or book (upon doing some research it was heavily inspired by Heart of Darkness and Apocalypse Now, haven't seen or read them yet so I wouldn't know but they are on the list now). The gameplay however drags it down so I can't recommend it at full price.

[b] Side Notes: [/b]
-I got the game for free from Humble Bundle back in 2018
-I played through the game using the Deadly Bullets Mod which does rebalance the weapons to make the game a bit more realistic. If you want an improvement to the gameplay then I recommend trying that mod out. If you want something closer to Gears of War then there is another mod (which I have not tried yet) titled Gears of Spec Ops Assault Recon.

(Spoilers!) Honestly, I tried to like this game. I thought the destruction effects were really well done and the voice acting was on point (as far as FPS war games are concerned). The individual map setpieces were well-done; I felt that the game over-all had a good flow to it. For me, the first problems started cropping up very quickly. Problem No.1: The AI. My goodness the A.I. is some of the worst I´ve seen in a long time. This issue has been lamented upon by many other reviewers, but it´s definitely worth mentioning here once more. Considering you are supposedly fighting U.S Soldiers, one would think a sense of self preservation would be a remote priority for people trying to "survive". Bum rushes, standing out in the open, it just looks and feels incredibly halfbaked. Considering you are a one man army (your squad providing some support with a sniper rifle and flashbangs), you mow down hundreds of Americans in... self defense? Segue to problem no. 2: The story... From the get-go I felt that this was just another COD-style story. The narrative quickly tried to do a 180 as our squad appeared to be mislead on the situation.  I was intrigued to see where this all would go. So, slogging through the incredibly boring and repetitive gunplay (cover, headshot, switch cover, headshot, repeat) I was hoping to see what the hype was about. But then, a series of fake decision-making moments occured. For a game about moral, you sure are shoehorned a lot into being the "shoot first- ask questions later" mentality. The phosphorous mortar scene bugged me in particular. Touted as a choice, it turned out it wasn´t... quite disappointing. Also it just boggled my mind the amount of people we mowed through in this game, who, honestly had no reason to continue fighting us. If there was one moment where someone had just started talking sense the story would have come to a screeching halt. At least Call of Duty campaigns find reasons to be clicking heads. I think this game had a lot of potential if it wasn´t so linear. The gameplay might have been more forgivable if it the story took it´s time to develop more and let the narrative really play out. Instead, buckle up for a wild ride with dislikeable heroes, no clear directive, horrible, uncontrollable events meant to shock you, and poor cover-to-cover gunplay. At least the music gave some good vibes. You´re better off playing Gears of War for a cover shooter with an arguably more provocative story.

I waited a very long time to play this game. I've seen it in lists and watched reviews about how great the story is. I have to agree that the story is intriguing and your team of operatives have interesting personalities, they don't drag the story down with too much unnecessary dialogue. 

The downside to this game is the gameplay mechanics do not hold up. The cover system is basically the same as Gears of War but it is very clunky. At times you'll be in a firefight and try to swap cover but instead you'll stand up. The sprint mechanic is basically useless. Instead of hold to sprint you have to toggle sprint. So if you want to cover a small distance quickly you just awkwardly two step and still have to sit through the heel sliding mechanic which is just the right amount of time for your enemies to target you and empty half a magazine into you. On the easier difficulties I can see this game being  more enjoyable because you can take more hits and recover, but on "suicide mission" there were a few ambush areas where I had to replay at least 20 times just because popping up to shoot calls every gun directly to your body. Also, in these same areas is where I experienced the aforementioned problem of your character just deciding to stand up instead of vaulting or switching cover. 

Aside from that the combat is pretty generic and if you're good with a mouse you can clear out areas with headshots pretty quickly.

Whilst having completely generic and forgettable multiplayer modes, and pretty basic cover shooter gameplay, Spec Ops; The Line offers a top 10 shooter campaign that says so much in so little time, and remains a classic almost ten years later. It's rare I become so invested and responsible for choices a character makes outside of my control, and the game makes very clever whilst not overly-manipulative psychological choices to slightly break the fourth wall and get you immersed. The game still looks really great too, with some incredible long-shots of Dubai amidst a sandstorm and some graphic character detail adding far more to the gritty nature of this world than some higher budget titles have attempted. Everything audio-related is also top-notch, from the voice-acting to the in-the-background but always present unsettling soundtrack. As mentioned, the gameplay is basic but has a couple of good ideas, such as the occasional use of sandstorms as a weapon and some basic squad commands, though I wish it was possible to control where your squad members move at times as their AI can be a bit dumb at times. 

I recommend playing on Suicide Mission for the best experience, as this makes the game feel intense whilst also not having too many challenging moments. Similar to when I completed Prestige Mode in NFS 2015 which was its hardest challenge, playing this game on its hardest difficulty, FUBAR, made me notice a few more problems that I wouldn't have otherwise encountered:

- The difficulty itself is unfortunately your standard shooter affair of making you die incredibly quickly, so quickly that it is sometimes impossible to pop out and kill one person without dying. As is standard with this kind of difficulty, there are really only a select few encounters throughout the entire game which are seriously annoying, with the last three levels having a lot of BS in them.
- Since you are required to keep your squadmates alive throughout the game else enter a fail-state, and they too die incredibly quickly, you unfortunately have to babysit and revive them far too much which gets very annoying.
- The enemy AI is strange as a whole. There were many instances where they simply didn't behave authentically, which is particularly the case for the suicide knife runners which just do not fit into this game at all. The normal soldiers sometimes charge straight out of cover as if they would fit straight into a Call of Duty, so I feel this should have been tweaked a bit.
- Checkpoint load states result in enemy bodies and their weapon drops disappearing, which in some cases can leave you with little ammo.

FUBAR is obviously doable, taking myself about 8 hours to complete, but I wouldn't personally recommend playing on it. It wasn't particularly fun and the challenge felt more artificial than fair. 

Despite only taking about five hours to complete, the campaign for this game is guaranteed to leave a lasting impression on you, as it did for me. Almost ten years later there's still not a single campaign out there that is as brutal and clever as this one is, and I hope a spiritual successor with a similar tone ends up releasing at some point down the road. 9/10.

Graphics:

For a game made using Unreal Engine 3, the graphics are really good. I have to give credit to the art directors for absolutely nailing the atmosphere of a desolated, sandstorm-ridden Dubai. Spec Ops: The Line, hands down, has some of the best set pieces in video game history. Distant skyscrapers, sand dunes, mist and sandstorms look phenomenal together. The graphics alone are enough to induce a sense of isolation and immersion in the world of this game. Although, upon close inspection, they are not that detailed or photorealistic, it’s the bigger picture that ultimately matters and comes to play. All the elements, when woven together, present a magnificent, atmospheric and immersive world to get lost in.

Spec Ops also has some of the best lighting in video games. I'm not talking about ray-tracing simulations, but rather the way lighting is used in the game to heighten the experience. Specific scenes in the game gave me goosebumps when I first played it, and my appreciation for it increased even more during my second playthrough when I paid attention to the more subtle lighting details in the game.
It receives an 9/10 in the graphics department.

Gameplay:

When Spec Ops: The Line was released, the majority of people who played it criticized the game for its outdated and lackluster gameplay mechanics and to be honest, I agreed to this during my initial playthrough. I bought it on Steam and played it on a PC, and the control schemes and combat mechanics were infuriating and irritable. The cover system, melee and sprint were confusing at best. The space bar was used to sprint, ‘F’ was used to vault over objects and melee when there were none. ‘Shift’ was used for taking cover and sprinting while taking cover. There was no jump mechanic, and the mouse sensitivity was insanely high even at the lowest in-game settings, implying a bad PC port. I had to lower the DPI of my mouse by a ridiculous amount, and then the main game was playable, but then navigating the menus became a nightmare because of (you guessed it) the low DPI.

However, during my second playthrough, I was able to modify the config file of the game and succeeded in remapping the key bindings and toning down the sensitivity, and only then I realized how grounded in reality the game is.

There is no jump mechanic in this game because soldiers don’t usually jump in the air whilst firing guns on the battlefield. The cover system and blind-fire mechanics also make a lot of sense because I was supposed to be an actual soldier fighting against actual people. The combat mechanics are realistic, and on-screen environmental objects can be manipulated. It makes you feel vulnerable and forces you to think of a good strategy in order to advance rather than shooting off everything. Ammunition is also very limited in this game, which adds to the feeling of helplessness and forces you to carefully take your shots and manage your resources.

The weather also affects the combat and style of gameplay. When advancing through a sandstorm, your bullet trajectory shifts to the direction of the wind, and so does whatever you throw at the enemies, causing a huge loss in accuracy, which then forces you to be stealthy with your maneuvers and picks. However, the game doesn’t feel like it’s forcing you to pick the best strategy. Sure, you can blast through enemies with limited ammunition, grenades and melees if you’re skilled enough. There’s always an option, and that’s the best thing about this type of gameplay. It doesn’t feel linear when it is actually linear. Combining this with incredible level design, manipulative environmental objects and realistic combat mechanics and sequences, it makes you feel like a real soldier.

Overall, the mechanics are pretty solid once you get used to them. The gameplay is very realistic and enjoyable, but the absolute joke of the control schemes and the bad PC port left a bad impression during the initial playthrough. Manually modifying the config file of a game just to play it properly isn’t what games usually require.

It receives a 7/10 in the Gameplay department.

Story:

This is where Spec Ops: The Line shines the brightest. This game was marketed as a “narrative-driven military shooter”, but people didn’t take the first two words of this quote as seriously as they should have. We played this game two times, in turns. My second playthrough was where I focused on the narrative, after remapping the controls. And, frankly speaking, the story it offers is nothing less than a masterpiece. I have never played a game with such a complex narrative with unbelievable amounts of detail and layers to the story.

To summarize, the game starts off strong. We are on a helicopter, fighting off tons of other enemy helicopters, until our vehicle gives in to a sandstorm and crashes down, and the scene cuts to black, and we get a cutscene about a Colonel named John Konrad who once saved the main character, Capt. Martin Walker, on the verge of death a long time ago, and he refers to him as a hero because of that deed. Some months ago, John Konrad was attempting to evacuate the city of Dubai because of the sandstorm. But two weeks before present day, Walker receives a transmission from a beacon in Dubai, in which Konrad seems to have failed the mission and has mysteriously disappeared, and the rest of the game is spent on finding out where he is. But it’s actually not that simple.

Turns out that John Konrad’s troop, the “33rd Infantry Battalion”, has turned rogue and is holding the inhabitants captive and preventing them from leaving Dubai. But Walker believes in Konrad’s motivations and sets off to find him, along with two of his crewmates.

Explaining the entire plot of Spec Ops is an ordeal, because it’s so complex and layered. At the beginning, you feel like being tasked to save Dubai and the world. But as the story moves further, your intentions become vague and you’re left wondering if you’re really saving the world or slowly destroying it. If you die during the initial stages of the game, the checkpoint loading screen offers you tips to defeat the enemies. But during the later stages, if you die, it breaks the fourth wall and displays sentences like: “Do you feel like a hero yet?”, and “The US military does not condone the killing of unarmed combatants. But this isn’t real, so why should you care?”

It all becomes clear once you actually look at the very subtle and fine details during the game’s play time. The foreshadowing, thematic environmental metaphors and dialogue development that I noticed during my final playthrough blew my brains off the roof. It all depended on the point of the game I decided to blur the line between fiction and reality.

This game has 4 different endings, depending on the choices you make during your play time. And the experience can be best described as traumatic, depressing, life-shattering, and so on. This isn’t a tale of saving the world. This isn’t a tale of heroism. This is the story of a man dragging himself straight to hell. This is a psychological breakdown of the subconscious mind of Walker and you as the player, as the choices you ultimately make in the game would tell a lot about you as a character.
It gets a solid 10/10 in this department.

Final Verdict:

Spec Ops: The Line is not a flawless game, and it’s not for everyone. It was a financial failure when it released, with less than a quarter million sales worldwide. Not many people have played it. It may bore off some people, confuse some, anger some… But for those of us who enjoy stories and immersion in video games, this is an absolute gem. It misses the “masterpiece” title by just a few points, because of the bad control schemes and PC port, the fundamentals of games.

It receives a final score of 9/10.
