Spec Ops: The Line is an interesting game. It's the black sheep of a long dead franchise and the result of an unusually good publishing deal the developer, Yager, secured with 2K where they essentially just got to make whatever they wanted. From these strokes of good luck came Spec Ops: The Line, a game that has nothing to do with previous entries in Spec Ops and everything to do with the horrors of war and the internal struggle of a soldier.

As always in my reviews, I talk about the gameplay first and the gameplay in Spec Ops is nothing short of generic. It's a third person cover shooter, basically Gears of War but more grounded and also worse in every way. Movement is clunky, mouse acceleration is always on (which will annoy anyone who has ever played a shooter before), and the cover system slows gunfights down to an agonizing crawl. Enemies range from tanky bullet-sponges to weaklings that die in a single shot, making me wonder whether this game was trying to go for realism or more of a gamey feel. Either way, the shooting is utterly unsatisfying and draining, having to toss out every weapon you pick up after just a few downed enemies due to the sheer lack of ammunition. It's not even like this is part of the theme, it's just an annoyance. No characters comment on having to scrounge for ammo and your companions seem to be getting by just fine with the M4s they hauled in. Meanwhile my protagonist is out switch between AKs, shotguns, pistols, and SMGs every five seconds just to gun down a room of enemies. Simply put, if you're coming into this game for the shooting, you will be disappointed.

If you're coming into this game from the numerous times you've heard the name in reviews of games like Homefront: The Revolution, Call of Duty: Modern Warfare (2019), and other modern-wartime games, then you might be more intrigued. This game's story does not shy away from portraying the horrors of war (massive content warning to anyone who is sensitive to that topic) and doesn't try to glorify brutality and war crimes like certain other games *cough* Call of Duty *cough*. White phosphorous in this game is just as terrifying as it is in real life, sticking to the skin and burning your enemies alive as they scream for your help. Civilians will be injured and even killed, you will be forced to shoot your own allies, and everything you think you know about the world the game takes place in will be tested. Unfortunately, the linearity of the game does railroad you into some sequences in an unimmersive way [spoiler](I noticed the civilians before I fired the white phosphorous and tried everything to not use it, but enemies kept blatantly respawning)[/spoiler]. The way enemies scream and curse you, the way civilians spit at your feet, and the way your companions treat you only emphasizes the point of the story. You are not a hero, there are no good choices, only between what you think is bad and what you think is worse. It's best not to think about Walker in the context of yourself though, I find the story is best experienced through a different lens. You are playing through Walker's story and get to make some decisions to an extent, but there isn't much agency for the player to take.

Another plus is the environments, which go from decent to simply draw-dropping. They're some of the best yet the most underrated parts of this game. As the game progresses, you move from the desert outskirts to hotels to city squares to skylines to ruins, [spoiler] watching as Dubai slowly falls to ruin and anarchy. In each level, you can see the fires and chaos start to spread further and further until the finale[/spoiler]. Each is detailed beautifully and horrifyingly with graffiti, notes, and corpses. The game itself looks great and runs fine, although there are some issues with the PC port (including the aforementioned mouse acceleration). Even on my laptop with an integrated GPU, this game manages to run at 30fps Medium Settings, not too bad considering its age.

To summarize, if you like a thought-provoking story and nice views, you'll enjoy this game. If you want to play a shooter, avoid this game like the plague. If you want to play multiplayer, God help you trying to find a server to play on. If you want to play a cerebral adventure that you can make a video essay about later, this is probably up your alley. There's not more I can say that hasn't already been said, this game is among the best I've played this past year. It's story has been picked apart countless times, but its impact still remains and its status as a cult-classic is forever cemented into gaming as an art form. Hopefully this game will receive more of the praise it deserves someday, but until then: Gentlemen, welcome to Dubai!

Pros:

1) War is painted in an ugly fashion, showing that even if your intentions may be positive, the process doesn't become any less wretched. The protagonist has his own inner demons to deal with as well, but I don't want to reveal too much.

2) Enemies aren't bullet sponges even on higher difficulties.

3) The graphics are pretty decent, especially for a non-AAA 2012 game.

Cons:

1) For the type of game this paints itself to be, there are a hilariously large number of enemies. There are apparently only around five-thousand survivors left in post-apocalyptic Dubai according to the narrative, but you kill close to a thousand soldiers just in an effort to save these people.

2) The time it takes to heal is exponentially longer than time it takes to reach critical levels of health, so be prepared to have to sit and look at your character hiding under cover pretty often.

3) Ammo runs low very often if you have a preferred choice of weapon. The game forces you to pick up random guns in exchange to mitigate this. This may seem realistic, but is not a fun mechanic in my opinion.

4) Your teammate AI can be frustrating to deal with pretty often. They will run ahead of you or dart across the line of fire and then get themselves injured, forcing you to frantically clear out the area before they bleed out so you can revive them.

This game is a great masterpiece. Yes, it's gameplay itself is generic and there are other games that made better use of the mechanics available in this game, as well as other games that explore the middle eastern backdrop and themes such as revenge and "war is hell". In fact, you could find a technically better game with all these attributes in Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain.

But what does this game have that Metal Gear doesn't? While Kojima-san is generally one to explore these themes, he does so in a way that makes a game more digestible for the masses. Walt Williams and Richard Pearsey instead took this story's darkness and violence to new levels, and went even further. They take the darkness of the situation and make it even worse for the player. The player is captivated and pushed to keep going further into this rabbit hole.

The decisions made by the player are not done mid-cutscene like Alpha Protocol or Mass Effect will have you do. They are instead made in fully interactive gameplay. Occasionally, if you take too long the choice may be instead made for you. Never are those decisions made for you made for the better, just so you know. Although, to be fair, no decision is actually better than another. They are, almost always, a matter of equally rotten apples and oranges, but they still affect you and the world around you in different ways.

I hurt with these men. I went through hell with them.

While the game plays this off as the protagonist not having any other options, I don't see it as his doing. I see it as more the player's fault than anyone else. That Walker would have been better off without the player's input. The same can also be said about the player being a victim of Walker's forced perspective and the plater being left no choice but to go with his words. The player and Walker both want the same thing, to be a hero. And because it throws the player for a loop, this game messes with you.

THis is a review of the single player campaign.  
Combat - Fun overall.  Combat mechanics, firing, and movement are fast, a little too cover focused, and definitely on rails, but none of that is a major issue.  The sense of rolling from one scene to the next with very little down time is exciting.  When the combat does slow down it is for a specific purpose (a cut sense or background point) then it picks right back up.  Combat pacing is spot on.  There is not a wide range of enemies but they mix them up and keep them coming plus add in a constant chatter between your two partners and the enemy means combat is never dull.  The ambushes feel a bit staged but they work.  It is an exciting running battle feel that just keeps building like going down a ski jump.
Graphics - visuals are mixed but solid for the game's age.  Combat graphics are strong, not great.  Environmental graphics stand out.  The backgrounds and vistas are great.  They feel expansive and huge or constrained and complicated at the right times.  The high up views of the city are impressive, think Laurence of Arabia wide angle shots - very engaging.  The local combat environments have a simple and repetative feel even with all the hotel and building decorations, yet you are busy fighting so they don't need to impress.  The travel sections (local rooms/halls/stairs) provide what you would expect considering Dubhai - beautiful opulence in the hotels front areas and utilitarian in the office buildings and back-halls. The visuals still holdup today in 2021 particularly on a high end machine.
Story - engaging is the word here.  The story is the stand out in this game.  Go into it with an open mind and it will pull you into a rabbit whole then if you pay attention and allow the game some leeway the progression to the last few scenes will take you to a very specific place that has a solid emotional impact.  My favorite aspect of the story (considering I like quite a few part of it) is your interaction with your two wing men.  Their banter and journey's are different than yours and the writers did a good job of developing them as separate.  It is also refreshing that they are not written to treat you as a hero.  They only go with you because they are highly trained soldiers following your commands and they want to survive, but they don't agree with you.  This helps advance your own progression and makes it feel that much more authentic when you finally arrive at that very dark place at the end.
OVERALL - I recommend this game.

Spec Ops: The Line is a story driven game with a third person shooter game facade. I have seen many reviewers gave negative reviews on this game and i believe there are two reasons: 

1. They probably had erroneous expectations for the game. 
With the TPS cover, many would think this game is a CoD-like shooty-shooty heroic game. And if they use this as the caliber, then Spec Ops: The Line is a pretty ♥♥♥♥♥♥ game - barely smooth control, mediocre graphics and guns.  As an amateur gamer who had seen the rise and fall of CoD, i think that is a normal reaction. However, this game is by no means to be that kind of game. Like i mentioned above, this is NOT a standard TPS.

2. The reviewers are too satisfied with the standard hero-praising FPS/TPS games and a change would make them feel weird. 

I am not criticising for the standard war-theme game lovers. That is just a matter of preference. In fact, part of the reasons for being negatively critcised is that the company intentionally made this game looks like a standard one. 

Spec Ops: The Line was released in 2012 and it was a commercial failure which is not surprised as the market of Gaming is constantly changing. Gamers love games with excellent graphics, strong visual and auditory stimulation and normally are usually reluctant to think deeper and try to understand the underlying theme that the publisher trying to deliver.

I don't want spoil the story so i won't tell. (sorry for wasting your time if you expect that)
I just want to say, as one of the Youtubers remarked in his video on Spec Ops: The Line, that this game can be a social experiment - look at how people make their decisions throughout the game and observe their emotion changes . When you  play, you will be faced with various moral decisions, especially you are under stress (and shock). And when you are finished, you will understand why the gameplay is of no significance.

Spec Ops is a third-person cover-based shooter that alternates between desert environments and crumbling urban ruin. You have two squadmates who can be directed to attack specific targets or heal a fallen comrade; they're pretty good at following orders in a timely fashion and, unlike some other AI partners, they're not highly prone to getting themselves shot constantly or hung up on the level geometry. Enemies are decently clever, more than willing to flank you, toss grenades to get you out of cover, or trick you into walking right into a Heavy Trooper's line of fire. 
While its gameplay doesn't do much in the way of innovation, Spec Ops is a competent shooter. But that's not why you should play it. You should play it because it takes everything about the modern military shooter and turns it on its head. You should play it because it has a story worth experiencing. You should play it because it's visceral, brutal, and will get in your head. Above all, you should play it because we need more games that focus on telling a powerful story, and any one that does should be encouraged. 
You have a large arsenal of weapons and grenades available, a dedicated melee button, and the rest of the bells and whistles of the genre. Ammo is scarce though which enhances the experience and the execution animations for downed enemies are brutal. You can also give limited orders to your squad. It helps out during tough firefights (and there are several), but keep in mind this isn't a squad centred realistic shooter like Rainbow Six or SWAT. The story is not a happy journey, bringing in a realism that war does not have a heroic ending like other games. This is a bit more gritty and real in that respect.

The gameplay isn't why this game is popular. It's the story. You play as Captain Walker of Delta force. You and your team are deployed to the city of Dubai located in the middle east. Your mission is to search the city for survivors after a natural disaster in the form of a massive sand storm destroyed the city.

NO SPOILERS - The whole game is a meta commentary about the genre of modern military shooters. Which is exactly why I think it's over rated. Meta isn't hard to do. It's the equivalent of your favorite actor who spent years honing there craft doing the one thing no actor should do. They break character look at the camera and talk directly to the audience. Imagine watching a film and the actor breaks the forth wall and starts talking directly to the audience. "Hello. I hope your enjoying the film. I was just wandering if you stopped to think about the implications this film will have on the film industry and society as a whole." It's easy to do and nowhere near as deep as it seems. The perceived depth is more of a trick than anything else. There are more elegant and intelligent ways to commentate on games, game genres, and there impact on the world besides making a video game that acknowledges that it's a video game.

Anyway the game is fine. It's overrated IMO but fine. If you played a lot of modern military shooters back when the genre was big in the late 2000's early 2010's go ahead and play it. If you didn't then maybe pick it up on a sail if you just want to see what all the fuss is about. GG I guess.

Spec Ops: The Line's gameplay is a boring, mediocre, and by-the-numbers cover shooter. Spec Ops: The Line's story is an Apocalypse Now-style journey into madness and meta-critique on the genre disguised as a typical 2010 war shooter. Many games since Spec Ops have tried to call out the inherent themes and violence within action games, but none have come close to how surgically, confidently, and effectively Spec Ops: The Line communicates that kind of critique.

There probably isn’t much I can say about Spec Ops: The Line that hasn’t been already covered by a thousand armchair critics and youtube hopefuls. It’s inevitably now more known for its twist than anything else, and it’s largely impossible for it to have its intended impact on a virgin audience as nobody will be picking this up blind. A lot of this also comes down to the change in the gaming landscape in the last ten years. The chest thumping military shooter doesn’t have its knee on the neck of the gaming industry like it used to, and while it still sells just fine Call of Duty is seen as rather quaint these days.

So yes, let’s just dispense with idea that anyone reading this has no idea what this game is about. Spec Ops is intended as a deconstruction of the military shooter, and is pretty openly influenced by Apocalypse Now and Heart of Darkness. You play as Captain Walker, voiced by Nolan North giving probably the performance of his career portraying a soldier’s loss of humanity as he and his squad push into a ruined Dubai after a devastating sandstorm engulfs the city, to locate survivors and lead an evacuation.

As you and your squad progress it becomes clear Dubai has become a tinpot military dictatorship under the rule of the subtlety named Colonel Konrad who stayed in Dubai to evacuate the city originally, against orders. Walker finds himself embroiled in a war against American soldiers, and goes to greater, and more morally dubious lengths to achieve an objective that seems woolier by the hour.

I’ve hopefully sold this spoiler free synopsis as a rather cool, and by the standards of 2011 big budget publishing, rather daring story. The problem is that this is not a story, it’s a videogame, and you’ve got to sell this concept to me mechanically. And however we try and cut it, Spec Ops is just a bland, rote third person cover based military shooter that never uses its mechanics in interesting ways. It’s just pop and stop shooting that was feeling very dated even back in 2011. 

There have been those that have defended the mindless shooting by saying that it’s all on purpose, you know, as part of the deconstruction, but I just don’t buy it. Sure, I find the waves and waves of identical soldiers kind of mind numbing but it’s not horrible – the mechanics are completely serviceable. In some ways, making the combat fun and visceral would help sell the idea much better.

So in the end we have this kind of average game strapped to a great story with some incredible performances, and an overarching metanarrative that to me just falls completely flat. The game admonishes you for enjoying killing, while making that killing enjoyable. It tries to induce guilt over war crimes that you, as the player, had no choice over. I understand the problem here – if you’d been allowed to avoid “the big moment”, most players would have considered this a failure state and reloaded, robbing the story of it’s impact. But to me this is just misusing the medium compared to film, which doesn’t need to justify 6 hours of combat to get to the point.

For what it’s worth I absolutely recommend Playing Spec Ops: the Line, as while I consider it something of a failure it’s a very genuine and interesting stab at something a little different. That it continues to generate discussion after nearly a decade is testament to this.

Its one hell of a game, and also one hell of ride too.

At first glance, this game looks like it's nothing more than your typical American patriotic shooter, BUT what this game offers is so far beyond that. As Captain Walker (voiced by Nolan North), you lead a squad through war torn Dubai, operating on nothing but half-truths and what you perceive as the right thing to do. I can't tell you how many times I just sat back, hand over my mouth and tried to comprehend what had just unfolded in front of me. I don't want to dig deeper into the story than that, just know that it's a wild ride that I absolutely never want to experience again. 

The gameplay on the other hand is nothing special. It gets you from point A to B, but I can't say that I was ever excited to clear another room full of enemies, I only got through waves of enemies in order to reach the next big story moment. It's definitely not awful gameplay, but it's just pretty run of the mill. Games like the Division, Uncharted and Gears of War have done this covered-based style of shooter much MUCH better.

All in all, this game will go down as one of my top 10 story-driven titles. I recommend this to anyone who can get through generic shootouts in exchange for an unforgettable, yet horribly depressing story.

While the events are highly dramatized, the game does a good job in depicting how a relatively normal person can devolve into something completely irredeemable. The game is a great modern adaption of "The Heart of Darkness" and updates the themes to include not only the state of shooters (at the time it was released) but also a critique American imperialism and the desire to always be the hero. 

You don't see many shooters which get recommended on the strength of its plot but this is a great, well told story. Highly recommend if you want to feel like a terrible person for a while after playing.

This is one of the craziest games I've ever played. I remember playing the demo version of it on ps3 years ago and i thought it looked cool, but never actually bought it. Now that I've played it fully, I can easily say that the game is a masterpiece. Gameplay is great, but the story though, its really something else.

If you want to enjoy a casual game, I suggest playing in the easier modes. IF trying to play at hardest difficulty, its possible but you're going to have to deal with 2 shot life and aim bots which you have to use a very small "window" of opportunity to usually get past them. I eventually managed the achievement while having to deal with constant checkpoint reloads because of some annoyance with the team AI or even against the aim bot AI which usually will be merciless throwing a nade and expecting you to be able to run to another cover while gunning you down should you even peak out or find another cover...

The story is mediocre and linear making some of the choices you make not have a huge impact on the ending as most of the story converges on near the same plot. It would have been nice to see player choice interactions having a major effect on the story plot throughout rather than just different endings. The story is only enjoyable on the first playthrough else it ends up getting repetitive as you already know how it pans out in the end.

The games controls are horrendous because its clearly a console port despite allowing keybinds but the fluidity is not even optimized. Taking cover usually works 80% of the time and when it doesn't it really messes up which can be frustrating especially at the hardest mode. The ability to command your teammates is a nice idea but it doesn't really seem effective in most cases. Most of the time its more efficient if you do things "your" way.

Story/Theme:
A great game I'd recommend to anyone looking for a story-driven war game. And it lives up to just that. It's War. You will experience everything horrible about War. Without giving spoilers, this game is best played without even looking at the details of what to expect with this game. Like the movie Moon, your best off just playing it and experiencing it. But it's war. It won't hold your hand. It's dark. It's gritty. And not everything is what it seems.
If you could handle games like Dead Space, then you can handle this. If you can't handle games like Dead Space, stay away from this. It's War.

Gameplay/Bugs:
Gameplay wise it's third person the whole way through minus the turret zoom ins which is through the crosshair FPS. Those moments are very few. The shoot mechanics feel great and it's defently an entertaining shooter game. There are tons of enemies and the game will challenge you, even punish you on whats considered "normal" difficulty. If you're looking for just a challenge like that, this game is made for you. There's no jumping and the sprint feels clunky and bad but it doesn't ruin the game. It is one of your typical "hide-behind-cover" games and offers to aim behind cover or raise your weapon over cover to blind fire. There are cut scenes here and there and you are forced to walk through places whilst the story unfolds, a typical form of A to B game.

Bug wise I experienced very few, mainly characters running right through me and walking around a corner and seeing an enemy spawn out of nothingness. One time I saw an NPC who had just died fly upwards into the ceiling and fall down again. There was also a cut scene rifle that stayed in the air despite moving my character around with another rifle. Like a duplicate had stayed behind and frozen in the air. All of these occurred only 1 time each.

Mechanics wise, this is a standard shoot-and-cover third-person shooter. If you're looking for exciting shooter gameplay, this might not be the game for you. Throughout the campaign, the shooting can become a bit repetitive and you're often forced to conserve ammo because it tends to run out very quickly. Bullets don't often find their mark and you have to aim carefully. Default controls are kind of confusing at first and sometimes doesn't respond well. Not to mention that the multiplayer doesn't have a lot of active players, considering that this game was first launched in 2012.
However, the story compensates for everything that is lacking in gameplay. The 5-6 hour plot alone is worth your time and effort. One certain quote made by Harvey Dent in The Dark Knight can pretty much summarize the entire story. Throughout the campaign, you're left questioning everything that is happening around you, and eventually, yourself. Sometimes, decisions are unknowingly made, and consequences of these decisions often hit hard. The revelation at the very end came as an intense shock. All in all, the dark and ambiguous tone of the plot is unique and not often experienced in other games of the same genre (arguably other genres as well).
Overall, given the mediocre gameplay mechanics and its dated release, the price of the game may be a bit too much, so I suggest getting it whenever a sale comes around. Still, the incredible story makes it worth playing.

[h1] SPEC OPS : THE LINE [/h1]
[b] THE GAME THAT SHOULD BE REMASTERED [/b]

Spec Ops: The Line, the last game of the series that started with Zombie Studio in 1998, is a group-based action game in the third-person shooter genre.
The city of Dubai, decorated with gigantic skyscrapers, endless beaches, and 7-star hotels, has been completely captured by a brutal sandstorm.

It seems that the sandstorm has an unnatural cause, but this subject will be explained in the following chapters.

Spec Ops: The Line begins with the dispatch of a 3-person expedition under the leadership of a Captain Walker to learn the status of a military unit that could not be reached despite all calls.

In this challenging mission, we have to fight not only with the sandstorm but also with the rebels as there is a civil war on the pontoon.

Taking Spec Ops The Line at face value exemplifies it as nothing special . It's core game loop is the same often found in many third person cover based shooters akin to gears of war , and spec ops doesn't try to innovate on any mechanical or game play frontier in this regard . The core shooting mechanics are rather janky and I found the control scheme very disorienting , the game was obviously made to be played with a controller and the fact multiple different functions are mapped out to the same key shows this . The shooting mechanics are perfectly serviceable and the game follows many of the same conventions as most other military shooters , aim down sights , regenerating health , linear level and mission design and 2 interchangeable weapon slots . The wide landscapes of Dubai do lend themselves to giving the game world and combat scenarios an air of interactability as sand dunes can be used to suffocate enemies but that's about it . But the moment to moment gameplay isn't where the game shines , not at all . The game shines in it's deeply gut wrenching narrative and thematic portrayal of different ideas . If you're reading this review and haven't played the game I highly consider you go and do so as going in as blind as possible will massively heighten the experience and is paramount to getting the most out of the game .

The game follows Walker , a military operative who's been sent in to assess the situation and state of Dubai , a city ravaged by sandstorms and currently under the occupation of the 33rd while simultaneously trying to save any surviving civilians . Your'e accompanied by your two wing-men Adams and Lugo . There are layers to what in my eyes makes Spec Ops' narrative masterful and intern what made it truly affect me and change my perception of the medium as a whole .

One of the main idea's players will get from Spec ops the line is it's clear disdain of the twisted perception of war and heroism which is deeply rooted in video games like Call of Duty which exercises and indulges in the darkest desires of man while commercialising these ideas . These games are ones that not only desensitises the idea of war by portraying it lightly and painting the complex conflicts that war resides in as a black and white affair ( one in which America is presented as a force of absolute good while all that oppose it are presented as absolute evil ) but also in it's twisted perception of heroism being attained by someone who commits such egregious acts of violence while all framing it as a viscerally interesting experience . In reality there isn't anything jovial about war and the affect Walker's actions have on his mind only spiral himself deeper into his darkest desires . Spec Ops the line provides a brilliant and reflective damnation of the modern military shooter which portrays war as less of a hellscape which scars those within it and more of a masturbatory affair used to feed into the players carnage .

Besides Spec Ops the line's commentary on games itself it's look into the psyche of soldiers and the effect of PTSD on them is gut wrenching . As Walker you'll commit horrific acts of violence as you over time forget why you even came to Dubai in the first place , your original mission to save any survivors has twisted due to Walker's twisted sense of heroism , he wanted to be something bigger than he was and in the end he wasn't good at it , he only brought suffering wherever he went and his hand wasn't forced to commit these terrible acts , he intern forced it upon himself . Walker continues his mad killing spree in an effort to justify his presence in Dubai and perhaps try to feel like a saviour when he was just a murderer . If you were a good person , you wouldn't be here .

The game asks the payer to weigh in the moral ambiguity of there own heinous actions by showing the effects of there actions in terrifying ways , the scene where Walker , Adams and Lugo discover that there were civilians caught in the fury of there phosphorus attack is a sight that instigates the idea that perhaps the actions of the player and Walker aren't in the name of justice and are just an act the journey of Walker is a futile one as it only carries carnage worsening the situation in Dubai . The loading screens massively impose this idea as there often asking payers directly how there actions affect not only others but there own psyche . The loading screens are also haunting and catch you off guard in the midst of your frantic firefights .

The culmination of the narrative and what happens to Walker is in the player's hands , they can kill Walker ending the cycle of violence or kill Konrad a man already dead , furthering the idea that Walker never faced or questioned his actions . As Konrad says it takes a strong man to face what he's done and truly ask himself have his action really helped anybody , do you feel like a hero yet ?( a bit on the nose i know ) .

In all the narrative is all used to show the horrific after effects of war on the mind , how horrific thoughts lay in every vacant corner of our psyche and how what happens on the battlefield emotionally stains us until we die . Honestly what I love about it's grim commentary is how many different interpretations it has and I felt like there are a lot of different thematic and narrative complications that I could've touched on . The game also carries some fantastic performances , Nolan North nails his performance as Walker , a stoic and brooding man who descends into madness perfectly and generally all the characters provide brilliant performances that entail truly there horrific circumstances . 

To conclude Spec ops the line provides a masterful commentary on moral absolutism and the simplistic black and white perception military shooters give of realistic real world situations , our twisted modern sense of heroism , a story of PTSD and the effects it has on man and questions our eagerness to commit atrocious actions and the mental ramifications said actions have on the player and characters , the saints and the sinners , the survivors and the dead . And it's honestly one of the most powerful narratives in any game , one that doesn't pull any punches and one that got to me and made me feel so bad in a way no other game has done . Truly a work of art which has quite a lot of problems but deserves to be played by everyone .

Spec Ops: The Line was a game released in 2012 published by 2K, it's technically the 10th game in the Spec Ops series however this game has nothing to do with the other ones in the franchise, I remember back in 2012 everybody talking about this game and it obtaining many awards for it's story, however unfortunately Spec Ops: The Line while being a critical success, bombed commercially and thus the franchise was canceled (personally I think it might be due to the fact that they tried to charge full price for a 8 hour game with below average generic multiplayer)

The gunplay and controls in SO: The Line are slightly weird but workable for the most part, the cover mechanics however are on the lower end in terms of quality though (i.e it's easy to get stuck and it can be annoying when an enemy chucks a grenade at you). Other than the game play the game isn't a headache to set up (the only annoyance I came across was having to download a third party program to hack the game into a 16:9 aspect ratio so that my eyes wouldn't hurt, oh and the game has mouse acceleration on by default with you having to mess around with the files to turn it off, but it's easy enough to just play with it).

I high recommend picking up Spec Ops: The Line and playing through it at least once (or don't if you want the good ending) however considering the campaign is only 8 hours long and the multiplayer is close to dead at this point I would recommend waiting for it to go on sale as I cannot recommend it at the current 32 CAD it's selling for.

SpecOps: The Line is a perfect testimony to the potential video games have for telling stories. In a time where games nowadays are nothing but glorified slot machines, soulless sandboxes, or pathetic excuses of narratives, playing this for the first time in 2020 was a great change of pace. If only developers nowadays had the guts to make story-driven games as bold and well-written as this.

The message is much more complicated than "war is bad." The Line confronts everything about the evils of war; from the brutal nature of it, the terrible choices it forces people to make, the people caught in the crossfire, how there are no truly good options, and to how it can make monsters out of men. Walker is a human, a soldier with good intentions whose will and sanity are broken down as this terrible warzone forces him to make decisions with no good outcomes. He's not a deranged killer, sociopath or psychopath, but this war truly breaks him and causes him to grow desperate and violent. Despite (unwittingly) shelling innocents with white phosphorus, something I condemn the use of for how terrible it is, by the end I can't help but feel... Sorry, for Walker and his team.

[h1]Story/Theme:[/h1]
A great game I'd recommend to anyone looking for a story-driven war game. And it lives up to just that. It's War. You will experience everything horrible about War. Without giving spoilers, this game is best played without even looking at the details of what to expect with this game. Like the movie Moon, your best off just playing it and experiencing it. But it's war. It won't hold your hand. It's dark. It's gritty. And not everything is what it seems.
If you could handle games like Dead Space, then you can handle this. If you can't handle games like Dead Space, stay away from this. It's War.

[h1]Gameplay/Bugs:[/h1]
Gameplay wise it's third person the whole way through minus the turret zoom ins which is through the crosshair FPS. Those moments are very few. The shoot mechanics feel great and it's defently an entertaining shooter game. There are tons of enemies and the game will challenge you, even punish you on whats considered "normal" difficulty. If you're looking for just a challenge like that, this game is made for you. There's no jumping and the sprint feels clunky and bad but it doesn't ruin the game. It is one of your typical "hide-behind-cover" games and offers to aim behind cover or raise your weapon over cover to blind fire. There are cut scenes here and there and you are forced to walk through places whilst the story unfolds, a typical form of A to B game.

Bug wise I experienced very few, mainly characters running right through me and walking around a corner and seeing an enemy spawn out of nothingness. One time I saw an NPC who had just died fly upwards into the ceiling and fall down again. There was also a cut scene rifle that stayed in the air despite moving my character around with another rifle. Like a duplicate had stayed behind and frozen in the air. All of these occurred only 1 time each.

Spec ops: The Line's gameplay is nothing but average, consisting of one killzone after another, and the action is repetitive and generic. But that's the point. Spec ops doesn't try to be a good "shooter", but rather tries to make a statement, and forces you to face the atrocities of war head on. The main character is Walker, a veteran american soldier, which is sent to Dubai with two other soldiers under his command , to find survivors from the 33rd division of the american fleet. The story shows what happened to the soldiers and citizens during the war. 

Walker understands that there is more then meets the eye in the city and that the 33rd division has become corrupted as the enemies they were trying to defeat. During the entire game you will have to perform morally wrong actions. Many people will not last untill the end, for more then one reason. Some will be sick of the terrible choices that the game forces them to make and just quit. Others will find the gunplay repetitive and decide it's not worth playing till the end. Oh but it is. The ending is showing everything you would never think of while playing and makes everything seems logical. It explains everything you questioned and will stay in your head long after you see it. This game exists purely to make you see why war should never be taken lightly, and why the addiction to military shooters such as Call of duty brings out the inner beast in us all. 

Never before have I played a game that made me feel so bad, and yet made me appreciate it. Only those that will play untill the end will understand the game's true meaning. You won't find a triple A shooter here, nor will you find exceptional production values, but you will find something deeper then you might expect. Don't let the generic shooting fool you, because you won't find anything else like it, once you finished it. So, how far would you go to complete your mission? When will you feel like you are crossing the line? Play and find out for yourself in Spec Ops: The Line.

The reputation of this game precedes it. Spec Ops: The Line is a frustratingly dull shooter hiding some of the best storytelling that games have to offer. I wanted to play it after hearing about it's "amazing story" but felt unjustified in spending 30 dollars on it, it was on sale recently for six bucks so I wasted no time in grabbing a copy.
Pros:
✅The Story.
 The game features one of the best war stories in any medium, you'll spend seven hours playing the game and what feels like a lifetime thinking about it. The impact spec ops has had on narrative storytelling in the game industry cannot and should not be understated. It's incredible.
✅The art direction.
 While often overshadowed by some REALLY ugly character models, even for 2012, the game's visuals are nothing short of excellent. On a technical level, this game's environments are breathtaking and detailed, it allows the game's graphics to still hold up today.

Cons:
 Immediately noticeable upon playing, this game has some jarring issues. Even for its time, the gameplay is incredibly outdated, counter-intuitive, unpolished and buggy. (Note: I played the game on the highest difficulty)
❌Broken cover system which often gets you killed 
❌Useless blindfire which often misses enemies directly in front of you, blind fire also extends your hitbox, which can get you killed if an enemy shoots your hands
❌Worst of all: Clumsy AI companions which run into full groups of enemies and get put into a "downed state" seemingly at random, failure to rescue them within a specific time window gets you a game-over

These issues are manageable individually but they're compounded by one of the worst checkpoint systems I have ever experienced in a game. You'll spend minutes playing defensively behind cover, then both of your companions will run ahead and get downed, you'll work your way up to save them, only to get shot in the toe by an enemy while sitting behind seemingly protective cover, that, or you'll get trapped between a grenade and an awkward camera angle preventing you from vaulting to safety. Just like that, you're stuck in an awkwardly-long loading screen waiting to start from the very, very beginning of the encounter.

It's just unfair.

Because of these issues combined with the game just generally not being that fun to play, I cannot recommend it at full price. I also recommend that if you do grab a copy, play the game on the easiest difficulty as to prevent the game's pacing from becoming boring.

Game play wise, its a third person cover shooter and is the weakest part of the game. You've played cover shooters before and they've been better.

Aiming, shooting, using cover and moving from cover just feels janky and they're some sections of this game that are downright infuriating because of how unrefined all of it is. That said, the game play is still almost always fun and was never so bad that I wanted to stop playing.

You should also know its a short game. 4-5 hours if you're good at shooters and 6 if you're bad like me. Coop and Multiplayer are dead. Definitely wait for a sale.

So then why should you Play Spec Ops: The Line? The story and your journey through it. 

Without spoiling anything, you're given a bunch of choices throughout the campaign and what happens after those choices often made my jaw drop. They're many twists and turns and by the end, love it or hate it, you'll feel like you went through something.

Its not perfect though. The twist at the end doesn't actually make sense when you think about it and many of the tough choices you make are forced upon you. 

You sometimes have to do awful things to progress through the game without having the option to not do them. And that often robs the story of its impact. There were several points where I tried to be the good guy or do the least worst thing in that particular situation and discovered I couldn't.

The game has an agenda and wants you to look at the characters and your part in the story in a certain way without actually giving you the agency to get there on your own through your choices.

It doesn't really matter what you do. And that may be the point of the story, but it did disconnect me somewhat from the narrative and characters and didn't make me feel the way I think the creators wanted me to feel by the end.

Bottom line, if you decide to play this game, play it for the story. That's what will stay with you. And despite its flaws, I was glad I played the game. It made me think and look at my world differently and inspired me to write this long review.

This game is definitely worth checking out. The dated gameplay makes it a little difficult to wholeheartedly recommend, but the story is interesting. Although I would argue even that aspect is dated to some degree for reasons that would spoil the experience. It's better to view this game in the context of when it was released - 2012, at an enormous high point for other shooters such as CoD and Battlefield in their skyrocketing popularity, when it was still tons of fun to shoot through hordes of mindless NPCs in service of progressing the "help the good guys, stop the bad guys" plotlines. You do the exact same thing in this game, but this time the game makes it clear that your comrades really don't want to be doing it, which gives the story a layer of self-awareness that was sorely lacking in the AAA shooters of its time.

I understand this game has a somewhat small yet very dedicated fanbase who love this game for what it is, and that's great, but I do believe it was a tad overhyped for me as a result. As I said, it's still worth playing even if only because it won't demand much of your time. (On the lowest difficulty, it took me only 4.7 hours.) Overall, despite its dated factors, it is still an interesting case of a mid-budget game with some creative and risky choices in an oversaturated genre. I wish we got more like it.

[spoiler] "Walking away and not playing the game" is not really a choice when the game itself is the medium. As someone who plays games for gameplay and dislikes the whole "cinematic experience" trend, this is the only game I could ever recommend based on reasons not related to gameplay. 

The story is easily the best I've seen- it can compete with pretty much any story in a high quality book, movie, or game. Unlike a normal story though, this one will keep you busy for hours, trying to piece it all together in your own way. The events are written vaguely, and there's a lot of evidence to support different theories for the events of the game (there's stuff to back it up as being purgatory, hell itself, a time loop, or an actual chain of events), so you can end up spending a lot of time coming up with your own ideas on what actually happened. A lot of interesting story-related things are missable though, so it's highly recommended to watch easter egg compilations if you want to see everything.

There are many themes to unpack, but much like the story events, you can discover and think about ones that make the most sense to you. Some people like to focus on how it shows the horrors of actual war, others might like to think about who the good guys were (if there are even any). There's even stuff that deals with you, the player, and whether you're good or not for even playing the game. Personally I found the most interesting ones to be futility, obsession and delusion, but there are many more. 

This all comes with a warning though- the game is dark. It starts nice and goes to hell very quickly. Its goal is to distress you, make you feel bad, and want to quit playing. It goes as far as breaking the fourth wall to do this, but that part is really well done and doesn't feel cringe. Having said all that though, the emotional impact it has on you, the way it makes you part of the story, and the way it makes you question yourself, is another major reason why it's so good.

The voice acting is perfect because of how believable it is. The the whole cast express emotions very clearly through all of their dialogue; you can hear their fatigue, anger, and frustration grow in a realistic way as they lose their sanity- it makes the game feel much more immersive. Their lines never sound out of place, and match every situation they're in. Music is solid.

The gameplay is generic and forgettable. It's okay enough for anyone to tolerate for at least one playthrough, I think. Guns mostly handle the same and combat boils down to clicking on heads after peeking from cover. The cover mechanics can be awkward on Keyboard & Mouse though; you may find yourself accidentally sprinting or disengaging from cover at really bad times. AI is decent, there are some tactics employed by the enemies, while your squad has decent intelligence and utility. I've had situations where both squadmates just run in the open and die though. I played on Hard, could recommend it if you want the gameplay to have extra flavor, I guess. Enemies can laser you on Hard, but don't do it too often, fortunately. They do seem to like doing it immediately after you peek or sprint from cover. 

Performance is fine. It seems to support uncapped framerates by default, which is nice if you're using a higher refresh rate monitor. Had a major bug- I couldn't walk up some stairs which I needed to, but I did manage to get past it by sprinting and turning the camera around. 

Overall, highly recommended to anyone who loves videogames in general.

Spec Ops: The Line is a game you play for the story, not the game itself.

Spec Ops: The Line is one of those games that should have rather been a movie instead of a game... or so I thought, until I finished it. This game tells a complicated story outside of the actual events of the game, but that story is directed towards the player, not the protagonist, which can't be recreated in a movie.

The gameplay is your standard covershooter from the early 2010s, without any special features that make it stick out, but I feel like it actually adds to the message that is being portrayed on a deeper level (or it could simply be lack of effort, I don't know). I guess that's it for the gameplay part... you move from cover to cover and shoot... that's it

Now, trying to talk about the story without any spoilers will be difficult, here it goes. You play as a dude with 2 other dudes, doing military stuff in Dubai, until stuff goes wrong, then very wrong, and then you reach the level of "oh ♥♥♥♥" wrong. The game starts off slow and boring, so it will be quite a drag to get through, but finishing the game made it worth it to me. Certain moments in the game will start talking to you as the player however, which you never realize, until you play through it a second time, then you will start seeing certain things (one moment I love the most is when you look into a monitor to... use a call of duty killstreak, you will see the reflection of your protagonist in it, with his cold, lifeless eyes).

If you are a patient person that can deal with some boring gameplay for the sake of experiencing a story, I still wouldn't recommend you try out Death Stranding, but maybe give Spec Ops: The Line a test run, the story does stick with you and makes you see certain games in another light, which is what i love about this game. This game isn't meant to be a game, it is meant to deliver a message, and by god does it deliver it. Do I recommend this game? Yes, yes I do, not at full price however, because you see the age in the game, but that shouldn't be a problem, since it is on discount quite often. How do I rate it? Taking into account that this game is meant to deliver a story, and not meant to be a game with it's focus on gameplay, I would give the game a solid 8/10, making it one of my all time favourite games of all time.

To accurately review this game in my usual review format, I'd have to include spoilers, but given that the only reason this game's worth playing is because of the story, putting spoilers in a review designed to recommend people to buy the game or not seems contrary to the point of the review in the first place.

So, I'll just sum it up fairly briefly: Spec Ops: The Line's morally grey narrative, heavily influenced by movies like Apocalypse Now, didn't convince me for much of the game. Some of it due to having had plot moments spoiled before, so naturally the heavy subject matter didn't hit as hard, but much of it because the shooting isn't spectacular and I felt that the completely over-the-top action didn't click well with the game trying to make me feel bad for my actions. The gore is ridiculous (and looks really amateur too), some of the cutscenes match Call of Duty's levels of absurd, and there's a brutal execution system that literally serves no purpose other than to give violent satisfaction (it doesn't stop enemies from getting back up or anything... it's just a few gorey animations and that's it), but by the last few chapters of the game it certainly started to weigh down on me, culminating in a suitably dark ending.

Besides the story, Spec Ops' gameplay is fine. It's a cover shooter, so staying out of cover is liable to get you killed incredibly quickly sometimes. The animations for getting in and out of cover are all very smooth and it's quite fluid, but it's certainly not perfect as it seriously made up the vast majority of my deaths when I was relying on it to save me but for whatever reason I'd be pushed out of cover or my character would refuse to get in it. There's not a whole lot of enemy diversity and the AI is quite thick, and right from the absolute first second of gameplay the game falls under countless military shooter tropes... turret sections, generic modern day weaponry (which is fair), hundreds of braindead troops to gun down, explosive barrels aplenty... but it is still quite a bit of fun, if not very easy when you're not getting kicked in the ass by the cover system. The only real times I died, even on the hardest difficulty (besides the one that's locked on first playthrough) is when I was rushing to finish the game and made silly decisions to hurry through it. Stick in cover until every enemy is dead and you'll barely struggle at all. It's pretty simple stuff.

Besides gameplay and story then, the visuals are fantastic, and so is the sound design/voice acting/music. It is heavy on bloom which you can't turn off, and I usually strongly dislike that, but I get why it was done. The bright, popping colours that fill Dubai wouldn't be the same without the saturation that bloom affords. Some animations are really off, but even those for the most part are pretty good. The audio is brilliant when cranked loud and the voice acting is quite solid for the most part, even if have Nolan North as the protagonist is a bit of a detractor. The dude can voice act, but he's so over-used it's just nuts. And his scream's kind of annoying... but anyway. The music's pretty good too in terms of both the original soundtrack and licensed songs which there are many, including appearances by Deep Purple and Jimi Hendrix which as a classic rock enthusiast made me very, [i]very[/i] happy.

If you're expecting anything with any decent amount of length to it then look elsewhere. This is a short game. It didn't take me 6 hours as it states. An hour of that was played years ago and at least an hour was spent in the menu as I left the game running. So in other words; buy this on sale. That being said, I'd be surprised if you're left unsatisfied. I feel like, given the repetitive nature of the gameplay, its length was actually perfect, and the narrative didn't feel all that hurried along either. There are collectibles, some co-op modes I've yet to play and a dead multiplayer, as well as a bonus difficulty unlocked after completion of the game, but none of those things particularly interest me so for me it's a play once and move on affair. The story's been told and the gameplay doesn't warrant a replay, so I've had my time with this game.

Would I recommend this? The thumb's up, so obviously the answer is yes. This isn't some cinematic masterpiece and I doubt it'll leave you heartbroken and dazed, but it is without a doubt more substantive than the vast majority of shooters out there. Whether the clash between gameplay and story bothers you or not is up to you, as is whether the gruesome moments have any real effect on you. Spec Ops: The Line Review: A Haunting Journey into the Darkness of War
"Spec Ops: The Line," developed by Yager Development and published by 2K Games, is a gripping and thought-provoking third-person shooter that stands as a landmark title in the genre. Released in 2012, this game is much more than a conventional military shooter; it is a profound exploration of the psychological and moral ramifications of war. With its intense narrative, morally ambiguous choices, and strikingly immersive gameplay, "Spec Ops: The Line" offers a haunting and unforgettable experience.

A Compelling and Dark Narrative
At the heart of "Spec Ops: The Line" is its deeply engaging narrative. The game follows Captain Martin Walker, a member of a special forces team sent to Dubai to investigate the disappearance of a previous mission's commander and his unit. What begins as a straightforward rescue operation quickly devolves into a harrowing journey through a city ravaged by sandstorms and civil war.

The story is a masterclass in psychological horror and moral ambiguity. The game explores themes of duty, sanity, and the consequences of violence. As the narrative unfolds, players are confronted with difficult choices and unsettling revelations that challenge their perceptions of right and wrong. The game’s writing is sharp and impactful, with twists and turns that keep players on the edge of their seats and provoke deep reflection on the nature of warfare.

Emotional and Psychological Depth
"Spec Ops: The Line" is distinguished by its emotional and psychological depth. The game delves into the psychological toll of combat, depicting the impact of war on both soldiers and civilians. The descent into madness experienced by the characters is portrayed with raw intensity, making the game's exploration of trauma and guilt both compelling and poignant.

The dialogue and voice acting are exceptional, with Nolan North's portrayal of Captain Walker adding significant weight to the character's internal struggles. The interactions with other characters and the unfolding narrative create a powerful emotional journey that sets "Spec Ops: The Line" apart from typical military shooters.

Intense and Strategic Combat
While the narrative is the game's strongest asset, the combat in "Spec Ops: The Line" is also highly engaging. The game features a cover-based shooting system that encourages tactical play and strategic thinking. The environments are destructible and dynamic, adding an extra layer of intensity to the firefights.

The variety of weapons and tactical options allows players to approach combat scenarios in multiple ways. The AI of enemies is competent, providing a challenging and immersive combat experience. The game's pacing is well-balanced, with moments of intense action interspersed with quieter, more reflective sequences that enhance the overall impact of the story.

Stunning and Desolate Environment
The game's setting in a post-apocalyptic Dubai is both visually striking and thematically resonant. The abandoned city, buried under a sea of sand, serves as a stark and haunting backdrop for the story. The environmental design is meticulously crafted, with details that convey the devastation and decay of the once-glamorous metropolis.

The use of sandstorms and environmental effects adds to the atmosphere, creating a sense of isolation and desolation that complements the narrative. The visual design and art direction are both impressive and integral to the game's immersive experience.

Moral Choices and Consequences
One of the standout features of "Spec Ops: The Line" is its emphasis on moral choices and their consequences. The game challenges players to make difficult decisions that impact the story and the characters. These choices are not always clear-cut, and the consequences are often morally ambiguous, forcing players to confront the darker aspects of their actions.

The game's exploration of the concept of "the greater good" and the impact of personal decisions on both allies and enemies is handled with nuance and sophistication. This focus on moral complexity adds depth to the narrative and makes the player's journey all the more impactful.

Conclusion: A Bold and Thought-Provoking Experience
"Spec Ops: The Line" is a remarkable achievement in the world of video games, offering a profound and unsettling exploration of the human cost of war. Its compelling narrative, emotional depth, and intense combat make it a standout title that transcends the typical boundaries of the military shooter genre.

In summary, "Spec Ops: The Line" is a must-play for anyone interested in a game that challenges their perceptions and emotions. It is a haunting and unforgettable journey that delves into the darkness of the human psyche and the consequences of violence. With its powerful storytelling and impactful gameplay, "Spec Ops: The Line" stands as a testament to the potential of video games as a medium for deep and meaningful experiences.

As third person shooters go, the individual controls are pretty good, the cover-based combat is reasonably smooth, and there's a nice variety of weapons to choose between. The main issue I have is with your squad members who accompany you for most missions.

The AI directing them is all over the place. Sometimes they'll use cover effectively, and fire on nearby targets, but other times they will run into the open, charge ahead to attack a distant enemy, or let themselves be charged or flanked, inevitably getting downed in the middle of the open. Which then forces your hand, as you need to rescue them before a timer runs out. The timer is reasonably generous though, but it's still annoying. This variable quality of AI support forced me to repeat sections several times before I had a good enough run to progress to the next checkpoint.

Also, giving your squad members orders is very imprecise. It feels like the game only wants you to give specific orders at key moments. For example, most of the time when I want the sniper to pick off a distant target, both squad members will instead run towards it to engage with shorter range weapons. Similarly, the game will decide for you when you can order them to throw a stun grenade. The only order they will reliably complete is reviving each other, but half the time that won't be viable because the downed member will be out in the open.

Overall, the game is good, but frustrating at points due to your squad members messing up.

Completely linear story until the end. The so-called "hard choices" the game boasts about are not choices at all -- there's one path to reach the end of the game. The plot tells you to do bad things, then rubs your nose in it while the npcs chastise you. Towards the end, the loading screens even directly insult you for playing the game. Avoiding doing said bad things results in infinitely respawning enemies until you die or do what the game wants. There is a single instance of what amounts to "Commit a war crime: y/n" for no benefit. Varied endings, but nothing effects them until the last five minutes. Every other choice only gives achievements. Very telltale-esque. Understand that the game is a linear story about a bad person in bad circumstances. 

The setting itself is nice, though. There's a lot of little moments that add to things, just sprinkled throughout the levels. Some areas can be briefly stealthed to listen in on enemy conversations. "Intel" collectibles provide commentary on the events leading up to your arrival, and your character's reflections on them. Enemies are far from brain-dead -- they'll panic and react to grenades and you killing people near them. The campaign is only five hours -- fortunately, it's a pretty well done five hours.

Pre-rendered cutscenes were very choppy for me, and had no sound until I replaced a file. Look on the forums if you have an issue.

The game itself isn't awful, but it could've been actually decent with just some tweaks by the devs.

[h1]The Good[/h1]
- The standard difficulty is perfect, it seems easy at first but you'll find yourself dying a lot the more you go on.
- Weapon selection/system was decent, there are so many good guns to pick from it's a struggle to only pick two but it forces you to pick whether you have more of a ranged or up close focus.
- It's not actually that good, but for a game that's 8 years old the graphics hold up well

[h1]The Bad[/h1]
- Stealth: This game shows you at the start that you can do stuff like use a silencer and if you aren't in combat and you tell your men to target some people, then they'll do it silently too. However all of a sudden it turns out you try do this later in the game and no they won't put silencers on, and so the entire map starts shooting at you because your squad chose not to do it silently, it's completely random whether or not they'll use silencers or not. ALSO, the soldiers are telepathically linked which means if one sees you for a split second before you silently kill him then the whole map will know and start shooting you. Long story short, you do [i]NOT[/i] get a choice of stealth and gun blazing tactics. This is a guns blazing only game, but 5% of the time they let you get a few silent kills first to delay the guns blazing part. So lame because the one section where I managed to get on a silent streak, it was really fun! But that's just not a playstyle the devs actually let you use for more than 5 minutes of the whole game. I even went back and replayed sections trying to get a stealth run but it appeared to be impossible every time
- Choices: This game was marketed as being all about tough choices and whatnot, but the first choice doesn't even happen 'til almost halfway into the game. And I could be really dumb, but a fair amount of choices are not at all clear and it appears there's only actually one thing you can do. Like one where they're like 'save this agent or save these civillians', but I couldn't see the civillians or where they went, and there was only one doorway and it led to the agent... did I just not see another pathway? was I meant to just wait in order to 'choose' the other option? I've got no clue. Other choices are just illusions, the 'choice' is proceeding or getting killed, and the rest of the choices don't matter, the story unfolds the exact same way. In the end no choice changes the ending, you decide the ending right at the end (Oh and there's no good ending btw, I read)
- Gameplay/controls: The genius devs had the idea to make the sprint button the same as the cover button, so if you run too close to a wall then you'll cling to it like a magnet, when you're trying to run across before being shot to death. Also whenever you come out of cover your character stands right up, instead of staying crouched. Also something you'd expect to give you cover do not, therefore you just stand there like a moron getting shot while you keep pressing the cover button. These things will result in unnecessary deaths and frustration. 

[h1]The Ugly[/h1]
- The Story: For the most part it's decent, but by the time you finish it I realised it just didn't make sense... I can't really say it without spoiling so... [spoiler]Basically its all in your head and your teammates don't see or hear what you see, but there's at least one section where some soldiers who 'dont exist' shoot at you and your teammates see them and shoot them too; and then it raises the question who actually is the enemies leader? Some say it's not Radioman, some say it is[/spoiler]. I just felt a little shortchanged by the story even though it was mostly good. Also the fact your mission is to help but at no point are you allowed to talk to your fellow Americans and say 'hey, how can we help?'
- Usually I factor playtime into my review, and although this was fairly short I don't mind because I got this game free. Some might be tempted to go back and do different choices, but I read about them online and like I said above, nothing changes from your choices; and in a game that forces you to go guns blazing the whole time, I don't want to go through that again.

[b]6/10[/b]

Spec Ops: The Line is a real hidden gem, that unfortunately nobody bought when it came out, but gained a cult following in the later years. It's a masterpiece of storytelling wrapped in a mediocre cover-shooter. The gameplay is nothing special, we've all seen better examples before and after it's release, but the unique setting, the great soundtrack and the deep, thought-provoking narrative makes this game a must play for everyone. Instead of romanticising war, this game shows us the real horrors of it. It's a disturbing, harrowing journey into a soldier's personal hell. The campaign is only 5 to 6 hours long, but 100% worth playing - it's an unforgettable experience.
Do you feel like a hero yet?

Spec Ops: The Line is an alright game. It's a pretty typical cover shooter but it tries to differentiate itself by emphasising the darker side of combat with a handful of grisly scenes. The campaign took me about 4 hours to beat. Going after collectables or replaying the campaign after unlocking the FUBAR difficulty would definitely increase this. 

Some things worth noting are that the online multiplayer appears to be dead, the game does [i]not[/i] currently run on Linux and required modding to get the audio functioning on Windows, and there are scenes of flashing lights that can be irritating (Chapter 11 has a prime example of this). 

The [b]TLDR [/b] of all of this is if you want a Call of Duty-style campaign with a darker twist, don't care about the multiplayer aspect, and can get it on sale for less $15 I would say it's worth picking up.

Honestly I was speechless when I finish this game and I do not even know where to start... 8 years was a year of great games, but this pearl passed off my radar. Spec Ops: The Line is a great proof that even less renown games can be great, in fact, I honestly think that this was one of the darkest war stories I remember to play. 

It is a short linear story game full of action and epic combats fights. You play as a soldier commander of a three men squad in a similar style of The Bureau: XCOM Declassified or even the Mass Effect games, not so polished as the others, but extremely satisfying. 
Trough out the game you follow the adventures and misadventures of this squad on a Dubai devastated by a massive cataclysmic sandstorm. I could keep talking and talking about this game, but despite it is not a new game, I do not want to spoil it to anyone that did not played it... 
Graphically, even compared with so many other games of that year it is not great, I came across with some inexplicable frame drops from time to time and an error message while loading the game once, but after check the files integrity it worked fine again. 
Last but not least the multiplayer. Unfortunately we do not have much to talk about it, since it is basically dead. But if you have a friend with the game available to play with you or if you are lucky enough to find a player to play with you, good to you, enjoy it! But if not don't wonder why and specially don't blame the game, it is a game from 2012, what did you expect.

Overall this was indeed a really great surprise, and I am very pleased that I notice that, better later than never right? 
A really nice addition to my STEAM collection!

The game that feels like the deformed love child in a love triangle between the video game "Bioshock", the book "Heart of Darkness" and the film "Apocalypse Now" and that a lot of people orgasm to for some reason is not as shocking and not as thought provoking as they claim it to be. A lot of the dark commentary on war crimes and atrocities had already been explored in Modern Shooters like the Modern Warfare Trilogy and Battlefield 3. Spec Ops: The Line is an interesting game with very few "moral" choices and has multiple endings depending on your choices at the very end. The gameplay and shooting is so mediocre and the enemy AI is often dumb but the story and writing keeps you playing. The infamous white phosphorus scene is forced onto players which is one of many examples of a lack of choices given to the player and is thrown for shock value and to guilt the player. The fact that 3 US delta Forces soldiers are shooting and killing rogue US soldiers throughout the game is weird and strange and doesn't make for a realistic scenario but it's nice to have a game where the bad guys are American scum. They kill more of their former mutinous comrades than the actual natives and insurgents of Dubai. This game does feel so pretentious, in it's attempts to guilt players by making them reflect on their violent actions throughout the game's story and makes you question your psyche and sanity. The AC130 gunship mission and nuclear bomb scene from Call of Duty 4 Modern Warfare has far more impact and shock value than anything in this game. Hell, even No Russian from Modern Warfare 2 has a larger impact! The fact that spec ops has multiplayer literally contradicts it's own themes and messages on modern FPS games and it's the worst most garbage tacked on multiplayer mode I've ever seen! The multiplayer is a prequel to the main campaign and shows the rogue US soldiers before Delta Squad arrived in Dubai. It's clear the publisher 2K forced the devs to add in a multiplayer mode to add more "value" and replay ability. I will give the game compliments though I love the setting of Dubai it is so beautiful and the voice acting is amazing especially from the local population. Although hearing Nolan North feels out of place since it sounds like Deadpool or Nathan Drake but he still does an amazing job. I wish the game had way more choices and that it had more humor from the characters and had them joking more to deal with the horrors of war and psychological damages to their mental states like the Bad Company games or even the Modern Warfare games to keep Spec Ops from being way too depressing and dark all the time. All in all buy this game for the singleplayer if you're curious about all the hype surrounding this game's story but do not play the multiplayer or cooperative they're both garbage and contradicts the main message of the game's themes! I would rather recommend the Modern Warfare Trilogy, Battlefield 3, or even Call of Duty Modern Warfare 2019 for much more fun and better gameplay. Spec Ops The Line is torture porn that hits the player over and over with guilt and shame and the revelation the whole game was a hallucination is dumb. As a story, this game succeeds. As a game, well the less said the better... let's just say it's aged very poorly in terms of gameplay in the same way the first Bioshock game has...
