This is a very scripted, linear, 3rd person war shooter... and I loved it all. 

Gameplay - there are multiplayer and co-op options. You play in a squad of 3. You can do some things to influence your squad members such as throw grenades, and tell them to heal one another, but it's nothing that needs to be managed regularly. There is an assortment of weapons throughout the game. Controls are pretty standard with cover, vault, reload and aim. 

Voice acting - the most recognizable voice in this is that of Nolan North (Uncharted etc). He does a great job overall and the other characters as well done also. 

Music - the game really shines in this area. The choice of music used sets the tone of the situation. Older songs were used that were popular during those times lends to the immersion. 

Story - this was a real standout for the game. The script illustrates that war lends itself to situations that are not just black or white and where it really succeeds is also showing the outcome of those decisions. 

Graphics - while it is an older game, the levels are well designed and the characters look decent.  The game does show its age overall graphically, but not so much that it breaks immersion in my opinion. 

Overall - a fantastic experience that reminds me of a game like Mafia 2, not so much in the game play aspect, but in the well written story, excellent choice of music and great dialogue/voice acting. I believe that if I had played this back in 2012 when it was released, it would have blown my mind. Completing it in 2020 still puts it up there as one my top scripted action games. It's not an extremely long game, but it is one hell of a good time with intense moments and then cause for reflection of the aftermath. Would highly recommend to anyone who enjoys these types of games. Due to the length/age, I'd recommend getting this on a deep discount ($5-$10), but it's well worth checking out.

[h1]Must Play.[/h1]
Spec Ops the Line Utilizes the unique advantage of Games as a medium, the agency of the player on the 'protagonist', to swiftly transfer the ownership of the guilt onto the player itself. What results is a near perfect concoction of surreal horror that is a must for anyone who calls themselves a gamer.
[h1]Pros:[/h1]
The game displays a thorough understanding of game design principles on the developers part, using subtly adaptive environments (to player's choices) to further its narrative, humanizing enemies (before combat), and something as simple as fade in - fade out transitions to make the player question the entirety of the game. These nuances are never made apparent to the player, most of them being missed in any given playthrough, leaving more horror to be felt when u do finally come across them (in a second playthrough or somewhere online).
[h1]Cons:[/h1]
The gameplay. Its mediocre at best and I'd recommend playing the game on the easiest difficulty (if u value ur time in this life) as it reduces the friction in getting to the best parts of the game. The combat is about as generic as a generic TPS cover shooter could be but, thankfully it allows u to skip most of it by sitting comfy behind cover and barking orders at ur squad m8s (at least in most instances) and depending on how u configure the controls, u could free a hand and utilize it to shove things down ur belly whilst ur at it.
[h1]Conclusion:[/h1]
Buy it, Play it. Tho maybe wait for a sale considering its 8 yrs old.

- 2012 graphics still hold up pretty well, and the framerate appears to be uncapped, or at least really high.
- Great voice acting (Nolan North!), and with just as much swearing as I would expect from soldiers in a war zone.
- Gun mechanics are straightforward but satisfying. Swapping guns and conserving ammo feels necessary, even on lower difficulty settings.
- The hide-behind-cover mechanic doesn't always work perfectly, but it's much more fun than games that make you run in guns blazing.
- Nice variety of guns, every weapon feels unique and like it serves a purpose at different stages of the game.

CONS:
- Short. It only took me 6 hours on difficultly level 2.
- Half the time I died was because the running and hide-behind-cover controls were wonky.
- Some of the gimmicky mechanics were underused, although maybe they'd be more used in harder difficultly settings (shooting glass to make sand pour out, squad commands).

What a trip this game is. It's part psychological horror, part standard cover shooter. The difficulty on PC is quite high, even on standard, likely to compensate for the increased accuracy of the mouse.

The negatives involve clunky controls (many functions dumped on the same few buttons), annoyingly sparce interaction points (cover, jumpable low walls - made more annoying by non-jumpable low walls that look exactly the same), the epilepsy bulldozer, the occasional bugs, and the tacky way the game talks directly to the player as if they were the main character.

You might think that all of that ruins the experience, but the game ends up being a blast anyway. Loads of fun, and the story completely deviates from your standard shooter into a hallucination-based fantasy.

This is a cover based shooter with a realistic military setting. But still very much an action game and not simulation. I would describe the story as a psychological thriller and as such you will get most out of it the less you know about it before you start. If you know you will like this game I would urge you to play it before reading my review for the best experience. If you are not sure, please continue.

[b]What I liked[/b]
- Apocalypse Now setting: The story and setting of this game are definitely the strongest points about this game. If you know the movie Apocalypse Now you will have a general idea of the type of setting they are going for. War is insanity. None of the glorification of it but all of “the horror”. Dubai also makes a fresh setting for this with all its luxury being demolished in acts of senseless violence.

- Character Arc: There is a real story being told with character growth. Things happening in the story have effect on the characters. The main protagonist at the start is not the same person as at the end of the game. They have different voice lines and look different. I like how apparent this was.

- Sand everywhere: Since the story unfolds before/after and during a massive sand storm the use of sand as a set piece is also creative in parts. It can be used as a trap in multiple instances where shooting a glass wall or ceiling unleashes a tidal wave of sand over enemies or it is used to create tension where a sandstorm swipes in during a gun fight. It also looks quite epic to see skyscrapers jutting out massive dunes of sand in the distance.

- Minigame-like sections: Most of the game is the well known cover based shooting that people know from Gears of War, Mass Effect or Uncharted. But I like how the game subtly tries to mix it up with these minigame like sections where you are for example mini gunning the side of a building to help your allies progress or shooting with a grenade launcher from the side of a truck. It really keeps the game fresh.

[b]What I didn’t like[/b]
- Iffy Controls: I had some trouble with the controls during parts of the game where it just takes too long to get out of a running animation or when you are melee attacking instead of vaulting over cover or vice versa. At the end of the game I also switched over to playing the game with controller which I regret not doing sooner. I would advice trying out keyboard and controller at the start of the game and going with what you prefer.

- Cinematic trail and error: This is a very linear game and that is fine. There are some very cinematic scenes where you do some basic actions to while chaos surrounds you. At best these are like the minigames I spoke off but some of these where a bit annoying. There was this scene where you have to run through a hallway while a chopper is shooting at you from the side. It took me multiple times to try and make it to the end but I got shot every time just before I reached cover. Then I tried it by vaulting over some cover that I previously walked around and made it. There was no noticeable difference in time. It even seemed slower then just walking around it. That took me out of the moment of an otherwise awesome scene.

- I don’t want to do this: I see why it is kind of needed to drive the story home but there is a moment where as a player I was like “No, I don’t want to do this” but the only other option was to close the game. The characters even say “There is always a choice” at that point. I would have hoped to have a second option that was maybe harder to find. If there is then please ignore this point. I might have missed it. I intent to replay it with different choices when the game is less fresh in my mind.

- Technical difficulties: The game mostly ran fine but I had one instance at the end of the game where I had to restart because my game became a slide show just after you are getting shot by a mortar.

[b]Why others should try it[/b]
Overall I liked the game. It wasn't perfect but it was a unique experience at the least. I would recommend it for its thriller like story that is more impactful because you are in control. The gameplay is fine but sometimes just feels off and less polished then other cover based shooters. PTSD: The Game

TL;DR: The Line played on FUBAR difficulty in one continuous playthrough is the best recreation of combat you'll find in any medium. It took me roughly 14 hours to get through, dying often and trying the same section repeatedly.

Full review (warning possible spoilers):

The effect of playing The Line on FUBAR in one sitting was revelatory. The Line does what video games do at their best: give us the experience of being somewhere and doing something without actually being there. In my playthrough controlling Captain Walker I spent many long, agonising, frustrating, exhausting hours getting him through one combat situation to the next.

I screamed, pounded my desk, and lost my sh**. The designers even sync the points in the game where both the player and Walker start losing it simultaneously. The controls are janky and even after multiple playthroughs I still found myself accidentally shifting Walker out of cover and killing him. Other times I'd be prompting Walker to swap his weapon instead of reloading in the middle of an intense firefight. 

The effect is that the gameplay elements compliment the meta theme underlying The Line's writing. The player becomes alienated from Walker as he apparently no longer responds to our input. The slip ups caused by the control scheme seem intentional; they mimic the way the human body starts failing to react the way we want it to after prolonged exposure to stress.

Moreover, the player's growing frustration with the sqaud mechanics mirrors Walker's own frustration with his men. You begin to berate them just as Walker does for perceived failings. Nolan North, Christopher Reid, and Omid Abtahi who voice Cpt. Martin Walker, Lt. Alphonso Adams, and Sgt. John Lugo respectively, do an impressive job of capturing the disintegration of Delta Force.

Each man ends up resenting one another - military discipline deteriorates and the squad is barely a unit in the latter stages of the game. The further you go in the game the further morale stretches and then fails. Neither the player or Walker is enjoying themselves, both are just looking forward to the next respite or the end around the corner.

As for the enemy in the Line, whether refugees or 33rd, their novelty wears off real fast. Soon you take glee in having Walker kill them, even execute them when they're incapacitated and no longer a threat.

On a continuous playthrough you sympathise with Walker to a much greater degree. Neither you nor he has had a break, and consequently both your decisions stop making much sense. I died a lot through my single playthrough, and after a while you start making mistakes with increasing frequency. I even started accidentally shooting my own squad members because they look so much like the 33rd. Fog of war indeed.

The end result is that you're worn by the last chapter. Your nerves are shot. At the end you - like Walker - are apathetic. He even throws down his weapon in the closing showdown with the 33rd, much to the incredulity and fury of Adams.

Love it or hate it, years on and this game still causes intense discussion.

Spec Ops: The Line at first glance may feel like a generic over the top action third-person shooter game but what lies within the story is something that I never thought to see in a military shooter like Battlefield or Call of Duty. If anything, this game is as close as to Black Ops 1 and 2 from the Call of Duty series in terms of story but with much darker tones. The story will make you ask, "Are you ever a hero? Or are you just playing hero?" You will make difficult choices and at the end, this game will make you question those choices if they were right choices. Or maybe not. There are multiple cutscenes and endings depending on your choices which makes the game replayable just to view what difference did you make depending on the choices you choose. 

Other than that.....Spec Ops: The Line fell short in a lot of department. The controls are probably one of my greatest complains as the character feels unresponsive. Perhaps its for added realism or something but a lot of deaths in the game had been due to how either unresponsive the controls are or how ♥♥♥♥♥ the controls are because a lot of your actions are tied to ether one or two buttons which could lead to you doing things you don't want to do. Difficulty is great and I do highly trying on the highest difficulty. The environments are fantastic especially running on the Unreal Engine. Destructible cover to interacting with the environment to kill enemies faster is always great fun when you have the opportunity to do so.....which the game doesn't give a lot unfortunately. The sound design is average though, usual military tunes but there are a few twists here so I dare say it serves it purpose.

There's a multiplayer and co-op mode but I never had the opportunity to try it so I can't give any opinions on it.

All in all, Spec Ops: The Line is a generic Third-person military shooter but with an interesting story that will put most modern shooter stories to shame. Unfortunately, its not worth it full price due to how bad the controls can be. Buy this game on a discount if you're interested in the story ONLY. Do not buy it if you're looking for gameplay.

Gentlemen, welcome to Dubai.

Spec Ops: The Line is a third person cover shooter built with the unreal engine. The controls and movement are troublesome at times but if you can get past them you'll enjoy it. The highest difficulties are the most challenging by default. Plenty of parts in both the campaign and cooperative missions are trial and error.

During the whole campaign you are the Captain of an elite Delta Force fireteam by the name of Martin Walker sent into Dubai to locate survivors of the 33rd Infantry Battalion. The leader of the 33rd Infantry Battalion is Colonel John Konrad who Captain Walker holds respect for. The further you delve into Dubai the more unstable the narrative becomes as other factors come into play such as the factions your fireteam comes into contact with, the atrocities committed and the desperation for survival and answers. The whole campaign of violence, vengeance and desperation unfolds as Captain Walker descends into a state of trauma, anger and guilt.

There isn't much lore behind the cooperative missions as they serve more as challenges which can be played alone or with a friend. I've played and completed all of the cooperative missions alone on FUBAR difficulty.

I haven't played the multiplayer but it should be known that the developers never intended to have a multiplayer feature.

The soundtrack is phenomenal and it fits the harsh atmosphere and firefights the characters experience during their stay. Dubai's atmosphere is desolate from the hell it has gone through caused by the sandstorms prior and during both the campaign and cooperative missions. Explosions on sand will kick up dust and even if enemies aren't caught within the blast, the dust blinds them. Certain parts of the environment are destructible when can be used to the player's advantage against their enemies.

I recommend giving Spec Ops: The Line a play not for the multiplayer, but for its campaign and cooperative missions. 

That is if you got the game before online game markets all took Spec Ops: The Line off their sites for purchase. I hope this game reaches the markets again some day, but still get this game if you can.

When I asked my friends to recommend me a story-rich shooter, this one was on the list. Did I get what I wanted? Hell, yes! Truth is, I never expected a war shooter to be so psychologically deep, so dramatic, so... mind-blowing. 
The story got me interested right away; I kept wondering what the hell was going on there. The further, the better - I had my theories on what would happen next and what the ending might be. ...And they turned out to be absolutely wrong. More than that, all possible what-ifs just won't leave me alone now. The jaw-dropping effect of the ending was amazing.
If you are more into action, don't worry. Spec Ops: The Line is pretty packed with that, too. In fact, there is a good story/action balance. They give us short time-outs to focus on whatever story pieces we get, and then all those shooting, shouting, and running starts all over again. Every now and then, though, I had to pause the game to give myself some time to think it over.
The controls weren't the best part of the experience, but still manageable. (You 'stick' to cover too much, can't turn the corner while in cover, lose track of the squadmates in multi-level or cluttered locations.) The combat was pretty challenging for me (on Normal, but I'm no expert on shooters). I died a lot (thank you, checkpoint system, you were very kind). It was often like 'Hey, haven't I already died in the very same way 3 minutes ago?' Symbolic... (I'm not telling you why, because it's a spoiler) Or maybe, it's just me...

[i] Another hero, another mindless crime (c) [/i] 
This game has some healthy philosophy behind it. Killing is NO fun, it's a chore, and you don't have a choice. Playing as a commander, you feel this burden of responsibility. You have 2 squadmates with opposite opinions (classic...), who would snap at each other, question your orders and blame you for all what's happening. Because, what the hell, Walker?
By the way, if you (like me) are used to watching your wounded buddies lie down to have some rest and then stand up at the end of the fight, don't get comfortable. Squadmembers' death results in gameover, so remember to tend to the wounded in due time. That is probably one way to say how important Adams and Lugo are for the story (they really are!).

I love stories. I play games for the sake of stories, because games are much more engaging than any other media.  Spec Ops: The Line is now definitely on my 'best story' list.

That said, this game offers an amazing game story the uses the gameplay to effectively tell it. Now, I specifically say GAME story because it isn't that spectacular of a tale on it's own; rather, most of the story is told through a way that uses the medium of video gaming to tell it in the most effective way possible. It's impressive, and even the one twist I did see coming hit really hard because of how I took part in it. It's very difficult to describe without going into spoilers, but it'll have you questioning everything, especially the excepted norms of shooters and player choice.

I don't really have many negatives. It's short, but that's honestly the perfect length for such a story to not overstay it's welcome. There were a couple parts where the scale was tipped a little too much on the enemy's favor, but it's rare to come across. I completely recommend this game. Just be prepared for some dark moments.

The main selling point for this game is its narrative, unfortunately the marketing was all over the place so I think that let it down in terms of sales. However, I can't blame them too much because selling a story like this, to the masses, is difficult.

In this third-person shooter, you play Captain Walker leading a fire team of three dispatched by Delta Force for recon. Your mission is to locate survivors in Dubai and radio for Evac, however like most games, you do more than that.

When you reach to Dubai, you find out what happened to previous battalion sent by the U.S. Army - known as "The 33rd" and a series of interesting narratives begin to weave their webs. In this game, you're forced to fight your own men, American soldiers, with the help of the CIA. You're forced to make decisions, questioning your morals while civilians are stuck in the middle of this warzone without any assistance or water.

The gameplay is your basic third-person shooter with a cover system. It works, but it isn't anything special. I found the gun-play satisfying, even if a little bland, but it worked with the type of story it was telling.

The multiplayer is dead, impossible to find a match and if you do somehow organise one, it is a broken, unbalanced mess. Multiplayer was clearly not the focus here, included only to please the publishers request and was apparently outsourced. The only things I liked about the multiplayer was that you could throw rocks which trick your opponent into abandoning cover as they think it's a grenade. I also liked some of the game-modes and how the story is linked to the multiplayer factions, kind of like a prequel to the campaign - except it doesn't make up for the fact that it's dead, horribly unbalanced, buggy and laggy.

Co-op seems decent, just needs more levels. The graphics are okay, the game runs well on Linux. There are a few bugs but nothing too common or game-breaking. I didn't like how the button for melee was the same as vaulting over cover which led to a few annoying moments, but it didn't take away too much.

So, if you're thinking of buying this game, I would certainly recommend it for the campaign, mostly for the story - not the multiplayer. There is an amazing attention to detail, so many small things I notice in the game that elevate the story or catch me off-guard on subsequent playthroughs. The plot itself is also open to interpretation with its multiple endings and symbolism. The voice-acting was also top notch with every character, it's clear the actors gave it their all in this amazing performance.

God is dead within this game.

[b]Story; the main focus[/b]
On first glance the game starts off as a typical third-person shooter but oh boy your ass is slowly eased into the an*l mind f*ck that is the story. The shifts and turns ,the constant questioning of your actions and even yourself as the player questioning if you ,yes you, could have find some other way. The questions shift from "what have they done?" to an instant of "what the f*ck have i done?".
The sender bender that is this venture into Dr Jung's house of psychological torment is the smoothed oiled Latina model bottom you wish for lad and it is the only spark that caught my eye. The voice acting and direction taken through the narrative is unseen by third person shooter standards .....by contrast i believe the TPS style is probably a choice made by the developers to distract the player from the actual nature of the game and create this false sense of understanding because hell you've played sh*t-tons of TPS you know the deal; goodboys kill badboys save the day, but no , this story is about the degeneration of a few good men's minds into a pile of insanity soup that Tzeentch would have a hard on for.

[b]gameplay[/b]
its fine.

Okay it isnt something to ride home about and declare it a masterpiece. You grab gun and hide in cover then shoot the enemy NPCs. Literally it. However environmental mechanics put this game out in the lime light , being able to shoot glass to send sand unto enemies killing them or blowing up parts of the setting to create a sand avalanche is the most satisfying thing than figuring how to put 8008 in a calculator in 5th grade.

[b]Graphics[/b]
Passable , it's outdated by today's standards but for its release year it was passable graphics and honestly doesn't need much to be run in today's age of hardware.
However where it shines is the art direction. The destroy and apocalyptic environments of Dubai after a natural disaster , the sense of paranoia and constant force of dead bodies and war crimes that make the Nuremberg Trials look like a kindergarten play day. Whoever was the lead art directer exactly knew what they wanted to capture and how to put on screen as if a giant middle finger pointed to morality and God himself.

[b]some negatives[/b]
Honest to God f*ck these hordes of enemies being constantly thrown at you and the need to die on repeat to understand the patterns to know where to go in a sandstorm. There are also some bugs with crashing but i suspect that is because i had this game running on max settings and had it running on max screen on my pc. The controls are strange to me especially the cover mechanics and gunplay, but once you get used to it its not that bad but its still very poor. 

[b]overall enjoyment and final conclusion[/b]
It's honestly a fun game to play and for the price during a steam sale its worth buying. Don't expect the greatest of third-person shooters but the story and the context this game puts you through is honestly a treat.

Completed this game 100% with all achievements and all difficulties excluding the easiest. Played co-op missions solo on easiest difficulties. Didn't play multiplayer as no one plays multiplayer anymore, or at least in my region.

First off, the negative points:
* Mouse sensitivity in this game wasn't ported over properly and doesn't allow fine tuning when aiming down sights. Most noticeable on sniper rifles.
* Border-less window not natively supported and requires 3rd part software.
* Shoulder view constantly resets and gets in the way when in corridor gun-play.
* Bare-bones tactical game-play. Hold command button, scan enemy, wait for AI to develop a brain and figure out how to pull trigger over enemies head. Useful for pulling aggro away from you. Essential in harder difficulties to eliminate heavies, snipers, and turrets.
* AI teammates would run ahead and get killed by enemies (Shout-out to the AA-12 in the pool level). Annoying the first time. Frustrating the fifth time.
* Running in this game is clunky and doesn't work well with cover system.
* Cover system isn't 'fluid' in movement. It had potential but was ultimately squandered by a static movement system. Some key problems that stood out were some cover areas not actually covering the player from gun fire and the inability to aim if the enemies was placed closed to the sidelines.
* There is one area where the game drops a heavy in front of you and the game starts flashing from darkness to light. Terrible game design. Not enjoyable.
* Heavy unit needed to provide more feedback to the player if they were taking damage. Wasn't sure if I was hitting their glass section of the helmet half the time. Resorted to using grenades.
* Game devs took a shortcut by shrinking the heads when head-shot. Resulted in a weird butt-hole neck effect. Hilarious but very noticeable.

Pros:
* First off, the obvious, one of the best stories you could come across in a video-game.
* Melee-reward system was awesome. Game rewards the player with ammunition from their specific gun if they perform a finisher on the enemy. Thought DOOM was the first game to do that.
* Overall, the gun-play is great once you get used to the sensitivity issues. Some would call it generic.
* Cool head-shot slow-mo effect. Some would probably feel it would get in the way.
* Dynamic voice-ines as the relationships progress through the story. A nice touch.
* Collectables aren't ridiculous in number like Ubisoft games and actually contribute to story. Easy to find if you pay attention.
* Though linear, flanking routes are there for the tactical player.
* Level designers have designed the levels with cover system in mind. Very rewarding for those who utilise it.
* Co-op missions were fun, though to enjoy it solo, I would recommend turning down the difficulty. Enemy numbers are clearly meant for two people.

However whereas the film Apocalypse, Now was inspired by Joseph Conrad's novella Heart of Darkness, this game just copies the film. It goes as far as featuring a soundtrack heavy with 1960's music -- not the obvious choice for the setting. At times I also found the presentation tone deaf, amidst the horror of war you have the usual action hero cliches: people surviving falls from an incredible height, one liners, and fighting "heavies" that won't go down without a grenade. However, in my interpretation the apparent tone deafness is explained at the end of the game's story. You just have to suppress your disbelief until then. The story also presents a few choices, none if which have real consequence apart from maybe your conscience. I did play the game through a second time though, just to see what would happen.

The game has a good selection of guns, which also have different firing modes etc. Different guns are better in different situations, so you do end up going through most of them even in the first play through. You also cycle the weapons due scarce ammo. I never ran completely out, but some sections I had to clear with a pistol or other such secondary weapon. You can also give simple commands to your two squad mates, and they are helpful at times. Sometimes they end up getting wounded, and then you have to step in to heal them. On the whole the AI is decent, and doesn't come in the way of your performance too much.

I don't think it makes much sense talking about graphics when a game is this old, but some lighting effects, especially amidst the frequent sandstorms still look good.

On the whole it's a pretty good game, and I would recommend it if you're a fan of shooters, or your library is wearing thin for whatever reason. Otherwise don't feel too bad about leaving it on the "shelf".

Spec Ops: The Line — A Story-Driven Shooter That Has Aged Remarkably Well

Spec Ops: The Line is much more than a typical military shooter — it’s a powerful, thought-provoking experience that challenges the conventions of the genre. Years after its release, it has aged exceptionally well, standing out for its gripping narrative, moral complexity, and unforgettable moments that stick with you long after the credits roll.

The gameplay is solid, blending tense third-person shooting with strategic squad commands. But where it truly shines is in its storytelling — the game forces you to confront the harsh realities and consequences of war in a way few games dare to do.

If you’re looking for a shooter with depth, emotional weight, and a story that resonates, Spec Ops: The Line remains a must-play classic that holds up even today.

[h1] Spec Ops: The Line, one of the best military video game stories ever! [/h1]

I'm the stubborn sort, I refuse ( or at least i believe I do ) to cave into popular choice and what people are playing at the time. As an example it took my 3 years before I played GTA 5 at all. But when I got around to playing GTA I was astonished, it was brilliant, it became one of my favorite games instantly.

So what does that have to do with Spec Ops: The Line. Well just like GTA 5, when I finally got around to playing it, I was amazed. This game is phenomenal, I'm not the sort of person who usually gets extremely invested in a games story but Spec Ops is an exception. It is really well written, right from the intro sequence I was hooked. The way the story is told and unfolds around you is really well done. The game does have some very dark moments and the plot twist and sudden changes of dynamic really add to the overall feel.

I have to say that I find Spec Ops to be very refreshing. It's not your usual go to the place and shoot the bad guys, go to the next place and shoot the bad guys and OOO guess what now go here and shoot some bad guys. Well... I suppose it is when you boil it down, but everything is disappointing when you break it down. It feels like every scene of shooting bad guys has a reason and it isn't just mindless killing.

One problem I have with the game is the option of choice, there isn't any. Whilst that isn't entirely true, there are some scenes with choice, those scenes are really linear story telling disguised into giving you the illusion of choice. However I understand that choice can't be included with a great story as it would take years and years to develop a game that would have a story malleable enough to fit literally any choices the player makes.

Another problem I have, and it's a slightly larger one, is with the gameplay. The gameplay in a shooter has to be good, and to be honest it's left leaving a lot to be desired in Spec Ops. It revolves around moving from cover to cover and peaking out to shoot people. It's extremely basic and the game doesn't really introduce anything new to keep the gameplay fresh throughout the roughly 5 hour story campaign. Again though, the story basically makes up for these short comings.

Well for the last 5 paragraphs now I've talked about the story, so maybe I should finally explain why I think it's so good. The storyline is stunning, well written and well directed. I was genuinely blown away by this games story, it's stellar yet, horrifying. This game has a military aesthetic over it but when you scrap away the surface it's really a gruesome psychological horror story.
When the game begins you think your just in for another military game. As you walk down the dusty path leading to Saudi Arabia however you quickly change your mind, it loses the typical shooter feel and takes a more serious turn. I'll try not to spoil any major plot points but basically, your a commander to a 3 man squad. After a large group of US soldiers go quiet in Saudi Arabia your sent in to find out what happened. But quickly you see that the situation is much more complicated than you anticipated. You now have to fight your way out against everyone, you never know who is on your side.

You'll find that you as the player will always be left in the dark just the same as your character in the game. This is genius, it means that everytime something happens or some plot twist hits when you least expect it, your left in the same position as your character. It really adds to the immersion. There are certain moments where you are left questioning what is happening and you never know what is correct about both your assumptions and your characters.

You'll find that you get really attached to your squad mates, I personally believe this just shows off the fantastic writing again as their characters are likeable not just unbelievably stupid and really only there to create tension. When their lives are on the line it will mean something to you and you'll have an actual reason to try and save them.

I would love to go more in depth into the story but I don't want to give away any spoilers too those who haven't played it yet. I really can't recommend this game highly enough, I know I am restating myself but this is one of the best game storylines I've ever had the privilege to play through. I can't speak on the multiplayer but from what I've seen online and read about it isn't anything to get excited about and I can't say I'm surprised.

Overall this games stunning story telling and stellar writing help both create a captivating story and really have you reflect on the horrors of war.

I always heard that Spec Ops: The Line had a crazy, psychological story and after experiencing it, I have to fully agree with everyone. It starts off like your average shooter, but the further down the rabbit hole you go, the more you start to see how insane everything becomes.

If you're into stories that make you think about the moral message to be human or someone's personal hell, I highly recommend playing Spec Ops: The Line. I went through a partial second playthrough to get some of the missing achievements and my perspective opened up even more to what was happening around me and the story made even more sense. You can finish the game around 7-8 hours and I walked away completely satisfied and engrossed with the characters.

Spec Ops The Line, a tactical third person shooter developed by Yager. This game really messed up with my head with its plot filled with dark and depressing moments. You play as Captain Walker, a Delta Force soldier sent on a mission in Dubai alongside Sgt. Lugo and Lt. Adams to evacuate civillians due to the sandstorms that have been hitting the city. From very early on you find out that things are not right and you are put in the middle of a war between the dammed 33rd battalion and the refugees from the storms. The game features few moments where you are given a choice to make which makes you think that you are affecting the story, but the twist at the end makes you question what the heck have you done. There was a choice in the game that was so dark and sadly can be taken only one way because it's the only way to move the story forward. Basically you have been tricked into thinking you can make a choice, but you can't. Like every third person shooter, this one features a cover system, you can take cover behind almost anything and vault some of the cover too. You have your standard weapons, but most of them have an addition attachment that you can use at any time while other weapons don't. Like I said, this is a tactical shooter so it means you can give orders, by holding the middle mouse button your chroshair turns into a tryangle which you point at an enemy and a teamate will take out the target for you, this does come quite helpfull in some situations if you are pinned down. Your teamates also will need to be revived from time to time, you can either do it yourself or ask a teamate to do it for you. There is also a stun command which rarely pops up and acts more like a quick time event. The AI for your teamates is quite good, killing enemies that flank your position, give you covering fire or like I said above, take out targets for you. The controls are also responsive and I didn't encounter many bugs or glitches. The game is developed with the Unreal Engine and it does show it with textures popping up, but it's a surprise that the loading times aren't really long and the performance in general isn't that crappy. The game features a coop and multiplayer but they are mostly dead so if you are getting this game for this then you are wasting your money. The single player is worth playing and if you have friends who you can play with, you will find the gamemode really enjoyable. I sadly couldn't get much of a chance to play it. However, I do reccommend it just for the great single player campaign.

not a very bad game if you're into this sort of thing but ultimately it's a fairly clunky and awkwardly-controlling shooter that, for me, left a lot to be desired. due to this, i can't recommend unless you're willing to overlook some slippery cover mechanics and poor ally ai for a story that, though done well in all fairness, is done better in other places.

the narrative it tells is easily the high point, and generally speaking that's what people are going to praise the most considering combat is so 4/10. fair enough, the characters aren't terrible and the whole "war is hell" approach it goes for generally is done pretty well. overall, the focus of the narrative is geared towards how the chain of command can leave individual soldiers blind on the battlefield, and how in the heat of the moment soldiers may make decisions they wouldn't otherwise with tragic consequences. as i've said, it's really not a bad story by any means, certainly above average for this kind of game, but for me it just wasn't enough to sell the end product on its own.

this is mostly because, as i've said, the gameplay leaves a lot to be desired. if you've ever played, say, Mass Effect 2, you'd have a pretty good understanding of what snappy, responsive controls for cover-based shooters should feel like. Spec Ops: The Line does not control this way, at least not for keyboard/mouse. sprinting feels overly slippery, the shooting is needlessly (and artificially) inaccurate. compounding this, you very frequently run out of ammo in your primary weapon, and this is not a game which has controls that lend themselves to effectively dashing around and scooping up new weapons from fallen enemies like the game seems to want you to do. i understand the premise and usage of camo being realistic, but enemies are often very indistinct-looking and distant from where you are, making firefights confusing in a way that is not beneficial to gameplay or the experience overall. half the time you can't easily tell where you're being shot from, which is very much detrimental to this type of game.

firefights do, occasionally, have mechanics where you can shoot an environmental object like a big window or something similar to bury many enemies in sand at once, but it happens so infrequently that it really doesn't add too much to break up the monotonous, gimpy firefights.

the final nail in the coffin for me was, ultimately, the fact that checkpoints do not restart you from after the cutscene. you have to wait for it to reload and hear the first few lines of dialogue from the cutscene again while you wait for the option to skip the cutscene to appear. this happens any time you die near a cutscene which will be often, if you play on a difficulty above normal. you have very low health. not a bad thing in itself, the low health does positively contribute to the challenge to a degree. but combined with the distractingly clunky controls and overall boring firefights this title wore on me very quickly.

2/5, cannot recommend unless you're willing to overlook the boring and fairly poor combat for the sake of the story it tells. in my own opinion, the story isn't worth that though. if you want a much better military action game about the horrors of war, buy Phantom Pain instead.

Maybe you have already heard about Spec Ops: The Line. The game that everybody keeps bringing up when talking about hidden gems and games that didn't get the attention they deserved. The definition of "don't judge a book by its cover". A game that stands out as something truly special. A game so daring and real that it's surprising it even exists in the library of one of the big publishers, 2K. Somehow YAGER got a lot of freedom with this project. And better yet, they dared to take this opportunity to create art that will forever be remembered for a story that goes against convention. An actual anti-war game, if you can believe that.

First off, don't expect too much from the gameplay. It's your very, very standard cover based third-person shooter. One gimmick it has is the usage of sand. Sometimes you can shoot windows or glass ceilings and let a big heap of sand in that buries enemies. And you can give your two squad mates simple orders but they are usually self sufficient. Other than that, the mechanics are nothing new. The gameplay is serviceable.

The environment can be quite the sight. It's Dubai but it got hit by a massive sandstorm and is now swallowed up by the desert. It's a very different take on the "post apocalyptic" scenery and it's as eery as it is beautiful.

You are greeted with a patriotic menu screen as well as the cliched team of bro-dudes. It all starts simple enough. Investigate the ruins of the city in search for answers as to what is going on. You immediately encounter bad guys and shoot them up. All in a days work.

Then, step by step, comes the part that is so lauded about this game. What starts out as something you have seen a million times takes a harsh and very real turn. Both on a meta level that directly addresses the player and with a story that confronts you with the depths humans fall to under extreme circumstances and pressure. You can witness not only the deconstruction of a genre that usually glorifies war heroism but also of a group of men faced with the nightmarish hell that is a war for survival, where decisions and responsibilities are demanded that humans are not meant to shoulder.

Gameplay's a bit console-like. Decent challenge but not too hard.

Story is amazing. Went from typical military storyline to something more psychological horror.

The twist is really well done. It has some replay value. Different endings. The background in levels when being replayed gives new perspective if you know where to look.

It makes attempts like [i]Medal of Honor: Warlighter[/i] - to try and say "war is hell" - look like a complete joke. One small example is when I came around the corner and saw someone running at me, so I instinctively sprayed them. It was an unarmed civilian woman, in the wrong place at the wrong time.

A larger example: In games like [i]Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare[/i], there are often fun little airplane bombing sequences, where you are blowing up a bunch of white silhouettes on an infrared camera. A moment at this game's peak shows precisely how impersonal and dehumanizing this "death from above" tactic is.

I played through the game in one sitting, on Hard, and I'd recommend you do the same, for the full experience. To become haggard and frustrated alongside the characters in the story.



By the way, the multiplayer is a result of the publisher outsourcing it to another studio, because they believed "it wouldn't sell without it". The developers themselves have stated that they didn't want a multiplayer mode, so do not hold it against them.

This game is absolutely spectacular. I am playing this in 2019 and I can't stress enough just how fun it is, how worthy an experience it remains to date. Sure the mechanics are a tad clunky, the lowest mouse sensitivity setting is still too high for any fps player, and if you're a real stickler, the graphics are one gen behind. But these ways in which the game have aged are nothing, made irrelevant by the timeless power of a good narrative and superb storytelling. 

Spec Ops suffers from one of the most generic, boring game titles I have ever seen. When a friend first showed it to me, I thought it was a CoD knockoff, a typical US army shooting foreigners shebang (with added sand) and I dismissed it immediately. It was only years later after I started playing fps games and saw reviews praising the dark and complex narrative of Spec Ops that I returned to this game. 

I'm just consistently shocked by how much this game gets right. Everyone always talks about the amazing story and how the story is presented to the player (the perfect way: through gameplay and not through expositionary dialogue), but it's not just the story, the gameplay is hella fun too. The sand mechanics are a treat whenever they come up, and little touches, like when throwing a grenade onto sand creates a smoke screen with the sand, make all the difference. The squad management system is barebones at best but it adds a little bit of freshness to traditional fps gameplay, like when you are being heavily suppressed by a turret you can command your squad to take out the turret while remaining in safety. 

Playing this game now I'm saddened by how little it seems the game industry has learned from this game in the past 5+ years. It's a challenge to the industry, a challenge to Call of Duty and other mindless, borderline racist fps games, and clearly this challenge has gone unanswered, basically ignored. This game is a Call of Duty killer. It poses a question about the "shoot first, ask questions later" mentality that Call of Duty promotes.

This game explores the real horrors of war. The terrible things that must be done for the greater good. The strain your mind feels after all the fighting. I got this title for free off the humble bundle store and even with the experience that I am about to share with you, I probably still wouldn't have paid full price due to the somewhat dull gameplay.

That being said, this is a game that you should wishlist.

The first half IS horridly dull, thrusting you headfirst in a chaotic firefight without any understanding of the situation. Over and over and over again. Nice setpieces, repetitive gameplay. 
What you would expect for a cool, crisp and professional army man daydream simulator you'd be rapt about at the age of 7.

THIS is a ruse. As you are continually forced to make choices with no information in some impossible situations, you find that your patience fades and the line you have drawn for yourself is gradually pushed back to allow for what you are about to do, for what you have to do.

You have no choice, or so you tell yourself.

You have to tell yourself this, because you couldn't do it if you didn't. Things become less clear, where do I stand with all this? What am I railing against? What is the right thing to do? Your mental state is fraying, suddenly the setpieces aren't helicopters shooting down the ceiling but wading through piles of screaming people that you don't even know if they are real or not. Zoning out in firefights as surreal visions rack you with guilt and confusion, your squadmates panic and call your name as they see it happening. 

Although at the time you don't know why they are doing it.

The game gets better as this goes on, enemies are now personal. From the fear and guilt of fighting foes that shouldn't BE your foes you now feel vindicated. These foes becoming more desperate, rushing you with knives and launching attacks with chemical warfare. Heavy units pin your position as hysterical soldiers scream orders to each other and hopefully put you down once and for all. The shooting galleries are gone, replaced with a vicious and desperate game of cat and mouse as you hunt them down from their hiding holes.

The gameplay is aggressive in design, jumping cover floors foes. Melee attacks crack skulls with visceral impact and enemies groan on the ground. Enemies who are mortally wounded feebly roll around as you beat their head in for bonus ammunition. This design has some downsides though as you find yourself standing up from cover when hitting the wrong input and being cold turkey dead if you need to pull back. New enemy spawned in front that you can't kill right now? Well you're ♥♥♥♥ outta luck, time to die and respawn. 

This is especially accentuated in the early stages of the game when you are stuck in drawn out shooting galleries and survival missions, the gameplay was just not built for it. On a minor note there are a few areas where you are given the benefit of stealth to soften up your opposition, obviously anything you do is going to trigger the alarm but you can get your squaddies to do some stealth kills. Later on it feels more natural and you get into a great routine, even to the stage where you completely flank all of them and massacre the bunch. 

It's not robotic either, they really panic when you push into their lines and they can't shake you out without being brutalized. This is dynamic to a degree also. The developers must have called in the AI techs from the original F.E.A.R game because the AI in this game is comfortable with the environment and presents a curated awareness of the world it inhabits most of the time. 

All in all the game IS short and quite linear despite moments that really stick out, this is a game for someone who isn't looking to invest in gaming but gaming EXPERIENCES.

And the game really is an engine for a fantastic story, there is no other medium that would have been this effective. 

Hold some funds ready for a sale and seriously, you need to experience this game at some point.

Dubai has been hit by the heaviest sandstorms in recorded history, John Konrad volunteered the 33rd to help with a relieve mission in Dubai after their tour in Afghanistan. You play as Captain Martin Walker who served with Konrad in Afghanistan, you have 2 Delta Force elites under your command for the mission, And you are being sent to Dubai for a recon mission. Once there you find the horrors of war find out what the 33rd did and go on your own mission; Revenge. The game forces you to make morally heavy choices, or choices will be made for you. I won't go in too deep because I don't want to give any spoilers, But I think it is a great representation of war and the effects of it.

Next to the Single player campaign, there are online multiplayer modes, There is PVP, which is pretty alright, there are plenty of gamemodes, customizations, There are not a lot of populated lobby's sadly, It mostly are the same few hardcore players playing Deadmatches only. There is also a cooperative mode on custom maps with pretty straightforward objectives. It is pretty cool but nothing special. I personally would not recommend buying the game for the online experience, But it is a very solid Single player game, and it might be fun with friends online in private matches.

Surely you won't need a cutting edge GPU to play this masterpiece on Ultra, But The graphics hold up pretty good, Even by todays standards the game looks great. The Controls are a bit wonky tho, the cover system has its flaws like cancelling cover, or not going into cover, But once you get used to this and learn how to play with these flaws you will be alright.

The gameplay is very solid, There is no free roam, or any real exploring, You walk the path that is chosen for you, You can make some choices which affect the story slightly, But this is not a bad thing in my experience, It reminds me a bit of the Uncharted Series, Very cinematic driven gameplay with an amazing story and a few very challenging shootouts you need to overcome. The game has 4 difficulity settings, You have to complete the game on Hard to unlock Fubar difficulity, Which is quite a challenge, but it certainly is very doable.

I completed the entire game with a controller with 0 issues, Surely the game drops in FPS when it is loading a new part of the map, but this seems normal to me. This is a very solid game and the Linux port runs great.

The game is banned in the UAE for its depiction of Dubai in state of ruin, the game also performed badly in terms of sales, I think this is a shame, It is a great game with a great story, It really deserved a sequel.

I would recommend this game for the single player experience alone I have to give the game a 9, It is worth every penny. I would not recommend it for the multiplayer unless you have a group of friends you can play it with.

[u] Gameplay [/u]
Spec Ops: The Line is a 2012 third-person shooter video game, It is the tenth title, as well as a reboot, of the Spec Ops series. The player controls Captain Martin Walker, who is sent into a post-catastrophe Dubai with an elite Delta Force team on a recon mission. As the game progresses, Walker begins to experience hallucinations and slowly realizes the horror of war.

[u] Review [/u]
This game is absolutely stunning when it comes to the story, I wasn't hooked at the start of the campaign. It felt like a typical shooter for the first few chapters but once I started to understand the story, I was blown away! It left a lot of question marks above my head half way through but it's all pieced together once you've reached the end.

There's plenty of choices to make during the game but it all leads to the same path, you're left with a couple of more choices right at the end which will be you're final ending. It's a very deep story line, showing you what war can do to a man/woman. It gives you more of an insight of how bad things can get.

[h3]Game Title:[/h3] Spec Ops: The Line  
[b]Platform Played On:[/b] Steam / PC  
[b]Hours Played:[/b] ⌛ Enough to still think about it years later  

[b]📜 Story & Writing (5/5):[/b]  
- Spec Ops: The Line delivers one of the most powerful and emotionally jarring narratives I’ve experienced in a shooter. The way it peels back the layers of morality, war, and the illusion of heroism is masterful. It doesn't hold your hand—it makes you question every decision and every motive.  

[b]🌆 Personal Impact & Setting (5/5):[/b]  
- Growing up in Dubai, seeing the city brought to its knees in such a haunting and believable way was emotionally heavy. Skyscrapers I recognized turned to ruins, iconic areas buried in sand—it was devastatingly surreal. That visual pain added weight to every step of the campaign.

[b]🧠 Ethical & Psychological Impact (5/5):[/b]  
- The moral ambiguity, the mental descent of the protagonist, the constant internal conflict—it all hit hard. The game doesn’t just challenge your skills, it challenges your ethics. You’ll walk away with questions, discomfort, and realizations—and that’s what makes it brilliant. It forces you to feel the consequences of war in ways other shooters never dare to.

[b]🎮 Gameplay & Mechanics (4/5):[/b]  
- Mechanically, it’s a competent third-person shooter. Cover, gunplay, and squad control all function well, though not groundbreaking. But here, the gameplay takes a back seat to the message—and that’s okay. It's the emotions behind each bullet that matter most.

[b]🎨 Visuals & Atmosphere (4.5/5):[/b]

An extroadinary game that on first glimpse might seem like a generic 'Call of Duty' esque action shooter with a tacked on story, but honestly, while it may be a generic third-person action shooter in the gameplay department, the story is something that will blow anybody away and a must-play for those that're fans of gritty storytelling.

"The US military does not condone the killing of unarmed combatants. But this isn't real, so why should you care?" 

This isn't a game of heroes. This isn't just about shooting hundreds of soldiers. It's about distinguishing between a definite purpose and hatred driven by bloodlust. About losing yourself in your own reality. About crossing THE line. 

Inspired by movies such as Heart of Darkness and Apocalypse Now, Spec Ops: The Line approaches the players with a negative outlook on their actions, constantly opposing and conflicting them by breaking the 4th wall via subtle messages or straight-in-the-face mockery: an effective method to make us feel bad by the end of the story, assuring us of our relentless and blunt nature as killing machines. A rescue operation in Dubai quickly turns into a slaughter: it doesn't take too long until our Captain Martin Walker and his elite Delta Team are forced to go lethal and things become much darker as they go along. But regardless of how many bodies keep piling up or what incoherent mess they got themselves into: the murdering doesn't stop and Walker faces his goal with full determination. Eventually, his commands lead to more casualties than he would wish for, unobtrusively losing his mind. The process of deterioration from a grounded leader to an unstoppable mindless killer is evident: his voice, his brutality, it's all affected to the point where the real threat ends up being him, or more accurately us, the players. 

The ingenious story of a soldier's personal hell is easily the highlight of this game, but one should not disregard the gameplay still! The control scheme screams Gears copy, but every single input is comfortably responsive and fluid. Shooting also works better than in most TPSes of that generation: no matter what caliber or size of your gun, they are accordingly accurate and work as intended. Our side-arm is not an irreplaceable piece of equipment and some guns allow us to attach a silencer for better recoil-control or switch between burst and full-auto, ammo pickups don't have to be taken per prompt and grenades are assigned to their own button: I'd say this is almost pure perfection, as far as smoothness goes, with one very minor complaint being the shoulder view switch mechanic, which can only be toggled when zoomed in. Even though the game may seem like a squad-based shooter at first, it's really not: your only means of commanding is pointing at enemies and targetting them once at a time, but the AI does a great job at taking them out. 

The game is running on Unreal Engine 3 and does show some dust (no pun intended) for the time it's been released, the particles, sand(storm) effects and character models, especially as they change over time, are awesome to look at nonetheless. Sound design is somewhat on the bare minimum side, but the mix of licensed and original music saves it by a long shot. I've not experienced a single crash, glitch or anything game-breaking and there is audio-logs for collectibles along with the unlockable difficulty setting FUBAR for a good challenge: a little replay value was needed, as the main campaign is rather short at the 5-6 hours mark. On behalf of 2K, multi-player modes are also included, but it's nothing short of an after-thought and clearly out of place, I haven't ever laid my fingers on it nor do I plan to. The additional coop mode is worth a mention though, so you can experience the horrors of war together! 

Even though I've been entertained by being forced to shame myself, which sounds so strange on its own, it's been a nice experiment for us to witness how maddening war can be and how we realize its ugliness when it's already too late. But as far as ambitious non-mainstream projects goes, this one too has been a commercial failure, but I feel like it gained popularity years later, receiving all the praise it deserves so much. Should be relatively cheap now so pick it up, you'd miss out big time otherwise.

[h1] The Line is in fact thin and linear, but it’s not without some merit	[/h1]
The two steps forwards that Spec Ops takes with the narrative comes in the form of synthesis and harrowing images. There are nice little details throughout the game that come off as bugs and such, but are truly just nice touches of foreshadowing and manifestations of the story. The game also doesn’t pull punches with certain images and material that certainly get brushed over in many pieces of popular media.  

The one step back in the narrative comes in the form  of predictable video game story pitfalls.  It has the journal entries that are easy to overlook and sometimes offer a conflicting ton.  One of the major themes is about the illusion of choice in video games. On top of that the game likes to mock the player for shooting people, but that is the only thing the game lets us do. There aren’t Big Daddies that only respond with violence if provoked, these are just fodder soldier enemies that shoot at you and can only be deterred by death. The situation it puts players in says more about the shortcomings of this game rather than video games in general.  

Everything gameplay wise comes off as lazy game design. Spec Ops: The Line is meant to be a direct response to shooters like Call of Duty and Battlefield (when they were focused on "modern warfare"). It somewhat succeeds in that regard, but you have to wonder why a game meant to be criticizing other bland desert shooters, is still a bland shooter itself. 

In the end, it is far from perfect, but it at least tried to be different in some ways.

If you're wanting a story, this is one of the best out there, and certainly worth it when it is on sale (or sometimes free with Humble Bundle). The lower difficulties are great, and there is some replayability factor, as there is multiple endings (and its worth going through the game again rather then just reloading a checkpoint). As you go up the difficulty, it really does ramp up, so if your looking for an extremely difficult challenge, this is also for you! There are however issues that may can your views on this game.

1)- you are forced to babysit two morons for AI that cant seem to do anything right. On the easiest difficulty, they are no issue as (other then the times you are required to use them) you can take every enemy out yourself.On normal, as the enemy intelligence increases your AI teammates decreases and will start to walk into grenades and not use cover. This means that they get injured and you have to run into the middle of the battlefield -with enemies all around you- and revive them or you have to start over. If you try to get one to heal the other, they both go down. On hard difficulty, this is extremely annoying as they seem to want to purposefully make you die over and over again. In the rare instances where you can use stealth, they will do it, but will often walk right in front of the enemy, thus alerting everyone. 

2) The way they implemented running, cover and vaulting. This game requires you to run from cover-to-cover, yet running is a nightmare-especially as the difficulty increases. When you start running, the only way to stop is to aim down sights, so if you turn, you turn like a tank while still running. This causes you to run past where you wanted to go, and usually into enemies. Running to cover is also annoying, as there's about 50% chance you'll run to cover, only for the game to make you stand there (rather then automatically putting you in cover like it should) and you end up with a million bullets in you. The vaulting system is okay, but it is a hit/miss situation if the game actually does let you do it or not.

3) Checkpoints put you in stupidly bad areas. I had one where the checkpoint put me standing up right in the middle of a field of enemies, and so unsurprisingly, I kept dying and having to repeat the bit over and over. Checkpoints are also few and far between, which on harder difficulties is really annoying, and you have to do several large gunfights before getting another save. There is no manual saving or reloading checkpoints other then the last one.

I had heard about Spec Ops: The Line for years before I actually pulled the trigger on it. All of the youtubers and reviewers I followed seemed to love it, claiming it had an amazing and inspiring story, and I feel that might be part of the reason why my review will be very different from the overwhelming majority of the others for this game. I also realize that I did not finish the game as of writing this review, which means my perspective is not complete. However, I simply could not find the motivation to finish this game.

I spent a bit of time wondering why this was, and I reached this conclusion: the story is simply not good enough to warrant suffering through the gameplay. I played this game with keyboard/mouse (my aim is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ with a controller), and the controls felt clunky. The level design is linear and boring, while also not always being clear about where to go next. The shooting mechanics are fine, but they are very basic and don't add much to the genre. Commanding the squad was the only part of the gameplay that I really enjoyed. It felt as thought the combat was simply there to stretch the story and increase the game's playtime. It never felt like integral to the story, creating a disconnect that made me dread the actual levels. 

As I implied earlier, I think my expectations for the story were much too high going into this game. Many FPS/TPS go the way of trying to show the bad side of war, and to be honest I don't think this game did it much better than any of them. Again, I did not finish the game or the story, so it might get better towards the latter stages, but from what I experienced it was not significantly better than other shooters I've played. 

I think this stems from the linearity of the game, as well as the unrealistic scenarios you get put into. It felt contradictory to go from dialogue where war is difficult and traumatizing, to a level where my two squad members and I have to kill waves upon waves of enemies to progress. It didn't feel like a dilemma, because I didn't have a choice. And again, maybe that changes later on in the game, but from what I had experienced, the story did not compensate for the stale gameplay.

From my experience, this game is certainly not worth the $30 price tag, though if you can pick it up on sale it could be worth a shot.
This game is not unlike your run of the mill shooters, it has a gripping story. It makes you care about the characters and questions your moral compass at times. Campaign alone is well worth the buy.

Spec Ops the line is one of the games I will never ever play again.

The Story itself is hauntingly depressing, and twisted on a narrative aspect, however for a emotional aspect, strangely personal. This game is true horror, and an incredible breakdown of the Call of Duty Military genre, and taking those ridiculous action movie tropes from the games, and utilizing them in a more realistic and effective setting. There was one scene. (You know the one. If you didn't TRUST ME, you will know.) That made me sick to my stomach, and I had to take a 2 hour break from playing through the game. This game is disturbing, depressing and horrific, and has an incredible ending that holds many layers, encouraging you to play the game again.

Gameplay 4/10 The cover shooting is half assed as ♥♥♥♥. It's so tedious getting picked off from AI from miles away, or wrestling with the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ controls. However, on a narrative perspective, I loved how the gameplay played out from a narrative setting, since in the beginning you are playing it like a modern military tps, going out of cover, and mowing down enemies like Call of Duty to the ending where you are literally at this point just surviving and fending for your life, spending dozens of minutes behind cover, without moving, just barely peeking out, as you hide again. Great transition.

Audio 10/10 The shootouts in this game has the most realistic audio I've ever heard. It makes you think about the "bad guys" you shoot, as you hear them desperately scream commands, as they panic, or even sound like they are on the brink of tears. Truly haunting. Sometimes I would sit back and listen to the audio in the shootouts. The background is also rich, and detailed, make the scenarios so powerful. The audio makes these moments timeless. Also the voice acting is Movie Quality. Total 10.

Story 10/10 The story is of course, the main seller. Being a story that seems so generic, after I have played the game, I was shocked to see how much detail and hints the Narration would give. Also the ending, 10/10

Multiplayer 0/10 .....

Overall you need to "experience" this game. It's an experience you will never get back, and one that will stick with you, true horror, where you will pause the game and think to yourself, "This scenario has probably happened in real life somewhere" It is horrific, it is ugly, and overall, the most memorable game I have ever played.

It is then that you, the player, realize that you aren't playing a character, you are seeing the world through the eyes of someone else, like a movie you cannot stop. The world starts to feel more hostile, the main character's actions start to feel more psychotic to you, nothing matters anymore. What once disguised itself as a generic run-of-the-mill militaric shooter started to show itself as nothing but a tragic story of a person who wanted to do good, but because you want to do good doesn't mean your actions won't have consequences.

It's not really a shooter, it leans far more into horror territory the more you advance. Something people should definetly experience for a great story that has no happy ending.

Some people might argue that is the point, but that just might as well be a lazy defence. The only saving grace from combat becoming boring is the occasional map interactions that you can find while in combat. For instance, you can fight during sandstorm or shatter glass above enemies so they could be crushed under tons of sand. If, by any chance you've liked the combat there's a special multiplayer mode with whopping FIVE players. 
Finally, the story is why the game deserves the praise. To keep the review spoiler free i will not say much. You play as one of the three members of Delta Force team - Martin Walker. Your only task is to do some reconnaissance to find survivors after massive crisis in Dubai, but you want to do more.

As for the actual gameplay, it's both loved and hated. Personally, I thoroughly enjoy the gameplay and find myself constantly coming back to play multiplayer and the co-op missions just because I enjoy the feel of this game and the world it has built. However, many people do think that the gameplay is underwhelming and the only redeeming factor is the story. I disagree, but that's just my own opinion on the playstyles it provides.

If that's not your style however, I would still get this game if you're looking for a powerful story that focuses on moral dilemma and the cruelties of war in this action packed roller coaster of emotion and confusion.

Most military games you play are the happy-go-lucky games where the squad gets along and things might be difficult for the characters, but everything ends up going there way.

Spec Ops: The Line does not do that. I found myself angered by command decisions, confused by some scenarios, and frustrated by some characters. While that does not typically sound like a positive review, it is the case with this one. Spec Ops is a game that does what it sets out to do and the money for it is not for replayability, or long campaign hours, because it has neither comparatively to a lot of franchise games; no the money is for the experience you get playing it- the stresses you get in if you allow yourself to be immersed.

That said, I was expecting more player-made decisions. I wasn't expecting a full blown RPG, but some of the hard decisions should have been left to the player- though I don't think it would have changed the story line. The controls were super funky and took some getting used to (I try to stick with the default controls). Space is run and shift is vault- what?

This game makes a strong statement, but does it in a way that can blunt its effectiveness.
The moral is that you, the player, are just as responsible for the descent into chaos as Walker. Just as Walker could have backed out and left at any point, rejecting what he perceives to be his orders,  so too could you have closed the game and ignored the objective prompts.

While it's an effective way to remark on how much agency we have regardless of how things might appear, the fact that the choice we get is extradiegetic with the rest of the game that isn't, and it's easy to sympathise with people who deny the player's culpability due to railroading.

This is going to be a multiplayer focused review since it's something that most don't tend to touch on for this game.

To quickly sum up the single player portion, some good writing and direction saves what otherwise would've been a very average shooter, although the plot can be a bit pretentious.

The multiplayer for Spec Ops has gained somewhat of a negative reputation throughout the years as the poster child for 'tacked-on modes' when the developers came out and disavowed it. It was claimed to be a mindless COD clone that didn't fit in with the 'serious' themes of the game. I don't agree that such narratives provide good reason to not include multiplayer. Look at Vietcong. Typically, multiplayer modes in shooters are just something extra, distinct from the main game. They're not part of the campaign a la MindJack. I don't see anything wrong with having two thematically dissonant games in one package, provided they're kept separate from each other, as is the case here. If anything, every shooter could benefit from having some sort of deathmatch game mode in them as in creating the campaign, a unique set of weapons & mechanics are created with it, that should always be at the very least interesting to fight other people with. There's also the chance it could redeem a bad single player.

Now that that's out of the way, if Spec Ops: The Line is a COD clone, it's easily better than any Call of Duty I've played. I'm not a fan of the Call of Duty formula. Big Red One is the only game in the series I've played so far where I actually enjoyed the multiplayer. Spec Ops: The Line however, takes it and pushes it ever so slightly in the tactical shooter direction. Not enough to morph it, but enough to create something that requires way more thought while still being an arcadey shooter at heart.

Spec Ops: The Line introduces stealth to the equation. Similar to The Last of Us multiplayer, sprinting reveals your position to enemies on the minimap, and thus becomes something you'll only do in combat, rather than just for general map traversal, which is something that greatly irritated me about the Call of Duty games. Your ability to easily see around corners, and over your head due to the third person perspective also encourages crouching in areas with low cover, in order to stay hidden. Couple all of this with the fluid map design where you can almost always get shot from more than one direction, and you'll have a game that actively encourages you to stay quiet at the risk of getting flanked. The mindless running around of the formula it takes as its starting point thus changes into a cautious type of map traversal, ideally with teammates to watch your back. Combine this with arcadey gunfights, in contrast to the deadly near instant-deaths in a typical tactical shooter like Arma or Red Orchestra and what you have is a genuinely unique experience that I would recommend to fans of both sub-genres. The time to kill is lower than most COD games, but not so low that you're screwed whenever you're exposed.

Now one noteworthy thing that Spec Ops does really well in multiplayer is the third person cover shooting. In spite of how simple it sounds, the gameplay loop of having you pop out of cover to shoot and pop back in when you get shot is something that multiplayer games rarely manage to achieve. The Gears of War games have such high TTKs that it's always better for you to stay out of cover, and take a few hits while dishing more damage, while other games like Rainbow Six Vegas have such slow cover animations and expose so much of you that it's better for you to just peek out normally. Spec Ops: The Line managed to hit that sweet spot. I had fights where my opponent & I were repeatedly popping out to take shots at each other, moving back in to regen health as soon as the other hit us, changing positions, and repeating. It was great fun. The TTK is such that you'll have a chance of surviving everything bar headshots & sniper rifles by moving in to cover as soon as you got shot, but not so high that it's ever advantageous to stay out. You're always one or two bullets away from dying.

Overall, I'd say multiplayer was the better half in this game.

Don't overlook it, and give it a shot.
