Honestly, this review is very late to the party, and if you haven't already played Spec Ops: The Line, I don't know what more you need to be told to finally play it. This game is a rare example of a "Triple A" title that also manages to make a genuine artistic statement with its narrative, and is an overall phenomenal game.

The gameplay is simple enough, it's a third-person, cover-based shooter, a formula that had been perfected in the "Triple A" space for years even back when this game was first released, and that fact is reflected in tight, responsive controls. Of note is that there are a number of opportunities to make use of the environment to deal with enemies, and when giving commands to your squad, there are fully-voiced lines that will reference unique features about your current location, which is a nice touch. However, the gameplay, while technically competent and lacking any significant flaws, doesn't stand out, either. That said, Spec Ops: The Line's gameplay only exists as a means to deliver on the story, which is the real reason you want to buy this game right now. Oh, and there's a multiplayer mode, but it was clearly tacked-on to satisfy publisher demands, and I'm not factoring it into my review at all.

To go into too much detail about Spec Ops: The Line's story would give away the whole plot, but, the basic premise is that  Dubai has been hit with massive sandstorms, and the city's elite evacuated in secret, leaving thousands of innocent people to die. A Colonel John Konrad volunteered to help with relief efforts, and ultimately, his entire battalion defied orders to evacuate and effectively deserted. A number of troubling reports made their way out of the city regarding the actions of Konrad's battalion since then, and they were all disavowed as traitors.

When a radio message is received from Konrad declaring his attempt to evacuate the civilians of Dubai a complete failure, a covert team is sent in to retrieve him, by force if necessary, led by Captain Martin Walker (the player character), who always viewed Konrad with admiration. Now, the more well-read of you may have already noticed, but if this sounds suspiciously like Heart of Darkness (or Apocalypse Now!, its Vietnam-era adaptation), you're on the right track. However, that's just the starting point, the plot takes some very notable turns from there, at times even deliberately subverting one's familiarity with the works that inspired it.

Suffice it to say, the story is nothing short of brilliant, and while the game runs about five to eight hours total, the pacing makes that the perfect length. In fact, I would recommend you play through the game in a single sitting, to maximize its impact. This is a game that everybody should play through at least once, if you don't want to pay full price, put it on your wishlist and grab in during the next Steam sale. Either way, do NOT deny yourself this experience.

Spec Ops: The Line is a very solid third-person shooter, with one of the most interesting takes on story of any modern day action game. 

The gameplay is nothing to write home about. Stick to cover, order your squad mates around. Regenerating health, two weapons. Pop out, aim and shoot. It's mostly Gears of War without much reliance on chainsaws and such. There's nothing about this game's actual play to make it really stand out, other than the fact it is solid, entertaining, and quite challenging at times. The shooting is satisfying, and should keep you satisfied through the game's average running length. 

The only real issues I ever faced were the usual annoyances with any third-person cover shooter. Running around like an idiot trying to stick to some object while you're being shot, instead of just being able to duck. 

However, the reason you play this game is for the story, and the way it is presented. It's the kind of open-ended, interpretive narrative that people write their thesis about. It is as much an exploration on the nature of war and atrocity, human nature, and psychological trauma as it is a shooting game. 

It's not the most interesting or profound experience you will ever have, but I think it's definitely worth going through at least once. Any vague hints will only spoil the experience, so I will only say that it's worth playing.

The soundtrack is very good and contributes a lot to the atmosphere. Even though the game doesn't try to recreate Dubai architecture exactly, the level design is done nicely and it's quite diverse. 
The AI does it's job, but it's not very smart (doesn't change location often enough, his head pops out of cover, your teamates often go in the middle of the enemies which is not realistic etc.), the only advantage is the 1-2 shot kill on Fubar, which makes you play the game more slowly, moving from cover to cover.

Anyway this remains a great game with a good story and a reasonable price. Strongly recommended.

Just finished this game, and I have to say it is one of the best narrative driven games I've ever played, period. This game explores the role of the player in violence, the horror and mission creep in warfare, and the way in which the circumstances of war can often lead to justifications and dissillusionment that are both harmful and deadly. This game from a narrative standpoint will challenge you like possibly no other game you have played. The writing and plot are flawless. The progression of the main charecters is impressive, both in the degradation of the mental states and the progression of how they feel towards killing. 

The level design in this game is some of the best I have ever seen. Not necessarily from the standpoint that it is layered and complex, because it is extremely liniar from a gameplay perspective. But the level design in terms of art, storytelling, and atmosphere is downright incredible. You will find yourself stumbling through the remains of a once great and opulent city. There are details everywhere of the people and life that used to be there. Now it's all buried under sand. The kind of enviorments and structures you find yourself in are varied and engaging, and most importantly tell the story that the narrative is trying to tell you. 

My big complaint with this game is the gameplay. Take a watered down, flawed version of the Gears of War combat system, and there you have this game. The cover system is oftentimes infuriating, many times not registering the space bar when you want to take cover or stop running. The execution feature is needlessly brutal and kind of awkwardly thrown in there (some may argue this could be a narrative choice, and I am willing to entertain that point of view). And most importantly, the gameplay is incredibly repetitive and wave based. Which again, people make arguements that this is a narrative choice. That is very possible, but the reality is that with games, the gameplay has to be engaging. If it's just another "Oh ♥♥♥♥, we got Tangos on the way!!! Take cover!!!" over and over again, it's gonna get old after eight hours. 

A recommendation I would make is to not play this game on the hardest difficulty. I did that, and I beleive it makes it needlessly frustrating to grind through waves of enemies. It only increases the frustration you will have with a broken cover system and other game mechanics. Play it on normal at least, even easy (although I prefer some challenge, so if I could do it again, I would play it on normal). 

All this being said, and some broken mechanics and repetitive gameplay aside, this game is without a doubt a masterpiece akin to Apocolypse Now. I'm gonna be spending a lot of time thinking and reading about this game for awhile. If you enjoy narrative, play this game. It is unmatched.

Here is my review: 

PLOT :

You are Martin, an idealistic soldier with high rank as captain. Along with your two partner and subordinate. As a military shooter game, the plot will drag you into philosophical questions about choices and your realization (as player) to continue fighting and also SO:TL will deconstruct the whole thing of being what is right and what is wrong in military combat with realitic touch how are you the hero of this story when you have to fight what you tought is right as your duty.

CONTROL :

Grab your controller or simply use mouse+keyboard, the control is pretty responsive with stunning graphic and dynamic camera movement that shows third person perspective which makes this game easy to enjoy and not really hard when you are in combat, I personally use normal mode and found its challenging because as in combat you have to think on every single move you have to do.  As main character, you can bring two type of guns and explosives where you can find along the gameplay or you can simply grab your enemy weapons after being taken down. As a captain, you can order your two partners (as AI) to use their skills in order to solve the thightness in some combats where they can shoot specific enemies or doing distractions to move forward. The gameplay set some realitic tone when it comes to your health system, you wont see any healtbar or indicator, just avoid massive of gunfires from enemy or you instantly being killed, your character can survive if your partners maintain their distance in order to save you if you are taken down. Probably, the annoying side of control system is when the cover system in combat have false detection in deciding to take cover or moving forward. 


VISUAL :

Enjoy stunning visual of post-disaster state of Dubai where sky scrappers are being torn and crushed buried among desert hills, walk and explore straight into miserable places of war casualties and what left that you will experience. Some parts are athmospheric and you may find some disturbing scenes (that involves with the plot) This game visual will touch your minds (literally) and your character mind when they face some odd strange situations where leads you into questioning, are you enjoying this kind of game, or you just feel something else. Moreover, this game have to offer interesting side of how music really influences how you perceive this game as serious but sometimes (in the early parts of games) it have the fun part of musical cues that can be enjoyed while you shoot everyone. The voice acting are top-notch and convincing that the characters you are playing have the situation as in the game.

FUN : 

SO : TL have good tier storyline where I assumed eventhough the plot sounds cliche at the first time (about a soldier being a hero and typical American shooters where glorifies its greatness and you act like another Rambo in this game, eventually, I was wrong. This games have no fun when you really think of how it projects what is great being American soldier or simple being a soldier when facing the outcome what you did on the entire gameplay. Yes, you do mass killing people and blow some ♥♥♥♥♥ to progress, its fun on video game medium. But when SO : TL approaches of realistic tone of this kind of genre. It has the plus point where I stated this game deconstructs what is kind of type shooter genre looks like mostly, and this game prove us wrong. 

If you like playing shooter game with great storyline and message, grab this game and experience your state of thought will be filled the consequences of various feeling on your main character decision and choice by the hand of yourself as the player in the challenging of combat system but still rewards you an thought-provolong experience.

The repetitive gameplay actually makes sense in the context of PTSD. Mobs upon mobs run into you, soldiers or rebels, intentions or goals make no difference. You just shoot them without questions asked, but an uncomfortable feeling lingers in the back of your mind. This is where the illusion of choice comes in, shattering the gameplay's monotony. The mechanics incentivize a certain action, but you always have the option not to do so. Even if the results are the same, the choices always feel meaningful. Just like in real wars, there is always an alternative that will cause the lest pain, but most people won't notice it until it's too late, when their psyche rules over their consciousness. Spec Ops is plays like your everyday run-of-the-mill military shooter. Shoot the bad guys, throw grenades, blow up helicopters, and take out that turret - all of which are common shooter tropes overused for a decade. For the first few chapters, there's not much to set Spec Ops apart from any other Call of Duty or Gears of War title. 

Except it isn't one. Taking advantage of the thoughtlessness by which the game's mechanics seem to be built on, Spec Ops is a game that takes the player's thoughtlessness while completing the game and uses it to question as to why the military FPS even exists as a genre. 

Whether you want to feel like an action hero or to have fun shooting targets, the game will make you wonder just what the hell are you doing.

Simply put, Spec Ops is one of the most underrated games of all time. The strength of it is in the way it tells its story, which is a way that you simply do not see in other games. It has a lot more in common with other mediums, such as movies, than The Last of Us ever has. It is truly phenomenal storytelling and direction. The cast did an amazing job. This game has a way of stirring your emotions and bringing out reactions in you, sometimes in ways that you didn't expect or even might disturb you.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
The gameplay is by no means bad, far from it, but it still consists of standard cover-based third-person shooter mechanics that we're all familiar with.

[h1]Story[/h1]
The story is the main reason to pick up this game as it offers a different view on war than what we're used to from these types of games, a view on the horrors of war accompanied by a very bleak, yet interesting, narrative.

[h1]Replayability[/h1]
There are 4 difficulties available (3 at the start, you'll have to beat the game on [b]Suicide Mission[/b], the Hard difficulty to unlock [b]FUBAR[/b], the Very Hard difficulty). In the higher difficulties, especially on [b]FUBAR[/b], it is pretty much a necessity to sprint from cover to cover and to command your squad; you will still die plenty of times though.

While the game has multiple endings (3, I believe), it doesn't really warrant a 2nd playthrough by the non-achievement hunters.

[h1]Multiplayer[/h1]
I doubt anyone that's interested in purchasing this title is doing it for the multiplayer, but if one is, then I suggest looking elsewhere as the multiplayer doesn't seem to have ever been a big hit and if there still is a small playerbase, then it would not be beginner-friendly.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
I would recommend purchasing this title if it's on sale as the story is a worthwhile experience.

[h1]Campaign[/h1]
Spec Ops: The Line is a game with standardized third-person shooter gameplay but with an aberrantly deep and powerful story with an unforgettable ending.

The game starts off with Captain Walker accompanied by Sergeant Lugo and Lieutenant Adams who begin as ordinary cliché characters who make cheesy remarks and below average quality humour jokes which is a usual formula for a game of this genre, however as the game progresses you encounter more and more horrific events which drastically deprives them of these characteristics and makes them cold-hearted soldiers. Instead of glorifying the image of being a soldier this game puts you through the relentless horrors and cruelty involved in a war zone. The conclusion is the absolute highlight of this game and features one of the best plot twists to date across all platforms of entertainment and that is what makes this game stand out from the rest of the other third-person shooters.

However despite how much I praise the storyline's uniqueness I can't exactly say the same for the gameplay. There is nothing wrong with it, but it certainly isn't anything special either; it's just average. If you've played another decent third-person shooter with a cover system this game will feel quite similar. You cover behind varying objects and peek your head to shoot when an enemy is exposed and when you have enough health to risk yourself being exposed. When you have taken damage you get back into cover until your health regenerates (kind of like Wolverine). Ammunition is scarce which makes the game more intense and makes it a requirement to determine whether a suitable weapon or a weapon with more ammo is a better idea in a situation.

You are accompanied with your allies for the majority of the game and them dying will result in a game over. This type of mechanic is usually detrimental to the enjoyment of the player because it becomes irritating and detracts from your ability to play the game and progress as you wish, however this is not the case in this instance. They help shoot enemies proficiently and you can even command them who to specifically kill and are able to use grenades even when you don't have any left, which can be used to kill people behind turrets, which adds a strategic component to combat. When a teammate is incapacitated you have a certain amount of time to heal him and get him back on his feet before he bleeds to death, but doing this isn't even necessary if another comrade is available who can heal the other comrade to health if you command him to do so. When your comrades are incapacitated it is usually due to your own incompetence rather than their idiocy since you have not been a helpful asset to the team, and are not killing enough enemy soldiers in time. (Unless you're playing on the "FUBAR difficulty" in which case your teammates will frequently fall in battle to add challenge to the most challenging difficulty setting in the game).

The game is set in Dhu Bai during a huge sandstorm which makes a great atmosphere for the game. Seeing and travelling from all the impressive skyscrapers in the middle of an intense sandstorm is spectacular.

Would I recommend this game? Well even though this is a "recommended review" I would exclusively recommend this to people who enjoy the third-person shooter genre. Lots of other reviewers on Steam claim this game to be an exception for third-person shooters however this game's main purpose is basically a big fat build up to the exceptional finale, so if you dislike third-person shooters in general this game will probably bore you.

[h1]Multiplayer[/h1]
The multiplayer segment of this game is an online service which involves you playing against other players with different types of modes which are unoriginal and monotonous. As I previously mentioned in the singleplayer section this game shines in terms of storyline, not gameplay, and the multiplayer option just feels like an inferior CS:GO or Call of Duty clone. Do not bother buying this game if the multiplayer aspect of games interests you.

Spec Ops: The Line is somewhat unique title that ditches away with the savior hero figure and takes a more realistic approach to the horrors of war. I think that an appropriate description is Apocalypse Now 2: Modern Warfare. The story, the characters and the music hint towards a spiritual successor to the 1979 Vietnam themed movie. Be warned, this is no Shaving Ryan's Privates or anything like that; don't expect to play this game and dream at night that you're a hero. 

The game startw with you leading a small team and proceed on a rescue mission in Dubai. Your main drive forward is the pursuit of your former superior and once life savior, Colonel John Konrad. As the story unfolds, you try to make sense of what happened and what is currently going on. I have played it only in the single player campaign, but the game menu list co-op and other forms of multiplayer. My run at a relaxed pace was a bit more that 7 hours, but your milage may vary by +-2 hours, depending on your skills and your desire to collect all the intelligence scattered across the game. The gameplay mechanics is a shoot from cover from 3rd person over the shoulder perspective. The run/sprint action is a bit awkward at first, but players should get used to it quite easily. There is no jumping, but you vault obstacles while running or from behind cover. What it lacks in freedom of movement and mechanics, it compensates by story, animation, voice acting and overall atmosphere. One thing worth remembering is that 33 is just the right-hand side of 88. Does that mean that it’s the right side, or that is just half the craziness? Well, play the game and find out!

- no vehicles to drive
- no night missions

Plus:

+ graphics are good and framerate is smooth
+ character textures “evolve” as the game unfolds, further adding realism to the physical traumas and scars.

This is another game that has a "Do Something" button.  In fact, it has SEVERAL "Do Something" buttons.  Almost every control the game has except for WASD has multiple context-dependent bindings, and you pray every time you use one that the game will decide to do what you intended.  This just adds to the confusion, especially when sometimes just nothing happens.  Or it LOOKS like the game has handed control back to you after a cut scene, but you can't actually do anything yet.  Oh, you blinked, or your attention was on a different spot on the screen?  Sorry, you just missed a control tutorial message you'll never get again.  Wait, did we forget to tell you how to use that?  Sucks to be you.  Q to throw a grenade?  Yeah, that makes ... um ... perfect sense.  NOT.

The main source of confusion, though, is that you start out on what seems to be a fairly straight-forward investigate-and-reconnoiter mission, that turns in short order into a rescue mission ... in which you can't actually rescue anyone.  Except for one guy, and then the next thing you know, within 20 minutes of beginning play, your rescue mission has turned into the game forcing you to fight and kill the people you set out to rescue in order to survive, you seem to be facing TWO enemy factions, both your own nation and both trying to kill you, and why the *@&$^@#^%$ am I here and what am I doing and why am I killing my own fellow soldiers and --

NOPE.  NOPE.  NOPE.  Enough.  Not doing this.  Too much crapsack, too much brain-hurts.

This game, at least in its opening phase, makes no sense.  Perhaps it'll all be explained further in, and the game will start to actually make sense, and perhaps you eventually acquire an understanding that there is some point to what you're doing, but ...  nope.  Too little, too late.  Spec Ops: The Line lost me in the first hour of undirected blind confusion and slaughtering everything that moves with no explanation of why I'm doing it.

Take Two had a generous beginning time window to gain my interest, get me invested and sell me on why I should play this game, and they blew it.

Spec Ops: The Line is not only a fantastic game in its own right but acts as a perfect time capsule for a generation in gaming.

The seventh generation of gaming was certainly one where the medium started experiencing some major growing pains, especially in regards to the kind of content it wanted to cover. Many development studios decided that they were done with the fun animal mascot characters and wanted to move in on telling gritty stories with human characters in more realistic environments but not being too sure on how to go about it. Given the large success of titles like Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare it became very common to see gruff military men in many games that took themselves way too seriously which made many titles come off as extremely generic and caused the industry as a whole feel like it was somewhat stagnating. Towards the later end of this came Spec Ops: The Line, a game to hold up a mirror to it all.

Story is absolutely one of Spec Op's strongest points. Set in Dubai after it's been hit by a massive storm Delta team is sent in to make contact with the locals and the previously stationed 33rd Infantry Battalion. As Walker and his team go deeper down the rabbit hole they begin to see the extremes both the 33rd and the populace were pushed to and endured along with the impacts it's had on them mentally, facing their own conflicts as they proceed. It's a game that manages to capture that more real, gritty feeling no other games did which is quite an accomplishment especially as it doesn't then glorify it. The game dabbles in many themes as you go along and offers a few different options to the player as they progress that help shape the narrative. With a multiple choices and many little details you might not have noticed the first time the game is extremely fascinating to replay.

The story is given even more weight by the absolutely flawless voice acting in this game. You might be sick of hearing the default voice of Nolan North in plenty of titles but I assure this game will show you what a little bit of solid directing can achieve. The rest of the cast all pull off equally incredible performances adding a much more real and raw feel to the dialogue. As the game also capitalises on its setting with excellent camera work and scenery design you'll get some truly fantastic shots as you make your way through the fallen Dubai, this accompanied by the voice acting create some incredibly powerful scenes.

Gameplay is where people tend to have issues with Spec Ops due to it being very run-of-the-mill. While it is true that this title doesn't really bring anything new to the table mechanically and is a fairly clunky third person shooter I feel like people do not appreciate how the gameplay is used. It takes that gameplay and weaves it perfectly into the narrative itself. A simple example of this would be letting you control characters when making story decisions instead of just pressing A or B, which means there are more options than you may realise if you're willing to think outside the box. It truly is a game that takes total advantage of the medium in many ways that because of that I find it hard to knock the gameplay aspect of it even if the moment to moment of it is somewhat generic. It's worth noting that game is not worth picking up if you are in it for the multiplayer. Adding to it being a time capsule is the fact it includes a tacked on multiplayer that is completely throw away which even lead designer Cory Davis referred to as "cancerous".

In closing if you're a player who wants a good story, engaging use of gameplay, or wants to see the kind of game that many in the seventh generation was always trying to be and then some, pick up Spec Ops: The Line.

Spec Ops: The Line provides a much different experience to other modern shooters in that the protaganist is far from the war hero that he thinks he is becoming, saving a doomed Dubai from an old military corps gone evil.

We are thrown in as you and your team of two embark on a scouting mission to gain intel on the progress of the evacuation of Dubai civilians under supervision by a military division who defied orders in favour of helping the people escape. However as the story progresses. This division is under the command of a general you once served with and state that you owe your life to, after being wounded and dragged from battle by this what is seen as a god like figure by our main protaganist. The perceived events that are taking place by our main character are called in to serious question as you willingly make decisions that truly prove that some of the worst things can be done with the best intentions.

Aesthetically the game is your run of the mill military style graphics with a slightly washed out colour pallette, however the ambience created by level building sets the game apart in terms of details and keeping in with the idea that you're in a city succumbed to anarchy and panic amidst a catastrophic natural disaster. Transitions between checkpoints and key changes in pace are executed flawlessly to suit the ebb and flow of realistic modern combat.

Combat feels similar to that of the Gears of War games, third person with an interactive cover/move system that allows for tactical movement without prolonged exposure to enemy fire, however is most useful for those who seek a challenge and try the game at higher difficulty.
Your two squadmates can be commanded to attack specific enemies to cover your movements or to concentrate fire to free up and area of the map for you to then flank the enemy yourself, a much welcome feature even though they seem to hit next to nothing (Assuming this is to increase difficulty and reduce you letting the squad deal the damage for you)
As mentioned previously the level design is a step above the standard lesser known shooter titles and allows for both tactical movements and easy concealment of secrets/collectables.

Overall, Spec Ops: The Line is a true independant game in terms of story and environment in which you as the player are left confused at how what you have just done was possibly misinterpreted and the effects it has had on the wider city of Dubai, it's inhabitants and the entire physche of a soldier just doing his 'duty'

Back for round three of my review for this game - both the first and second reviews were ... not quite what I wanted, mainly because I hadn't beaten the game on the harder difficulty settings (specifically Suicidal & FUBAR), until now.

Pros:  

- A surprisingly great third-person action game!
- Solid graphics (for its time, and even now, 2018)

- Unexpected sequences at times gives the game a very unique advantage over other, similar games

- Generally speaking, the overall ‘mechanics’ of the game are solid, fluid, and feel ‘good’
- Decent, generally believable chatter/dialogue between characters
- Decisions you make can drastically change the game/story – I really liked this!
- It's a solid challenge (even on 'Normal' mode)
- Most importantly, it's FUN!  Finishing a ‘combat sequence’ feels good/rewarding


Cons:

- Very awkward ‘default’ controls (likely because it's a console port – tweak as needed!)

- Insane mouse sensitivity (you may want to check out this link:  https://pcgamingwiki.com/wiki/Spec_Ops:_The_Line#Change_general_sensitivity)

- Player’s AI squad mates are incredibly stupid at times, and function more as meat shields than anything else. They become a liability at times on higher/FUBAR difficulty modes, as they tend to rush blindly into battle, and are ‘downed’ within seconds; have fun playing medic

- On the higher difficulties (especially FUBAR) the game becomes incredibly frustrating at times.  Every 'battle' is more intense than the last, dying becomes the norm, and your patience WILL be tested

- “Ammo is sparce in Dubai” … unless you’re the AI.  Accuracy, ammo conservation, and ‘Executing’ enemies becomes extremely advantageous!

Final Thoughts:

If you haven’t played this game yet, do so – you’re absolutely going to enjoy it (if you like this style of game).  I’m truly impressed with the overall story and development of said story as the game progresses; and I don’t typically care THAT much about stories in military games.

That said, I'm not sure I can recommend the higher (Suicidal & FUBAR) difficulty modes.  On FUBAR mode (and Suicidal at times), many of the battles (I found) become/became ‘memory fights’ – learning the sequence of the battle, which enemies you’re fighting, where they come from, how many of them are there, how much ammo you have, and so on.  Is this a bad thing?  Not necessarily!  Many people (including myself) enjoy difficult games that you can come back to - this game definitely falls into that category when playing on Suicidal & FUBAR modes.

This is the quote that I find myself repeating as the end credits roll in Spec Ops: The Line. Since the game's release in 2012, I have spent small amounts of time dabbling within the game's demo that was released for the Xbox 360 as well the full release for when I purchased it here on Steam, but the game never captured my attention enough to commit to finishing it and I often found myself lost behind the confines of chapter 3 upon attempting to replay it and properly asserting myself back within the story. Yet, the other day I chose to gamble once more on the prospect that is Spec Ops: The Line and I am glad that I did, for this time I finished it. Many believe that The Line is its own entity, despite having the Spec Ops title tacked onto it. Spec Ops is a long running franchise that had its start on the original Playstation as a semi realistic tactical shooter that served to immerse players within the various different roles of the military. As the franchise grew, each installment grew more formulaic than its predecessor, as the last Spec Ops title to release was Spec Ops: Airborne Commando in 2002, which was a top down shooter. Fast forward a decade and here we have The Line. The shell of Spec Ops: The Line is a generic, third person, cover shooter with bare bones squad mechanics. Ever since its inception the Spec Ops franchise has attempted to set itself apart from the rest of the cannon fodder military shooters on the market and The Line upholds that creed. While the game's shooting mechanics are generic as can be, the differentiation comes in the form of its story, the horrific yet realistic imagery that it portrays, as well as the effect that this hell has on protaganist Martin Walker's mental state. Throughout the game, the player is taken on a journey as Delta Squad attempts to do good by the people they were ordered to rescue. Upon the opening of the first chapter, the game's credits list each of the developer's names as one would expect, but at the end, the subtitle "Special Guest: *insert player's name*" displays on screen. That is where the heart of The Line lies, within the choices you as the player make. For the choices are not Walker's or even that of his squadmates, but of yours and the player must suffer the consequences of those choices and actions because of it. Spec Ops: The Line is a meticulously crafted piece of media and deserves to be played by hardcore audiences, avid gamers, and even bro dudes racking up killstreaks. Well done.

This game is something special. This may be an ordinary military shooter on the surface with its derititve albeit solid 3 person shooter gameplay. However, before I comment on the story, I want to say this game looks fantastic when cranked to full settings. The environment comes alive with fantastic lighting, textures, shadows etc. Now the story of the game, which I will not spoil, but lets just say its a truly innovative story for video games. It is not your typical gung ho military call of duty badassery kick ass gun toating pro america military story. This is a truly haunting experience that will stick with you for a while after completion. The characters of Walker and his teamates along with Admiral Konrad, are some of the most memorable chaarcters in gaming because of their distinct personalities and character arcs, plus their respective voice actors do a fantastic job. This game made me quesiton my own morality, making me ask myself, what if the events of the game were real and what if I was living those events would I make the same decisions in real life as I did in the games story? I don't know honestly, but this game forces you to sit back and ponder the horrors of war and forces you to see as General Sherman once said "War Is Hell." This game has only a few drawbacks, as I mentioned, the deritive but solid 3rd person shooter gameplay (it can get somewhat repetitive, your AI partners can be dumb sometimes, and the tactical squad based gameplay boils down to pressing one button for two different outcomes and occassionaly dropping sand contextually on your enemies. [spoiler]So what do I think about the themes and the message of Spec Ops: The Line after all those years? It was really innovative in its execution and fresh back in the day, but now it can feel extremely heavy handled. We all were quite naive back then and we soaked all of that self-loath on our gaming activities and the excessive, mindless consumption of many different shooter games. That being said, nowadays gamers need to be treated much more fairly and they don't really like to be moralized how bad their habits are... especially from people who are all smug being a "culture critic" without having any substance to their claims and being generally dishonest.

Spec Ops: The Line has many very ungraceful moments in its campaign that trick players in very controversial way. Fortunately, it also leaves some clever gaps that save the message from being completely condescending or even outright hostile to the people playing it. This is greatly shown in the game's ending sequence, where the player has the final decision. In this one moment of surprise and extremely clever writing you have an option to disagree with the author's conclusion and vision. You still can stand up from the game firmly holding to your own opinion. It may be hard to catch on to that and get everything on your first playthrough, but the question is clear, the decision is yours and I'm really glad that we ended up with it instead of getting a ham-fisted moral. [h1]I'm Not A Bad Person, You're A Bad Game[/h1]

In Spec Ops: The Line you are given the role of Captain Generic Tough Guy and given a simple mission to go to Dubai and rescue/kill Colonel Kurtz from [i]Apocalypse Now[/i]. To the shock of everyone who has never played a video game, seen a movie, read a book, or experienced any sort of narrative in any context, things go to ♥♥♥♥. 

Your expectations are set up for this to be a standard forgettable modern 4-hour single player third person shooter experience - corridors leading into shooting galleries with waist-high cover leading into another corridor leading into epic cutscene. Repeat until done. From a gameplay perspective Spec Ops follows this unerringly, and while the gunplay is satisfactory it's purely a vehicle to advance the story. 

As any review will tell you, the only reason anyone played or remembers this game is that story, which I was looking forward to. I expected some 'moral choices' in the vein of games like [i]The Witcher[/i], where you have to stop a train from running into a bus of schoolchildren by rerouting it to a puppy farm. That sort of thing.

[b]Warning: major spoilers for Spec Ops: The Line[/b]
The reality is even less interesting and more two-dimensional than that. About halfway through the game you are forced to [spoiler]commit a warcrime/mass murder of innocent people[/spoiler] completely unintentionally and without the option to not do so. I went around and checked. There's no other way to progress the story. 

Afterwards, the shocking reveal that [spoiler]you were actually killing [i]civillians[/i] and not, you know, the [i]bad[/i] kind of faceless NPCs[/spoiler] is supposed to really trigger a guilt response, but I can't feel guilty about something I literally had no choice in. Not even "hey man, it was him or me" kind of choice, it's a "if you want to play Spec Ops, you're going to do this". 

Anyway. It wasn't any worse than any of the hundreds of murders of random NPCs I had just killed to get to that point, or the hundreds more I would kill on my way to the next cutscene. And it's hard to weep about the above when every 10 seconds you get video game-y bullet time effects and gratuitous explosions of heads from headshots from a simple pistol shot. 

Futher undercutting any sort of emotional resonance this game is going for is the weird sense of humor of Colonel Kurtz, who is only slightly less over-the-top than Handsome Jack from [i]Borderlands 2[/i]. You get quips like "aw, you shot that guy? he was my favorite!" in your radio as you mow down dozens of identical baddies.

All that together makes for a very schizophrenic experience - Spec Ops wants to have its Games Are Art™ cake and eat it too, and fails on both ends. 

[h1]TL;DR - Final Say[/h1]
Spec Ops: The Line has mediocre gameplay and an emotionally exploitive story that is designed to make you feel bad, but doesn't go far enough and doesn't even look at itself before pointing a finger at you. If you want to be manipulated or have your emotional rug pulled out from other you, there are other games that do it far better and are more fun, too. Give this a hard pass.

The fact is, the broad strokes of this game reveals it as the generic 3rd person shooter it is, not the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ it is trying to be. So if you play this game, just save yourself the time and play on easy, and don't bother overthinking any "choices" you think you may have none of it matters.

[h1] Intro [/h1]
Let's start with why I bought Spec Ops; The Line in the first place. Well, it was for the story, because it was the only thing I heard about this game- "Story! Story! Story!". So I had to try this game out. And after completing it I can say that there is two major assets this game is made out of- story and gameplay. But the problem is that one those assets is compelling, interesting and sometimes breathtaking, while the other sucks major dic*. I can first talk about the good part. 


[h1] Story/Plot [/h1]
The story of this game is about a group of three soldiers that are sent to half-destroyed Dubaii as a rescue mission. Their mission is to save civillians and find out what shady business is taking place in the sandy ruins of Dubaii. And then everything spuns out of control. First there is only the physical conflict that drives Spec Ops, but then you understand that the main conflict is actually mental, but nearly everything about it is a spoiler. And it is that mental conflict that makes everyone love this game's story, because the physical conflict is the thing that always gets in the way of the "real" conflict. And that leads into the pinnacle of all the physical conflicts in this game- gameplay. And oh boy, the gameplay surely is something in this game. 

[h1] Gameplay [/h1]
Boring, repetitive, frustrating. You can choose any of those words- all of them are perfect in describing the gameplay of Spec Ops: The Line. I personally played the game on what the game presents as "Normal" difficulty, but it felt like I was playing on at least "Hard". I alway felt like I was pushed into a corner and had to peak and kill enemies one by one. And it always and I mean ALWAYS felt repetitive to be in all firefights. Every area felt the same, only some of the Areas had more holes that enemies could crawl out of than the others. The thing that bothered me the most about Spec Ops was the cover system- it was bad. I mean really bad. I played with controller because I thought that if it was originally made for controllers then it would not be that bad. But it was. You use A/X to go into cover, the same button you use to run(btw- If you press A/X while walking you will start running and the only way to make your character walk again is to stop completely and then start walking again, which was frustrating, escpacially in firefights). The cover system itself is close to non-existant. [h1] Overview [/h1] 

Spec Ops: The Line is a 3rd person shooter centered on the catastrophic collapse of Dubai amid raging sandstorms that decimated the cities infrastructure and communications to the outside world. You play as Captain Martin Walker, who leads a three-man reconnaissance team to survey and assess the situation; errant communication and the discovery of slain US soldiers leads Captain Walker’s men into the heart of the unknown.

There’s a lot that can be said about Spec Ops, but to avoid spoilers it’s tough to delve into some of the symbolic themes and subtle ques the game throws at you. Having played through the game multiple times, you really start to see the game’s strengths in story-telling, character develop and dialogue. On the other side of the coin, you also feel the gameplay becomes a begrudgingly stagnant towards the third act of the game, especially during heavy combat.

When you begin your journey, you’ll be trekking through the desert on a standard recon mission when things turn sideways near instantly and you’re in the middle of a treasonous bloodbath with no clear virtuous side in sight. The chaotic nature of the story, mixed with clever dialogue really sets the tone for something exciting. Captain Walker, Lt. Adams and Sgt. Lugo all have very diverse personalities from the start, mixing a symbiotic relationship between dark comedy and the serious overtones of war. 

Spec Ops offers some of the same when it comes to your modern shooter; it offers a cover system much akin to things like Gears of War and Call of Duty, an array of small arms, long guns and explosives to defeat your enemies which can be found or recovered from the corpses of various enemies, and a melee option. Melee is all but useless in the game, though, with firefights being too hectic to properly utilize.

Enemy AI is average at best, even at higher difficulties. The highest difficulties being “Suicide” and “FUBAR” [the hardest difficulty] you’ll often notice enemies stopping in the open, face the wrong direction or have detection issues where they won’t even notice you, which is especially noticeable in Chapter 14. That being said, enemies do have some positives to help level the playing field. They’ll provide cover fire for their troops, blind fire, throw grenades if you stay entrenched in cover, flank your position and call for backup when applicable. 

The game itself is a linear story progression with several instances of heavy-handed decision making that slowly splinters the atmosphere of the game depending on what you decide. Interestingly enough, your partner AI will react and respond differently depending on the choices you make. Again, these changes are subtle, but if you notice them it makes the game a bit more satisfying to play.

Probably the most creative aspect of Spec Ops is the dialogue; it truly sets it apart from other shooters. As Captain Walker and company progress the storyline, your relationship with your Lt. and Sgt. become strained and significantly more volatile while the commands you give become hostile and blunt. Your uniforms become haggard, torn and bloodied, and Captain Walker’s reaction to killing enemies loses its cool and becomes more psychotic. It’s easily my favorite part of the whole game.

The main game aside, Spec Ops does have a co-op option which follows specific missions and not the storyline and an all but dead multiplayer ability. Neither were the main focus of the developer due to them distracting from the harsh reality of war the main campaign explores. If you don't have a partner to play with or bought it too late to try the multiplayer, you were never missing much.



[h1] Pros [/h1] 

[list]
[*] The dialogue is wonderful. It does a great job fleshing out the characters in an otherwise short game.
[*] Gun and explosive mechanics are well done and interact with the environment [explosions cause blinding dust, some destructible cover, being able to bury soldiers under sand…ect]
[*] The game has multiple endings, all of which are thought provoking. 
[*] The music – The game does a unique job of incorporating music that is going on in the game itself instead of layering it over the game just for the player [I.E. a city-wide broadcast radio]
[/list]

[h1] Cons [/h1] 

[list] 
[*] The helicopter scene mid game is an immersion breaker. It should have been a basic cut scene or removed entirely.
[*] The last minute bolted on co-op/multiplayer seems like a waste of effort that could have gone into improving the main campaign.
[/list]

It provides a game of adequate length, plenty of curve balls, some great character development and plenty of twists to keep it interesting. I don’t feel it merits the stellar reviews some have given it, but it does try to break the mold of the modern day shooter and for that I can appreciate it.

For all the games I’ve played throughout my lifetime, Spec Ops: The Line has to be up there when it comes to being one of the weirdest that I’ve encountered. I don’t mean that it’s weird in the traditional sense, either – what I mean is that’s there’s so much going on, and so much the game tries to achieve and stir within you, that it’s honestly hard to know where to start talking about it.   

Since that’s the case, let’s start with the basics; the gameplay and graphics, actual solid and concrete features that are easily observable. Unfortunately, as becomes rapidly apparent as you start playing, these are features the game is deeply lacking an abundance of in the quality department. This is very much a generic cover based shooter that you’ve probably played a thousand times before, and it’s not even a good example of that genre. It doesn’t feel engaging or enjoyable to play, and in fact pretty lacks anything that make it special in any way. Indeed, the only lasting memory of the gameplay I have is how the fiddly controls (especially regarding cover) are what killed me more than anything else.  

This is a problem that is then only exasperated more by the dismal visuals on display. While I accept this came out five years ago, the actual graphics are merely tolerable when compared to other titles from the same time period. I’m also aware that considering the game's tone, the dull looking nature of every landscape you encounter is clearly a deliberate design choice. The real problem is just that everything’s so... Forgettable. You’ll pass through area after area completely passively, retaining no information as to what they may have ever looked like. There’s simply nothing engaging to grasp on to; no dramatic vistas or battlefields, and no compelling gameplay to try and counter this defect. It’s the purest definition of bland.
 
Yet – and here’s where things start getting weird – it’s clear Spec Ops: The Line never really cared for these matters in the first place. What it really wants to focus on, and the whole purpose for it existing in the first place, is how it’s a brutal deconstruction of the military shooter genre as a whole. This is a title that rips apart so many ideas and beliefs common to all the other similar titles around it that it’s honestly difficult to keep up. The idea that America is always there to save the day, the glorification of the army and war in general, even the idea that you could put violence into the form of a video game and call it entertainment... All these topics and more are picked up, scrutinised, and then torn to shreds. 

It’s startling to see, and effective for the most part, but it’s not perfect. There’s a deep problem ingrained in the message that's trying to be conveyed here, and to demonstrate this, you only have to take a look at the pivotal moment that occurs around the halfway point. Its dark, presented to you without compromise, and will make you feel incredibly miserable for a good while afterwards. It’s also the stepping stone by which the second half of the game really ramps the story and its moral message into high gear, with practically everything setting you down a emotionally dark path – loading screens and all. 

The problem is this, however – you’re forced to do it. There’s no alternative way out, much as you might like to find one; the only way forward is to commit the atrocities set out in front of you. Yet since you’re so railroaded into doing this, the game telling you you’re an awful person afterwards feels a big hypocritical; you were never given a say in the matter, after all. To commit to a terrible analogy, it’s like me making you a delicious sandwich, placing it in front of you, and then criticising you when you actually decide to eat it – considering the way everything has been presented before the outcome, the outcome itself simply doesn't make sense. 

The developers have argued in interviews that there is another option to take; simply turn it off. Yet that feels completely at odds to the way every other video game in existence works -  you’ve paid money and invested your time into this product, so you’re naturally going to wish to proceed and not just give up halfway. Besides, if the developers are stating that the best course of action is to stop playing – why create anything after this point? Why develop it at all? The fact this experience takes the form of a video game is both its greatest asset and its greatest curse – it needs to force you to do things to proceed forwards, but by doing so it fundamentally weakens their impact.  

There are other smaller moments throughout which provide some form of actual choice, and it’s actually these that fare a great deal better. One in particular saw an intense situation physically panic me, pushing me into making a terrible decision. It was only after the event that I realised there was a better solution I could have taken, the realisation of which made me feel terrible in a distinctly more organic way.  This isn’t really a critique of the other emotional moments the game places in front of you – far from it - it’s just a shame that these moments of true choice aren’t a little more prevalent. 

Spec Ops: The Line, therefore, is a lot to take in. As a piece of entertainment, something to actually have fun with, it’s a complete and utter failure. Whether it’s actually a good game is hard to answer as well, because I’m not sure how you define “good” in the context of something that’s as dark as this.  As a think piece, however - something to look at, examine and discuss – it’s a sterling success. It’s made me question things long after I put the controller down, and you only have to glance at the internet to see how much discussion this has created. That’s why it’s so weird and so much in a class of its own – and something that is, despite its many faults, well worth your time.

Spec Ops: The Line – War is not a Game

The Experience: From Soldier to Monster I first played this as a random purchase on console, and I’ve never regretted it. Never before have I felt such hesitation to shoot at pixels. Why? Because the game makes you doubt every target—friend, foe, or civilian. Eventually, I just shot everything that moved, purely for my own survival, accepting the crushing guilt that followed.

The Story: A Dirty, Ugly Masterpiece The story doesn't make you a super-soldier; it’s a direct punch to the face. It tackles themes like PTSD and the absolute filth of war in a way no other shooter has ever dared. There are no "positive" endings here—it only gets more depressive, and that’s exactly why I love it. It’s the anti-hero shooter.

The Impact: Emotional Scars The game forces you into decisions that don't necessarily change the plot but destroy you emotionally. Do you use your last bullet to end someone's suffering or let them burn alive? The consequences are staged so well that you’ll find yourself swallowing hard. It leaves you feeling worse after playing than before—and that is its greatest achievement.

Verdict: Spec Ops: The Line is the most emotionally taxing shooter I have ever played. It shows the true, ugly face of war.

Recommendation: A MUST-PLAY. You need to experience this for yourself.

Spec Ops: The Line – Ein Schlag direkt in die Fresse

Das Erlebnis: Vom Soldaten zum Wrack Mein Erstkontakt war ein Zufallskauf auf der Konsole, den ich nie bereut habe. Ich hatte noch nie in einem Spiel solche Hemmungen, auf Pixel zu schießen. Man ist sich nie sicher: Ist das Feind, Freund oder Zivilist? Irgendwann habe ich aus purer Angst um die eigene Sicherheit auf alles geschossen, was sich bewegte, und das schlechte Gewissen einfach in Kauf genommen.

Die Story: Dreckig, hässlich, ehrlich Dieses Spiel hinterlässt einen mit einem furchtbaren Gefühl – und das ist Absicht. Es gibt keine Helden in Spec Ops. Die Story rund um PTBS und den Wahnsinn des Krieges ist fantastisch inszeniert. Egal welches Ende man erspielt, es wird nur noch depressiver. Endlich mal kein Helden-Shooter, in dem man der Übersoldat ist, sondern eine bittere Lektion.

Die Wirkung: Emotionale Schwerstarbeit Kein anderer Shooter hat mich emotional so mitgenommen. Die Entscheidungen, die man trifft, sind oft rein moralischer Natur: Beende ich das Leiden einer Person mit der letzten Kugel oder lasse ich sie bei lebendigem Leibe verbrennen? Die Konsequenzen sind so hart inszeniert, dass man mehr als einmal kräftig schlucken muss.

Fazit: Spec Ops: The Line zeigt den Krieg so hässlich, wie er ist. Die Qualität der Story hebt es weit über alle anderen Genre-Vertreter hinaus. Man muss es selbst erlebt haben.

Empfehlung: ABSOLUTE KAUFEMPFEHLUNG. Ein Meilenstein des Storytellings, den jeder Gamer einmal gespielt haben sollte.

What a dissonant experience this game is! At first, it excites you with the production and the set pieces. Then it gets quite repetitive and a bit boring cover shooter. Then the story takes a very dark and twisted turn. The game is still a repetitive cover shooter all the way through and its gameplay mechanics get old really fast. It is not a long game, but the gameplay overstays its welcome in the first few hours. The cutscenes and the dialogues during the game are what drives you forward to find out more and then it grips you so much - you are willing to "suffer" through the uninspired shooting and covering. 
A couple of scenes work really well. A few, punch you in a gut and make you feel miserable. The second half of the game is not fun, narrative-wise. This is a one dark story. Despite a few endings - none is a happy one and the game won't leave you feel satisfied and pleased with yourself. Good stuff!
If you love shooting and blowing stuff up, if you enjoy war violence - the game is for you and is a great fit in all but the story. If you are not into those things - the gameplay is worth your patience for the plot and the characters. 
Also, the twist at the end might send you playing the game again, so there's a bit of a replayability factor there.
So in summary, good graphics, quite a few great set pieces and scenes, derivative shooting and covering and a one great story you will remember long after you've finished the game.

[h1]TL;DR: Don’t judge a book by its cover: SOTL is nothing short of a masterpiece. An average TPS with a very well crafted psychological story and narrative.[/h1]

When it came out, like most people, I didn’t care. Another cover-based TPS following the Modern Warfare hype train. Not my cup of tea, so I passed on it. Then, a lot of people started to praise the game and it gained sort of a cult following. I wanted to see for myself, so I picked it up for dirt cheap while on sale. 

As I said above, it’s a rather basic cover-based TPS with squad command elements and a few gameplay elements related to sand, like sandstorms. The gameplay itself isn’t brilliant - not bad but rather generic and sometimes clunky. As for the graphics department, the design is really cool but the execution is, again, generic. 

But what really shines is the story and the narrative. I never felt that much involved in a narrative with a TPS game before. Without going into spoiler territory [b](and I REALLY advise not to if you plan to play it)[/b], Spec Ops is very psychological. Every choice is a burden to carry further on; everything you experience has a meaning. And as the story progresses, it gets you into a very uncomfortable side of warfare which is always toned down in favor of heroism in this kind of games. 
I also consider SOTL as a proof that a game can be very deep and emotional without going the “Quantic Dream” way, where the story is top notch but the gameplay is lacking, weird, or even almost absent (like Heavy Rain). I love those games too but they’re more interactive movies than games while SOTL is a game first and foremost. 

I really, [u]REALLY[/u] recommend this game. Its psychological and philosophical aspects are very well done to the point where it becomes more of an experience than just a game. If you like Silent Hill, Jacob’s Ladder and things like that, you’ll love Spec Ops: The Line.

Spec Ops: The Line is the playable Apocalypse Now in present day Dubai. Gameplay is banal yet fun in contrast to its story which is thrilling but uncomfortable.

Featuring average linear shooter mechanics, the game lulls the player into a sense of traversing in known realms. The premise of Spec Ops: The Line wouldn't work with an all new innovative gameplay because it requires knowledge of the genre in order to build on expected player behaviour. It's a pleasant cover shooter, despite its finicky controls.

Initially, Spec Ops: The Line is rewarding to play. The beautiful scenery is second to none and the music is reminiscent of almost every anti-war film about the Vietnam War. Even if mostly destroyed, the pomp of Dubai is as colourful and impressive as the vegetation of the tropics. Mundane effects such as the shaky camera in cutscenes, the death animations and particularly the slow motion headshots give the impression of playing an action-packed Hollywood movie.

Slight spoiler ahead.
[spoiler]About halfway through, depending on the player, recognition with the main character Walker and his choices slips away. The imagery becomes unbearable dark, the actions inhumane and all should've ended way earlier with the exfiltration of your squad but [i]you're not done yet[/i]. Cognitive dissonance starts to build, which even the developers mention in their loading screens, alongside various other fourth wall breaking statements, e.g. "You are still a good person." quickly negated a few chapters later by "If you were a better person, you wouldn't be here.".[/spoiler]

It's fun to play, it feels good landing headshots in a row hearing Walker scream “Kill is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ confirmed!” but over time, the player sees more and more of the horror that stems from the actions of him and his kind. Spec Ops: The Line is a unique and invigorating experience.

Hey do you want a game that makes you feel like rotten slime all the time but is oddly super enguaging? Are you curious for what video games can be as a medium other than just cheap fun entertainment? Then this is a game for you. This game is great.

The campaign which is the only thing that matters in this game (there is a crummy stock multiplayer tacked on but you can safely ignore it), is relatively short. I completed it in around 6 hours and a not insignificant amount of that time was spent dying. With a price tag of 30 smackums this may seem a little short but a couple thing. 1. This is probably the most important to me, considering the other forms of entertainment we spend our money on, dollars per gaming hour is normally incredibly cheap. Even with this price tag you are probably breaking even with a movie theater experience and this game is no batman vs. superman, it is incredibly compelling and worth it. That being said I'm a cheapo and grabbed this game during the steam summer sale.  
It's next biggest shortfall is the clunkyness of the combat system. A lot of its weaknesses actually play to the advantage that the atmosphere is trying to project however the cover system in a cover shooting game is inexcusable. A lot of my aformentioned dying occured do to my inability to predictably go into and out of cover and or jump over cover to progress at key moments. That being said  this is not a shoot em up. It is an interactive drama disguised as a shoot em up. So its shortfalls in this area doesn't impact the experience of the game as much as it would in a battlefield clone. 
One last thing is that if you look closely enough especially at earlier events in the game once you understand a little better what is happening you might find some things that seem like plot holes. That being said if you are looking that hard you will be enguaged enough to not really care about them. 
Now for the positives:

In summary, the shooter mechanics aren't great, the story is great, and you will feel bad when you finish it and probably end up writing a review on steam for the first time recommending it to complete strangers.

You also have some basic commands for your squad, such as focus enemy, stun enemy or heal ally.

What recommends this game though, it's the plot. The characters are evolving and changing as the story progresses. The plot gets interesting halfway through and during the last chapters there are chances you could guess how's it gonna end, especially if you have seen some particular film classics. There are also some decisions to be made which will influence the ending, especially the choices in the last chapter.

It is filled with characters that evolve as you move forward, characters that feel real, characters that respond to the situations in front of you. This game's tale begins as one thing and ends as another.

Plenty of cut scenes to ensure that you feel the story, your objectives and your men's mental and emotional conditions. I believe that the story IS the core of the game. Yes, the shooting is fun and everything, but staying true to the message of the game which is the story is the primary concern while playing this game. 

So much emotions are packed into each sector of the game, after 4 hours I already felt the weight and burden of the protagonist, and truth be told - I started to feel tired. "Tired but having to move forward" is what the game is about, so it is a joy that the developers were able to make its gamer feel what the heros' feel. 

CONTROLS and MECHANICS
The controls are a little quirky at times. Sometimes, I'd initiate cover and nothing would happen, thus I'd get shot - a lot. Other times, the game would insist that I move cover to cover or stick to cover needlessly, which is annoying. I found myself dying over and over because of the issue I had with the control system. It was ruining my immersion with the story. Thus, I had to turn down the difficulty. Like what I said earlier, the story and immersion is the main concern of the game. 

Shooting rifles feel nice, the recoil is good. The sound, complements the gameplay very well. What  tops these, are the satisfaction I got from landing head shots down to blasting a bad guy with a big old shotgun. 

One bad thing I can say is the gameplay feels repetitive: bad guys shooting at you, you hide and shoot back until they are dead. I did enjoy the area where you had to stealth-snipe your way through a well guarded building. Apart from that, everything is repeated. Since the game is acceptably short, its repetitive nature is not that big of an issue.  

VERDICT 
A must play! Bare with the repetitive game play and you will be rewarded with a story worthy of your time.

While it's not a great game, far from it actually, I'd say it's barely passable as "average", the story is where this game shines, albeit dimly. No, it doesn't bring anything new to the table, but, it definitely works with what it has at hand. SO:TL sacrifices inventive gameplay to show the player the horrors of war, where "just following orders" can lead, and what happens when you go "too far".

Don't get fooled by its appearance. Go in as blind as you can and you will come out with an experience that few video games offer, right up there with Metal gear solid 2 Sons of Liberty.

(SPOILERS)

Perhaps the most brilliant metanarrative ever implemented into the medium, and linear cover-based shooting that perfectly compliments the game's views on modern FPS campaigns and desensitizing video game power trips. Filled to the brim with symbolism and small details that open up hundreds of doors for different interpretations, Spec Ops is a work of art on every level.

A very mediocre military, third-person, cover shooter guided by a crazy good story (emphasis on crazy). There's a few cool mechanics like shooting glass and drowning your enemies in sand, or using a grenade to kick up sand to distract your enemies, but let's be honest: no one gave this game a thumbs up for the shooting. The level design is also INCREDIBLY linear, but there are a number of cool set pieces that would feel right at home in a Call of Duty campaign in terms of scope and sheer destruction.

The story wears it's influences on it's sleeve. If you like Heart of Darkness/Apocalypse Now, you'll really love this. Just be warned: this is some morbid, gut-wrenching stuff, and not just in terms of blood 'n' guts. It's emotionally draining, to say the least. The twist at the end is done well, but I can see why people might be put off by it. And do try to find all of the intel scattered around each level. The writing makes it worth it.

The game is as long as it needs to be; about five hours.

I wanted to give this game a thumbs-up, but the poor level design, clunky shooting and awkward cover system made it the opposite.

The game deserves a lot of credit for trying to do something interesting with a "standard shooter", but it just isn't all that compelling.

The story is too vague, shallow and short to really be compelling. It is definitely a cut above its peers, but the gameplay will leave you frustrated out of the experience. Opportunities for emergent gameplay and imaginative solutions to problems using sand and destructible glass are ignored by the developers except for in certain situations where you are prompted to do so. That aspect of the game was an outright fabrication.

You die -way- too easily, and many of the enemies are respawning bullet sponges. A lot of the level design is very, very poor, which is odd considering how pretty the game can be at times. For all its big open vistas, though, the game is a corridor railroad, both in story and gameplay. A corridor through a bunch of sandy buildings in the middle east. You've done this before.

The cover system seems unfinished, with actions that are common in other games being locked off or remapped to strange button choices.

I found all the main characters completely unlikeable, and all of the choices felt empty and contrived by the end. The story only gets interesting after the game has already slogged through several hours of nothing, by which point are the majority of players have either quit or lost interest. A watched pot never boils, but this game's stove isn't even on. The pace is excruciatingly slow. 

Ultimately this is a 6-7/10 action game with an 8/10 action game story. If you really need something to shoot, pick it up for under $10USD at absolute maximum.

But believe me when I say this, [b]it is worth it[/b]. I must warn people going into this game that it is an amazing experience, but not to mindlessy shoot things, but rather to immerse yourself in a game that can be brought up in a discourse about video games as art.

This game's story is on par with that of Bioshock: Infinite and its moral choice mechanics are very similar to that of Undertale. The setting reminds people of Call of Duty and that is 100% intentional to give people expectations just to mercilessly crush them in a brilliant manner.

Spec Ops: The Line is not perfect, but it deserves a playthrough by every gamer who considers the medium fascinating, because this game makes great use of almost all tools a developer has to deliver a very unique experience.

This makes the player legitimately make the decision for themselves instead of tricking the system into leading them to a certain ending.
Adding to these awesome decisions are at times very trippy cutscenes with actually fu(ked up imagery (especially when you fu(k up a whole mall with chemical weapons... ahem Syria).
This is only enhanced with a really good setting – an apocalyptic Dubai post-huge-sandstorm – an atmosphere that isn't really in any other game.

Spec Ops: The Line is something... more than a game. Obviously it [i]is[/i] a game, because it features gameplay--specifically, gameplay where you and two squad mates are sent into a war-torn Dubai on a recon mission that turns into something so much more. Spec Ops has the most basic, mundane third person shooting that one can wish for: you can hide behind cover, you shoot humans with guns, your health recovers by waiting, and there is a ton of sand. 

But that's the point of Spec Ops. A mundane facade designed to undermine your expectations, because nothing can prepare you for what the game's story puts you through. There comes a point where you stop shooting the enemy and you question what you're even doing--you get so caught up in the gameplay that you don't even realize the decisions you're making, and furthermore, the decisions out of your control.

Spec Ops: The Line is, essentially, a deconstruction of the modern military shooter genre. It grabs hold of the likes of Call of Duty, Battlefield, and other contemporaries and asks them: why?

This is a game with a considerable level of morality to it, unlike the usual 'Gung-Ho' ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.
Having said that, I found it most entertaining and highly enjoyable and for the price, I would most certainly recommend it.

Amidst the awkward controls, the dated 2012 graphics (even for their time), and the mostly run of the mill 3rd person cover-to-cover shooter, lies a gem of a game, mostly due it's superb storyline and unique narrative. [h1]Spec Ops: The Line[/h1] starts off a bit slow but once you picked up on the pace of the game, it quickly turns into a very entertaining and thought provoking experience.

I'm gonna start reviewing the game from a gameplay and technical point of view. The 2012 release looks barely OK in 2017. It's not horrendous and I'll admit certain parts of the game look really good for their time, but even 5 years ago there were prettier things. The gameplay is your typical 3rd person action cover-to-cover shooter. Nothing you haven't played before, nothing revolutionary, just OK. You're in control of your character and two squad mates who you can order to help you to take down the enemy and provide covering fire. They can use flashbangs and revive each other but that's just about it. You can carry only 2 weapons, from a variety of assault rifles, submachineguns, snipers, shotguns, pistols and heavy weaponry. You can also have up to 3 different types of grenades. Ammo is not as generous as you might expect and truth be told that adds a little bit of difficulty and immersion to the game but overall there's not gonna be an issue. The controls are little bit awkward and for me it was a sore spot for the overall enjoyment of the game. Running from cover-to-cover is weird and you might die as a result of poor mechanics since sprinting and taking cover is the same button. Really poor design choice but again, nothing too serious.

There's not really many types of enemies. Soldiers, snipers and heavies, very little [i]mechanised[/i] combat with turrets/vehicles but I'd be a liar if I didn't say it wasn't fun. Not the best fun you've ever had but enough for you to push on through the campaign. I have to be honest here and say that there's really not much else to talk about the gameplay. It is as generic as it comes, I can understand people liking or not but for me it was as uninspired as it comes. The maps and level design were interesting at times and the environment of Dubai looked pretty nice for most of it's part. But the game is not about the way you shoot and kill and people, but rather the [b]who, what, why[/b].

Spec Ops: The Line storyline remind me of the first Black Ops game. Kind of weird how both have the word [u]Ops[/u] in their title right? I don't want to spoil too much of the story but I will try to provide context for the game. You're in control of Captain Martin Walker and his two squadmates, First Lieutenant Alphanso Adams and and Staff Sergeant John Lugo, part of the elite Delta Force, send to Dubai during one of the worst dust storm season the region has ever seen where [i]The Damned[/i] 33rd Battalion of the U.S. Army is stranded after returning from Afghanistan. The 33rd is trying to help to evacuate the civilians out of the city but upon your arrival you notice that something else might be going on. The premise piqued my interest and the way the story unfolded over the course of the game had me at the edge of my seat. I wish I could divulge more information but sadly that would take away from the story. Naturally, the game's been out for over 5 years so really spoiler warnings might be unnecessary for some but if you're one of the lucky few who haven't experienced this yet, I feel it would be a shame if you didn't do so first hand.

The game explores a variety of themes directly from the nature of warfare. If there's an anti-war game, I guess Spec Ops: The Line would be it. Nowadays you can rightly claim that some of the tropes and themes of the story have been explored before in other visual and interactive mediums, but the game has a great narrative supported by brilliant dialogue and an otherwise excellent soundtrack, with polarizing characters who you will meet. You have choices in the matter too; it's not RPG level type of divergence, but certain actions in the game will have lead to different outcomes.

I have to add that I would love to see this game made into a movie or a miniseries even. If I could imagine [b]Three Kings[/b] with a note of [b]Apocalypse Now[/b], this would be it. The game has attracted a variety of theories regarding the meaning of its story, the characters and I think that is a sign of pretty good storytelling.

Spec Ops: The Line is not long, ~6 hours, but it's guaranteed to provoke some interesting feelings and thoughts upon completion. It's not the most difficult of games but there a few challenging situations especially on higher difficulties. I definitely recommend this game for everyone who enjoys action games and people who want a decent story and rich characters in their games as well. Do not be deterred by the mediocrity of its gameplay cause underneath all that game lies a great storyline and the feeling of completing the game will make you wonder about all that you experienced.

Spec Ops: The Line is a decent third person action shooter with an amazing single player campaign story! You play as captain walker, a delta squad leader who thinks that he is helping the survivors in dubai with his actions but not everything is as it seems... There are also plot twists in the story which might surprise you and would also entice you to play more to find out more of the story.

The gunplay is pretty standard but decent. It is basically a cover based third person shooter with a good variety of guns. The game is also really challenging on a higher difficulty as you can die in around two shots and that would encourage you to make use of the cover system more if you do not want to die. The character models looks really dated at the time of this review, however the environment (e.g Buildings, shops, desert, etc ) looks really detailed and beautiful.

The multiplayer and co-op of this game is basically dead at the point of this review as I could not find anyone in matchmaking. However, you can still play the co-op mode alone or with a friend. There are only 4 missions in the co-op mode and they are really short and is also not replayable as the same mission would play out the same way everytime.

In conclusion, the single player campaign has a great story with a serviceable third person shooter gunplay mechanic. The multiplayer and co-op matchmaking are dead and not worth checking out. If I were to rate this game, I would give it a 6/10!
