Wow, I don't think I have ever played a game that is this emotionally charged. I'll get more into that later, for now let's talk about the game in general. 

Admittedly, the gameplay isn't really anything special, it isn't a lot more than your standard Third Person Shooter. It does contain some interesting mechanics involving the sand that is everywhere in Dubai. It isn't a very long game, but its main attraction is the story. It does take a little while for the story to really get intense but it is worth the wait. The events that take place in the story, as well as the way the game tries to make you feel bad about what you are doing is amazing. Also, be warned, the game contains some fairly graphic looking things at a few stages, but if you are playing a shooting game, it probably won't bother you.

The game will place moral choices in front of you more than a couple of times throughout its length. They all carry weight on you and your character, these aren't just your typical "give the object to person A or person B", you are playing with peoples lives in these decisions. 

The game takes a fairly obvious anti-war stance, showing what can happen when things go really out of control. It is a need perspective that not a whole lot of games really take advantage of. 

The PC port works great, never had any issues on the 760 I was using when I played it. It is a pretty nice looking game.

There is a multiplayer portion to the game, I don't know a lot about it because it isn't very populated, but from what I've read, it's a standard team based multiplayer portion. Like most of this game, it isn't very unique.

If you are on the fence about this game, it usually dips pretty cheap during seasonal sales, so get it then. It is absolutely worth that. There aren't many games that I feel I would be happy spending 60 dollars on, this is absolutely one of them.

Spec Ops: The Line is far more than what it was advertised as. In fact, I would say this game was marketed more poorly than any game I have ever seen. What is presented as "Call of Duty in Dubai" is actually far more. It makes a lot more sense when you describe the game as "Heart of Darkness/Apocalypse Now in Dubai." The story takes most of it's cues from those two works far more than Call of Duty or Battlefield.

Gameplay wise, this is a solid cover based third-person shooter. The shootouts you find yourself in take place in incredibly well designed areas. This becomes even more apparant when playing on FUBAR difficulty (which I highly recommend playing on once you unlock it) when you really have to use all aspects of the environment (cover, choke points, etc.) if you want to survive. The gun play is nothing particularly special but it is most definitely competent and doesn't feature any pesky playforming sections or areas where the controls just don't work. Unfortunately the enemies are pretty much all the same with the exception of heavier units but I never really found myself caring all that much. It works and it works well (better than some games that aren't narrative based).

If you're looking for the next great shooter you'll be disappointed. Those looking for a different kind of shooter experience (I'll leave it there at risk of spoiling what makes this one very special) will be in for a treat.

In terms of achievements they are mostly grind related and you can always replay chapters to pick up collectibles so it wasn't particularly troublesome. FUBAR mode kicked my ass though so that could take a bit depending on how skilled you are at third-person shooters. Overall though it was quite fun to 100% this one.

It's a must for any serious gamer, especially a shooter fan, to play this game AT LEAST once in your life.

This might be one of the few shooter games where killing an enemy puts me at unease.

You play as Martin Walker, commander of Delta Forces, who is on Dubai trying to evacuate the civilians from sandstorm. The 33rd Divison went there first, but never returned, so it is up to you to continue their task... or not.

I mispredicted the game would take the usual cliche "rescue mission gone awry because someone screwed it up" - but I was wrong, completely wrong..

With its gripping storytelling, the game it delves to the traumas of war, the ambiguousness of war (that war isn't black and white), and. most importantly, how accustomed we are in murdering faceless people as entertainment. The game started with the usual heroic "we're going to save the day, lads" pro-war stance shooter games usually have, but as you progress, it turned its head to portray how terrible trying to act as an hero can be.

I also like the minor details. In every cutscenes, you're given options how to deal with conflicts presented. E.g., should you rescue the civilians or an agent? Should you shoot the enemy or let them talk first? Should you shoot that guy, this guy, or... abandon order at all?

The consequence doesn't have major effect, but it opens up different reaction and dialogues. Even the smallest ones like standing in front of your teammates while they are ziplining. The environment is also rich in details: barricades are destructible, bullet goes through clothes, etc; sometimes giving you different tactics to progress through the levels.

The cons of this game - well, the covering system sometimes doesn't really work well. So sometimes it's kinda difficult to move from one cover to another. But mostly it's not really a problem. Also, the game punish you for running and gunning; it's more tactical shooter like, so if you're coming from Call of Duty or the like, you would need to adapt.

There is a scene about an hour into Spec Ops: The Line, generally the one people who have already played the game will recognise as the "game changer" scene, that forces you to walk through a landscape of smouldering, writhing soldiers. Some beg for help, others just quietly choke on their own oozing fluids. And its around about this time that the average player will have an epiphany. 
"It takes a real cold hearted psycho of unimaginable cruelty to do something like this," they will think.
Of course, the fact it was THE PLAYER that did it is exactly what makes this game unique. (THE PLAYER, an American soldier, NOT a Saturday morning cartoon villain who twirls his moustache, cackling gleefully as he kicks puppies and heils the swastika, or shouts "JIHAD!", or whatever is most fitting these days.) 
You see, Spec Ops: The Line is the anti-Call of Duty. And it doesn't so much deconstruct the Call of Duty games as it does strip them down to their bare reality, shove them right up the player's ass, and ask: "Just how cool do you think war is now?" 
The above mentioned scene in Spec Ops: The Line very obviously mimics a scene from CoD, involving bombing soldiers from an airborne drone. At least, it mimics the bombing people part. The moments after, where you witness the results of the bombing, are very specifically added. And this is the purpose of the game.

Many will have noticed that in the Call of Duty series the focus of the games are entirely on the fast paced, pulse pounding, fifty-soldier-a-second-murder-rate action part of war, and never once do the games force you to witness the consequences of your actions. (Except for that "Crawling through the city nuke scene," but really, that was many years ago, and the tones of the games have changed drastically since then.) Spec Ops: The Line is happy to give you the pulse pounding action, and it even does so with similar over the top spectacle as can be found in the CoD series, but it never strays far from making you stare the horrific results of those actions square in the face. Likewise, the characters in Spec Ops: The Line grow ever more twisted, tortured and insane, clearly reflecting the reality of the horror around them. The player, be he or she a person of reasonable intelligence and not a sexually frustrated teenager, (you know who you are,) should hate themselves by the end of the game, not feel like a hero.

"This game doesn't sound like much fun," I hear you say, "What about the actual game part of the game?"
Fair enough. Lets talk gameplay.  In terms of gameplay, I must be honest, Spec Ops: The Line isn't a perfect, and certainly isn't much to write home about. Its a reasonable third person shooter with functonal cover mechancis, reflecting Gears of War more than CoD, in point of fact. Even these basic mechanics, however, are a bit flimsy at times. On curved walls it seems a bit ambigous as to whether Walker, the protagonist character, will shift up the wall upon you moving the thumbstick to the right, or leap up out of cover like a man doing an interprative dance of a meerkat on the lookout for predators. These instances are rare, however, and the gameplay is for the most part fast paced, epic, and enjoyable. The gameplay really is, however, just a means to drive the wheels of the story forward.

Lastly I would like to add that Spec Ops: The Line is also hands down the most breathtakingly beautiful game I have ever played. The sheer amount effort that must have gone into making the enviroments, that turn a war-torn Dubai into an artistic masterpiece, more then makes up for the average gamelplay, and then some. This game, a shooter that has you blowing off heads, simultaneously makes love to your eyes with an absolutely stunning gallery of gorgeous level designs.
 
There is another scene I'd like to mention now, before ending this already overly long review, where you and your soldiers drop down into a cave, the floor of which is a carpet of hundreds of lit candles. And, as you and your soldiers walk over these candles, your clumping boots extinguishing the little pinpoints of light, leaving paths of darkness in your collective wakes. This visual metaphor of these soldiers and their purpose, (soldiers snuff out lives beneath their mighty tread and leave darkness behind them, for those sexually frustrated teenagers who didn't get it,) created in such am original and strikingly beautiful way, is why Spec Ops: The Line is one of my personal favourite games. This massively overlooked game, indeed not perfect by any means, was a risky project of passion by a group of developers I feel should have got more recognition for it. I commend those developers, and very much recommend the game to anyone who has the right mindset to appreciate it.

Spec Ops: The Line has one of the most intricate, ominous, and heart-wrenching storylines I have ever seen. Playing this game, you truly feel that every action you take has a lasting effect. With each ultimatum you face, it is difficult to decide between what is easy, what is ethical, and what is right; and it's even harder to decipher if you chose correctly.

The gameplay, cinematics, and dialog throughout the game are incredibly immersive. You use your surroundings, you flank the enemies, you work together with AI teammates… When commanding my teammates to take out an imminent threat, I once heard the character shout, "Take out that shotgunner on the stairs to the right!" I couldn't have been more specific myself!

I'm not sure I have ever been as captivated and emotionally tied as I have been while playing Spec Ops: The Line. Though the campaign goes quickly, I would [b]HIGHLY[/b] recommend this game to everyone who could handle the intense story. It really does take you past the line you never thought you'd cross.

Before I jump into my review of Spec Ops: The Line, I feel I should disclose the fact that I only played this game for a little over half-an-hour.  If you're thinking, "30 minutes is not nearly enough time to tell if a game sucks," I would say, "not if the game in question sucks as much as Spec Ops: The Line."  That is because the game is so monumentally clunky and insipid, anything else about it that might be considered 'good' is crushed instantly out of existence (I'm looking at you, storyline.)  The mechanics are really the main problem, centered as they are around a cover system that is clumsy to use and  a cliche of just about every shooter ever made and marketed for the Xbox demographic (sorry, 10 year-olds.)  There are squadmates you can order around, but there's no point to actually doing it because it's so much easier and faster to just kill the bad guys yourself.  The level design is linear to the point that even the outdoor maps feel like running down a hallway (if the hallway only ever turned left or right, because heaven forbid we might get lost or something.)  The gunfights themselves are repetitive, probably due to the fact that they are low-skill/ low-intensity yawn-fests, made even more frustrating by the reliance on cut scenes which are probably intended as set pieces but only end up robbing you of any potential feelings of accomplishment.  The main gimmick on offer seems to be the ability to shoot piles of sand conveniently located over the heads of the bad guys, which is stupifyingly silly in a game that ostensibly wants to be taken seriously.  Many people have praised Spec Ops: The Line for it's strong narrative, but the problem is that whatever engaging story was to be found past the 30 minute mark was buried under a pile of soggy, flaccid game design; I just couldnt muster the willigness to put up with the lack of fun and the boring gameplay to find out.

If you like war games and shooters, you need to play this game. Not because the action is intense and brutal (which it is), but because the story is intense and brutal.	 Never in a game before had I felt the atrocities of war so acutely. This game made me not only realize how horrible we can be, but how EASILY we can slip into hell, especially on a battlefield. That type of statement pulled off in a game that was fun to play is in my mind a genre changer. God help other military shooters for what they will have to do to keep up with this. 

I have a few gripes about the game, they are not small, but they are demonstrably overshadowed by the storytelling.  The cover system sometimes is very inadequate, you step away from walls you did not mean to and get shot in the face. And sometimes you cover to walls you did not mean to and expose yourself in that way too. I feel they could have made the order system better as well as you have no control over where your team members go, just what targets they kill, and if you are lucky enough to get the prompt, who gets a flashbang before getting gunned down. The order system does have the benefit of being simple and therefore keeping you focused on the pace of the story, but this gets countered a bit in a few sections where your friendly AI gets killed by running ahead of you and into the open.   You do have to save them which puts you in terrible spots. I can only think of 2 spots this happened to me more than once, so it’s not that big of a deal. What is a bigger deal is that towards the end of the game the checkpoint saves get ludicrously far apart in my opinion. I would have to play one section over and over, just because the guy (a very heavy trooper) at the end of the section what giving me issues. In another section, the same sort of thing happened but I had next to no ammo when it put me at the checkpoint (I was not low on ammo when it saved)…that was a bit of a drag. 

ALL of that said, on a scale of one to ten the game would be in the high 9s no problem for how well done everything else was done. Buy this game, play this game…but by something happy for yourself too. You are going to need it after the war.

A descent into the depths of the human soul.

Videogames are still a rather young art-form mostly catering to an adolescent or adolescent-minded main audience which works both as a benefit and a detriment. On the one hand videogames are very free in how they express themselves compared to e.g. movies because your role as the player is a uniquely interactive one and the unhinged nature of many games has proven inspiring for decades of aspiring artists. However this playfulness becomes troubling when games start to depict real events, namely wars. While you could make a case for WWII-era shooters like the older Medal of Honor parts as "documentary games" the only reason they could get away with showing war, argueably the most horrific thing humans are capable of, as entertaining and fun is that the world wars have for the most part been delegated to the history books now and its millions of victims are brought up in a discussion more in a way that you would discuss a gripping chess game.
With modern shooters the situation is a bit different. The moral implications of portraying currently ongoing human tragedies as entertainment for the youth of the nations that are responsibly for quite many of them is very troubling. I don't believe the games we play have such a huge impact on us that they would convince an otherwise stable human being that brown people are inherently our enemies and more animal than man, but they contribute to a society that turns a blind eye to catastrophies unless they happen in their backyard.

Enter Spec Ops: the line. What is superficially a typical military cover-shooter is actually more of a psychological horror game with action elements (not that you could tell from the terrible trailers). You follow a soldier's quest for glory and victory which turns into a downward spiral into madness. In the end the soldier's incentive to be a hero in this story (and in extension the player's motivation too) are dwarfed by the atrocities he has commited. I won't spoil anything but many scenes of horrific violence made me feel rather sick and it's very rare that a game ever gets to me on such a level. Other games have tried to do similar things and tug our heartstrings and guts, yet in my opinion these scenes come off as pretentious and clumsy at best. In Spec Ops: the line the descent into madness of our main character feels a lot more genuine and cleverly made, starting with the subtitle "the line". It can refer to several memorable moments in the game or basically the line you cross when you go into a war game trying to be a hero, a narrative that as mentioned before is cleverly and drastically dismantled. In the end it's made clear that the only moral choice you can make is not to play.

The only downside to the game is the very standard gameplay. It's necessary to lure you in with the similarities to other modern shooters and then hit you repeatedly over the head with a hellish experience but many people will unfortunately be turned off and never even get to the bits that make Spec Ops a memorable and important game. The action set-pieces are not really the game's strength but the thick atmosphere more than makes up for it. 

Play it, think about it and then reevaluate its peers, the call of dutys and battlefields of this world - it's like going from apocalypse now to michael bay's pearl harbor.

Spec Ops the Line is a good shooter with excellent art direction.

But the story is two things at once and I am not sure which: The first is a "War bad" shooter with a series of good narrative tricks and fourth wall breaks to dazzle, trick, and belittle the player, showing how valorous conduct in war can easily lead to war crimes.

The second Spec Ops the Line is a tragedy, where four or five different factions are all locked in a crucible, all trying to do the right thing, and every one of those right things ends up colliding in a train wreck, the player included, such that by the end credits everyone is a cruel murderer including the civilians.

I am not sure which story the authors wrote here. I am not sure anyone knows. The first story is a hacky subversion, a trollface parody of COD saying ">implying heroism actually exists." The second is a very human tragedy that logically and internally consistently  produces an enormous amount of evil from good people trying to do good things.

Most people see the former (The game is absurdly unsubtle with the jabs at the player) so I expect the former is what was actually written, but I really hope... probably wish... the true Spec Ops is the second story.

The gameplay of this game is almost entirely ordinary; It functions well as a cover-based shooter but does nothing overly complex or groundbreaking. The most prominent features of the game are its story and underlying messages, concerning both war and the interaction between the player and the game - arguably, the interaction between all players and all games.

I strongly believe that this game is one of the most powerful arguments available to convince the average person that video games have great potential as a serious creative medium.

I knew this game would mess with me but I still tried to not get burnt. I failed. I didn't fail miserably but I still failed and I'm not scared to admit it. 

    In a world where indie titles seem  to have cornered the avant garde and ofputting side of the market e.g Binding of Isaac, Limbo, This War of Mine it's neat to see such a high value title go in such a different direction from other mainstream shooters. 

    The overall look of The Line can be summarized as a typical shooter set in present day Middle East but with a slight saturation to the lens. It's not overdone and it seems to fit the mood of the game. Almost a sort of festering humidity at the edges of your vision. It becomes an unsettling contrast later in the game I find. 

    But what isn't unsettling about this game!

    Gameplay is your typical cover based action. Firefights tend to become pretty pitched at a fairly early point and I found myself dying several times even on normal difficulty. The gates that activate enemy NPC's are not very well hidden which makes it easy to see future setpoints and ruins the illusion somewhat. Nevertheless it's given a pass because that is not the intended focus of the story. 

    Ahh the story, such a dumb beginning. Barely a plot to justify inva ding a city and then it builds. The suspence. The questions. The unease. I barely know why I'm here, why am I killing these people. And yet it's the only way to progress. Once the gears are in motion it's either continue playing or uninstall the game. And it's too good to uninstall.

    Sounds of weapons and enemies feel kind of flat and repatitive but the dialogue more than makes up for it. I'd put this squad dialogue as probably the best I've ever heard. Right up there with Alyx Vance or The Sands of Time narration. It just fits and is so well delivered. It kept me way more interested than all the firefights I was engaged in.

    Single playthrough had me at six hours which is more than enough to feel sick about yourself. Also there are a lot of choices in the game which lead to an alternate ending which I'd love to tackle someday. For now, I'll take to heart the horrible lessons of modern day war and stick to playing Renowned Explorers: International Society, a game where I can suceed while being predominantly friendly.

Does playing a game through a screen like this justify everything we do? All the harmful actions we perform, all the lives we've taken away, all the lives we've ruined from such chaos? Few games will ever actually ask that question, and fewer still will tell you that it doesn't. At some points in this game, it almost feels like it DOESN'T want you to play it. It wants you to turn around from the monitor, walk away, be a better person than who you're watching in the story. 

What appeared to be another generic shooter to perhaps many people, was a wolf in sheep's clothing. While some people are right, yes, the gameplay is nothing special, it's decently polished. No gamebreaking bugs, or even small ones really (As far as I saw), and yeah you might enjoy some parts. But after a while, you may find yourseff weighed down...weighed down by the horrors you've seen...horrors that aren't even real, but they still stay with you. 

This game is like going into University, where you've accepted a certain truth your whole life. In this case, the truth is that you're a hero and every game makes you a hero. But like that surly university professor you take without realizing his nature, it tells you one thing. Question what's around you. Is everything really what you think it is?

Do you feel like a hero yet?

I have to be honest, this game got to me, got inside my head and made me feel things I didn't think a basic, cliché, third person shooter could. There are plenty of games that show you violence, plenty of games have you run through all sorts of firefights and battles that are visually stunning making you feel awesome. You walk away from most firefights in this game feeling many feelings; sadness, guilt, horror and sickness. You start the game as a strapping commander of a small team of Special Forces, the serious "Captain America" type and sarcastic joker. You are entering the city of Dubai, struck by devastating dust storms trapping the 33rd and all the civilians they were trying to evacuate and of course, you know the CO of that unit, he was a good man who helped you in a past theater of war. All very, run of the mill story of a canned modern shooter. This is remarkably misleading. As you work your way through the city you find that order has utterly collapsed, you help soldiers under fire from apparent insurgents and as you go farther, you find American soldiers rounding up and gunning down civilians. You are forced to defend yourself when the turn their fire on you. It tears your team up and it is simply the beginning. The game constantly confronts you with choices between one evil or another. No one is the good guy, each side commits atrocities against each other, and if you hope to survive, you have to do the same. There are literally a pair of achievements named "Damned if you do" and "Damned if you don't". The game drags you through the mud watching soldiers, civilians and even your own team die. Your character's dialogue slowly devolves from in control tactical commands to screaming obscenities at the enemy and eventual hallucinations. This game brings themes from Apocalypse Now and The Heart of Darkness into the gaming world and confronts us with the true horrors of this level of violence. You don't walk away from this game feeling good about playing it, the game even goes meta, insinuating that you caused this violence; you could have shut it down and walked away at any time, why did you keep going? They are questions that demand answers. It is a game I think all gamers should play; it rocks you, makes you feel uneasy and forces you to appreciate the true nature of violence. The gameplay itself is smooth and user friendly. Basic squad commands and different guns give you multiple approaches to different combat scenarios. The gameplay is linear and simply escalated as different guns and enemies are introduced with smarter AI and better fighters, much like most of the Call of Duty franchise, although this game, I enjoyed more. Overall, this game is deeply dark and challenges you to confront its own violence. I believe that anyone who plays shooters should play this game to remind them how horrific true violence is; there is nothing wrong with playing our video games that are violent, we just can't become numb to it and this game keeps us grounded.

I get what the game was trying to do here, but for me, at least, it just doesn't work. 
The game REQUIRES you to treat it like a CoD or Battlefield game, otherwise it doesn't make any sense.
The plot railroads you into situations where you might logically just sit down and say "Hey, guys, why are you shooting us? We literally haven't done anything to you." But, hoping that the audience is used to shooters where you just shoot people for poorly explained reasons, the game just hopes you don't think for more than two seconds about what's happening. 

Likewise, the fact that the character (and game)-defining moments railroad you into a 'choice' removes all feelings of personal responsibility and empathy that they spend so long building up. Call me cynical, but if you give me a game and force me to do something to progress, that has the same impact as follows:
"Hey, you literally -have- to kick that puppy to continue the story"
"Okay, I guess."
"OH MY GOD HOW COULD YOU, YOU MONSTER"
Of course, these forced 'choices' are required, because barely anyone would actually chose to do it this way if they were given the choice. Most people aren't ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ psychopaths. 
BUT the story requires you to act like a psychopath in order to make sense. This lead to me, trodding along acting fairly sensibly, then the game forcing me to do something horrid, then scolding me for doing that thing that it forced me to do.
There were one or two moments that actually let you choose what to do at some points, and when one of them went wrong, that was when I actually felt terrible, because it was MY choice that lead to this, and not the the plot railroading me.

I came out of this experience a bit unfufilled, really. I had acted sensibly, trying to make logical choices where I could; not killing civillians, trying to stop people from shooting me on sight, even going as far to flashbang soldiers to see if I could just get their attention for a moment. Of course, this doesn't work, because the plot demands that you kill people. Frankly, this gave me some cognitive dissonance, because, to me, it was abundantly clear that we were fighting the 'bad guys' for no reason, and yet there was no way of acting on this understanding. Then, later, the game shouts at you "WHY DID YOU KILL ALL THESE PEOPLE?" Gee, I don't know, because you didn't give me a choice?

I almost feel as though Spec Ops plays it's hand too soon, immediately trying to make you feel guilty for the people that you were forced to kill not ten seconds ago. This results in that cognitive dissonance I mentioned earlier. I know I'm fighting these guys for no reason, and that I just killed them in a super-not-okay way, but I had to, because the plot demands it.
I think the story would have made so much more sense had they acted more like a modern shooter, romanticising things like WP, or drones, biological weapons or something, and giving you the choice to use them, but tricking the players into doing so because why wouldn't you? It's way more fun, cooler and easier than having to shoot everyone yourself, right? Instead, the game actively dissuades the player from using WP, which detracts from what it's trying to do, which is trick players into becoming a psychopathic war criminal.

Compared to something like CoD or Battlefield, this game is definitely leagues ahead in terms of story. Maybe people who are really into the shooter genre might get more involved in this story, but me, coming from more RPG-esque games, where choice is commonplace, this just felt linear and annoying, because I knew what I wanted to do, but I just wasn't given the option. Still, points for trying to reverse some genre tropes and using your shooter knowledge against you.

YAGER might be masters in subverting expectation. [i]Spec Ops: The Line[/i] is a rare surprise that goes in so many unique directions that it is a wonder 2K approved it. The game takes place in Dubai, but rather than war-torn, it has been destroyed by sandstorms. Dubai is noticeably different from how other "war" games depict the Middle East: Dubai is beautiful, full of large skyscrapers with dazzling interiors. The amount of sand that has destroyed Dubai adds to its level design in fun an imaginative ways. A lot more of the subverting comes within its narrative and I'm not going to spoil any of that - however, even more impressive is how the characters change as the narrative and the tone of the game changes. The characters become angrier, and their interactions with the world (both within and outside of gameplay) become more brutal as a result. I can't reveal the enemies without spoiling some of the story but understand that you don't spend the entire game hunting down a terrorist cell, or fighting against some sort of rival military. If I had any issues, it was that combat is mostly generic - from what I'm led to believe, this is intentional as the [i]Spec Ops[/i] wears the mask of a generic third person shooter to hide what it is really about. However that doesn't change the fact that it can be a bit of a slog. I also feel that weapons are too similar to one another and thanks to conveniently placed ammo boxes you almost always have sufficient ammo - eliminating any reason to pick up and try out the different weapons throughout the game. There is also the multiplayer which the developers themselves called a “cancerous growth” on their own game... yeah, I wouldn't waste any time on it. Many have referenced this game as a great example of "video games as art" and I won't dispute that, however I would rather say that [i]Spec Ops: The Line[/i] is less of a video game and more of an experience.

Based upon the classic novella by Joseph Conrad, Spec Ops: The Line deviates from previous entries to tell a harder hitting story. While the gameplay mechanics are stock standard Third Person Shooter, the soundtrack and story help sell a world on fire.

You assume the role of Captain Martin Walker, a man in charge of a small three man squad.  As you enter a devastated Dubai, you realise that your simple reconnaissance mission isn't all that it was cut out to be. You are taken down paths you would normally never take and when you make mistakes, the game lets you know in glorious fashion. That's not to say you can't have fun with this game. Just remember that you shouldn't be surprised if after the first few chapters, ♥♥♥♥ hits the fan. This is based on the story that was the basis for Apocalypse Now and if you're going to play this game, you might as well give that a watch.

While the gameplay is fairly simple and standard, TPS, there are a few things that make playing Spec Ops: The Line, a little more interesting. One mechanic is the ability to direct squad mates toward targets. Can't quite get someone yourself? Let your scout/sniper handle it. Want heavy unit control? Let your explosives expert deal with that. As you get bombarded with enemies from every direction, don't forget that your squad mates don't have to help on autopilot. I do have to note that the controls for me were a tad finicky. However, I can simply place that down to my casual gaming status. This other interesting mechanic doesn't affect gameplay as much as the squad control does, but it does help sell the story's descent into madness. As you progress through the game, Captain Walker is placed in increasingly morally difficult positions where one decision now can affect how the game will play later on. Due to the emotional stress you are placed under by your decisions, melee attacks start becoming far more brutal. What used to be a simple elbow to the face, progresses until you end up pummelling a person's face with the butt of your gun before finishing them off with a street justice execution.

All in all, this game is a fantastic experience and certainly challenged me both gameplay wise and morally. I began asking more questions of how simple decisions now can affect how life will be later on. While the decisions you make don't alter the story drastically, whatever choice you make certainly feels like it carries a lot of weight. I guess what I'm trying to say is, this game is a fantastic piece of storytelling, even if the gameplay is your standard TPS. If you are looking for a game that challenges you in more ways than just the gameplay itself, then it is most definitely worth it.

It's been four years since I played Spec Ops: The line. Since then it's lingered in my mind, occasionally taking me back and causing me to relive the horrors. Even now, I'm still not sure what genre to place it in. Action drama or action tragedy perhaps? Whatever genre it's in, I know this:

It's the number one of all time.

In some games, the only way to lose is when you turn the game off and stop playing. Here, it's the only way to win. And I strongly doubt many players have won. Your desire to finish, to see what comes next, is expertly pitted against your better judgement. Almost always the former prevails over the latter.

Of course, there are those harping on mediocre 2007 gameplay or shoehorned in multiplayer. I surmise that they have completely missed the point. It's like criticising a masterwork painting for being in a shoddy museum or having a dirty frame. This is doubly true because Spec Ops' message is about being in such a museum, poking fun at the box it comes in.
Poking fun is entirely the wrong word, so instead let's call it poking nauseated revulsion.

If you have a timemachine, go back to 2012 and tell yourself to play it. If you lack such a device, reading this review alone probably spoils too much. Part of the experience was going into it thinking it was Modern Warfare 2. The real reasons to play it now are academic, archeological. Also the soundtrack is pretty good.

[h1]My Thoughts on Spec Ops: The Line[/h1]

[h1]The Port[/h1]

This game's port is relatively solid, for the most part. It's stable, has a decent options menu with all the options this game really needs, the controller support is weird in the way that, when it is plugged in, every button prompt is replaced with the controller ones and you need to quit the game, unplug the controller and then start the game back up in order to get them back. This game didn't need an advanced options menu or magnificent control system or any of that ♥♥♥♥. It's simple and it works. Normally I would complain about how simple it is but, like I said earlier, this game doesn't really need any of that. And I'll explain why later.

[h1]The Graphics/Performance[/h1]

The graphics in this game are absolutely stunning. Beautiful shadows, incredible geometry, fantastic textures, awesome lighting effects, great particles, fantastic use of ambient occlusion and pretty good animation. It is a truly stunning game, but it isn't all that perfect. There are some weird textures here and there, weird models, animations and particles and some shadows look less than great, but it is both a visually stunning game and a visually pleasing game. The performance in this game is amazing too. It runs extremely well as my rig, an FX 4300 OC'd to 4.4 GHz and an EVGA GTX 750 ti, as it goes all over the place between 70 and 150 FPS maxed out. It really varies but it stays above 70 FPS all the time so that's awesome. Seriously fantastic job with this Yager.

[h1]The Story/Atmosphere/Characters[/h1]

♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. This game was the most insane experience I've ever had in a video game in my entire life. The story is possibly the best story in a video game ever for many reasons. Alright bare with me while I try to explain this. The story starts out giving you the thought that it's a run of the mill third person "♥♥♥♥ YEAH MERICA" shooter but as the story goes along it turns out that ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ were you wrong. At some point in the story this "thing" happens that I will not spoil for those unlucky few who haven't played this game that just ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ turns the whole story on it's ass. From there the story just goes into a downward spiral and it goes deeper and gets more depressing until the last couple hours and it gets to the point where you just have to sit and take in what the ♥♥♥♥ you just experience. 

I have never had a game have such an impact on me before, and I thought that Life is Strange ♥♥♥♥♥♥ me up, to the point that I actually, during a cutscene, sat there for the entire cutscene and just ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ think about what I just saw. I started to cry cause I felt like absolute ♥♥♥♥ for what I did and it takes quite a bit to do that to me. I've never experienced something that overwhelming in a game before in my entire life and I've heard similar stories from other people so I'm not just being an over-emotional ♥♥♥♥♥. The atmosphere takes many different turns but for every turn it takes it is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ perfectly executed. Not really much else to say there. 

The characters in this game are ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Oscar worthy with how good they are. The writing in this game is on a whole other level with how well written it is. All the dialogue that occurs throughout, all the subtle changes in the callouts you and your squad make, the actual performances of these ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ voice actors, to everything that has to do with a character in this game. It is all absolutely fantastic. Every character is believable, well voice acted, well written, well spoken and extremely well executed. One of the few games to get the whole spectrum for this ♥♥♥♥.

[h1]The Controls[/h1]

Now here and the gameplay is where this game kinda lost it with me. The control scheme is not very good. Like at all. It's clunky as ♥♥♥♥, weirdly mapped, hard to use and movement is just honestly awful. It's very run of the mill third person action that I thought was honestly ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ awful. The only saving grace, for me, is that the gunplay is actually fairly decent. Playing with a controller isn't that bad but compared to other games it's not very good either, mouse control is fine though it works well without much problem and everything is very responsive but I'll be damned if it isn't a clunky piece of ♥♥♥♥ that, given how amazing this game's story is, the graphics, and every other technical aspect, really could've been so much better. But hey some people didn't mind it so maybe whoever's reading this won't mind it either.

[h1]The Gameplay[/h1]

The gameplay is so basic it hurts. It's cover based, third person, SUPER basic combat that made me not want to play this game. It got ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ irritating with how many times I would die due to the retarded controls and how many times I had to stop midway into moving and try to take control of my character again. The cover system isn't bad but I've had a fair share of times where it would just not work. Actually getting into firefights isn't all that bad though. The Line is, unfortunately, as relevant now as it's ever been. If anyone ever wondered if the COD franchise had a single original or thoughtful bone in its body, those hopes are dashed now, as Activision continues to churn out remakes to commercial success in spite of critic fatigue. "Art" continues to be supplanted by advertiser-friendly "content" that sacrifices innovation and any meaningful message for the sake of engagement. Meanwhile, all over the world, people are clamoring for war against someone else, eager to cosplay an action movie hero, shooting first and asking questions never. People continue to be hurt by those in power who claim to know what's best for everyone. Mass shootings and veteran suicides continue to plague the US, symptoms of a mental health crisis, among other issues.

The Line asks "Hey, y'know those twelve+ games you've made glorifying consequence-free violence against enemies who strongly resemble groups of real world people but without any nuance or context, while rewriting history and depicting war as generally cool and good? You ever think that might be a BAD thing?" I am *not* at all saying violent video games are the cause for the world's ills, nor that The Line is somehow the cure, but even a mere attempt to address those issues through the atypical medium of the modern military shooter is worth at least considering. The fact that it's no longer available for purchase is a tragedy, doubly so because any (unlikely) re-release will be sans the offending music, and I can think of no song more fitting to The Line's tone and message than a warped, distorted version of the US's most patriotic song which was performed originally as an anti-war protest.

At this point, the cat is out of the bag when it comes to The Line; its trick is no longer a secret and its intended audience was unlikely to pick it up even before the high seas were the only way to acquire a digital copy. I could talk for literal hours (and have, previously) on why, despite its flaws, this game is so ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ important. The ending scene alone is gut punch after gut punch of simple lines that nevertheless manage to fall like hammer blows against the protagonist's shattered mind and the player themselves. While MW tries to make gritty claims about "drawing the line where you need it" while pulling any punch that had even a chance of hurting its customers, The Line actually explores very fun, advertiser-friendly ideas including: Martial law, military interventionism, jingoism, the fog of war, civilian casualties (accidental and otherwise), torture, lynching, PTSD, survivor's guilt, chemical weapons, and honest-to-god war crimes.

If you have the means, you should ABSOLUTELY play it. Stop reading reviews, no more articles or video essays, just play it and see what you feel and think for yourself. If nothing else, it's one hell of a conversation starter and more food for thought than 90% of the games, shows, and movies available today.

Spec Ops: The Line is an enjoyable third person shooter. The game mechanics are solid and as a result the cover-based shooting feels incredibly natural. Spec Ops is at its best when the fluid game movement is showcased in gorgeous action set pieces. The graphics are fantastic, this is as true in 2016 as it was at release. What truly puts Spec Ops above the run-of-the-mill third person action shooter is its story and disturbingly realistic depiction of  the brutalities of war. The story is based off of two other works: the novel, Heart of Darkness, and the classic film Apocalypse Now--which was also based off of Heart of Darkness. War and the decisions it forces humans to make are the heart of the story. The game is incredibly graphic, which the developers use in their favor. Not once did I think the game was graphic for the sake of being graphic. Each moment that incited shock felt horrifically natural and succeced in blurring the lines of morality--as war has done and will continue to do. A standard run through of the game will take around 10-15 hours, but that can be extended through collecting all of the Intel or playing on the unlockable FUBAR difficulty. All said and done, I thoroughly enjoyed my time with Spec Ops: The Line. I definitely recommend checking it out especially if it's on sale. The multiplayer community is, for all intents and purposes, dead, which is to be expected at this point, so if you're looking to check that out it's not going to happen. The campaign, always the focus of the game, is strong enough on its own to leave any player satisfied even without the multiplayer. 

TL;DR: Fantastic narrative, solid cover shooter, would recommend.

It's not often that a shooter game leaves you feeling gut punched at the end of the story. 

When you shoot down enemy soldiers, some of them aren't quite dead and lie on the floor squirming or screaming in agony. Several times I found myself putting an extra bullet in them.

At first I told myself it was out of mercy. 

Later I realised it was because watching them crawl away feebly attempting to draw breath through destroyed lungs made me deeply uncomfortable. This typifies Spec Ops: The Line perfectly. 

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
The game is not so much about butter-smooth mechanics or mowing down hordes of enemies, but rather about inviting you to question your decisions, to face the consequences of violence and to think about what it means to leave a trail of corpses like in so many video games before. Of course, we're talking about a videogame, an entertainment product where Hollywood brings out no end of violent films every year; it's fair to say humanity still enjoys violence as entertainment, although we've moved away from slaves fighting lions and have embraced technological substitution to feed our thirst for excitement.

[h1]Shoot to Kill[/h1]
Spec Ops: The Line is no different, where you're faced with wave after wave of enemies to kill and creative ways to dispatch your foes into the afterlife. In this sense violence is glorified, with your character and his teammates calling out succesful kills in increasingly excited tones, and with time slowing down when you hit a headshot allowing you to admire your handiwork as the man who was trying to kill you and your friends drops to the floor in a limp heap. At the same time the cost of warfare is apparent, with your character looking increasingly harrowed and beaten up as the story progresses. 

[h1]Contradictions[/h1]
Other reviews have pointed out the apparent hypocrisy in this construct - to present an exposition of violence meant to be enjoyed whilst simultaneously berating the consequences and, by proxy, the player's enjoyment of said violence. This wasn't a concern for me - I was far too busy both enjoying and worrying about the feeling of discomfort I got every time I shot another man down.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
The critical look at violence and the way it's juxtaposed with wave after wave of bad guys for you to kill means Spec Ops: The Line is a sublime mix of stereotypical shooter game combat and a deep discomfort that only grows as the story progresses.

Spec Ops: The Line is often quoted as one of the best war dramas which actually makes you feel the impact and the negative sides to what you're doing, and to actually show the horror or war.

Well, not quite. First of all, the game looks beautifull. Set in a Dubai city buried almost completely following mysterious sandstorms, staring a disappeared and apparently now brutally reigning american division as your main opponents, and you sent as a rescue team, this game has great potential, but falls short due to two main errors made.

First of, the storytelling. The way in which you get set up to eventually be shooting (without any attempts of communication) at CIA Agents and american soldiers, is completely unbelievable. It tears a gigantic hole in an otherwise very interesting story, which i particularly liked for its unique setting.

And second, and more importantly, there are ENORMOUS flaws in the gameplay design. Not only is the game the definition of a sloggy tunnel-shooter, it tries its hardest fo fullfill every stereotype possible, from the pinned scenario where you're hiding behind tiny bits of debris taking out 50+ people shooting at you from the remnants of a skyscraper, to the obvious helicopter shooting through the side of a glass window sidescraper, to actually falling off a skyscraper, surviving a 200+ meter fall, and finding yourself in a corner at the start of another level tunnel with nothing but a pistol with 8 bullets in it and 11 enemies facing you down immediatly and simultaneously. The amount of times i had to restart that section to go for a 100% headshot rate and to grab one of their guns before the shotgun-guys ran me over was mildly annoying to say the least.

Enemy AI has massive deficiencies. They will go for certain pieces of cover, and eventually lob grenades at you if you don't kill them, but they keep peaking their heads out without actually properly returning fire, and most of the time they won't react to your grenades and simply die. Their only advantage seems to be their sheer number and considering the setting you could've replaced them with something akin to zerglings instead of american soldiers (FEEL BAD FOR SHOOTING THEM DAMNIT!!)

Lastly and most importantly, we have to talk about the interactive-cognitive dissonance of this game because it sets to bar for it in every video game ever. What is ICD? It's the difference between what the story is telling you, and what you actually do in gameplay. You sneak down a stairway, spotting two US Soldiers discussing how they want to return to their green farm from this desert nightmare and wish to find peace. Then one of them eventually walks up the stairs to you and you have to shoot them both in the face. No disarming, no dialogue, kill only. You find camps of survivors and refugees who have been murdered, just to make sure, yes, those deserted americans you're shooting HAVE to deserve to be killed AND you're still supposed to feel bad about it, but never lets you do anything to avoid confrontation of the bunches of enemies placed in the level tunnels, like talking them into surrender, taking them down in non-lethal ways or disarming them. You can't feel bad for enemies that you can't choose not to kill, which is why the game ultimately fails to be as dramatic and meaningfull as it tries to be. Also, the sheer amount of super soldier stereotypes thrown at you (for example the aforementioned falling off a bloody skyscraper) makes it impossible to relate to the actions of your "heroes".

Right, this review is late, but sometimes it's good to see a more modern perspective on games. 
Spec Ops: The Line is pretty ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ awesome. If you (yes, you! Reader!) are too lazy to read the blurb, this game is about Captain Walker (voiced by the King of voice acting, Nolan North) and his team of Delta Force operatives who are sent into Dubai to find out what happened to the 33rd Battalion who attempted to evacuate Dubai before lethal sandstorms swept the city. Naturally, the 33rd failed. (If they'd have succeeded, it'd have made for a boring game, don't you think?) When you get there, you find that everything's gone to sh*t and anarchy has ensued, because humans can't help but tear each other apart whenever any form of disaster happens. (Humans, what a bunch of bastards, right?)

I know what a lot of you are thinking, having seen the title and the blurb- yeah, I know it sounds like a mediocre third person shooter with one or two cool parts, nothing to get excited about. That's where you're wrong. This game manages to capture you with a powerful narrative in which you are forced to witness the atrocities that happen in the aftermath of a disaster, and you even do a couple yourself. That being said, this isn't a game where you just see some awful crap and do some yourself, what the game does is show the emotions of Walker and his team. You see the effects that the harrowing scenes have on them and you watch them slowly descend into madness. You can make choices in what you do. Sometimes one choice is the smart thing to do, but is not necessarily the more moral choice. At times, you'll be forced to make the worse choice simply to survive, or to make things easier. 
The story isn't just the good thing, although that would have most people hooked. The gunplay is a bit normal, but it's solid. Most weapons have alternate abilities that can change the way you play, or the tide of a battle. For example, the M4, one of the more common weapons. The alternate fire is a suppressor, which allows you to have an element of stealth. You can silently murder enemies, meaning you need to fight less of them when they inevitably catch you, whereas other weapons just make themselves more effective, such as the AK-47, another common weapon. This one has a burst fire mode as well as automatic, meaning you can accurately pick off enemies in a manner that would be difficult with a fully automatic weapon. 
The level design is linear, but the beautiful -and wrecked- environments will command your attention. The environment isn't all about looks however, there are many ways you can use it to turn the tide of a battle, maybe by shooting out a window to allow tonnes of sand to crash down upon anyone unfortunate enough to be standing next to it, or by turning around a turret and decimating the enemy forces. 
And now, the graphics. The game has aged well, thus far. It won't satisfy graphics wh*res (because they're never satisfied), but they still look pretty amazing, even today. 
The game runs like a charm and holds up a solid 60 FPS, and very rarely begins to tank.

It is console experience, so you are hindered down but I will let it slip since I have a softspot for Gears1, probably due to it inventing the gameplay which modern fps is now rinse&repeating. Since Gears was the first game to do this covershoot thing, it's allowed to do so and this Spec Ops right here, does have scenery in videogames which you have not seen before. Dubai deserts after sandstorm and thus atleast visually it's something new, even if it rides on the same old gameplay which gets old after 15mins of playing.

I only bought this game because it is available on Linux and I heard it is kind of good. "Kind of good" is an understatement. It can be seen as an "Anti Call of Duty", because the setting of the game could also be as well the setting of the next Call of Duty edition. But the story develops in a direction where Call of Duty (most likely) never will go: no glory, just madness. Even though the game starts in quite a standard way (not only in terms of story and setting, but also in terms of gameplay), the direction changes quite fast.

Speaking of gameplay: it is a solid cover shooter. The cover mechanics work quite well (most of the time), the shooting part is good and the AI of the enemies is really good. They are more than just cannon fodder and put some real pressure on the player. The gameplay itself might be standard nowadays, but the implementation is top-notch. The overall game experience is what you would expect from a AAA title, which is a big surprise, considering the topics covered by the game's story.

I have a few points of critique, but those points rather fit to modern shooters in general:
[list]
[*]It is rather short (it took me ~13h to finish the game on the hardest difficulty, and I'm not really experienced in playing cover shooters and thus was dying a lot)
[*]The levels are very linear (but you can also see this as a metaphor for the freedom of choice you have or haven't in the game)
[/list]

Still, for the price it's usually at, it's way worth it, if not for the great soundtrack and narrative at the minimum.

I do NOT recommend this game. It's painfully clear that the makers were trying to make a point with the game, story and gameplay. But it's extremely heavy handed, in your face and sometimes makes absolutely no sense.

So let's start from the beginning. The game is a Modern Military Shooter and it's got every single trope from these games, including regenerating health, bland cover mechanics, billions of soldiers, rambo-style firing from the hip, unskippable cutscenes and more testosterone than a juvenile detention camp.

It tries to be dark, realistic and gritty, but then throws you in a situation where you mow down 50-60 enemies all on your own (or with your two teammates). There are even situations where AG (Air-to-ground) missiles strike the ground not five feet from you and all that results in is a bit of an action scene in slow-mo, a building falling apart but you escaping unscathed. It's got a serious problem with keeping it's setting and tone. Is it dark and realistic? Trying to make a moral point? Is it a dumb covershooter? It can't seem to make up its mind about what it's trying to be.

The gameplay is bland, bordering on downright dull. It's just moving to a battle arena area, mow down 30-50 enemies, move to the next cutscene, new arena. Rince and repeat. It's incredibly dull and if it wasn't for the story, I would've quit after less than half an hour. It's that dull.

It's very obvious the point of this game was to make a moral point in killing and what you're actually doing in a game like this. Killing hundreds upon hundreds of soldiers. Yet the game never gives you an option to stop and ponder these things. Nor does it give you any meaningful choices. Oh, so you want to berate me for using white phosphorous on a bunch of american soldiers, and accidently on a bunch of civilians? Sure, but then give me an alternate route! You can't berate me for making a choice where I had no other choice. 

Then there's situations which are obvious "shooter traps". At one point, someone you care about is killed by an angry mob of civilians, and you're put in a situation where unless you wait for a few seconds, it's going to be the airport scene all over again. Try to walk through the civilians, they nearly one-hit kill you with a push. It's blindingly obvious that the game wants you to shoot the civilians so that it can complain about what a horrible human being you are later. Now, there's actually a way out of that situation that does not involve massacre, so I'll give the game that.

The game at one point makes a quip at how killing civilians isn't allowed in war and adds a contemptful "But you don't even care". Don't presume to know me, my dear game. It pisses me off.

But on the whole this game is frustrating, extremely heavy handed, DRENCHED in MMS tropes and has bland and dull gameplay. Unless you love these kinds of games, please stay away! It's raising some questions, but it does is so extremely "in your face" that it just becomes tiresome and preachy.

Spec Ops: The Line is not the awesome war narrative i had hoped it would be, but instead it is the gritty, harsh reality about the morality and insanity of modern warfare. It tells the story that happens every day in conflicts around the world, the harsh reality and burden that many soldiers fall into. War is not fun, war is hell, and Spec Ops: The Line shows the true hell it is.

I will start by saying, this game does not want you to buy it. And I am dead serious about that. The developers even said as much themselves.

But lets say you were considering buying it anyway. What is Spec Ops? Its a standard cover based third-person shooter. Ever play Gears of War, Kill-Switch, the recent Ghost Recon games, or GTA5 and you know what I mean. Slow paced, but throws more at you. But that's not why you're considering it anyway, its the story.

Well let me get back to that first statement that may have confused you. This game is about "subverting traditional game tropes" which is an asinine way of saying its story really resonates with people concerned with the surface of storytelling. How it does this is by presenting scripted scenes to the player that are sad, then telling the player its their fault it happened. All this hinges on the player being emotionally connected to what's going on. And by going on, I mean dead civilians. Something which has always felt cheap and uninspired. Especially when you as a playerr know its completely disconnected from what you're doing.

That's the problem here. The game takes a huge gamble on whether you emotionally resonate with fictional people you have no connection to. And does this with scenes it forces you to participate in to progress. Which brings us to the real problem with this game. How you win, is to not play it. This was actually said by their staff. You're meant to buy this game, and if you want to be considered a good person, you'd turn the game off immediately. Yes they are trying to make this into a moral judgement on you as a person.

Keep in mind the pricetag they're asking here. As well as the fact this came out before Steam refunds even existed. At the time you would have had to have bought a retail copy and traded in for either store credit, or not even a 1/5th of what you payed for it. Yet what they're expecting from you, is to enjoy being told something they made is your fault, or spend money to NOT play a video game. Some have called it art because of what they were trying to accomplish. To which i say, making an artistic statement doesn't cost people money to understand it. And if you think it does, you're not an artist worth caring about.

I've avoided spoilers here because they're irrelevant to bring up. They're not what makes this game a waste of time. The game itself does, by existing.

This game is the game equivelent of a mix between 'Predator' and 'Full Metal Jacket' i.e. it's the 'Aliens' of video games.

Sans full-on analogy, basically it's generic and predictable action (yet satisfying, a la 'Predator') but with a very well written narative. While you may initially feel the whole "Been there, done that." gambit, it'll suck you in if you let it, and leave you very satisfied with the [end] experience.

There is a good reason I brought up the aforementioned movies: There are paralells to be drawn; you see, while not a great movie (or even good, by reasonable standards) I can't help but love 'Predator'; it has a certain entertainment quality, that while generic, that just stands out and is entertaining. 'SPEC OPS: The Line' is very much in that vein, with one HUGE difference being it has a very well thoughtout script, or at least they were abitious. The pacing could definitely take a queue from the likes of the 'UNCHARTED' franchise...but then again, what series couldn't? That's why I harken back to 'Full Metal Jacket'. While that film was ultimately a masterpiece, it's pacing (along with all Kubrick films) was somewhat lacking; SO: The Line seems moreso to suffer from frantic pacing rather than the slow-draw of a Kubrick film, yet missed pacing is jarring either way, with similar effect.

Yet...Just like FMJ, the pacing seems to make sense within the source material to deliver an ultimately satifying experience.

Lastly, the 'Aliens' reference. You see, while not a cinematic materpiece, 'Aliens' is enjoyable on almost every level, so long as it isn't taken too critically; sure, it's a 'B' movie wrapped in celeophane, but made with such care it just becomes that much more entertaining; and that's what SO: The Line is -- A generic shooter with an exceptionally encompasing narative that, while not entirely original, is extremely entertaining and engaging.

- It is in no way tactical (not a con for me, but it's advertised otherwise, so better be clear on that)

[spoiler]There's no choice that matters, and worst, no choice I felt implicated into.

Unlike what is said in most reviews, the player actually has no influence on game's plot and can make only four decisions during the whole game that decide if he still can think like an average human thing or becames a mindless killing machine, or, as Walker likes to name it, „a soldier” (snipers' ambush, Gould's rescue, mercy killing Riggs, Lugo's death), but after all it makes no change to the game. And this is where in my opinion this game loses all the impression it is supposed to give, even though it has one really great solution that tries to keep it – using a bloody finisher on dying enemy grants player with extra ammo and grenades, but if you will just shoot him once more to let him just die, you get nothing more than your satisfaction.
Honestly, I'd just give up after that phosphorus action. Instead, Walker blamed Konrad for everything (even though, at that time, he was rotting at the top of one of skyscrapers) and started to look out for revenge, putting his team to very high danger just for his personal needs. Just stopped thinking as a soldier, as a commander and as a human. And, after the whole game, it turns out there was no mission and Walker just wanted to be a hero and save someone that didn't even ask for any help. - Usability is a mess. Sometimes there are cutscenes which you can't skip. The savepoint is right before that cutscene. So, if you die at higher difficulty levels (i.E. "FUBAR") it'll get played over and over and over and over and over again. Yeah, I got it, they're rounding up civilians. Again, and again, and again.

Your team is mainly occupied with blocking your sight or not following you - sometimes they rush forward though and if they weren't almost invincible they'd be dead in a second. Sometimes they even shoot through walls.
- The game is, as it is with many mainstream-shooters today, very unrealistic. The most unrealistic things are theweapon damage and the health recovery. And how the soldiers behave. In fact you play rogue soldiers who fail following orders and then you get blamed for "decisions" in a "all war is bad and you are bad" manner.

I didn't play it for a while... and now I remember why I stopped playing Spec Ops: The Line. The idea was good, but the implementation is a mess. If you have at least a bit of a clue you'll hate the game, because Spec Ops: The Line is very good at one thing: Destroying the high opinions you've may got from all the good reviews. [h1]What an experience![/h1]

[i]TLDR: This is any of the great anti-war movies in game format. If you liked those, you will like this one. Gameplay is standard shooter, but the game has a strong story with a gut-wrenching moral ambiguity[/i]

[b]Gameplay[/b]
The game has the standard 3rd person cover-based shooter gameplay as many do. It has the nice twist of team commands for sniping, throwing grenades and focusing fire, all context-sensitive. Imho most thrilling are the few situations where you can't use your team early on - thats when the gunplay becomes more intense. Also there is the "drop sand on enemies" mechanic. But thats only useful for about 5 times in the whole game.

[b]Design[/b]
The UI is quite nicely done and lacks the health bar or so - everything is more or less focused on the main character. Colours and graphics are nice, and it is quite enthralling to see the characters (and parts of the environment) become more and more ragged, deteriorating with the story progress.

[b]Story[/b]
This is where the game shines most. If you watched any of the great (anti-)war movies like Platoon, Apocalypse Now, Full Metal Jacket: this is what the game shows you and lets you experience. The moments of feeling goodlike while you mow down hordes of enemies are halted by scenes which contain everything from moral difficulty to outright horror. Try keeping humanity in an inhuman environment. What can I believe of the things I am hearing (and seeing)? So, a road to hell (paved with good intentions) comes as a playable experience here. Pick  your own flavour of bad outcome.

[b]Resumeé[/b]
Nice one. I picked it up during a sale and was smitten with it. It is mostly a one-playthrough thing unless you are completionist and want all the achievements. You can also replay certain chapters, just to see how different choices play out. Surprise: most play out bad. But bad is good when in context of a warzone. Or at least it makes one think. And that it was SOTL does. Recommended!

When I first heard about this game, I loved the idea. A shooter which forces you to make morally gray decisions while trying to get outta Dodge in one piece. While the game had the core premise well enough, I was sorely disappointed.

PROS
+Cover mechanics and gunplay are mechanically well-fleshed.
+The ending makes a number of things that I scratched my head at make sense. Not all of them, but a number of them.
+There are a number of situations where you do something and just sit there for a minute, amazed at what you did.
+Your AI teammates do actual damage (unlike some other games I know). This may seem like it should be par for the course, but it was refreshing because not enough games have an AI that can actually hurt the enemy.
+Definitely has the atmosphere down pat.
+Game can make you feel terrible early-on for crossing a line, then later forget there was even a line.

CONS
-There's still a lot of things that didn't make sense, even after the end.
-Over-use of Juggernauts. Where they should feel like a mini-boss, they felt like "just another bad guy, but tanky"
-Music didn't help that often. Sometimes, it helps a scene hit home. More frequently, it's annoying background noise, and made me feel annoyed more than anything else.
-One particular character was singled out and it looks like the developers were too eager to make him look like a bad ass instead of letting his actions speak for his character.
-Game tried too hard to beat you over the head with "You're bad! You're bad!" instead of taking a subtler approach. Sometimes, it's necessary. More often, it backfires. Again: let the action speak for itself.
-There's a number of things the game made me do that I didn't want to, both good and bad. Then the game tried to make me guilty for stuff I couldn't say "No" to.
-Squad-based combat mechanics weren't fleshed out, and feel completely useless. Just an add-on to try and make the game have more of a tactical feel, which requires more than "Attack this target," "Heal a downed partner," and "Throw a flashbang, but only at certain times."
-Game isn't sure whether to be realistic or "standard Gears of War cover-shooter," and chooses the latter when the former would have served much better.
-Despite numerous decisions to make, only one changes the ending. It would be nice to have it change across numerous endings based on what you did.

I'm seeing a ton of positive reviews, so I'm probably missing something or seeing too much into it. Either way, it felt like an idea that was poorly realized. Hopefully, the sequel will have a more subtle, expansive way of telling a tragic story.

Some checkpoints are placed with the storytelling in mind but not the replayability, so you get them right before cutscenes or world presentation (a long trek), that works if you quit and start the game another date, but, on the same session, that means if it is followed by a tough fight, it gets annoying fast.

Once you get past the annoyances, firefights are good, and level design helps by not being 100% shooting gallery and giving plenty of alternate ambush routes (which you dont figure until after you get past the shooting gallery so you feel dumb for not taking the clever route, but at least that would help to spice a second playthrough). Due to the design every weapon actually has uses, there are big health sinks you can use the smgs on, long range enemies for snipers, close range for shotguns (and shotguns can be decent at medium range although aiming may be tougher), big groups with lots of suppression that just require explosives of any kind and so on. You start with the simple weapons, and by the end of the game you are using the one-shot-kill sniper, and pro-rifles with noob tubes or m32 6-round grenade launcher with infinite ammo and short reloads. If you notice, the boss enemies start spawning closer and closer to you, forcing you to stop cowering and learn how to beat them, give you less room to hide, and get more personal as the game goes (you have to be the one that kills them, not your ai allies), that the good progression I felt during the game.

All things considered, remember to buy it.

This game is unusual.

On one hand--the storyline is fantastic.  It doesn't exactly try to force morals on you.  It doesn't tell you WAR IS BAD, but rather it forces you to make terrible, awful decisions, each choice akin to dropping a plate full of turds on a marble floor, and then the game tells you to clean it up.  Except when you clean it up, you make everything even more smeary, and it just gets worse and worse from there.  By the end of the night, you decide to clean up the floor by cleaning it up with C4 and a general disregard for OSHA compliance.

By exploring the gaming trope of "You are the Hero" you muck things up exponentially, and it's a terrifying blast to watch the main characters gradually descend into the worst mental pit imaginable.  A lot of people got ruffled because of a scene where you had to deploy white phosphorous (Usually referred to as Willy Pete) on a group of soldiers and the results are catastrophically hilarious in the worst way possible.  But I loved this, why?  Because it tells several things-that people in war have to make terrible, terrible decisions-do we kill one group of people to rescue others?  Do we as soldiers, and on a larger scale we as people, often have to make decisions that are damning, and that isn't portrayed nearly enough in games?

Yes, yes we do--people weren't happy because of the lack of control in this scenario, but it's that lack of control that makes Spec Ops so compelling because let's be truthful, sometimes we need to speak with the ugly reality of things that even when we are the heroes we are just as much the villains, and sometimes we have to become the villains.  Sure, you COULD try to sneak around what are dozens and dozens of people, except you're in the middle of brought daylight and you have absolutely no bearings of your surroundings.  It's a terrible idea because it could lead to failure of the mission, but it's a desperate plea from gamers who want to retain some control in a game where the only control you have is to stop playing.  That alone is brilliant in my opinion.

The gameplay on the other hand is a bruised apple-it's a third person cover based rail shooter, which is probably one of the most painful words I can type out in a review.  Perhaps the developers made the gameplay this bad on purpose, to fit in with the story of, "War is never fun, it's not fun in the story, nor will it be fun in this game."

Except there are a ton of sloppy design mechanics--the run button is shared with the cover button, but sometimes cover isn't properly applied.  The vault button to hurdle over cover and obstacles is a seperate button-instead of combat being one fluid movement, it ends up becoming this disheveled janky mess where often times, if you actually remember to hit the vault button, sometimes you realize that you can't even vault over that item, or even better, you try to take cover behind an object but good luck because it's a corner, so you either end up just standing around getting shot at or you end up taking cover on the wrong side of the wall.

Also, The bad guys are mindless drones, spawning out of mid-air.  At first, killing men dressed as US Soldiers is unnerving-these are our people!  And then after a while?  It just becomes a chore.  "Oh look, another way to artificially waste my time!"  Maybe another thought on war-how easy it is to stop associating them as people, but rather, as mindless objects that we must cross.  Except you don't get that feeling in here, you don't get that regret, and you don't get the PTSD that comes with killing a man that may have a child just like yours and is just doing his job.  You just think, "GOD THIS GAME IS THE WORST."  If this was in any other game it would be criticized for being a bad game, and I don't think this game should get spared because of it's message or some clever metagame that says that it's intentional.

This game would be so much better if the combat wasn't a terrible mess of what feels like half assed ideas-I don't know if people try to cover up some of this with the thematics of the game, but I feel like it was just overall terrible design decisions.  If this was in any other game?

The game also suffers from having absolutely useless companions-they don't feel like they do much good at all besides occasionally taking out snipers or heavies or turrets, but in reality you can do this just as well by yourself.  The few obstacles placed in your way, like a sniper or such where you HAVE to use your companions never make it feel as if they're useful, but rather an obligation, as if the game developers said, hey lets make the player remember these guys exist and then don't use them for anything else besides banter.

Then there was the time we were pinned down by snipers as part of the story and my sniper was telling me that I had to get rid of them-what?  You're telling me I have to do your job when you're five feet away from me?

Honestly-I recommend this game for the story alone.  I would under no good conscience recommend it for having fun and a good time but instead as an experience to walk away from.
