I am an Army infantry combat veteran. I don't say that to brag, only so that you'll know when I critique the realism of this game, I know a little of what I'm talking about.

I love shooter games but I have never had the emotional connection to any game before this one. Normally it doesn't take much thinking to blow away animated bad guys. But in Spec Ops you quickly get drawn in to what you are doing. I read a couple articles about this game before playing it. Most talked about how the creators of the game wanted to create a game where players thought about what they were doing when they killed in the game. In that, they succeeded. I have never played a game that sucked you into the battle the way this one did. Normally in a game I would clear an area and then poke around for ammo and secrets. The first few times I played this game I got so caught up in the rush of the game that I routinely charged forward without stopping to pick up ammo and often found myself with little ammo left which would be more similar to real life than most games. With that said, here is my review of the game. Do not read further if you want to avoid spoilers....

GAMEPLAY:
I'm normally not a fan of 3rd person shooters, but this game worked pretty well. The controls take some getting used to, specifically in the moving to and from cover aspects and cycling through weapons. But I thought overall the game really sucked you in to the emotion and the adrenaline. This is actually a very short game, though I was glad it was after my first time through as I felt I had literally been through a war zone playing it. It took me a while before I could play it again. Ironically I've actually come to enjoy replaying this game which is probably not what the creators intended. I'm fairly good at separating games from reality and this is actually a pretty good shooter in my opinion.

WEAPONS:
One of the things this game gets right in my opinion overall is the weapons. For the most part you can pick any weapon and get through the game with it. M4's are accurate but don't have the stopping power of AK-47's. M2 .50 cals kill anything but overheat quickly. For the most part it's pretty realistic.

GRAPHICS:
The graphics are pretty good, even for a game that is not very new. Once you've played through it and can stop long enough to take in the scenery it's actually pretty cool and very well done.

THE NITTY GRITTY:
Overall I really liked this game but the grunt in me couldn't let everything pass without complaint....

STORY:
If you can suspend disbelief the story is actually pretty compelling. But if you stop to analyze it falls apart pretty quickly... The premise is interesting and serves the purpose of creating the scene needed for the game to work. But...a more or less never ending sandstorm??? Your character is sent to see if there are any survivors in Dubai but at several points in the game you can see clear skies above you. Why couldn't recon satelites be used to see what was going on??? You can also see the ocean nearby at some points. What would stop a submarine from getting in close to land a recon team or a rescue force and maintain communications?

CHARACTERS:
Everybody has to be a Delta operator or a SEAL these days, but a captain, a lieutenant, and a sergeant as the team? Come on guys. I can buy the early fights against the "insurgents" but once the team meets and kills Lt. McPherson of the 33rd, how does the rest of the 33rd know the "Delta" guys are bad guys? Why can't the Delta guys talk to the 33rd soldiers they run into???

CHOICES:
One of the main themes of the game is that you shouldn't just mindlessly charge forward killing everything in sight as most shooter games want you to do. The game tries to imply that you have a choice, specifically to stop playing, killng, etc. Unfortunately the game doesn't give you a choice most of the time. There are one or two occasions where the "choice" you make can lead to slightly different outcomes, but overall you don't have a choice unless you stop playing the game altogether.

The mortar/white phosphorous scene is the prime example of this and the pivotal scene of the game. I admit, the first time I played through that scene it got to me more than any other game scene has. The problem is, in real life you would have a choice. In the game you can either use the mortar to masacre the 33rd troops or you can try to shoot it out with them with small arms, in which case you are guaranteed to die eventually. Why can't you go around them? Or sneak by them? I can think of several other options other than the ones you are permitted to choose.

Again this is a powerful scene but as a mortar man myself, it strays pretty far from reality. Your using a 60mm mortar... regardless of the round it's not going to do much to a Striker. The game makes a big deal of white phosphorous/willy pete rounds. Sure, against unprotected infantry WP rounds can be pretty deadly but its primary function is to be used after high explosive (HE) or delayed impact rounds have been fired and have opened up fuel lines and other combustible material. Then the WP is shot in to light the combustible stuff on fire. I understand what the creators were trying to do here but the scene stretches reality quite a bit.

As a military man I have to complain about the game not being EXACTLY correct but as I said in the beginning I really recommend this game to anyone that wants to really feel a game pull you in. You will hate yourself for liking this game but in the end it's worth at least one play through.

- Fun to play if you like 3rd person shooters
- Great graphics for a 4-year-old game
- While somewhat predictable, the plot is still above average for a game; certain parts are quite intense in terms of action
- Ability to command your other team members to focus their fire on specific enemies
- More realistic than average game in terms of damage
- More realistic with ammo management (it's not as widely available as other shooters tend to be, and often times you will be forced into using various weapons simply because your favorite gun ran out of ammo)

Cons: 
- Commanding teammates is a bit limited, would've loved to see more control in this regard
- No character or skill building / development
- No weapons customization
- Aiming with a controller can be difficult
- Linear gameplay
- Take cover navigation can be a tad wonky in sticky situations
- About half-way through the story line, you can guess the plot twist because of the heavy amount of clues

The game is definitely worth checking out if you're a fan of games like Gears of War.

I must admit that I did enjoy playing this game. The action was good and the scenery of a Dubai under the after effects of a powerful sandstorm made for a very memorable experience. However, I still can't recommend "Spec Ops" to anyone. The graphics are good, even for an older game, and the squad "banter" is often amusing and reminiscent of old B action films. 

However, I bought this game because of the so-called "serious" decision-making that was advertised as adding another level to what is ultimately a rather flashy but simplistic squad-based FPS. Sadly I was extremely disappointed by the fact that none of the decisions had any real relevance to the actual course of the storyline, leaving a totally linear narrative that I completed in 9 hours (and I'm not an FPS gamer either). For the most part, the "big" decisions felt forced and it seemed like the player was being left with no other alternatives except for choosing between "bad" and "even more depressing". A more open gameworld might have allowed players at least some ability to problem-solve their way around the suggested alternatives and come up with more inventive strategies.

A more open narrative would also have added immensely to the experience, instead of trudging from one chapter to the next along the rails of a dead straight narrative arc. Possibly the inclusion of some sort of temporary base of operations in the city from which to launch various smaller ops that contribute to the progress of the story through their completion, while one continues to advance the main plot simultaneously. Nevertheless this is not true of "Spec Ops", which can only perhaps be viewed as a contemplation on the savagery of modern warfare and the fact that it leaves no one involved completely untouched: In the end, it might be better to think of this as more of a moralising play than a typical FPS...

Spec Ops: The Line is a cover based third-person shooter in which the player controls one Captain Martin Walker. The player also has some control over Walker's crew, Adams and Lugo, in terms that they can be commanded to kill specific enemies on the battlefield. The entire game takes place in a post-war zone Dubai, where Walker and his crew have been sent out on a reconnaissance mission.

At the time of writing, it has been nearly three years since Spec Ops: The Line released initially. The game has definitely stood the test of time in every aspect imaginable; the story, graphics, gameplay and soundtrack have all aged beautifully. For the time, the graphics were above par for shooter titles, and they're still outstanding to look at today; especially the way Walker's face becomes more and more disfigured by the turmoils of war as the campaign wears on. The use of dynamic lighting is also some of the best that I've seen in early-era last gen games. The city of Dubai, as sand-swallowed as it may be, is massive and stunning to look at.

I will also add in a quick note here that the game does not suffer from any type of performance issues, at least in my experience. I always maintained a stable 80-120 FPS throughout the duration of the game while capping out at 144 FPS, and there were no crashes, glitches, or bugs.

The gameplay is solid for a shooter, there are no clunky controls. The entire control scheme is similar to that of the first Gears of War title; which is not unusual, seeing as Spec Ops was indeed crafted using the Unreal Engine. There are slight annoyances, such as when you're running you will sometimes stick to a piece of cover. Other than that, the control scheme is smooth and nearly flawless. As expected, there are tons of shooting sequences... almost too many at times. Around every corner there lurks another gang of foes who are waiting to rip Walker to shreds bullet by bullet. Like any good military style shooter, there is also Intel to collect.

Where Spec Ops: The Line really shines is within its story, and its soundtrack. This game has one of the best soundtracks of any shooter that I've ever played; from the rocking classic tunes to the Louisiana bayou styled twangy guitars, the tracks never get old no matter how many times one plays through the game. The same can be said for the story, which has a possibility of four endings once the player has reached the end of the ride. While I won't say a lot about the story, for those that have not played the game yet, I will say that Spec Ops definitely ripped off the original Black Ops, but I personally think this game does it way better. 

A once respected high ranking military man who gradually goes crazy over the course of the campaign, only to have a huge twist revealed at the end. There are lots of feels-hitting areas between the beginning and end of the game, and the player can become very attached to Walker, Adams and Lugo throughout the time spent within the title; making it that much harder on the emotions when something goes awry. This aspect is where every single Call of Duty ever created has failed, and it's why people love Spec Ops: The Line. The game does spend a good amount of time carving out the characters, so that they don't just become more expendable jarheads in another military shooter.

If you haven't played Spec Ops: The Line yet, and you're in the market for a good third-person cover based shooter, definitely pick this up. It will be one of the greatest storylines in a shooter that you've ever experienced, and it's sure to stay within your memory for years to come. There are also many replay factors, and reasons to go back to the title; whether it's as soon as you complete it, or a couple years down the road. However, I cannot justify $32.99 CAD for a title that is almost three years old, get it on sale.

This game's slower and the gameplay suffers from Generic Military Shooter Syndrome, and I found myself sometimes annoyed by the cover mechanics and lack of anything new brought to the table. Spec Ops: The Line is a game that both suffers and benefits greatly from its title. On one hand, the name “SPEC OPS: THE LINE” is generic to the point of being the product of a military combat Mad Libs, fitting in nicely between such titles as “HARDENED SOLDIER: PAID IN BLOOD” and “WAR PAWNS 3: DOUBLE BARRELED IN SUDAN.” The cover features bold lettering, unhappy dudes toting unhappy guns, and an explosion, all tinted in the most vivid shade of the color spectrum; brown.

	You can spend three seconds looking at the box and think you know exactly what you're getting into. Middle East. Helicopter crash. Militants. Shooty-shooty-bang-die. Done. 

	Of course, you'd be wrong.

	Don't misunderstand me, all those things are indeed present in the game, but I'm of the belief that the true brilliance of this game, and its title, is that it wants to [i]appear[/i] like all other bland military shooters, and it wants you to  [i]play[/i] it like all other bland military shooters, because the game's message and play-style is fashioned out of that expectation of you. The best way to experience Spec Ops is to go in figuratively blind. Trust me on this. Stop reading this review, stop reading any Spec Ops reviews, and just play it. Seriously, go away. Simply put, the more you know about the story, the message, and what the game is truly up to...the less effective it is.  

	That said, a video game review isn't worth much without the author injecting as many off-topic blog-tier musings as possible (hello, Polygon.com) so I'm going to continue writing and hope for the best. 

	I truly believe that Spec Ops is of a unique persuasion in that the game dislikes the player. Spec Ops gives the player choices, but first concludes that if the player begins to actually play the game, then at some basic level, the character that we—the players, control has disobeyed orders and lost. The more we play, the harder our character loses. Choices rarely appear to be actual choices, and are instead framed as typical video game 'do or die' situations; do this action, or the game ends. Shoot these people, or you die. Press this button, or get overrun. Press forward, or don't complete the level. 

	Of course, all video games could be boiled down to this idea, really. Mario  [i]should[/i] jump on the Goomba and get to the end of the level. If you decide to have Mario just run into the little guy and die on World 1-1...you have (in a way) completed the game. You finished the story of Mario. 

	This isn't how we approach video games, though. It's not how we approach media in general. Yet, Spec Ops toys with this idea and asks to player to reflect [i]why[/i] they pressed on from level to level. [i]Why[/i] they continued to shoot. [i]Why[/i] they continued to kill. We the players might respond with “That's just what I was supposed to do,” which gives a much clearer perspective into why games work like they do these days. Why destruction is seemingly the only action that most games can trust players with. Why spectacle is so much more developed than emotion. Why this game, out of all games, came packaged with an achingly dull progression-unlock multiplayer component.

	I recommend this game, Steam. Thanks for acting like you care, bud.

Perhaps intentional design, perhaps not and most likely subject to the perceptive cognisance of those lost in the immersive sea of Dubai's blood stained sand.  

For when the credits roll and you ponder the rich story [url=http://www.engadget.com/2012/07/04/stiq-flicks-spec-ops-the-line-and-apocalypse-now/]inspired*[/url] by Joseph Conrad's novella Heart of Darkness and influenced by Francis Ford Coppola's iconic Apocalypse Now, Spec Ops The Line is elevated past common war time yarns denoted by the computer game genre.

Where the repetitive Gears of War, run, cover and shoot mechanics overrun, thankfully the avant-garde psychical linear narrative blisters continuously, frequently exposing enough underlying ethical wounds to metamorphosize the title from combat to psychological horror.

Endowed with multiple endings, I researched for a definitive authoritative source that would define which ending is lore and which ending was designed to be deceptively tangential, thus further encapsulating this deep and vividly imaginative work.

Special mention for the soundtrack and the inclusion of Deep Purple and Jimi Hendrix.  Highly recommended and an additional play-through from an alternative perspective encouraged.

This game has by far some of the most frustrating mechanics of any game I have ever played.

Let's start with the basics: it's a cover-based, squad-based third-person shooter.  Well, except for the fact that there is one magical button for sprinting/cover/rotating out of cover/healing your teammates.  Roll a dice to figure-out which one the game will pick to do this time!  Want to heal your squad member?  Sorry, you're rushing into the meat grinder like a maggot straight out of basic!  Want to sprint to that cover?  No dice chief, it's at a slight angle so instead you're sprinting next to the cover until you mash the button enough that your character decides to commit suicide.  But there is cover, so I guess you could call it "cover-based."  Don't even get me started on the grenades.

Oh, and did I mention your squad?  Your two helpful teammates with minds of their own, who love to run out of cover and get shot and bleed out and force you to replay the same section over and over because they are too stupid to just stay put and keep their heads down.  I don't know whether I spent more time replaying chapters because they died or replaying chapters because I kept shooting them in the face.

Thankfully the third person mechanic saves everything.  As long as everything you need to shoot is on your right.  If it's on your left you're out of luck.

Issues aside, my favorite part of the game are the setpieces.  Those wonderful scripted moments where something completely out of your control happens in a masterful stroke of storytelling and you have to play the same thirty-second section again and again for over an hour because the scripted event accidentally kills you.  Whoops.

The story is well-told, the atmosphere is perfect, the music is fitting, and the characters' development is superb.  It's a great Heart of Darkness adaptation and a nice parallel of the modern problems with US jingoistic foreign policy and military hero worship.  Even with all of its problems, I'd still recommend playing through it for the story alone.  Just make sure you choose the cake-walk difficulty to avoid tearing your hair out.

It's essentially the gameplay Gears of War meets a story heavily influenced by Apocalypse Now/Heart of Darkness set in a semi-apocalyptic Dubai.

Let's get this out of the way: The gameplay is mediocre at best. It's a 3PS with your standard cover-based combat. There's nothing interesting about it, and plenty of games have done it better. All that said, it's functional, it's visceral, and it feels good when you finally manage to break through a particularly difficult corridor.

Now, I'd heard people talk about the story and the "twist," and I'd been wary. Most media involving critiques of modern American military involvement still seems to either have the characters "go native" (like Pochahontas or Avatar) or has the character portrayed as some kind of hero (Hurt Locker or American Sniper) despite their violent and harmful actions.

What Spec Ops did was very clever, though not entirely novel. People familiar with Apocalypse Now and/or Heart of Darkness will recognize right away the ambiguity of the introduction. You are DELTA SQUAD, from America, and you're here to ... do something? Save people? Look for survivors? It's never really made entirely clear what you're doing in the wreckage of sandswept, arid Dubai. You know that you're supposed to be rescuing somebody, but the game is ambiguous. 

The villains also seem to be mysterious and ambiguous. The first group you fight are survivors of whatever happened to Dubai, but soon you're fighting an American detachment called the 33rd, led by a shadowy figure named "Konrad" (a very unsubtle nod to to author of HoD, Joseph Conrad, as well as the main 'antagonist,' Kurtz). Very soon, and very quickly, you seem to abandon your mission in order to take vengeance upon Konrad.

This is where the story gets interesting. This is where the twist begins.

Despite some awkward pacing around the middle, I felt that the reveal was slow enough that I had about an hour or two of wondering and trying to piece things together before I was shown what was actually happening. Your character is suddenly forced to make unpleasant choices, and you have to wonder whether or not that says anything about you. Probably my favourite detail is that a little past the halfway point, the load screens stop giving tips and start making accusatory statements.

"This is all your fault."

"How many Americans have you killed today?"

As this is happening, the player character (voiced by Nolan North) becomes increasingly strained. Instead of saying "Tango neutralized!" or "Heavy target down!" he starts garbling in an exhausted rasp "THE ♥♥♥♥♥♥'S BEEN KILLED" or "ONE LESS BASTARD TO WORRY ABOUT." Combined with the wear and tear of his clothes and a fresh wound after every cutscene, you really feel the character's mental state start to decline.

Noticing this for the first time made me realize that this was a game that was very much trying to push away from other games in the military shooter genre. It wasn't the run and gun propaganda of CoD MW, and it wasn't the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ insane conspiracy theory garbage of CoD Blops. This was a game that was trying to ask you what YOU thought was right, by giving you a certain amount of power and encouraging you to abuse it as you saw fit.

The ending was satisfying. Not as satisfying as Brando staring into the distance and repeating the famous lines "The horror... The horror!" but it was still satisfying to see the game play out in a way that you almost expected, but didn't really want to see.

Anyways, 7/10. The gameplay is a 6, the story is a solid 8.5.

This what it? This was the cult classic shooter every video game hipster this side of the solar system ranted and raved about? Really?  Okay, where to begin...



First and foremost, the game was four hours on the normal difficulty.  Four.  That's about a dollar an hour for what I paid this game for on Steam, so whatever,  But definitely not worth the $30 it's worth normally.  Beyond that, the game doesn't really successfullly subvert the shooter genre like a lot of people like to say it does.  Why?  Because you, as the player, never have any real decisions to make.  The game tries to make you feel bad for doing things, except you have no choice but to do them.  If I could choose not to do bad things but I did them anyway, mistakeningly or otherwise, I might feel bad about the bad things my character does in the game.  But I can't, so I don't.  Beyond that, the story was pretty convoluted.  Some of the crap the characters do is overtly sabotaging their mission and they don't seem to notice until after the fact.  


The rest of the narrative is pretty much "find this guy, so you can find that guy, so you can find THAT guy", and that's pretty much  it.  It's a quest to find a bunch of different dudes who are in the game for fewer than thirty minutes so you can find the next guy who will be in the game for fewer than thirty minutes and that's pretty much it.  On top of that, the suppossed delta operators act like anything but.  None of them seem like they've ever held a weapon before in their respective lives.  The player character inexplicably has two rear iron sights on his rifle and fires it with the stock under his armpit.  The dialogue is also horrible.  Additionally, there are military inaccuracies out the wazoo.  There are two officers in your "squad", but delta doesn't recruit officers.  A fireteam is at least four guys, but your team has three.  The 33rd Battalion has way too many guys to actually be a battalion, and the guy leading them is also a delta officer (again, even though there's no such thing).  Why is a spec ops guy leading an infantry unit?  Who knows.  This game makes zero sense.  Moreoever, you carry about half the actual combat load of an actual soldier, so have fun constantly scrounging for ammo after you burn through your whopping 120 rounds in your primary weapon.  



Your teammates are also completely useless.  They can't do anything unless you tell them to, otherwise they just get in your way.  Ocasionally, they'll even get downed and you'll have to revive them, even though there is no such system in place for your character.  If you go down, you die.  Which is horribly frustrating, considering you'll sprint when you mean to slide into cover and vice versa due to the bad controls.  All in all, this game is just bad.  It doesn't really succeed in anything it tries to do.  The only part of the game that really got to me was one of the endings that you can affect, and even then, the game couldn't fight its compulsion to be lame and cut the awesome pan-out and the music just as the full effect of the scene was setting in.  



The game's cutscenes are abrupt with rapid transitions and violent cut-outs of music.  There are fewer than ten commonly-encountered weapons in the whole game, and none of them can be customized.  Which, is kinda ridiculous, considering delta guys get absolute autonomy over their gear.  Your companions are noisey and incompetent tag-alongs who constantly shout at you, giving away your position.  Even the gunplay is mediorce at best.  Buy the game and give it a go if it's on sale.  Otherwise, avoid it like it's the plague.  This game was atrociously bad.

A wonderfully, terrible third person shooter that you can finish in a weekend. Spec Ops: The Line will draw you in with its generic box art and derivative gameplay, and then flip you on your head and stomp on your gut because you're a terrible person. 

The game opens in medias res with (all together now) a helicopter chase scene wherein you mow down other helicopters with an infinite ammo minigun, until one of them crashes into you. flash back to the beginning where our protangonists are on a mission to find out what happened in Dubai after a record sandstorm hit. You fight some local insurgents, explore some interesting sand infested buildings, and slowly learn about a CIA operation and a rogue American Infantry unit. 

After about an hour of run-of-the-mill shooter story, things start to get a little strange. First you start killing other American soldiers in self-defense. Then you're trying to figure out if you can trust the CIA agents or not. pretty soon you're raining down white phosphorus on an entire platoon of your fellow soldiers and innocent civilians!

Wait what?

Yeah, it only gets better from there, and the best part is the story ramps up so smoothly and the gameplay is integrated into that story so well. The loading screens start off with helpful hints about gameplay then slowly shift to unnerving messages directed at the player in real life. The animations of the characters even change over time! The early game will see Cpt. Walker punch or rifle butt a downed enemy to finish him off, but later on he starts getting more viscious by shooting them in the face while they beg for mercy. Even the mission objectives are integrated into this mad scheme. They start off like any other game: go here, defend this, eliminate that. But then they change: obey, murder, and so on.

Often in games we see a sort of cognitive dissonance between what the game is telling us about a character and what the character actually does in the game when we're controlling them (see the Tomb Raider reboot). Spec Ops is both a great example of how to not have that problem AND is the greatest display of cognitive dissonance AT THE SAME TIME!

I could go on, but the Extra Credits team has already articulated my thoughts better than I can. I do have a few closing thoughts though. First and foremost, yes the gameplay isn't very good. You run. Your gun. You take cover. Enemies spawn in obvious spots. It's all very early 2000s shooter. However, that's all done on purpose to highlight and critique those very same generic shooters. Second, this is strictly a single player game. There is no multiplayer, nor should there have ever been (although maybe they also tacked it on just to show a point). 

Finally, and most importantly, I'd like you all to remember: you choose to play this game. You choose to do all those horrible things. Really, the only way to win this game is to stop playing it. But even then, you'd still be losing.

Spec Ops: The Line. There's one title I had never really noticed, until I came across it on a top something list of good games of some kind. It was lauded for its story.
The short version of this review is: everybody else is right, this is a recommendation, play it.

But why? Well, the game is a cover based, third person shooter. It gets the mechanics right except for one strange exception, being the melee button and the cover button being the same one. It's a reasonably small gripe, even if it caused a few deaths.
Graphically, the level design goes from OK-but-really-generic to very interesting and in service of the story and its progression. You'll have to get past the initial genericness of it, it's worth it. Technically, the game looks fine. It doesn't have anything revolutionairy going on, but that's not what Specs Ops is about.

You play as captain Walker, who, along with two team members is sent to Dubai on a reconnaissance mission. After finding something else than they expect, Walker decides that they're on a different mission now. But during this mission the line between what's right and what's wrong continues to shift and fade.
It's this story that's different from other games. Not the graphics, or the voice acting (which I think is very good btw), or the animations. Or rather: it's the idea that the game is more or less a character study, the type where at the end you think back and remember details that suddenly make sense. Or better yet: the details you missed that you notice the second time you play through it (these details are really a testament to the developer's devotion, massive thumbs up). It's is a pretty intense trip, and on the one hand it's about as much fun as it is to watch Apocalypse Now, but on the other hand, screw that and give this game a chance.

[u] What is Spec Ops [/u]

[olist]

    [*] An interactive story, about war and doom ;
    [*] A "tactical" 3rd person shooter.

[/olist]

[u]What I liked about it[/u]

[list]

    [*] I got hooked quite fast. It is not that original, but it works just fine: 
Things have gone horribly bad in Dubaï -> Who did it? Why? What are we supposed to do?
 [b]The plot is fast paced, and numerous twists keep you thrilled all along[/b]. If you want you can collect intelligence to get a better understanding, which is always nice for this kind of game.
You can  [b]make choices that will influence the story[/b] at some points, which is IMO one of the best features in a game.

    [*] The great art and atmosphere. In a few words, I would call it [b]dark and surrealistic[/b]. As should be something as senseless and terrible as war. It carries the story, through ambient music, visual storytelling and symbols. I think it works perfectly. During the fight, it is all bullets and screams, but when things go quiet again, what is left ? [b]Blood, fire and sand [/b]. Also, I must add that even if the city is ruined, some places in this game are still beautiful (e.g. some luxury hotels).

    [*] I found the gameplay fine and  [b]challenging[/b]. The shooter being "tactical" means that positioning and cover is important and you can give orders to your NPC team mates. Compared to Mass Effect 1 (I did not play the others), the team controls are bad, but I found 2 things I liked best: there is not so much scattering when you aim (which is something I hate about RPG shooters) and your characters moves are smoother (you can jump over obstacles, knock ennemies down and finish them later, etc.). Also,  [b]stealth[/b] killing is sometimes an option, which is great! (yeah, I am quite the sneaky fellow, usually).

[/list]

[u]"But... there is some bad stuff, right?"[/u]

It is not perfect of course. I think the gameplay could have been better, especially team controls, and I was expecting more player choices from what I had heared. However, these are secondary complaints.  [b]This game does very well what it was intended to do[/b], and IMO, it is the exact definition of a [i]success[/i].

[u]Why you should play it[/u]

You will see terrible things.[b]Innocents will die[/b]. Perhaps friends. It will not make much sense. You will be [b]angry[/b] at who is responsible for all this. Sometimes, you will have to [b]make hard calls[/b], and accept the [b]consequences[/b]. Sometimes, you will just [b]have no choice[/b]. You will be confused, pressured, anguished, but you will have to [b]keep moving on, down into hell, because it is your duty[/b].

But ultimately, if you are ready to pay the cost, you will know the truth. Maybe...

“The truth, Walker, is that you're here because you wanted to feel like something you're not: A hero.” Without wishing to spoil anything, these words were spoken in the recent game Spec-Ops: The Line. One question that often comes up with video games is what advantage a game has over a movie or a book? The answer to that is the level of interaction that a person has with a game’s world and story. I’ve read movies and books that can get a person to think about the actions that a person may take, but I have never seen or read anything that makes me question my own actions. This is where the game Spec Ops: The Line comes in, and it really does do a great job at responding to the actions of the player with actual consequences unlike other games. While the gameplay is very standard the story telling is probably some of the best stories told in video games in recent time.
A recent problem with the game industry is the slew of modern shooters paving the way for very uncomfortable themes. For example Call of Duty: Ghosts’ story is about America building a doomsday cannon in space- and the game has no self-awareness whatsoever. The game doesn’t get much better when the player gains control of the cannon and nukes all of South America. So the theme to Call of Duty: Ghosts comes across as being that America should build a death weapon to kill everyone who isn’t American. Thank goodness for Spec-Ops: The Line coming along and showing us how a deep and complex story should be told. While the gameplay is certainly standard in this game, it goes along with telling the absolutely excellent story. It’s one of the few games that everyone should play. Whether one plays games or not, it’s a game that gets people to think with its innovative story telling.
	Spec Ops: The Line is based on the book Heart of Darkness by Joseph Conrad, which was also the inspiration for the movie Apocalypse Now. The basic plotline of those pieces is that a Colonel in the army goes native deep in the heart of jungle lands and starts ruling over the native population. That’s not a spoiler, for those who are wondering. It is established very early on in Spec Ops: The Line that Col. John Konrad (the main antagonist) is ruling over the native populace. The game also doesn’t borrow that much from Apocalypse Now or Heart of Darkness. The reason that the Colonel has decided to ditch the US army and go native is that a recent sandstorm has struck the Middle Eastern city of Dubai. After the major politicians and other VIPs leave the city Konrad is ordered to abandon the city and come home to America. Konrad chooses to stay in the city along with his unit, the 33rd infantry, which would become known as the “Damned 33rd.” The colonel and his troops made one last desperate escape attempt, but failed miserably. The city went dark for six months before American forces received a radio message from Konrad asking for aid.
	Enter our protagonists, Captain Martin Walker and his two NPC (non-player character) subordinates. The first thoughts that I had going into this was that it was going to be another Call of Duty clone. I was expecting another gun ho, nationalistic war game about how great it is to go to war. However, the game pulls a massive fast one though when, in the context of war, the game has the player do something unforgivable. I know that I felt like crap after it happened. After this event, Walker’s mind begins a massive descent into madness and brutality as he moves toward a goal that is becoming increasingly blurred. What I like about the game’s story is how it starts. The player starts with the expectations they would have about any modern game, which makes the grand twist all the more shocking. Those who tend to look at modern shooters with disdain would especially find the moment to be a huge shock to them when they find themselves questioning their own morality. 
However, some people though may find the tone to be a bit wonky at times, especially in regards to the gameplay. One bullet from your gun is enough blow an entire enemy’s head clean off, with bone sticking out of the neck stump. It also does that thing where it slows down the gameplay so you can get a good look at your freshly slain kill. These features do seem to go against the actual message of the game, but I feel as though this was intended to let the player lose his or her self in the game before the game yanks on the collar and pulls the player back down to reality. On the other hand, however, it’s almost like if someone flashes you in the parking lot and then yells at you for looking. I never asked to see those violent kills in Spec Ops, so I wouldn’t be surprised if a few people were turned off because of this. Keep in mind, though, I could have stopped playing at any time, so that’s what makes me believe that the game was making me lose myself in the first half and then begin the spiral into madness. One of the more important questions, though, is “how does the gameplay work?”
The gameplay itself is a basic third person cover based shooter with tactical elements. I think that the third person really goes along with creating a sense of disconnect between the player and the character. This makes it so it doesn’t feel like the player is just being lectured by the game and goes to show the effects these actions can have on a soldier. If it had been in the first person a lot of what it was trying to say would have been lost. No one likes to be told how to feel. In Amnesia: The Dark Descent the game had a sanity meter which would tell you how scared you should be, which seems to say that the developers were not very confident with their own work. While the final confrontation is as much confronting the player as it is Walker, if it had been done from the first person perspective it would have felt more like a lecture at the player forcing them to feel bad. As for the tactical part the game, it’s probably the weaker aspect. You point at a group of soldiers you particularly don’t like, and your explosives guy will blow it up. You point at a faraway enemy you don’t like and your sniper guy will shoot it. These effects don’t go toward much and are barely used because it’s does not take long before you realize that it is easier to eliminate the middle man and just shoot them yourself. The tactical part of the game falls flat so what else is there?
A unique selling point to the game is its use of sand. Sometimes you can shoot out windows to have a huge ton of sand come crashing down on top the enemies, but it’s hardly worth mentioning. It’s not going to make any one jump up and down. What I found most interesting about the gameplay was the development of the character shown through his actions. You can perform executions with your enemy. At first it start as a way to end someone’s life painlessly, but as Walker’s mind collapses he starts wanting to cause as much pain to his enemies as possible. This is also shown in his dialogue during combat. At the start he would shout “he’s down” and by the end of it he would shout “F***ing stay dead!” I do like how well the gameplay goes to show Walker’s descent into madness. One other thing that I love is the focus it keep as the game progresses.

This isn't just a game, it's existential art.  This should be required playing for every high school student in America.  It forces you to question your own ideas on what constitutes a hero, what an enemy is, what the nature of duty is, what is good, what is bad, what is right, what is wrong, what is honorable, what is dishonorable, what is justice, what is moral, and who gets to decide where to draw the line.   

The story pivots around the central character's hero complex and his need to validate this egoistic image he has of himself.  He makes bad decisions and commits to them even when the outcome of those decisions leads to disastrous consequences.  He never takes responsibility for his poor choices, because his ego won't allow him to, but instead insists that he "had no choice".  By the end of the game the player, too, will feel his/her expectations challenged.  This metagaming experience will leave a lasting impression.

This game has a pretty thick narrative that mostly plays out in dialogue between the various actors as they move through the world.  Cutscenes are concise and to the point.  There is no filler here.   This is very much a modern day retelling of the Joseph Conrad novel 'Heart of Darkness'.  The story had me hooked from beginning to end.  The writing is that good!

Gameplay-wise it functions like many third person shooter games (Gears of War, for instance).  Some of the mechanics can be wonky, but not to the detriment of "enjoyment".  You can carry two weapons at a time and 3 different explosive types (grenade, sticky bomb, and flashbang).  You can swap for weapons you come across, and you can find ammo and explosive boxes to refill what you're carrying.  There is a plethora of weapons and they all have their pros and cons.  There are also places where you can man turrets or gatling guns.  

Combat involves alot of taking cover and picking your shots.  Doom this is not.  It's very easy to get torn to shreds by a hail of bullets in seconds if you're not careful.  There are no medkits, your health regenerates when not taking damage, but your team-mates can be incapicated - injecting them with morphine helps get them back into action (if they bleed out first they die and you restart at a checkpoint).  

The graphics are gorgeous.  The game has beautiful scenery with a rich tapestry of colors that belies the dark nature of the world you inhabit.  It has it's share of gore, but it's a story about war which is always messy.

The voiceover acting is impeccable.  The sound design is solid.  The soundtrack is amazing.

Multiplayer is a mixed bag, but if you have no interest in the singleplayer game and it's metaphysical storytelling then you should probably go play Battlefield or some other brainless shooter instead anyway.

[b]Spec Ops: The Line[/b] is a thirdperson cover shooter with an interesting setting. The game looks and sounds appealing, but it falls flat on its face when you actually play it.

Most of the weapons (especially the assault rifles) feel identical with the only real differences being lightly modified stats and a different mesh. There is almost no enemy variety. You will play the whole game only encountering reskinned versions of the same enemy. However, the game will occasionally throw a heavy or charger at you. Even then, they do not add enough to the combat to bother.

On the topic of gameplay, the controls are weak. I found myself pressing spacebar or shift on accident and quickly dying because of it. By default, spacebar is sprint, cover and revive. Shift is for your melee attack (which is completely useless) and leaping over cover. Even after rebinding them, I still do not believe they work very well.

One of the most praised aspects of this game is the story. It's certainly better than the gameplay, but that isn't saying much. I will admit that the darker perspective is refreshing but I never felt interested or involved in the story at any point.

In the end, you are supposed to feel bad for the things that "you" did. However, you are forced to make the majority of these bad choices to progress with the game. There were only a couple choices you can actually make and none of them have any real effect on the story.

[h1]The Story[/h1]
A three-headed Delta squad led by yourself is sent on a rescue mission to the once beautiful city of Dubai - now a wasteland covered in sand. In this hostile environment you are to find survivors of the 33rd Infantry Battalion who volunteered to evacuate the civilians of the city, afterwards received orders to abandon them and leave but disobeyed and broke contact since.
Throughout the game, you will see what happened in the five and a half months and how the order of command in the city turned around.
As it is, I think it's not a great story but it is beeing told in a unique way that shows a perspective you are normally not shown by the media. At the end of it, you will be able to emphasize with everybody but yourself - you might hate yourself, you might want to kill yourself (not in real life, mind you, but as the character you are playing) and you will regret everything.

[h1]The World[/h1]
Dubai is beautiful - it has always been and even all those sandstorms couldn't take the beauty of the city away.
What however takes aways it's beauty are the tributes of war and the things that have long left the definition of 'war' and go into the fields of mutilation and violation. 
There is quite a lot of detail - many posters and grafiti with different messages - some from the old face of Dubai like expensive cars and then the messages of the survivors, sometimes written in bloody red.
The textures are ok for the age of the game I guess and they are not your main focus anyway, they are pretty mushy at places, though.

[h1]The Characters[/h1]
[olist]
[*]The first man of your squad is 1st Lieutenant, heavy gunner, Alphonso Adams - a really loyal and devoted soldier - at the beginning, that is. However as the story progresses his attitude begins to change... for better?
[*]Additionally, there is Sergeant John Lugo - your man with the Eagle Eye and the trusted engineer of the force. He makes it pretty clear what he thinks of the whole mission and the choices you make and his opinion is mostly not in your favor - you can image that this will not become better in the hot wheater of the desert.
[*]Last but not least there is yours truly Captain Martin Walker, the character you get to play and make the decisions with, for your team. Decisions you won't like, decisions that are bad and worse - but that's just how decisions are in a [i]war[/i]. His mental stability will begin to fade in the heat of battle and you won't know whats true and whats not anymore - whats good and whats bad - who is a friend and who is a foe. It becomes clearer that he suffers from [url=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Posttraumatic_stress_disorder]PTSD[/url] - which is not too unusual in the light of the situation.
[*]But wait? I am forgetting John Konrad - Colonel John Konrad, commander of the 33rd Infantry Battalion who intended to help the people of Dubai but damned them instead... or did he?
[/olist]

[h1]The Gameplay[/h1]
It plays as a third-person shooter with quite a lot of tactical elements.
[list]
[*]Control your squad: You can order Adams and Lugo to attack certain targets, it is also possible to ask for a distraction in the form of a flashbang. However be mindful that in the case of them going down, you have to get your men back up.
[*]Stay in cover: The game has a simple cover system and you definitely have to use it - or die. Thankfully the linear levels are designed with a lot of cover in mind, so you will find something to crouch behind [i]most of the time[/i].
[*]Use your environment: Sand... sand everywhere - but why not use it? Shoot windows and glass roofs to unleash a sand avalanche upon the members of The Damned or make your bullets find some explosives positioned near enemy cover.
[*]To be or not to be: It's your [i]choice[/i] - you make a call to live or let live... or do you? You get to decide between bad and worse, there isn't anything else in a war anyway... is there? Whatever you do, at the end of it, you have to go through with it and live with what you have done. You can keep telling yourself, that your hand was forced and there was no other way but is this what you really think?
[/list]
[b]However[/b], there is a big problem with all this: the movement. 
I used to play this game with mouse and keyboard, but just couldn't navigate really well from cover to cover like this and soon found a lot of bullets in my belly, so I switched to my XBOX360 controller which made moving easier but aiming all the harder. Therefore, I could only play on the lowest difficulty and still died quite a lot.
Enhanced was this problem by the fact, that the damage you take is quite 'realistic', meaning you can endure some 3 shots at most. There is a regeneration system but it takes so much time to recover from just one graze that it makes the firefights feel like walking through instant glue.
This resulted in me quitting the game so many times - I could play through it, after all, mind you, but it was no fun at the beginning.

[h1]The Sound[/h1]
You will get to enjoy quite nice and atmospheric music while you play - provided by Robert Darden - the Radioman of Dubai. 
The voice acting is good but not all too good in my opinion, at times it just wasn't matching the situation however at others it perfectly did.
[b]But[/b] I experienced a lot of sound bugs such as hearing my own steps behind me, noise while inside of a sandstorm - which was [i]not[/i] resulting from it and the like. This often hurt the atmosphere and, therefor, decreased immersion.

[h1]The Verdict[/h1]
At the end of the day, the game has a great anti-war attitude which is shown directly through the eyes of a high-ranking soldier suffering  and losing himself in what started as a rescue mission and ended as a suicide commando. 
[b]Nevertheless[/b], it's being held back a lot by the gameplay, which feels poorly ported.
If you can live with the problems it has and manage to maneuver your squad safely through the sandy wasteland you are in for good a story.

Spec Ops: The Line. From all the praise, I was expecting something unique and different. I can't say I got any of that.

Good things first. The setting. Sandstorm weathered Dubai is something truly unique, I can give it that. Skyscrapers buried in sand with the constant threat of storms where civilians and armed forces try to survive is absolutely fresh. The strong glaring sun and bloom, although most of the time very distracting, added to the hot weather feel.

Voice acting was quite nice. Felt pretty good to listen to although some lines were really awkward but that's just the script.

Sand worked quite nicely as a mechanic also, although it kinda died off the further I went on in the game.

Well, the bad things. Let's start with the big praised and awarded morale. Did the game make me feel like a hero? No. Did the game make me feel bad? No. Why? I was wondering, why would it? I was stuck on rails. I went on how the game wanted me to go and suddenly what I did was wrong in the end. But I didn't have much of a choice. It was like reading a book. There was only one outcome. There were a couple choices to be made but I felt like they didn't make much difference. I picked one option and I was told, "Well, that's how things go". There are three different endings but I'll just say nothing you do between start and end matters. I couldn't feel bad for "Wakuhs's" (player character) choices because I couldn't affect his larger choices and I couldn't relate on him at all.
Maybe I was supposed to feel sorry for the characters but the thing was that my squad was "The Bro Delta Squad" kind. I didn't like the fact that I was a superior and my squad could just act like brats because we were such bros. It made me feel annoyed and I wanted to personally end my squad mates. So whatever quarrel we had made me want to slide under the table in shame. The civilians were angry for a good reason but they felt like complete idiots. Our objective at one point was to issue an evacuation order but I felt like I might have missed something. Why haven't the civilians left? That makes them stupid, except the sandstorm keeps them there. So they can't really leave. So why are we trying to tell them to leave in the first place? That makes us stupid. If our solution was to round up some nice vehicles and then escort them but no. Our plan was just to tell them to leave. Tell a bunch of angry mindless civilians to march into their doom.

Gameplay. Clunky, sticky, unresponsive at times. Aiming and shooting was plausible. Running and using cover, awful. Spec Ops: The Line falls under the category of games that handles most things with just one key. Running and taking cover happens from space. However, other things such as vaulting happened from shift. It just didn't feel natural. I felt like cover related actions should've been in one button and movement related in another. On top of it all, my character didn't feel like staying in cover sometimes. He would just pop his head out and refused to take cover. Firefights felt like a chore because the enemy threw grenades with pinpoint accuracy constantly. There were times when they threw grenades through my cover as well. So I couldn't stay in the cover for more than a second or two. I had to retreat away from the fight because I was pretty much as far as I could be from the enemies. Once I returned to the cover, another grenade was lobbed at me. Not really fun. A cover shooter that punishes you for using cover?

tl;dr
Pretty average cover TPS. Morality executed poorly. Clunky controls. Nice story, voice acting and visuals though. Not a super long game. If you enjoy a good story, get it. If you favor gameplay, don't get it.

"SpecOps: The Line" is a succesful reinstalment of a serie that fell from grace after promising begginings. "The Line" leaves behind realism and goes for action TPS with tactical elements. And does the job just fine. 

When it comes to technicals and mechacnics, "SpeOps: The Line" is just another, cover-based, generic TPS. It looks good, sounds good, plays good. But nothing mindblowing. Higher difficulty levels means more HP for your enemies and less for you. Playing on hard means your enemies will be quite a bullet sponge while FUBAR makes the game a bit tiring as great majority of levels has poor rail-design. It does improve but too late - when you come to the point where you can do some maneuvering and commanding you teammates makes some sense, you will be just few steps from finishing the game. But, to give credit they deserve - fighting in those locations is very interesting and exciting - pity the devs did not put such an effort earlier. Also, issuing commands is unintuitive. So I'd keep to normal difficulty to get the best from the game. 

The plot and narrative is where the game shines. You wouldn't be far from thruth saying thet "The Line" is computer adaptation of Conrad's "Heart of Darkness". It's a story about duty, honor, surviving, doing what's right and what's needed - the story about preserving your humanity. The game probes the 4th wall as the prrotagonist - and indirectly player himself - faces morally challanging situation and is being asked some uncomfrotable questions. Questions you may not like the answers when the time comes. And the grand finale gives completly new look at already interesting plot and available solutions.

So to make the long story short - "SpecOps: The Line" is a good shooter with great story, definietly worth playing and I will be looking forward for any future "SpecOps" titles.

Spec Ops the Line is an interesting game. On one hand its a refreshingly different from other shooters but on the other hand it is frustratingly the same and often feels its missing out on its full potential.

     Spec Ops the Line is a 3rd person shooter that is inspired by Joseph Conrad's novel "Heart of Darkness" which also servered as the inspiration for the film "Apocoalypse Now." You play as Captain Walker as him and his troops Lugo and Adams work their way through the ruins of Dubai  which has been ravaged by sand storms, and there is lots of speculation as to why the U.S. Army's attempted evacuation of Dubai failed. The plot to the game is filled with interesting insights into the characters of the game and it has some surprises in store for the player.

    Let's start with the games strengths. Spec Ops the Line does for sure succeed in most of the aspects. The gameplay is good, if a little generic for a 3rd person shooter. The story is great for sure, it delves into the mind of Captain Walker as these horrors occur and the game presents moral choices which are genuinly really difficult to decide. I'll talk more about this later in the review. The voice acting in the game is top notch (Walker is voiced by the always excellent Nolan North) and the character writing is great here. The game features a great soundtrack and solid sound design. The graphics are good and surprisingly despite the whole taking place in the same desert destroyed city the setting is never boring and actually one of the games strongest points. The game also features some more sureal moments that are some of my favourite parts of the game. The work effectivly and are a smart way to mix things up.

    Now, Spec Ops the Line does have some slip ups for sure. The game first of all is short, I beat it on normal in 5 hours which ever for shooter standards is pretty short. It features options for stealth gameplay but i found my AI team mates would often screw up my attempts at stealth by running around like they're in open combat as well as sometimes even opening fire with unsilenced weapons. I also found it a little ridiculous that an entire infantry batallion would stay behind in a ruined No Mans Land of a city without trying to get any kind of help when they started running into trouble. But that's mostly just me nitpicking, it probably won't bother most people. There's also a plot point involving Walker that I can't get into due to spoiler reasons but it really makes some things that happen in the game make no sense.

    One thing with the game that lowered my opinion of it the most is actually how in a lot of ways I feel it didn't live up to its potential. First off is the interaction's with your AI team mates during combat, you can give them a couple orders but with the exception of telling Lugo to snipe somebody i rarely used these which didn't make me feel like much of a team. I found they also were kind of idiots in combat occasionally, i saw Adams and Lugo shooting walls sometimes and running in an open area with heavy enemy fire which didn't really make me feel that they were well trained soldiers. I mentioned earlier in the review that the sound design is solid and that's true, but that's it. It's just solid sound design. It feels so cookie cutter and generic, modern military shooters have extremely high standards for sound design in my opinion because so much of the sounds in this game feel artificial and soft. Battlefield is the best reference point i can think of for amazing sound design in a military shooter game, Battlefield sound design really highlights what's possible for shooters like this. 

     So, I saved my favourite thing about this game for last. Spec Ops the Line has some choices you have to make in the game. The way these choices are presented to the player is possibly the most well done I have ever seen in a video game. This isn't like a Bioware game where your choices are clearly laid out for you and you have to chose. In Spec Ops you simply find yourself in a situation and it leaves it up to you what to do. It doesn't give you any hints and it doesn't tell you your options, you simply have to actually think about it and make a choice. You also have a time limit on all these choices which adds to the tention but you have no idea how much time you have left. You have to look at the situation and see if you think time is running out or not. It's realistic and it makes some of these situations really intense. It also shows how easy it can be for things to go bad when you have to make a tough choice in the heat of the moment. In my opinion this is the absolute best way a game can present the player with complicated choices and I really hope more developers use this design philosophy.

     Overall its a pretty solid game that I can recommend for sure, especially if its on sale. 7/10

It is pretty damn obvious that clear majority of human kind would not commit war crimes or other atrocities, as normal reality permits our minds to stay intact. So far in my life I have only played two games with such moral complexity that I would say as a gamer, you HAVE to play them. One of those games is Shadow of the Colossus and the other one is.... Spec-Ops: The Line. I'm not going to spoil the big plot twists because this is a game that spoilers will ruin. I can't stress how much you need to play Spec-Ops: The Line. Anyway, over all Spec-Ops: The Line is a sophisticated deconstruction of the modern warfare genre and one of the most down right brilliant games I have ever played. So when you start Spec-Ops, the first hour is nothing special. You play as Captain Walker, a special forces operative on a mission to rescue civilians in Dubai because massive sandstorms have totaled the city. The game starts as your typical, generic, linear, modern-warfare shooter as you meaninglessly gun down "enemies". It's not until after the first hour when the game starts getting interesting. You quickly find that things are not as what they seem then plot twists unfold and by the end you are left thinking about who is really the bad guy. Usually I say that a good game connects gameplay, narrative, and design which Spec-Ops: The Line does this flawlessly. The design starts off very modern as the story and gameplay are utterly generic. But as the narrative starts to dive into the psyche of Captain Walker as he goes totally insane, the design of the dull environments seamlessly transitions into looking and feeling more vivid, colorful, and surreal. Gameplay isn't anything special, you just shoot tons of people like any other modern warfare game but it's amazing how the narrative contextualizes and comments on the gameplay by asking questions like who were those people, why are you shooting them, why does that make you the hero, and what is any of the killing even worth? The gameplay also feels clunky and stressful which these mechanics intentionally feel this way to serve as metaphors that help express some of the major themes of the narritive during gameplay. The narrative paints most of your actions in the game with a coat of moral ambiguity which makes Spec-Ops: The Line profound, brilliant, and complex. As for the plot, it is driven by Captain Walker's coherent character arc as he and his squad are isolated and thrown into a hostile environment and any humanity is stripped away along with compassion, reason, and rationality until only a monster remains. But it's brilliant how Spec-Ops questions the morality of the player by involving them in the gameplay because we essentially control Captain Walker. This raises some interesting questions about the relationship between player and player-character. Are Walker's actions merely our own? Or do we just represent the last thoughts of reason in his damaged mind as he railroads us into committing more war crimes. Even the gameplay starts reflecting the narrative as Walker goes more and more insane, his hallucinations slowly start becoming intertwined with gameplay until you aren't even sure what is real or not. This game is a masterpiece in storytelling and you just have to experience it.

Most of the positive reviews of this game praise the story, and rightfully so; it's based on a number of military novels containing similar themes and is written quite well. It sets the scene and atmosphere of the game: our protagonist is fighting with their own morality and mental strength in a nation plagued with disaster. It starts out averagely enough, but quickly spirals out of control as the story progresses. However, the story is all that's good in this game.

[h1]Setup[/h1]
Before even starting the game, I tried to enable borderless fullscreen, but it's not supported. To someone with one monitor, this might be pretty trivial an issue, but it's still a legitimate one. For games that don't support it, it's easy enough to use thirdparty tools to fake it, but this was not the case here. When I tried to change the windowed resolution manually, it was automatically clamped, meaning that it was impossible for me to resize the window to fit my native resolution. While this isn't a problem the developers should be responsible for, they [i]should[/i] be responsible for not including the feature in the first place.

In addition, the game is forcefully letterboxed, so it won't stretch to any aspect ratio it doesn't support, including over two monitors or on a super-wide monitor. While this can be hacked with tools like Flawless Widescreen, it's still annoying.

When attempting to edit the game's configuration files to see if there was anything I could do about my problems, I was greeted with encryption. As far as I know this was manually implimented and not a standard feature of the Unreal engine. Thankfully, more tools exist that can decrypt these files and allow the user to edit them. I learned later that there is forced mouse acceleration that cannot be disabled by normal means; I was able to turn off the acceleration, normalize the sensitivity, turn off the awful bloom, and fix a few other issues I was running into by editing and re-encrypting the files.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
The controls are uninspired, and in some cases completely broken. The cover system was clearly designed for controllers, with the button to vault over cover the same as the melee button, causing you to often beat your cover with your gun before you're able to vault over it. The sprinting in this game works like the "roadie run" from Gears of War and similar games, meaning you can only run in a mostly straight line and can't sprint left, right, or backwards. I suppose the saving grace of this is that you can hold a direction and press sprint to quickly spin around and run in that direction, but the fact that it takes [i]ages[/i] to stop running without pressing a button like crouch feels incredibly awkward and got me killed a few times. Additionally, the sprint button is also the take cover button, and the cover snapping either works [i]too[/i] well, causing you to snap into cover when you're trying to run away from enemies, or doesn't work [i]at all[/i], causing you to stand there awkwardly as you try to take cover, or worse, make you sprint into the open and get shot to death. The sprint/cover button is also the "jump off of ledge" button, which makes no sense; shouldn't it be the vault button? To make matters worse, [i]it's also the use turret button[/i]. Clearly, the controls took some time to get used to. It doesn't help that there's no urgency to the game, save for a few sections, and the time-tested "sit back and snipe everything that moves and wait for your health to recharge" tactic works [i]far too well[/i], and is sometimes your only option on the harder difficulties.

Unsurprisingly, enemies are bullet sponges in this game, at least on the second hardest difficulty, which is the highest unlocked when first starting the game. Very few enemies take a single headshot to kill, and most later on in the game will take two from the lesser powerful rifles and pistols. The game also features "heavies" which see implementation in so many other games it's become average, and these in specific lack suitable tactics to taking them down. At least in other games there are gimmicks that can make fighting one easier, but no, not this time. It's shoot it in the same spot until it stops moving. It gets old very quickly and their resilience to bullets is uncanny.

The maps are incredibly linear, with little explorative value aside from finding the (usually very obviously placed) intel pickups. Lots of invisible walls and things that look safe that aren't. Map triggers sometimes fail to occur, causing hangups in gameplay and/or checkpoint restarts.

[h1]Graphics[/h1]
The game is... okay to look at, despite the graphics appearing dated in many places. However, where and when it was noticable, the drop in quality is very apparent, especially for the characters' faces. The scenery looks pretty low-res for a last-gen game. I will admit, the environment textures look pretty good with lots of detail, but this quickly falls off as you lower the settings. The game also runs horribly on my machine, even though I can run more modern games on higher settings without issue. Also, explosive container fireballs are garbage.

[h1]Sound[/h1]
The voice acting is incredibly repetitve, with hordes of cookiecutter enemies all spouting the same selection of 10-20 lines every few seconds. The scripted sections are voiced very well, however, and add more emotion and depth to the story. The sound effects are pretty good, but are lacking for a few of the guns and explosions. Overall, very good sound design, though the constant blaring rock music got pretty old as well, especially with how frequently the background music was reused. The music really didn't add much to the game besides annoyance, and there's very little musical ambiance aside from it.

[h1]Story[/h1]
The game has an inspired story with great writing that honestly would have worked better as a book or a movie than a videogame. You're led around on a string as the story reads itself to you, helpless to the hell around you, despite being given a number of supposed choices in the game (and set up for a few more, but contrarily these aren't actually choices and the game will kill you if you don't play along [spoiler]like that part with the mortar, snipers appear on the buildings around you if you don't use it, and even if you kill them, [i]they don't stop spawning until you die[/i][/spoiler]). There are four endings, which all take place in the same penultimate sequence of the game, and affect nothing but a short cutscene change. Your actions during the course of the story and your reaction to the moral choices proffered do not change the endings you can get.

Simply put, there's too much story to consider for what the game is. They tried to make a game around a story that was too ambituous, and it shows. There are a few sequences that offer moral choice, but either force you to choose one action, or the choice ends up being meaningless. Maybe they were trying to convey a message by doing that, but all it ends up doing is disappointing me with the thought of what could have been in a more polished game. To top it off, the ending is depressingly laid out, despite the thousands of lives that could have potentially been saved by your actions (even if you did just [spoiler]slaughter hundreds of people that may or may not have been trying to do the "right thing"[/spoiler] and [spoiler]kill 42 or more civilians, depending on your actions[/spoiler]). No matter what you try, the game forces you make it worse.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
Overall, there were few times I actually had fun in this game, and that fun was quickly squandered by the horrible gameplay elements, repetitve voice acting, and negative story. I can barely recall myself smile, gasp, or show any kind of emotion at all at anything the game tried to do. The story is interesting, but even if that's your thing, the gameplay could likely ruin it for you.
Not worth full price.

To get into what made Spec Ops the Line one of the best games of the 7th generation I have to first shed a little background on the game.

Spec Ops the Line is a sequel to the Spec Ops games released in the 90s. It was originally planned to be a new IP but was made part of the Spec Ops brand for sequel bait. This is important because this ties into what Spec Ops the Line was advertised as. It was advertised as a big budget modern military shooter with an interesting setting but overly generic game mechanics and plot premise.

What we got was an elaborate satire of modern military shooters. Spec Ops the Line starts out similar to how you'd expect a big budget AAA game to start. You are a squad of soldiers, sent in to investigate a crisis, and you have to cowboy in and shoot some brown people.

However the game plays with this a lot. What was the exact nature of your mission? Why are the enemies so hostile to you? Why are your squadmates talking erratically about you? There are so many questions raised and the game delightfully gives you answers that you don't want to hear.

Spec Ops the Line's writing is very top notch. It satirizes the heroic power fantasy nature of modern military shooter plotlines and characters. And it plays with the idea of "how would killing hundreds of people change you as a person". 

Beyond that the gameplay is sound, it has Mass Effect style squad combat and fairly generic multiplayer. The singleplayer is what you get Spec Ops for, and it remains one of my favorite games ever for its message and its post-modern view on the 7th generation of video games overall. The main gripes I have with it are due to the linear nature of the game, and due to how the plot is written it isn't as replayable as you might think. But it still is one of the most breathtaking games I have ever played, and one I dearly recommend to people who want to play a game that'll make you feel uncomfortable and uneasy with your objectives.

White phosphorus is a material made from a common allotrope of the chemical element phosphorus that is used in smoke, tracer, illumination and incendiary munitions. Other common names include WP, and the slang term "Willie Pete", which is dated from its use in Vietnam, and is still sometimes used in military jargon. As an incendiary weapon, white phosphorus burns fiercely and can ignite cloth, fuel, ammunition and other combustibles.
White phosphorus can cause injuries and death in three ways: by burning deep into tissue, by being inhaled as a smoke, and by being ingested. Extensive exposure by burning and ingestion may causes fatal result.

Burning:
Incandescent particles of WP cast off by a WP weapon's initial explosion can produce extensive, deep second and third degree burns. One reason why this occurs is the tendency of the element to stick to the skin. Phosphorus burns carry a greater risk of mortality than other forms of burns due to the absorption of phosphorus into the body through the burned area, resulting in liver, heart and kidney damage, and in some cases multiple organ failure. These weapons are particularly dangerous to exposed people because white phosphorus continues to burn unless deprived of oxygen or until it is completely consumed. In some cases, burns are limited to areas of exposed skin because the smaller WP particles do not burn completely through personal clothing before being consumed.

Smoke inhalation:
Burning white phosphorus produces a hot, dense, white smoke consisting mostly of phosphorus pentoxide. Exposure to heavy smoke concentrations of any kind for an extended period (particularly if near the source of emission) has the potential to cause illness or death. White phosphorus smoke irritates the eyes, mucous membranes of the nose, and respiratory tract in moderate concentrations, while higher concentrations can produce severe burns. The Agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Registry has set an acute inhalation Minimum Risk Level (MRL) for white phosphorus smoke of 0.02 mg/m3, the same as fuel-oil fumes. By contrast, the chemical weapon mustard gas is 30 times more potent: 0.0007 mg/m3.

Fume inhalation:
Long term inhalation of derivative fumes causes a condition called phossy jaw or osteonecrosis of the jaw, which is a painful, debilitating and ultimately lethal condition that afflicted factory workers involved with the manufacture of matches that contained white phosphorus. The mechanism for necrosis is clot formation leading to bone ischaemia or infarction, leading to the putrid rotting of the bone of the lower jaw. For this reason, the Berne Convention (1906) was enacted to forbid the manufacture, sale or purchase of matches containing white phosphorus. This condition may also be caused by high doses of lead, cadmium and bisphosphonate based cancer drugs.

The assumption that white phosphorus is considered a chemical weapon, and thus constitutes a violation of the Chemical Weapons Convention, is false. During the testimony of Prof. Michael A. Newton at the United Nations Fact Finding Mission on the Gaza Conflict he said "the law is clear that there are some authorized, perfectly valid uses of white phosphorus munitions".

The disaster of "contextual" keys is shown here like in no other place, with the spacebar serving three drastically different functions and the left shift key two, making for "humorous behaviour in combat situations".

  - Want to revive a squadmate now that you ran accross a crossfire to the place he was downed? Too bad, press space before the game deigns to aknowledge your intentions and you sprint out of cover to your death.
  - Want to jump over the cover you just hugged? Too bad, this cover is 1 inch too tall, you run out of cover making a melee attack in a random direction. Usually into enemy fire.
  - Want to get out of cover to another chest-high wall next to you? Too bad, the game doesn't recognize that as a viable spot, so you get shot in the head as you stand up. Wait, you got the prompt? Great! Unfortunately, you just ran to the other wrong side of the cover, putting you in plain view of the enemy forces.
