Spec Ops: The Line is a third person cover-based shooter. Your mission in Dubai is to save some people, but how far you go to save them,  the further you will go into insanity. 

To give my opinion about the experience of playing the game, I have to say it, at first it felt generic to me. ( like the trailers felt generic to me) I didn't really care about anything or anyone. The game felt like a parody of modern shooters, because it was so generic. But after I reached a certain point in the game I finally saw what makes this game so special. And that is letting you feel the pain of making choices in war.

There were some gameplay parts that were exciting but most of the time it wasn't. The only thing this shooter has that other shooter don't, is the use of sand, which hasn't been used that much sadly in the game. You can use your A.I. partners to help you. Sadly, you can only order them to throw flashbangs or target enemies. So you can't really execute big tactical moves with them. But I have to say on the hardcore difficulty I played the game on they sometimes were useful. Except when you have to revive them...  There are stealth missions, that are just 'kill these 3 people and than just go on shooting again.' I had really hoped that they would expand on those parts just for the variety. 

The levels are really well styled with a lot of detail. But, in many places, it doesn't look that amazing graphically, I think the reason for that is due it being an unreal 3 game. This also contributes to the game looking often like a generic shooter. 

I really liked when the game let you made in-game choices because they felt well thought out. This occasionally stops the game being a 'shoot everything that moves' game, and allows you, for example, to make a choice whether to kill or not to kill someone. But, often you will be shooting everything you see, which struck me as strange. Sadly, these choices have no effort on the game ending. You will always get the same two endings to choose from. Once I completed the singleplayer I reloaded a save to see the other ending I didn't choose. I also reloaded some missions to get 3 collectables, most of the time they are easy to find, because of the invisible walls. The collectables told some other stories. Also helped with the achievements, which are easy to get in the game. 

I would really recommend this game to anyone who is interested in war. The game really made you confront with what you done and makes the line between good or bad people invisible. It also made me think about different aspects of war while playing it.

Mechanically, it's fairly prosaic -- third-person, cover-based, regenerating health, a variety of modern weapons, a couple of companions generally.   The checkpoint system is somewhat obnoxious but checkpoints are fairly common, and if you repeatedly fail the game will start providing you with extra ammunition and even suggest lowering the difficulty (which you can do at the cost of restarting your current checkpoint).

It is not a terribly long game, so don't be expecting a 40-hour run. 

There are some technical quirks like encrypted INI files (google around for decryption / encryption utilities) with settings that the menus don't let you change otherwise (notably, depth of field, radial blur... and mouse acceleration!).  It's a minor inconvenience since tools do exist, but just be aware.

SPOILER: For some reason, the actor that set up all these difficulties for you is off the hook because he was dead while he was bantering throughout the script and giving orders to US troops to constantly attack you.  Huh?
There is actually no way to get through this game without "making a bad decision", it's all about creating guilt for both sides of the conflict [both sides being American soldiers].  The horror of war is a side-show.   There are much more realistic ways to portray the horror of war.
Our soldiers who DON'T behave as portrayed in this game.  In reality, our troops [yes, I am ex-military] behave well in the middle of carnage caused by the countries which do not.
Yager is obviously too cowardly to portray the real merciless killers of the region. They are the those who crucify civilian captives because of intolerance, carry out armed massacres of school children,  make slaves of young girls, who ignore their shame when 1/2 their army deserts allowing the capture of a billion dollars worth of military hardware, etc.   
During later scenes in the game, after Yager has tried to make you feel worthless, you see screen loads saying alternately: "It's all your fault", "How many Americans have you killed today?" and "You're still a good person".   Huh?  I suppose the last comment is the "suicide prevention" cover for a very nasty group of programmers intent on presenting American ethics in the worst possible way.  
Rigging it this way for purposes of creating anxiety is part of the creepy low-life cashing in on our supposed "guilt". The many torn US flags are symbolic of Yager's mindset.

If ever there were a game that would benefit from a complete remake, it's Spec Ops: The Line.  It's a thought-provoking and aesthetically interesting title with a lot of flaws.  The gameplay is incredibly basic whack-a-mole cover shooting that's at odds with the emotion and believability the narrative is trying to convey, and there are plot holes and moments where the game forces you to do horrible things, then beats you over the head for doing so as if you had any choice. 

All of these flaws make piecing together the narrative in your head a maddening effort, because the game seems so confident in the story it's trying to tell, with some very meticulous details thrown in for those who take the time to notice them, yet due to the plot holes it doesn't make any sense unless you subscribe to some kind of interpretation that allows these holes to exist.  Ultimately, the game just feels like it was rushed.

But you should still play it.  There are a lot of things it does right, and a number of moments that you've probably never quite experienced before in a shooter.  Your squad's descent into madness really keeps you on the edge of your seat and makes you want to progress through the game just to see how they'll interact with each other.  And this is, without a doubt, Nolan North's most intense role.  The audio alone is worth the price of admission, which thankfully is quite cheap these days.

[h1]AT A GLANCE[/h1]
(Full review follows below)

[list]
[*][b]Game Name:[/b] Spec Ops: The Line
[*] [b]Original Release:[/b] 2012
[*] [b]Genre Tags:[/b] Third-Person; Shooter; Story Rich; Action; Psychological
[*] [b]My Overall Grade:[/b] A-
[*] [b]Estimated Playtime (Campaign):[/b] 8-14 hours
[*] [b]Multiplayer Aspect:[/b] None
[*] [b]Recommended To:[/b] Established fans of the genre; Those intrigued by the genre; Aesthetes; Strong narrative advocates; Game atmosphere connoisseurs
[/list]

[h1]REVIEW[/h1]
[b]Spec Ops: The Line[/b] is a modern-combat, over-the-shoulder shooter set in a post-cataclysmic event themed Dubai.  Unrelenting sandstorms have all but destroyed the city entirely; and the evacuation (aided by the US army) was a failure.  You go in, with your two Delta Squad buddies, to try to assess the situation and rescue any survivors.

The combat is solid, if not simple.  You take out enemies in standard over-the-shoulder shooter fashion mostly, with some ability to dish out commands to your squad members.  The atmosphere is top notch, and the visuals can be quite stunning.  The voice acting is solid, but some of the lines are cheesy in trying to be funny.  The controls are good, and the game itself is stable.  The gameplay is fun, but a little limited.  You won’t see very much variety in terms of squad commands, grenades, or guns; and can only have 2 equipped guns at a time—which fits the story but somewhat limits gameplay.  Still if you switch your weapons out here and there, picking them up from fallen foes (which you probably need to, as ammo is scarce) you can get just enough variety.

One major strong point for the game is the story.  And not just the story itself, but the way it is told.  The pacing of the story keeps you moving from one combat scene to the next, intrigued with the notion of finding out what comes next.  There are some minor decisions to be made here and there; they don’t have a major effect on the progression of the game—they more so just allow you define the character you play.  The final decisions you make, however, will determine which of several endings you will see.  (You can see all endings by replaying just the last level, no matter the other decisions you made).

Another major strong point for the game is the atmosphere.  The setting and general theme of the game are constructed quite well.  It is a bit Hollywood-style sensationalist with the sandstorms completely destroying Dubai; but at the same time it’s pretty awesome because it makes for quite a novel setting for a modern-combat game.  However, it does put a restriction on the variety of locales in the game, but that’s OK.

All in all, [b]Spec Ops: The Line[/b] is a very well put together, story-driven, third-person shooter experience with a great setting.  Highly recommended for fans of a good story, modern-combat FPS/TPS, and a powerful atmosphere.

What is Spec Ops: The Line in a nutshell? Imagine 'The Last of Us" but set in a military shooter context... and perhaps not quite as brilliant. The characters are not all that deep nor easy to get attached to. Perhaps however, this is a saving grace as the emotions and journey that Captain Walker (the protagonist) and his two squad mates; Lugo and Adams endure brings out some very real themes of remorse and dread.
It's somewhat ironic really; the makers of Spec Ops: The line have given us some very mixed signals where the game entices you to play quite aggressively to overcome all your foes and yet has a strange way of making you feel evil no matter what choice you make. There are not a great deal of choices to make in this game but the few you do make will haunt you every time the game yanks you out of the action for a cinematic to tell you the next chunk or bite of story.
This for me is where this game is weakest. The game play has you playing through what for the most part is a very solid third person shooter and then slaps you in the face with realities and horrors contrary to the fantasy and glory of shooter campaigns like Wolfenstein (the recent one), COD and Battlefield.
While it can be argued that it is, as many shooters, a shooting gallery leading you to play through to the next cinematic, it is indeed unique as it will challenge you and strive to make you feel something real. About 5 hours in I thought; "Yeah it's nice to have a story in my mindless shooter, but I probably won't remember this one." Having completed it now (3 hours of game play later) I can certainly say the ending gave context to the game which now has burned its story firmly in my memory.
Now enough on the touchy feelie ♥♥♥♥! Let's talk about the game-play:
The controls overall or are quite straight forward but the cover mechanics leave a lot to be desired. While it is nice to have a game which allows you to break free of cover easily, sometimes this can work out badly for you when needing to lock into cover elsewhere when getting flanked from multiple directions. It is useful though when a grenade lands close by and you need to move to another cover point -which happens A LOT! This is probably because too many contextual actions are assigned to the A button (playing on an Xbox-One controller).
The guns feel great and each feels unique and appropriate for various engagements as well as play styles. You will quickly find your favorites and gravitate towards them. Personally I liked the M417 Semiautomatic Rifle and the Scar-H with under-slug grenade launcher but the pistols are great too. The game does give you some jizz time with grenade launchers and turrets but not even close to enough time with the RPG or the AA-12 which are incredibly powerful but only available for the arse-end of the game.
The AI is not overly punishing in that they won't rush you constantly. They will put you down very quickly if you keep your head out for a few shots too many. Also they love to throw grenades. Most of the time I died because they would flush me out with a 'nade and there'd be nowhere safe for me to run. You quickly learn to target the lobbers first. I played this game on the highest available difficulty of the three available before first play-through. I suspect the additional difficulty which unlocks at the end is meaninglessly hard like the 'Veteran' difficulty in COD campaigns. The hardest initial challenge level is a sweet spot. There were sections which I had to replay up to 8 times before I'd make the checkpoint. Thankfully this was due to needing to learn the best tactic and angle of attack as well as strategically allocated my resources -specifically grenades. Of which there are frags, stickies and flash-bang. Whenever you hear something about Spec Ops: The Line - you only hear about its message. Well, when I played it, I didn't see any messages - nor did I care. I wanted to enjoy the game, and "enjoy the game" I did.

"War is Hell" is a phrase often understood in fiction portraying armed conflicts. Combat can be a scary, deeply unsettling experience that weighs on the mind, however noble the goals.  

Most military shooters aren't about that. Sure, they pay lip service to it, with narratives about intricate government conspiracies and pixelated atrocities (remember "No Russian", anybody?) 

but at the core of the experience, the player isn't considered. He and his digital avatar are both rewarded (achievements, game progress, etc.) for shooting down everything in their line of sight. Regardless of how many people you kill, at the end of the day, you're still the good guy. 

Without being Spoilertastic, you should play this game because it makes you think about how wrong that notion is. 

You're player character's still a one-man army,  and killing is still the only way to progress through the game. But with each life you take, both you and your player character learn to hate and fear your aptitude at violence, looking for some reassurance that your actions were justified, or at least, whether or not you had a choice.

When I put the controller down, I didn't feel like a bad person. It didn't make me hate myself. 

But it did make me think: how complicit was I in what transpired in the game? And if I was complicit, is it really okay to play games like this?

[h1] War is hell. [/h1]

Yet we all make our choices. Where Coppola put [i]Heart of Darkness[/i] into the Vietnam war era, Williams puts it into modern day Dubai. This game is not your average shooter. As with most story-driven games I do not care much for gameplay - which is average, yet solid - or visuals - which are mostly good; there are lots of contrasts here: from bright desert day in Dubai to darker scenes which look far better in my opinion. The voice acting is phenomenal, the sound design is theatrical right along with the soundtrack which makes you feel like you're "playing" [i]Apocalypse Now[/i]. You will likely feel the urge to complete the story in an uninterrupted playthrough.

What many negative reviewers failed to notice is that the game leaves you the option to quit playing at any time - right to the very end. It's main reasoning is proved by the vast majority of players [i]not[/i] quitting despite all the choices they have made and even despite all the points where it's the [i]only[/i] alternative to the events unfolding. There is no Kurtz eerily whispering [i]"The horror! The horror!"[/i] here, but the early [i]"Death toll: too many"[/i] which is ironically reprised in one of the possible endings mocks us for not stopping earlier just the same.

I suppose [i]The Line[/i] has it's shortcomings in multiplayer though I wager it was never really intended for that. Aside from the lackluster MP the game is remarkably bug-free and runs with a stability that is sadly uncommon nowadays.

[i]Spec Ops: The Line[/i] makes for an extraordinary shooter that will stay with me for a long time and certainly come to mind whenever I think of [i]Heart of Darkness[/i] or [i]Apocalypse Now[/i]. Yet it is even more: a compelling argument for peace.

Spec Ops: The Line is a third person shooter like no other. I just finished the game and was it worth the purchase? Yes. Definitely. Spec Ops shows significant strength in its storyline, bearing similarity to how Deus Ex: Human Revolution has you chase a rabbit hole which gets deeper and darker with every step you take. It may seem to be just an ordinary third person shooter at first, but as you continue not all is as it first seems.

The game also throws in some moral quandaries as you progress, forcing you to judge the crime of the other Dubai inhabitants. For the most part you really have to think about your decisions, and that is where Spec Ops: The Line really shines. Some decisions, however, felt that they had a lot of weight but ended up doing little, which was a shame, but understandable. Some aspects of the story do really stand out though, even if you are given no choice by the game. Your squad mates feel like living characters that react and evolve to the unpleasant situation you are thrown into, and Intel pickups gives you a nice background on the people you are gunning into the ground. As the game continues your actions eventually leads to Scarecrow-esque psychedelic trips, giving you time to reflect on the people you have killed though out the game. The game comes to a very satisfying, eye opening end which nicely finishes up the experiences.

The visuals are stunning and the performance is very good. Running on a GTX 770 it pushed into 120 frames per second. the only issue to me is the lack of AA, which I forced though the NVidia control pannel. I also ran this game with flawless widescreen to increase the FOV, which was around 70, to about 100. The use of flawless widescreen may have created bugs with some weapon scopes and highlighted some pop in of off screen characters, but those issues were entirely self-inflicted.

The game had a decent length of about 11ish hours, and most of that time felt well spent. However the combat and third person shooter aspect of the gameplay was not on the same level as the rest of the game. Keep in mind I played on the hardest difficulty available at the time. The combat was very frustrating as a person who plays a lot of shooters and whose accuracy is pretty decent. The game additionally suffers from the old "press space for everything" and many times I wanted to swap cover and instead healed my AI squadmates or ran out into the open into the unforgiving bullets of the enemy. The AI for the most part is good, but has an extremely annoying tendency to go down in the middle of nowhere, usually with a LMG and lots of enemies surrounding him and start to bleed out, forcing you to run clumsily towards him and die. Repeat many times and furiously quit the game. The game also suffers from difficulty spikes, usually at the end of a long fight when a heavy (similar to a PAYDAY 2 bulldozer) strides confidently onto the field and kicks you right back to the start of the fight. Some sections I had to repeat as much as 7 times to pass the arena section, each time dying on that last heavy. I would recommend playing on a lower difficulty as the harsh combat would often make me appreciate the story less as I came -fuming- out of an arduous combat section. The main problem is that this time of combat is 80% of the game, and when 80% of the game is a chore you better hope that the story was worth it. Luckily it is. The game has a bad case of Ludo narrative dissonance, the game clearly wants you to feel the pain of death in war, but has you murder hundreds of faceless soldiers.

The soundtrack was quite nice, very atmospheric, but nothing legendary in my opinion, although the Radio Man has a good selection of rock songs that play thorough out.

War is a horrible thing and this game is an experience you will not forget. I'd recommend this to anyone.

Since the essence of Spec Ops: The Line is well known by now, I'll lay it out straight. The game is set up brilliantly. You buy this for the story, and you play along as it dips you into insanity with the characters. The gameplay itself is average (movement mechanics felt a bit clunky at times). But it's not the gameplay that pulls you along through the game. It's that story and the way the game starts punching you for playing it to the end. In a way, it's less of a shooter than a highly-interactive movie.

Another note, the scenery itself is quite beautiful (it is Dubai, after all), and yet manages to give off an unsettling atmosphere. Even while everything around the characters is becoming ripped apart, the scenery still gives off a good effect. Who knew the desert could be so chilling?

There is no glorified ending. There is no glorification of anything, really. And that's what's so glorifying about this game.

I got really curious about this game after reading other reviews.
When I started playing I thought at first that it's just another regular shooter and didn't get the fuss, but as I advanced I found out I was partly wrong.
In terms of gameplay, this is mostly just a regular shooter, but in terms of story and atmosphere, I've never seen anything like that!
Unlike many other shooters and war-games in general, this game doesn't try to make war look like 'fun' or anything heroic. For the first time (as far as I know) a video game tries to deliver the true meaning of military conflicts, as much as a video game can.
You get to feel the impact on the people and how devastating it can be, for both the civillians and the soldiers themselves.

If you're looking for simple 'fun' with shooting and killing, this game isn't necessarily good for you, as it explores the darker sides of war and has quite a few moment which could make you feel sadness, anger, and such things.. But not fun.

Unfortunately the gameplay doesn't bring anything new and innovative to the genre, and I even found it boring at times. You get to play with one main character which can, at times, command other two soldiers, so there's a little tactical thinking through it all, but mostly it's just a regular shooter.
The story completely compensates for it, though, and throughout the game you'll have to make a few difficult moral choices.
At first I was a little disappointed when I found out they have no actual effect on the story, but I realized that they're there for the psychological impact, and that's what the game is based on.

So, in short, gameplay is mehh and it does get a little repetitive - but for the sake of story it's worth it

But that's not all of course.
The soundtrack is absolutely amazing, as it's masterfully integrated into the game.
The original soundtack for the game is mostly made up of rockish-style tracks - which is very refreshing for the genre and for video game music in general, and also some licensed soundtrack (couple of tracks from different artists such as Jimi Hendrix and Bjork) which greatly contributes to the game and as I said, the music is involved in the game amazingly.
If you're of the type who pays attention to the music in the background, you're going to enjoy this one!

That's it though, and eventually, these things are fully forgiven, as this game gave me a strong and interesting experience, and left a very good impression on me.
Seems to me like the devs really worked with their heart and soul on this one, and I hope they'd work on more things like that.

The best possible way to experience 'Spec Ops: The Line' is to go into it thinking that it's just another run-of-the-mill modern warfare 'Call of Duty' clone. 

That's how I first played it, and boy did it blow my mind wide open as it progressed. By the end I knew I would be picking it up again and again. I swear by my love (predominantly) for the 'Metal Gear' series, but as a stand alone title, 'The Line' is by far the most engaging, complex, and well-crafted game I've ever encountered. 

I won't give a synopsis of the title's story (astonishing as it is), I'll leave that for you to discover at your leisure, but I will say that 'The Line' is both a visual as well as a psychological marvel. On the highest setting, the graphics are incredible -- the dead ruins of the city of Dubai are brought to life in a breathtaking array of colors and detail. However, from a gameplay standpoint, 'The Line' may lose some people: controls seem copy/pasted out of any generic third-person shooter and can seem slightly unresponsive at times. If you're a fan of simplistic gameplay, you'll be satisfied, but that's not to say the game isn't challenging (especially on FUBAR difficulty). On the subject of sound design, 'The Line' shines again, featuring stellar voice acting from the likes of Nolan North ('The Line' is his best performance, in my opinion), haunting music from popular artists as well as a brilliant original score, and finely tuned sound effects such as gunfire and explosions that will thunder through your speakers/headphones. 

I would recommend 'Spec Ops: The Line' to anybody who is ready for a mature story regarding the psychological effects of war on soldiers and what it means to be a "strong man".    10/10

Spec Ops: The Line is a Third Person Shooter that's focused around story rather than gameplay.

This game has a pretty unique blip on my radar, and for good reasons. Simply, all I can say is the story alone is worth purchasing this game. The basic premise is about three Delta operators: Adams, Lugo, and Walker. They were sent out on a mission to rescue any survivors found in the desolated sand-wasteland of Dubai. You play as Walker, leading your squad to carry it out.

Now this doesn't sound like a complex plot, it sounds incredibly simple, even. But the whole undertone of the story is what it's all about. Without giving away too much, Walker has the good intentions of saving all the civillians he can, and eliminating all evil that walk around them. However, it gets very psychological and personal, as Walker, and you, realize that the choices you thought were justified and well, turns out to be the exact opposite of what they are. It mentally breaks Walker down, trying to lead with his mind intact, trying to figure out good from evil, what he's doing right and wrong. The choices you make, sometimes there's never a good choice, it could be a lesser of two evils, but that's not saying much. War is hell, and sometimes, your best isn't enough. This is what the entire game is focused on: this, and the deeper meaning. It's truly an engrossing story that will leave you wanting more. I promise you won't regret it.

The gameplay is less spectacular, it's your standard cover-and-shoot type. It's pretty textbook if you wanna look at it that way, as there isn't much to do besides... Well, cover and shoot, but there is a good amount of different weapons to use. One thing I do like though is that battles take place in lots of locations, the desolate presentation of Dubai is very immersive and nice to look at, so you can be doing close quarters battle in a broken building, fighting on a large battlefield, or snipe from across buildings. The varying locations do mix up gameplay a little bit, but it's still rather basic. It does work however, and it is still fun, just nothing really pops out.

The game isn't too long, it could take you about 4-5 hours to finish the campaign. However if you wanna play the story again but with different choices, you can probably clock in another 3 if you skip cutscenes.

Multiplayer is there, but this game has a very low population, I doubt you'll find anyone, so I can't give off my impression there.

There is a Co-Op mode where you can play the campaign with a friend, who plays as either Lugo or Adams. That's very fun and it works pretty well. If you got someone to play with and wanna enjoy the story together, that brings up something fun to do as well.

Overall, Spec Ops is an amazing game with a deep, enriching plot that is sure to leave a lasting impression on you, that's what it's all about, even if the gameplay is pretty textbook stuff, and the short length. However, you won't regret buying this, I recommend it.

Spec Ops: The Line gets a little to much praise for my liking, but that doesn't and didn't stop me from realizing how great of a game it is and really enjoying myself as I went through it. There is a bit to much flattery thrown at the game with it being called unique when it really isn't that unique even within the videogame industry. This wasn't the first time civilians are killed in a videogame, or the first time Americans as cast as the enemy and it isn't the first time war crimes are acknowledged. What is unique though is the massive effort put in to give the player a strong sense of ownership over the matter that is complemented by a development philosophy that ensured even the tiniest of details in the background pushed that agenda forward. Spec Ops might be a competently designed shooter at best and I may think that people see it as having more artistic value than I do, but that doesn't stop it from being a great overall game with a strong narrative and commitment to its theme. That alone sets it apart from most games in its genre and the reason that I recommend that you play this it sooner rather than later.

Spec Ops: The Line is a game everyone needs to play in the exact same way that Grave of the Fireflies is a movie everyone needs to watch. I'm not saying this ironicly, I mean it with all cincerity. 

We civilians gain by not only the destruction of our enemies (thinking WWII, Iraq, Afghanistan) but we also gain from the destruction of those we send to destroy our enemies. Very few, if any, media really tries to get you to think long and hard about what we really ask our military to sacrifice for our freedom.

Spec Ops: The Line

Before I start my review, I would like to say that this game is OK, but nothing spectacular. It has received a lot of hype about the "terrors of war", when it doesn't deserve it. While there are many crucial decisions to make which can be difficult, it's not nearly as horrific as people claim.

[h1]Positives:[/h1]

+ Nice selection of weapons - assault rifles of various kinds, several shotguns, pistols, RPG's, sniper rifles and grenades (sticky, frag, stun). 
+ Storyline is nice.
+ Decent graphics, nothing more.
+ Cover system works well most of the time, fun and engaging shootouts - with the occasional epic one.


[h1]Negatives:[/h1]

- Important storyline audio is played during firefights, making it hard to hear characters that are speaking - it's quite annoying. I don't really know much about the plot other than the basics.
- Game takes around 7-11 hours to complete, which is pretty short.
- Stupid loading screen messages which fail to taunt you about your decisions - "Do you feel like a hero?". Lol.
- There is no way to make a "correct" decision in this game. While some say this paints an accurate picture of war, I find it disenchanting. Whatever you decide to do in Spec Ops: The Line you are ultimately ridiculed or punished for, even when it seems the most logical to do. You're basically a war criminal no matter what.
- Level design is meh, not much variety - mainly desert landscapes and the interior of buildings. While this is appropriate for the setting, it could've been made better. Sometimes it's a bit drab/bleak and this is where the lack of high quality graphics don't help.

Overall Score: 6/10

Well.
My mind...wow.
Just. Wow.
I went into this as any other shooter fan did: I expected a good fight, to come out on top, save the day, and maybe hit on some scantily-clad lass with an Australian accent and a nice bum.
But I was bloody well not expecting this.
The game begins with your usual scene of exposition: Dubai has been twitch.tv'd. A huge, unstoppable sandstorm has ripped the city apart, killing thousands, wrecking buildings, and (obviously) dumping sand everywhere. What used to be the shining holiday destination is now a wasteland reminiscent of Fallout. Minus the mutants, of course, since this game's punishing enough already without a Deathclaw trying to perform dental surgery on you. Your former friend, a Colonel Konrad, was sent in with the 'Damned 33rd' to try and rescue civilians, but goes silent.
Weeks later, you hear back from him.
So, since the message isn't all too cheerful, a small Delta Force squad is sent in through the storm wall to find out just what's going on. Average bunch of gaming heroes: You've got Lugo covering you with a sniper rifle, Adams keeping them in cover with a heavy machine gun, and, of course, you're in charge.
Captain Walker.
So, as it goes, once you pass through the storm wall, your first experiences with enemies come from the Insurgents attacking the Damned 33rd's men. Cleverly, almost all weapons in the game have the option of a secondary firing mode. Your starting rifle and pistol can be supressed, preventing enemy detection, the SCAR rifle has the grenade launcher function, the classic AK47 has the option of Burst Fire or Full Auto, and so much more. Being a heavily cover based game, it's important to know the effective range of your weapon, and this is smartly done by developers. With short range weapons (i.e., shotguns), your targeting reticle will change colour to display how much damage your shot will do: If they're out of the way of your shot and will only get spattered with pellets, the reticle turns a light pink. When you're close enough to tear them in half with a shell, your reticle is the good old red you'll come to enjoy the sight of in a tough fight.
So, after you save a Damned 33rd soldier, it becomes apparent that the once respected battalion, and its commander, have gone rogue, no longer under the US army jurisdiction.
Damn.
That means you're an American, and to stop these guys from keeping an iron grip on the city's surviving inhabitants (Who, I might add, have apparently waged war on their oppressors), you'll be fighting Blue on Blue: Friendly Fire.
Of course, once you see the combat, you'll see that there is no chance that they'll even consider stopping to ask what you're here for. Opposing troops sprint out of doorways and vault fences with all manner of commandeered firearms to stop you from getting out of the city and calling in the cavalry. A shot to the head will send time into a brief spin of slow motion, just so you can really appreciate how well you shot him. It's almost a pat on the back: "Nice one, player, you totally kicked him in the face with bullets. Now he isn't going to be able to do oppressive American rogue army things. Good work."
Though...there's a point where that pat on the back becomes a knife to the spine, the game taking almost a dark pleasure in [i]twisting[/i] it every so often. If an enemy goes down, you can 'Execute' them. At the beginning of the game, Captain Walker will punch them in the face and possibly knock them out, maybe shooting them in the head if they're lucky. But as time passes, and you begin to see [i]exactly[/i] what Dubai has been doing behind the sandstorm, these become arguably a bit more...hands on, shall we say.
After all, no finer skull-crusher than the end of your rifle, right?
Continuing on from how it breaks the squad down, the game will occasionally show you signs that Walker is breaking. His originally professional tone upon a kill ("Tango down!") will begin to twist and snap into an audibly darker tone ("Got the ♥♥♥♥♥♥!"). Your squad will notice Walker breaking. They'll start snapping at each other. Arguing for brief instances at first, shrugging it off as just a bit of friendly banter. But further along the line, these arguments become more drawn out, and over more serious things.
And I dare not even mention some of the atrocities the game will force you to commit to carry on. One such choice sees you overlooking the 'interrogation' of a man you've been pursuing for answers. If you open fire on the interrogators and attempt to save his life, his men will kill a set of civilians they...'requisitioned'. Should you just sit and watch, you're going to be watching these psychopaths dragging out his punishment. They open fire by his head, next to the heads of the captured civilians, and kick sand in his face, culminating in the strangling of your contact.
Either way, it's a choice: Your mission's asset, or the lives of the innocent?
However, in spite of its incredible accomplishments in the fields of combat, soundtrack, voice acting, story, gameplay, and level design, there are, as with all things, a few shortcomings.
Firstly, the cover system can be, at the worst times, confusing and unresponsive. Your sprint button and cover button are mapped to the same button, and it's tap to sprint. This eventually means that you'll be pinned down with heavy fire and looking to move forward up the field, and you'll vault your cover, prepare to run...
...and instead, Walker jogs towards a nearby wall and stands there like a gormless tosser as you repeatedly spam the sprint button.
Next, there's the...[i]questionable[/i] elements of the game. Whilst this is not really a shortcoming (on the contrary; they were choices and tasks brutal enough that I briefly paused afterwards to breathe steadily at what I'd just done), it seems that the problem with them is that they were too good. No other game thus far has managed to recreate the horrors of war as well as [i]Spec Ops: The Line[/i]. No other game has shown the devolution from hero to monster as well as this, and with physical evidence of Walker's decline showing his uniform beginning to rip and tear, armour becoming visible, bullet wounds, cuts and scars all becoming apparent as you and your squad drag yourselves through extreme gunfights and brutal environments. Not only that, but the good folks at twitch.tv make their appearance known every so often by sandstorming the battlefield, making it impossible to order your squad to do anything and making it damn near impossible to see. And with these storms, the men's eyes become redder, and more glazed, as they see things that nobody should ever deserve to see.
And the difficulty...damn.
Now, I will openly admit that I'm...mediocre, when it comes to shooters. I pick up weapons that look familiar to me, aim for the head, and hope that they're not better than me.
Here?
Everyone was bloody well better than me, and that was on [i]Normal[/i]. I died a good ten times per mission, even more on later levels. On one play through, Walker must have personally met Satan a good two hundred times. So I can thank the developers for making the hardest difficulty (lovingly named 'FUBAR', or '♥♥♥♥♥♥ Up Beyond All Recognition') locked until you've proved that you're good enough to fight through the hard mode.
So, if you want to pick this up, I'm not stopping you. Nobody is.
But just remember: Walker only does what you're making him do.
Do you feel like a hero, yet?

The mechanics of this game are fairly standard for a third person shooter (cover shooter, chest high walls everywhere). The game feels like a console adaptation for the most part and there are some frustrating aspects to controlling the main character, like the occasional refusal to take cover or vault over objects. As a single player experience, the best of this game lies really in the setting and storyline. Desert storms taking over Dubai skyscrappers makes for an excellent environment that feels fresh and original. The single player campaign is a harsh, cynical twist on the typical oversimplistic, jingoistic narrative that most military shooter games tend to favour of late. It purposefully makes you reflect on the consequences of your actions, the horrors of indescriminate war, of lives and humanity lost.

A 3rd person shooter with simple controls. What makes Spec Ops The Line great is it's narrative. The story is really the only thing it has going for it, but that's all it really needs, I never even touched multiplayer, and I never will because the story is just very good. Instead of making you a badass killing machine, Spec Ops The Line want's to show you the horrors of war, giving you choices that have no good outcome, and making you do horrible things. It's also worth mentioning how great the characterization is; how Walker is trying to be this "good guy, help the people" kind of person, but, just keeps making bad decisions, or how his two comrades are very sarcastic in the beginning of the story and deteriorate to angry soldiers who are completely serious. In short: Spec Ops: The Line is game you want if you like a good story, and I have to say it's a dam good one, for 29.99 though? No, get it on sale (I got it in a humble bundle). If you're sick of the usually "you're a military badass" campaigns you see in your cods and bfs, and if you like a good story, this is definitley the game to buy.

The game is nice. I have 2 remarks – about gameplay and about story.
[b]Gameplay.[/b] In short: it actually is quite good (but I agree that there are types of people who would not like it). 
Before buying I have read professional review on top review site (forget which one) that gave the gameplay very bad scores. The reviewer claimed that he was shocked how easy his character dies while his comrades are almost invulnerable. After completing the game I was missing several “intel” locations. So I went online, googled (top result) walkthroughs to find out were the missing “intel” was and redo the chapters to collect the “intel”. As walkthrough was on youtube I watched in disbelief how person doing the walkthrough fights “the end game turrets” mostly simply standing and exchanging fire from afar (and not with long range weapon either). That was ridiculous, because turret is supposed to be almost invulnerable from front and turret is supposed to kill you very fast. So I guess only reason why the walkthrough guy was able to win the firefight was because he probably was using lowest difficulty (or/and probably some cheats). I also suspect that professional reviewer I mentioned in beginning was same type of player who loves to run with the shotgun against fortified position and expects to win.
So if you love to slaughter waves of enemies simply by running into them this game is not for you. Me, I personally find that automatic health regeneration makes character incredibly tough. Quite often it is more beneficial to simply absorb fire while you maneuver to better position rather than spending ammunition by shooting back. However you must always make a judgment call which position really is better one and you have to maneuver.
I would also note that level design is good. It has surprising variety of mission types. Waves of enemies are quite manageable and enemies never suffer “never ending” syndrome. Learning curve is very ok with first missions (“chapters”) being easy and demanding very limited tactical knowledge that changes latter. I agree that keyboard controls could be better.
[b]Story.[/b] In short: it ok, not as good as some claim.
The story is very good in sense that it forces casual player to think about idea that “enemies” are not bad and do not deserve to die. If this is your first realization that quite often there is truth (right) on both sides, then you would probably go away quite shocked. The most epic moment is also very emotionally done. However to tell the truth this is neither the first time this idea is presented nor this is the best way of presentation. The biggest problem for me was complete lack of choice of action (while in game dialog repeatedly claimed otherwise). I read the interview where developer explained that the bad path was intentionally chosen because in life the good is not rewarded (Here I simplify what he said). While that is technically true. It would be completely untrue in case if in real life you would have option to see the results of your mistaken action and then “reload” and do it differently. If in real life you would have reload button you could easily avoid almost all the bad moral situations presented in game. Actually in real life you can avoid some of them even without “reload” just by applying common sense and prudence. The actions taken by main character was simply childish and idiotic. That broke my “suspense of disbelief” and unlike many other people I felt no real guilt for gameplay actions (but it was emotional nevertheless). However citing the end game “it takes a strong man to deny the reality” – maybe that is the case with me ;-).
That said I must note that “bad ending” actually makes the game into non replayable. Why you would want to repeat the suffering once again?

[h1]A word of advise: This game is not COD. It also isn't Battlefield. Or any other war shooter.[/h1]
I usually don't read reviews when Im really interested in a game, boy was I wrong here.
This game offers choices. Lots of them, and one more brutal and morally despicable than the other. It's just that, I didn't get this until more than half way into the game. This game doesn't throw "decision points" around like "press F to ignore the geneva conventions". So, think of your actions. Consider consequences. It's not a really linear game. 

And now to the actual review.
You lead a party of three Delta Ops into the City of Dubai that was supposed to be evacuated due to heavy sandstorms almost six months ago. What you search is the remains of the US Evac team including its leader and civillian survivors. What you find is death, despair, war crimes and five hundred million metric tons of sand.

For the graphics and audio, SpecOps keeps on proven grounds. Graphics are as good as UE3 can be. Sound is nice, with a very functional use of background music. The enemy soldiers could have used a few more lines to make their shouts less repetitive.

The scenery is a sad but beautiful apocalypse set in UAE's Dubai, desertified by extreme sand storms. The chapter "The Edge" was visually astonishing, backgrounds in the panoramic shots look a little static but still blend in really nice, The constant change between the hot desert outside and cool building interiors was refreshing and prevented boredom.
A special factor is the high verticality in the game. Dubai is a city of heights, and the game let's you feel that. Basements to rooftops, up and down dunes, a literal pit formed by high sand walls clinging to the many skyscrapers.

The gameplay followed that of a shooter: ambushes, firing from cover, two fairly useful AI teammates you have limited but effective control of. I am an experienced shooter player, some parts still made me to turn down the difficulty to "normal", as I simply died too often, but that's personal I guess. I found no particular glitches that "killed" me, so I guess the game is fair. Beware, ammunition is as scarce as you would expect in a desertified dead city.

For my personal experience, I  really liked it once I understood how the game actually works. It was difficult enough to be challenging, but not unfair. I also liked that the character models change over time to represent the ordeal they are advancing through.

The story begins as casual recon mission and quickly descends into unforgiving survival when the lives of all remaining city inhabitans lie in your hands. Will your choices relief the situation or make it worse? Who is your actual enemy? Are you an Angel of Life or Death? And, depending on your decisions, the game changes to: is it real what you see? Why did you actually come here? What the hell have you done? This game is somewhat "Apocalyse now".

For conclusion, I came to Dubai to help and rescue, and, considering my personal ending, I believe I became f*cking Hitler. I killed those I wanted to protect, starved all I did not kill, melted refugee kids with banned weapons and became a walking war crime. In the end I was happy with my gameplay, but dissapointed in myself.

10/10 should probably rethink real life ethics.

Spec Ops: The Line is not a game. No, I refuse to call it a game. Instead, a more fitting way to label this piece of work would be, 'art'. Plain and simple. Just as the 'Fountain' by Marcel Duchamp was a big slap to the face for the art commmunity on 'What is Art?', Spec Ops: The Line does the same for the Gaming Community on, 'What are Modern Military Shooters?' It takes the Badass, Stone-Cold, Heroic and invulnerable killing machine protaganist typical in your everyday Military Shooter and tears it to pieces with its masterful story.

This poigant work will really help making you wonder what it means to be a hero and needs to be played in order to be understood. To be honest, I feel like I ripped off the developers for buying this game when it was on a $6 deal.

The less you know, the better the game.
________________________________________________________________
Story

Dubai was hit with a series of sandstorm that ravaged the city and turned it into a Kid's Sandbox basically. Colonel John Konrad, a decorated Officer in the US army and the 33rd 'Damned' Infantry Regiment volunteered to help the evacuated the city. Nothing was heard from them ever since until 6 Months Later when a Distress Signal by Konrad himself reaches out to the world. This is where you come in. You're Captain Walker, leader of a 3 Man Delta Team Operative sent to investigate Dubai for any survivors. (Cliche, Badass 3 Man Special Forces Protaganist trying to get stuff done and take care of business where others failed.)

This is about as much as you need to know to understand what's going on.
________________________________________________________________
Gameplay
(AI)
Enemy AI seem to be good enough, alway shouting out what their doing and responding to each other in turn. There are 4 types of enemies Regular, Close-Combat, Sniper and Heavy. * = can be armoured, ie more durable
Regular* - The Grunts. SMG/Shotgunners/Assault Rifle all day, everyday. Shotgunners tend to charge at you which can be a danger
Close-Combat - Remember that Banzai Soldier from World at War? This is him except that its 1 hit kill, he dodges and insta-kills you with his knife when he gets close (Yes, no QTE)
Sniper* - He snipes? Also has shiny red laser sight which you can see since its tagging you
Heavy* - Always comes armoured and just like the Bulldozer from Payday 2, his face is his weakspot. There are 2 varieties of the 'Heavy', M249 Saw or AA12. Either way you're boned as they love walking straight up to you... Jerks

Don't worry about your AI though as they are okay-ish enough to get stuff done though they tend to go suicidal when you issue an attack order. They have no problem in getting kills or distracting enemies and will always shout out enemies of interest during a firefight such as, "Shotgunner coming from the right!". Take note that this needs to be heard as battle lines are not subtitled. What can be annoying though is when they take too much damamge, they need to be revived and you have a time limit but you don't have the ability to be revived (On Hard, idk about normal and easy)

(Core)
The meat of the game comes from being a Cover-Based Third Person Shooter reminiscent to that of games like Gears of War. Basically, you sprint form cover to cover (Using a Toggle Key 'Space') and rely on Regenerating Health. The lower your health, the more bloodied your screen becomes in addition to being Black and White (CoD anyone?). There are 15 weapons in total give or take which felt the same with only the diffference being its 'Alternate Function' key which is 'C'. There are also 3 grenade types, Frag, Sticky and Stun which are pretty self-explanatory. You can carry 2 weapons and all 3 grenade types at once. However, you are only limited to 3 grenades per type making the total number of grenades which can be carried to 9(3 Frags/3 Stickies/3 Stuns). Different from other games is how ammo is obtained here. While there is still the basic, 'pick up ammo from dead body so long as same weapon' concept, what Spec Ops has added to spice it up is that in this game is that you can actually Execute wounded enemies to get ammo for your current weapon type. Because you know.. Executions are fun. Be fast though or they'll bleed out to death(GoW anyone)

In a nutshell, it's your run of the mill Third Person Cover based shooter like Gears of War or Future Soldier.. Just like any other games where you're the unstoppable saviour of your country.

(Command)
As Leader, you have control of 2 Squad Mates who use order via the MMB. They are:
Lieutenant Adams
Your Heavy Weapons Specialist carrying the M249 Saw. Order him to attack an enemy so long as their close and he'll do two things. FIrst, he unleashes hell on them with suppressive fire from his weapon. Second, he throws a frag which finds its mark 90% of the time, the 10% due to the enemy running away from it

Sergeant Lugo
Your Sniper. Order him to attack an enemy from long range and he'll kill the guy so long as he has vision. Though it takes some time for him to pull the trigger, its usually a 1-shot kill

As you can see, the command aspect in this game is very weak but simple enough to make life easy.

(Environment)
Alongside your Red Explosive Containers, you also have the sand which can either help or hinder you. Firstly, Sand can act as either an alternative form of Explosive Barrels. Secondly, throwing an explosive into a pile of sand would create a sand cloud which effectively stuns all nearby enemies for a nice amount of time, similar to Stun grenades if I'm not mistaken. Later in the game at set stages, you'll come across Sandstorms which does two things. Making you unable to issue orders and increasing weapon spread. Extremely frustrating, especially on harder difficulties (15+ deaths on Hard)

Nothing revolutionary here really though I'll admit its interesting in theory.

(Misc)
Collectables are available in the game and are called Intels. The number of intels available in each level is shown by pressing Escape. It offers backstory to the world of Dubai and its inhabitants. As of the time this review was written, no Steam Trading Cards are available. Checkpoints in this game seem to be fair enough. 1 checkpoint pre and post engagement.
________________________________________________________________
Music and Sound

I like the music. It's nice... very Vietnam War-esque and is also perfectly timed and well-executed. It's either Gung Ho adrenaline fueled action or music that make you muse over your actions.

Sound also seems to be quite good though the sound of the AA12 doesn't seem to have too much force behind it. Other than that, the sound can of this game can really make firefights here intense, especially on higher difficulties.
________________________________________________________________
Graphics

It looks nice enough if you really care so much about it. It's able to capture the violence and carnage you unleash (Yay carnage and violence cause that's what every military shooter needs right!... right?)
________________________________________________________________
Mutiplayer
There are two types of Multiplayer here.
Co-Op
2 players, 4 levels. A bit of a challenge when communication between the two is lacking. Can be fun for the first few times though I believe that it will lose its charm as fast as you finish it
Competetive
4v4 PvP from what I heard though sadly the cream of this game comes from the SP hence why I never bothered to try it out.
________________________________________________________________
Overall

Story is honestly speaking the saving grace for this game. It's what made it so spectacular as the entire gameplay is bland, rehashed and has been done countless times though it can be argued that the very fact that it copies its gameplay from other Military Games is what makes this so good. This is because of how Spec Ops question our beliefs on said game. Must buy.

This game has done more work towards games being considered an artistic medium than any other game ever made. Period. This game is art. It isn't some floaty pretentious nonsense from the xbox live arcade, the developers of this game wanted it to invoke actual emotion in the player, and that is exactly what it does. Fear, confusion, anger and sadness. 

Self-loathing.

I doubt that a game has ever made you really cry before. I mean you're in charge of your own choices, what do you have to be sad about? if you screw up you can start again. We live in a society that consider games escapism. Even a good story well told in a game is often hard to take seriously. Spec Ops is not escapism, it is a massive sucker punch in the stomach. It wont make you cry... it's not that sort of experience, but it will tell you a lot about yourself. It will make you ask questions about why you do some of the things you do. Spec Ops deconstructs what we have made to be "normal" in modern games with such aptitude that I haven't been able to play a military shooter the same way since.

There is a small amount of ammuntion at disposal as well. These two components allow for some stratigic and intense shoot-outs.

Not exactly the best thing to hear about a recommended game, but stick with me. At first the game sets itself out to be just another Third Person Shooter about killing insurgents and rescuing the ol' Americans. The gameplay, while fun, is nothing revolutionary. Take cover behind chest high walls, and take turns pelting lead at each other at 900 feet per second until one of you falls over. It is still fast-paced and fun.

To be honest, that's the only thing about spec ops that is fun. Stick with me, it's not that this game is boring. Quite contrary, in fact.

Without wishing to spoil much, at one point in the game, Walker (the main character) unintentionally does a really bad thing. The kind of thing that makes you feel really bad about him and yourself. From that point, you follow the character into an everlasting descent into madness, doing more and more questionable things, things you, the player, may start to disagree with.

Your thinking reflects that of the men in Walker's command, cautious and frightened of him as he tries to rationalise comitting terrible war crimes as just and necessary. Eventually you feel so disconnected from what he is thinking, and the game just gut-punches you at the end, and kicks you while you're down, pulling possibly the largest rug from under your feet.

If anything, this game is very worth the purchase, just for the story alone. It is not fun, or empowering, but damn will it make you feel like a miserable pile of sorrow. And yes, that is a good thing.

I am a little disappointed by this game. Somehow I expected it to be a FPS when I bought it, but it turned out to be a third-person shooter. "Oh well", I thought, "as long as the controls don't suck".... which they do, sadly. Taking cover behind objects is too often a hit or miss and sprinting makes your character uncontrollable. I even bugged and got stuck on staircase after vaulting over a wall. Picking up weapons is a bit iffy sometimes. The voice acting is sub par.

The AI is nothing special, multiple times the enemy slipped from cover and decided it was a good idea to change their magazines, right there, out in the open. Enemies just keep running straight at you and shouting the same voice clip over and over. I haven't seen any flanking or whatever tactical movement, which makes it feel like one big virtual shooting gallery, but I guess that is the type of game the creators were going for.

The gameplay is quite repetitive, since there are only ~5 types of enemies and the shootouts are mostly the same. The shotguns seem useless most of the time and the snipers are very situational.  At some points you are forced to swap weapons because you run out of ammo, which forces you to try out some of the other weapons. Still the standard assault rifle and the AK did the job for me. The sand mechanics feel more like a gimmick than really substantial part of the gameplay, but the idea is nice.

The storyline is ok. The only real problem that I have with it is that game forces emotion on you with melodramatic cutscenes where you can only walk and (mild spoiler) [spoiler]the main characters (who apparently already know what is going to happen half of the time) point out all the bad decisions that you make. I can imagine the game director looking over your shoulder saying "THERE, did you see that? You're such a terrible person for doing that." I got the feeling that it did not really matter which choices I made, the end result would still be the same.[/spoiler]

Apparently, if you need to open a locked door (metal or wood - doesn't matter), you just unload your shotgun at it once or twice and then try the door knob. Works every time!

Oh and then there is the reiterating loading bar.

On the positive side: The graphics and animations are nice. The atmosphere in the game is really strong and the game is incredibly colourful for a post-apocalyptic desert setting.

For me, the awesome atmosphere this game has to offer does not outweigh the iffy controls and repetitive gunfights. You may think otherwise and you can enjoy this game if you play it in a few sessions. I would only recommend it on sale (bought it for 3,39 eu). Spec Ops: The Line will certainly entertain you for a few hours, but there are enough better alternatives.

Spec Ops: The Line (SO:TL) basically isn't a bad game, but I still wouldn't recommend to buy it for the following reasons. While the setting and level design are unique and fresh, the game's mechanics and presentation suffer from some horrible, horrible issues that shouldn't be there in the first place, considering that Ghost Recon: Advanced Warfighter (GR:AW) and Star Wars: Republic Commando (SW:RC) got those things right over half a decade before SO:TL was released.

[b]1. Squad management[/b]
Seriously, a squad-based tactics shooter, where you cannot control your squad? Where you cannot tell them to stay put, but instead have to watch them run off like headless chickens and get themselves into hopeless situations, causing you to fail the mission? Where you cannot order them to cover you, or advance on your command? Bloody ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ hell! The amount of frustration this game causes by squad mates that are about as intelligent as a slice of moldy bread is insane. GR:AW and SW:RC do this whole squad thing about a million times better with explicit orders you can give your whole squad or individual members.

[b]2. Health and Death.[/b]
Okay, I get it. You're not Rambo, and guns are lethal. But apparently your squad mates are Rambo, because I cannot imagine any other reason why they are capable of withstanding punishment that would kill you three times over. And when they finally drop, you can get them back on their feet in a few seconds. So while your mates are Rambo McBulletsponge, you seem to be a fragile piece of china that gets smashed when an enemy even looks at you. Also once you drop it's over, because the magic healing syringe apparently only works on NPCs. In SW:RC you can also "revive" fallen squad mates, but they can do the same to you (and are actually quite clever in covering each other to get you back on your feet if you drop).

[b]3. Gun play[/b]
What's the difference between a FAMAS and a 417? What's the difference between an AK-47 and a M4A1? The weapons feel and play far too similar to warrant the variety, and you generally pick the one that has the most ammo available (either right now, or from what you expect in the next room/section). The only exception are situations that either require a particular weapon (sniper) or where you lose all previous weapons. There are far too many weapons that serve the exact same purpose and have the exact same gun play, making them completely redundant. Also, why the hell would an army battalion use so many different weapons with incompatible upgrades/extensions/calibres? It doesn't make any sense.

[b]4. Enemies[/b]
Seriously, ♥♥♥♥ heavy troopers. Just ♥♥♥♥ them. Guy with open helmet that exposes face survives several large caliber rounds (or frag grenades) to said exposed face. Are you ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ kidding me, SO:TL? For real? If you design enemies to visually have a weak spot (like open helmet), then FFS don't make that visual weak spot invulnerable! GAAAAHHHHHHH. Don't make me think there's a particular tactic to one type of enemy, when they just have twelve times more health than the other mooks! Damnit!

[b]5. Story[/b]
What really ground my gears was the repeated talk of how everyone had a choice, and that there was always an alternative to some course of action, but then the game goes around and forces you into a hamfisted linear rail road plot. No, you can't not use the phosphor grenade mortar. No, you can't not steal the water (and damn everyone left in the city to death by dehydration). No, you can't not destroy the radio tower. And so on, and so forth. Bascially, the only decisions you can make is which of two achievements you get in a particular situation. And that's a lame excuse, both for story and achievments.

If you're interested in the story, a few "Let's Play" videos on YouTube will serve you just fine, and save you hours of frustration.

The game mechanics don't offer anything special and may even lead to frustration from time to time. Storywise, you could hardly find a match in the military shooter genre. The less you know in advance, the better. Keep your questions for after finishing the game, there will be a lot of them.

What does stand out in this game is the gripping tale of a small operator squad that find themselves in the middle of a Dubai that was declared a no-man's land. The game will remind you of how cruel war can be, with some particular scenes and levels being not for the faint of heart, reminding us once again that war isn't always a conflict of villains and heroes, just a bunch of unfortunate encounters and events.

With that said, there is something that doesn't feel right about Spec Ops: The Line. The way it tells its story doesn't really match your typical cover-based TPS conventions. As you progress, the disparity becomes even more apparent, as the game seems to have trouble deciding whether it should be entertaining you with a series of explosive, ridiculous fights, or whether it should delve deeper in the psyche of the main character. It tries to do both anyways, and that leaves some to wonder whether things should have been done that way. SPOILER: [spoiler]The ridiculous fights could be justified as the MC's mental instability grows stronger, as he continues to justify his actions and do his best to be a hero. That's a bit of a stretch though.[/spoiler]

For the typical sale price, I'd say it's worth it, if you like emotional war stories and TPS games. Just don't ask questions about the multiplayer, it's dead and sad.

Spec Ops: The Line was probably one of my favorite games of 2012. Few games have stuck with me as well as Captain Walker's odyssey into madness and atrocity.

The gamplay is as uninspired as they come: it's essentially a functional, but largely uninteresting combination of a Gears of War-esque cover based third person shooter, with the weapons, theme, and color-pallette of a modern military shooter (ala Modern Warfare). The set-up for the story isn't much different: Middle Eastern city experiences a natural disaster, US soldiers sent into find out who survived (including fellow American forces), and run into seemingly hostile Arab insurgents. However, (at least in terms of the plot and theme ) I quickly encountered many twists and turns that quickly undermined my expectations of what this game was actually about. I won't delve into spoiler territory, but what started out as the most bland shooter I'd seen in a while, over time turned into maybe the most intelligent and interesting.

That said, the gunplay never really experiences the twists and radical changes the story does, which is a bit of a shame. I understand the gameplay was supposed to be deliberately derivative and unengaging for the purpose of where the plot takes you, but I still feel there were opportunities to radically change things up which would only add to the power in the storytelling and messaging in Spec Ops.

Spec Ops is one of those few linear story-based games that I have actually bothered to play through multiple times, because the tale it tells is worth experiencing with new eyes once you see it through once. Spec Ops to me signals that even the most reactionary game genres can be incredibly story-telling and metaphorical mediums. If only developers can find ways to not have to sacrifice gameplay for artistic merit, but Spec Ops is still a step in that direction.

Most military games start with shooting at whatever that decade's topical enemy is. Spec Ops is no different; you are greeted by a group of insurgents who yell at you in a language you can't understand and you put them down. You might be able to justify shooting them; they were being aggressive, and you were defending yourself.

But is there a point where you can't justify what you do? What does it take for you to stop and realize what you've done was brash, reckless and wrong?

I cannot recommend Spec Ops for its gameplay; it's a cover-based shooter with somewhat wonky controls and little variety. Story-wise however, it's a military shooter that leaves a strong, lasting impact depending on how you play it. A lot of games have some sort of tragic death of a squadmate to demonstrate "the horrors of war" after mowing down hundreds of faceless enemies - Spec Ops will make players regret pushing forwards at all. The genius of the game is that a fair portion of the regret experienced is self-inflicted, making it sting just a little bit more.

When do you stop being able to justify your own self-defense? Does it take a landscape littered with American soldiers? The charred remains of innocents? Firing into a crowd of confused civilians?

When is violence justified, and where do you draw The Line?

This is perhaps one of the most immersive games I've ever played in my lifetime. It's a scathing critique on modern modern militiary shooters, and pulls it off by juxtaposing the surrealist fantasy of FPSs and the real world effects conflict has on people.
First and foremost, I should point out that this game is not fun. This is intentional, and if you play the game you will understand why. The developers didn't want to deliver a power fantasy, they wanted to call you out for wanting to live those fantasies in the first place. Be warned, this game will make you feel like a terrible person. Yet this is exactly why I love this game so much.
After completing The Line, I felt horrible. This was genuinely the first game that made me feel guilty over my actions in the game, despite being forced to do so in the game. It's an experience I will never forget, and even impacts my experience when playing other games.
Perhaps one of the most impressive features The Line pulls off is its choice system. Choices are never given to you in a dialogue box, instead relying on the players to see the options presented to them. By doing this, the developers are essentialy saying "We trust our player base is intelligent enough to make their own decisions", a far cry from most AAA games developed these days.
In conclusion, buy this game.

Spec Ops: The Line is a big question mark for the military shooter genre, disguised as a 3rd Person Shooter. The major point of the game is the story, the journey of three Delta Force operatives within the doomed city of Dubai. The focus is on the progression and the change of the characters and the world that turns more and more surreal and a mirror of the madness you descend into.

You start the game as you would a lot others, shooting mostly arab-looking opponents, running and gunning into the outskirts of Dubai... but you will certainly not finish the game as you would most others. The twists and turns of who is the actual opponent is a very nice thing, morality gets murky very quickly and some of the intel you find will make you think a lot about your enemy (very nice format to introduce collectibles into a serious game). The only fixed point in the swirling madness you walk into is the main character's certainty that he is doing the right thing. You be the judge if that is the case....

Some of the most striking bits about this game are the visuals and the sound. It isn't the most technically impressive title, even considering its age, but the way the sand-filled city of Dubai is presented to you is simply stunning. A very important thing is that the visuals will evolve together with the story and the characters: in the beginning the world is what you would think it is, bleak desert, with some remnants of civilization hanging around, but as you advance into the Heart of Darkness, the landscape will change accordingly. Inside the crumbling towers you will find the luxury mixing with brutality, surreal scenes painted with lots of colors, contrasting very sharply against the state of mind of the characters. 
The visual transformation of your character and your squadmates is equally impressive and important in driving home the messages of the story. You start out as proper looking soldiers coming to the rescue, but by the end of the game you will look like demons murdering dozens upon dozens of soldiers... and then the game will ask you: "How many Americans have you killed today." And you might feel an urge to put down the controller/mouse and walk away from the game at that point... it is one of the possible endings, refusing to finish the game. 
The sound and voice acting evolves similarly. In the beginning of the team your small team of Delta operatives behaves and talks like you would expect from elite soldiers. Your opponents and the world around you also sound proper. But there is a very subtle change happening to all these things along the game. Your orders go from the likes of the calm "focus fire on my target" command to bellowing furiously toward you comrade: "I want him dead", and your squadmates will respond in the same way, from professional acknowledgment to a disturbingly savage war-cry. 

The genius in all this evolution is that it happens almost unseen, and the atmosphere of the game is so powerful that you won't always notice the changes as they happen. You will just be surprised at some point of the game that... wait.... when did we start shouting obscenities at out enemies and each other? Why the hell did I just execute a wounded US soldier with utmost brutality? Why did I just gun down that civilian? 
The "tooltip" messages that pop up on loading screens will also change... at first they will be actual tooltips, but as the madness progresses those messages will turn increasingly more intimidating ("Do you feel like a hero yet?" "If you were a better person, you wouldn't be here."), rubbing the salt even deeper.
That fact that the changes are subtle but powerful is the whole point of the game, as is the fact that it is very good at sucking you into its world and making you miss all these little details when it would still matter.

Gameplay-wise, Spec Ops: The Line is good enough to carry the story. The TPS shooting mechanics are a bit stiff, aiming  isn't as smooth as it could be... but combat is gritty and action-packed enough to be entertaining on most difficulty levels. For the best experience I would recommend Combat Op or Suicide Mission difficulty depending on your skill. These can make the combat challenging enough that the whole "war is brutal" message isn't lost, but not as unforgiving that the combat would blur out the message of the experience. The tactical part of the game is very shallow, you can command you squadmates to attack a target you choose, heal each other, and occasionally to do a specific action (stun, flush). It is very barebones, and the AI isn't particularly bright either, but it is good enough.
"Good enough" is the staple of Spec Ops: The Line's actual gameplay mechanics. It isn't really good, not very memorable in itself, but not bad either.

I do have one major problem with this game however: what the bloody hell are "Kill x amount of people with y gun" kind of achievements doing in this game? Who's genius idea was that load of steaming something? Actually why are there even achievements for this game? That seems to be completely against the spirit of the game...
