If you're looking for a thought-provoking and emotionally intense gaming experience, I highly recommend playing This War of Mine. This survival game offers a unique perspective on war by focusing on the civilian side of the conflict.
In this game, you play as a group of survivors trying to endure in a war-torn city. Your objective is not to defeat enemies or conquer territories, but rather to gather resources, make difficult decisions, and keep your characters alive. The game creates a sense of desperation as you scavenge for supplies, deal with moral dilemmas, and protect your shelter from hostile forces.
What sets This War of Mine apart is its emphasis on the human cost of war. The game delves into the psychological and emotional struggles faced by civilians caught in the crossfire. Each character has a unique background, skills, and personal story.
The day and night cycle affects gameplay dynamics, as you must balance resource gathering during daylight with the dangers of venturing out at night. 
Whether you're a fan of strategy, survival, or narrative-driven games, This War of mine is a must-play.

Обзор на This War of Mine: Stories - Father's Promise DLC

Очень радует, что студия поддерживает свой проект, несмотря на то, что основные их силы сейчас брошены на Frostpunk, и радуют нас обновлениями. Скромно, без анонсов и громкий заявлений, студия выкатила дополнение “Fathers promise”, которое является частью нового режима “Истории”.

Этот режим превращает игру из выживалки, в которой сюжет играет второстепенную роль, но все равно цепляет, в линейную новеллу. Нет, это всё ещё та же самая игра, с убежищем, ресурсами, нападениями, с вылазками, во время которых происходят леденящие кровь события, но теперь в центре повествования только отец и маленькая дочь.

И, черт, пока многие требовали добавить в игру зомби (непонятно зачем, TWoM вообще не о том), я втайне мечтал о сюжетке. Не историях персонажей и локаций, которые подаются воспоминаниями в биографии, записками и заметками, а полноценной сюжетной линии. 

Чуть ли не визжа от восторга, я купил season pass, запустил игру и погрузился в нее, рассчитывая на новые ощущения. И не ошибся, новый режим раскрывает осаду Погореня совсем иначе чем классический, и даже если вы уже успешно закончили игру за все возможные комбинации персонажей, уверен, что “Stories” позволит вам получить новые эмоции.

В первую очередь хочу сказать, что 11Bits проделали большую работу при разработке этого дополнения: несколько новых механик, новые и переработанные старые локации, новое убежище и, что самое важное, сюжет.

У убежища есть своя фишка: оно состоит из двух частей, причем перебраться из одной части в другую можно только перебросив через расстояние между проломами в стенах навесной мост. Это очень свежая идея, которую можно развить дальше: почему бы не дать игроку возможность строить лестницы из подручного хлама прямо на локациях для вылазок?

Помимо этого, во время вылазок теперь можно разговаривать с жителями Погореня, расспрашивая их о интересующих вас вещах. При этом, кто-то с радостью ответит на вопросы, кто-то потребует оплаты за информацию, а другие откажутся говорить, попросят отвязаться от них, а могут даже пригрозить главному герою.

Появилась новые локации: “Магазин игрушек”, который мы, кстати, видим на экране при запуске игры в режиме историй, “Аптека”, “Дом брата”, “Церковь”. Также переработаны “Аэропорт”, “Городская больница”, “Бензоколонка” и “Заброшенная школа”. Все они сделаны в характерной для “битсов” манере, все локации атмосферные, погружают в атмосферу агонизирующего Погореня. Это очень круто.

Завязка сюжета проста: после смерти матери девчушка замкнулась в себе, а единственной ее связью с внешним миром и одновременно надеждой на выживание остается отец. Драма заключается в том, что после бомбежки им пришлось перейти в другое крыло дома, оставив все вещи, а сама Амелия медленно угасает от болезни.

После одной из бессонных ночей Адам теряет сознание от истощения, а, когда просыпается, то видит пустую постель. Дальше развивается практически детективная история: обезумевший от горя, но очень решительно настроенный отец ищет свою дочь и ее похитителей по всему городу.

Я прошел длс, оно не очень длинное, всего часа на три геймплея, и могу сказать, что сюжет мне не понравился. Основная проблема сценария в том, что концовка никак не вытекает из основного повествования. В желании сделать мощный твист в конце польский писатель позабыл о логике, и это его подвело и вместо чувства опустошения, которое должно было возникнуть у игрока по задумке разработчиков, я почувствовал только разочарование. А это при том, что большую часть игры я прошел с большим интересом.

И, как мне кажется, в режиме “Истории” важно именно качество сценария.

Резюме: Замах на рубль, а удар на гривенник. Видно, что “битсы” старались, видно, что проделали большую работу, разработали множество нововведений. Но главная проблема дополнения в том, что сценарий очень слабый.

С другой стороны, ради того чтобы освежить впечатления и вновь погрузиться в атмосферу осажденного Погореня, заплатить такие деньги не жалко. Опять же: будем надеяться, что сценарии двух новых историй окажутся лучше проработаны.

11Bits - очень креативная студия, доказала, что может делать игры, которые в первую очередь рассказывают истории, цепляющие за душу. Но на этот раз у них не совсем получилось, и оценить их продукт больше чем на 6 из 10 я не могу.

Дальше будут СПОЙЛЕРЫ.

Я настоятельно не рекомендую читать этот раздел, в котором я постараюсь объяснить, почему сюжет дополнения такой слабый, если вы ещё не прошли дополнение.

Серьезно, потом играть будет неинтересно. Режим “Stories” - это не выживание, а линейная история, поэтому, если вы не хотите испортить впечатления, не читайте.

Как я уже сказал ранее, финал практически никак не вытекает из основного повествования. Всю игру вам намекают на то, что дочь у вас украл брат, которого затем убили повстанцы, чтобы использовать девочку в качестве пропуска, и покинуть город через открытый по требованию ООН гуманитарный коридор.

В итоге оказывается, что сам Адам, не в силах смотреть, как умирает его дочь, отправился в аптеку брата на поиски лекарства. После того как лекарства не помогли, он отнес дочь к доктору Ефимову, который только констатировал смерть. Отец, не выполнивший обещания, похоронил дочь, но, не в силах принять ситуацию, впал в состояние ретроградной амнезии. А потом очнулся и бросился по своим же следам.

Это очень дешёвый и очень слабый финал. Но даже так ситуацию можно было бы спасти, если сделать в процессе повествования больше намеков на то, что Адам сделал всё сам (намек ровно один, один из персонажей узнает мужчину, но тут же отказывается от своих слов, стоит Адаму сказать, что это не он).

The game's premise is simple yet powerful: you control a group of ordinary civilians trapped in a besieged city, struggling to endure the horrors of war. Instead of playing as a soldier or a hero, you assume the roles of everyday people trying to survive in the face of scarcity, danger, and moral dilemmas.

The gameplay revolves around resource management, exploration, and decision-making. As you scavenge for supplies, make crucial choices, and fortify your makeshift shelter, the game forces you to confront the harsh realities of war. Balancing the needs of your group with the moral consequences of your actions creates a gripping and emotional experience unlike any other.

What sets This War of Mine apart is its remarkable storytelling. The game beautifully captures the human side of war, focusing on the struggles, fears, and desperation of its characters. Each survivor has their own unique background and personality, and their stories unfold as you play. Witnessing their emotional journey and seeing the toll war takes on their psyche is truly heart-wrenching.

The art style and sound design further enhance the game's atmosphere. The hauntingly beautiful visuals portray a war-torn city with remarkable attention to detail, while the somber and evocative soundtrack perfectly complements the bleakness of the narrative.

This War of Mine is not a game that provides a sense of power or triumph. It's an introspective and thought-provoking experience that compels players to contemplate the nature of war, morality, and the human spirit. It challenges our empathy and forces us to make difficult choices that often have no right answer.

If you're looking for a game that transcends traditional war games and delves into the human condition with unparalleled depth, This War of Mine is an absolute must-play. Just be prepared to have your heartstrings pulled and your worldview challenged in the process.

After surviving the game on my 6th attempt, and spending about 50 hours on this game, I just want to share my opinion on the game.

To start off, I apologize if I make any mistakes in any of my statements. I wrote this to the best of my knowledge, which may not be extensive as I did not search up much of any additional information online, and based it solely on my experience. Also, although I have 'recommended' this game, this review will mostly be negative. Verdict is at the bottom.

The good points:

1. Game concept. I really liked the idea of playing as helpless citizens in a war-torn city, and how under these circumstances, experience with my own senses how normal people can be pushed to perform questionably immoral acts just to survive. I felt that the game did a good job showing this sense of desperation and hopelessness in war.

2. Atmosphere. Very important part of the game. The atmosphere coupled with the music undoubtedly makes you feel like you are in a despair filled war-torn environment which draws you into the game.

Negative points:

While the concept is good, I personally feel that some of the execution is lacking which killed my immersion. 

1. Player Characters. While scanning the reviews prior to purchasing the game, I was under the impression that there was going to be a story behind the characters, expounding on their personalities and motivations and such. I was disappointed to find out there was no such thing. All the characters just repeat the same lines with no character development. 

2. Impact of actions. I was excited about the experiencing of moral dilemma, making possibly immoral choices just to survive. However throughout the game, I fail to feel the impact of my actions, the impact is merely conveyed through some barebones character remarks which sometimes feel very stupid. For example, your character can get sad and keep complaining nonstop about stealing from some random house, but other times I can straight up murder civilians and steal from the hospital and my characters ignore those actions completely. The way they measure morality in this game is just not consistent. You also don't get enough meaningful interactions with the NPCs, and I barely feel the army presence throughout the game other than just from text.

3. Combat and Stealth. Kills the immersion. The NPCs behave very stupidly. Sometimes, NPCs somehow sees you through multiple doors. Sometimes, NPCs completely glitches out and stands at a certain spot, making you stuck in your hiding spot. You run through a door and the NPC forgets you are there. Initially, I was excited about sneaking around but at some spots it gets really annoying due to buggy NPCS. Combat is also not intuitive and you can accidentally employ exploits to wipe out enemies.
Additionally, I was expecting to be able to experience real-time raids on my house and I would have to fight them off. However, this all happens off-screen during the night, and all I get is a screen showing the details of the raid. 

4. Health penalties. Very annoying part of the game. I get the need to be realistic with physical and psychological health, but at some point I felt it was pure RNG. Characters can never recover from slight injuries and sickness despite so many days of sleep and medication. Sometimes characters get constantly sad despite successful defense from a raid. They keep complaining and worrying about the next raid even though I have upgraded to max defense. And I am not only complaining about these "bad luck" moments. On my final playthrough I went almost the late half of the game with no sickness, injuries or sadness even though I murdered citizens and stole from a hospital. In fact they became content a short while later after I performed those deeds. These are the same characters that got sad for a long long time after I stole insignificant stuff from some random house. 

5. Saving mechanics. The game autosaves when you complete a night. I feel this is a negative point because you are forced to complete a night before you are able to quit the game. Beside that, if you make a single mistake like forgetting to bring an item during your night scavenging you will be forced to restart the entire day. There is also no speed up mechanics so if you want to perform multiple tasks during the day, you will be forced to wait between each task. I think it doesn't take anything away from the game to allow you to save before the night.

I really like the concept of this game and think it could be a great game. I was really absorbed into it on my first few days to the point where I literally sat there for 10 hours straight. However there are many flaws (in my opinion) that slowly killed my immersion throughout my playthrough which eventually led me to just wanting the game to end and move on. 

My verdict: I really have mixed feelings. I would recommend buying this game on a discount, as the concept and atmosphere still provides a decent experience and is worth the money. However I would not buy it for the full price.

"This War of Mine" is a remarkable and thought-provoking survival game that immerses players in the harsh realities of war and its devastating effects on civilians. Developed by 11 bit studios, the game offers a unique perspective, placing you in the shoes of ordinary people struggling to survive in a war-ravaged city.

Set in a fictional city under siege, "This War of Mine" takes a departure from traditional war games by focusing on the civilian experience rather than the military. You control a group of survivors, each with their own distinct skills, backgrounds, and personalities. As you scavenge for supplies, manage your shelter, and make life-and-death decisions, the game creates an intense and emotionally charged atmosphere.

One of the standout features of "This War of Mine" is its moral ambiguity. The choices you make in the game are never easy, and they carry consequences that can profoundly affect both your characters and the overall narrative. Should you risk your life to help a stranger in need, or prioritize the well-being of your own group? These dilemmas constantly test your morality and force you to confront the difficult decisions people face during times of war.

The gameplay mechanics in "This War of Mine" are engaging and realistic. Each day is divided into segments, with daytime dedicated to managing your shelter, crafting essential items, and reinforcing defenses, while nighttime becomes the critical period for scavenging in dangerous locations. The scarcity of resources and the constant threat of violence create a tense and nerve-wracking experience, capturing the desperation of survival in a war zone.

Graphically, the game presents a hauntingly beautiful hand-drawn art style. The attention to detail in the environments and character animations, coupled with the melancholic soundtrack, further enhances the game's somber atmosphere and emotional impact. The sound design plays a crucial role in immersing players into the world, effectively conveying the despair and tension that permeate every moment.

"This War of Mine" goes beyond the confines of entertainment; it serves as a poignant social commentary. The game highlights the plight of innocent civilians trapped in the chaos of war, shedding light on the struggles, hardships, and resilience of those affected by armed conflicts worldwide. It prompts players to reflect on the moral complexities of war, empathy, and the importance of basic human values.

In conclusion, "This War of Mine" is an exceptional game that stands as a powerful testament to the human spirit in times of unimaginable adversity. Its gripping narrative, thought-provoking gameplay, and atmospheric presentation create an emotionally charged experience like no other. By offering a fresh perspective on war and the untold stories of those caught in its crossfire, "This War of Mine" transcends the boundaries of a traditional video game and becomes a powerful medium for empathy and reflection.

As someone who was amongst a family of Balkan refugees I may hold a somewhat different perspective to TWOM compared to some other gamers. Anyone who's been in a real war, or at least knows well someone who has, will be quite moved and possibly overwhelmed - but at the same time appreciate - how gritty and realistic this game is. I'm not sure "fun" is what I would call it. It's most certainly engaging to play in the sense of progression and challenge like many "fun games" tend to instil, but there are times when the game is simply too depressing and all too real to match that description. It's clear that 11 Bit Studios knew exactly what they were doing while developing this: although their country did not experience a genocidal war in recent memory with a city undergoing years of siege like Sarajevo did (which the game is based on), Poland also has had rough history and hardship so there's no doubt the developers could really understand and empathise to a degree with the struggles and futility people faced during the utterly pointless and disastrous Yugoslav wars (as well as many others throughout human history to the present) while they developed this title.

This is not the only game with harsh anti-war themes (Spec Ops The Line comes to mind, another terrific war game), but it's the first I've noticed that puts full emphasis on the civilian perspective. Depending on the slightly different game modes, the player spawns in a randomly generated story with a group of civilian residents residing in an apartment block, each with their own backstories, personalities and gameplay strengths/weaknesses. The objective is to survive the randomly generated number of days till the war ends by looking after the characters' moods, hunger/energy levels, and scavenging for useful material. During the day they must use what resources they have to modify the apartment block, grow/cook food, and craft tools and weapons. The latter is used during nighttime when the player chooses and controls one of the characters to venture to one of the surrounding neighbourhoods to scavenge for resources. If the character is killed, then the story must continue without them until either the war ends or all characters die.

From a technical perspective, the game is well-made. A lot of the imagery feels like a drawing or painting, although the experience is essentially 2.5D. I encountered very little bugs, and even then nothing that broke away from the atmosphere. The controls do take some getting used to though: when you control a character during the night missions you are essentially playing a blend of point-and-click and 2D-side-scrolling action/shooter. This can make some combat and stealth scenarios bit awkward at first, so don't be surprised if a character or two gets killed on your first couple of playthroughs. Initially, it also means you may be confronted with tough decisions that may make you feel almost as depressed as your own characters when they're forced to go through with them. TWOM is one of those "The more you play, the more you learn and the better you get" experiences, so if you have the patience you will eventually be able to reach the one positive vibe you can find here: the war ending. Doing so unlocks new modes and characters to play with when you restart a new scenario.

The TWOM stories are also worth getting, but be warned: they are VERY sad and depressing (*especially* Father's Promise, oof) so if you find that too much to handle then just focus on getting The Little Ones DLC and supporting the charity pack. Even absent those, you'll seldom find a game as bleak as this one. If I were one of the cover artists, I'd be filled with tears just drawing those up. Well, maybe the also-brilliant Frostpunk comes close though that is still at least based on fiction. At any rate, TWOM is a game that every gamer should try. You will rarely find a game so full of heart and meaning. It won't be for everyone, but whether or not it was made for you, it will be one of the most important experiences you may ever face in a video game.

this war of mine is a survival-strategy game developed & published by 11 bit studios. it released on PC in late 2014, then came to mobile platforms in 2015, PS4/xbox one in early 2016, and nintendo switch in late 2018. instead of playing as a soldier on the front line of war, you play as civilians and their experiences hiding inside a damaged house in a besieged fictional city's warzone. it does a good job showing how war affects people in more ways than you could imagine. the game is all about survival, you're not a a part of the two warring factions, in fact your characters are scared of/powerless against both the main faction and the group rebelling against them. you are just helpless survivors caught in the middle. you start off in a damaged house with a small group of survivors, each character/survivor having their own backstory, giving them different stats, different traits, etc., such as one guy being a good cook, using less resources than other characters to make the same meal, or another character being faster than others, making him a good option for going out and scavenging at night. there's even a character who is pregnant! 

again, the main point of the game is surviving. it's pretty difficult, but it's handled extremely well as far as realism goes for a video game about war. the gameplay plays almost like an ant-farm, as you can see from the side and have a 2.5D viewpoint. presentation-wise, this game is amazing and you can tell that the city is war-torn and been ravaged through. the story is there, and is effective, but there's a lot of scripted interactions that can feel repetitive, especially in multiple playthroughs. however, there's also a heavy-handed feel to these interactions and many other moments in the game, such as whether or not you give up food or not to another struggling group. maybe later you return and they all starved to death. just the thought of that happening irl makes my skin crawl. the game does a great job conveying all of that to the player.

there's great resource management in the gameplay with tons of crafting and base-building that any survival fans will feel familiar with. however, it is done with pristine quality and attention to detail, especially for a game that first released in 2014 and was one of 11 bit studios earlier games. having now 100%'d this, I'm excited to eventually get to a lot of 11 bit studios' future games, including the next couple of titles they published after this war of mine, which includes beat cop & tower 57 (2017), and frostpunk & moonlighter (2018). i can't recommend this game enough, especially when it's on sale for 80% off, making it only $3.99 USD which is an absolute steal.

With so many military games out there people sometimes might forget how nightmarish war actually is. This War of Mine is a game that truly immerses players in the horrors of war and the difficult choices that survivors must make in order to stay alive. Set in a besieged city, the game puts you in charge of a small group of civilians struggling to survive in a world where every decision can mean the difference between life and death.

The game's unique focus on the civilian experience of war, rather than the more traditional military perspective, sets it apart from other games in the genre. The game's visuals are stark and gritty, effectively conveying the harsh realities of life in a war zone. The haunting soundtrack only adds to the game's atmosphere, perfectly capturing the feelings of hopelessness and despair that permeate throughout the game.

What really makes This War of Mine stand out, however, is its emphasis on player choice. Every decision you make, from who you choose to scavenge for supplies to whether you steal from other survivors, has real consequences for your group's survival. The game forces players to confront the harsh reality that sometimes there are no good choices, only choices that are slightly less terrible than the alternatives.

Overall, This War of Mine is a powerful and affecting game that will leave a lasting impression on players. It may not be the most enjoyable game to play, but it is an experience that is well worth having.

Although it is easy to exploit the combat system and take away the well-established dread of murdering someone that part of the game revolves around, this war of mine offers an insightful perspective into the consequences of modern-day armed conflict for civilians. The game is from the perspective of these civilians, and their turbulent psychological well-being as they are deprived of necessities such as food, shelter or even cigarettes and coffee. it is immersive, thought-provoking and sticks with you long after it is played.

I recently played 'This War of Mine,' and I have to say, it's a truly gripping game. The game's setting, a war-torn city, is portrayed in a realistic and haunting manner that pulls you in from the start. As a player, you must lead a group of civilians through the chaos of war and make tough choices to ensure their survival.

One of the things I loved about the game was how it made me think. The decisions you make have a real impact on your chances of survival, and often there are no easy choices. Whether it's deciding who gets to eat, or whether to risk going out scavenging at night, every choice feels weighty.

The game's mechanics also add to the sense of immersion. You must scavenge for resources to keep your group alive, and every decision counts. The game has a day/night cycle, and during the night, you must decide whether to stay put and try to defend your shelter or risk going out to find more supplies.

However, the game can also be frustrating at times. The resource management aspect can become repetitive, and the AI can be unpredictable. There were moments when I felt like my characters were not behaving as expected, which led to some frustration.

Overall, 'This War of Mine' is a game that is definitely worth playing. It's an intense and thought-provoking experience that will stay with you long after you've put the controller down. The game's atmosphere, storytelling, and mechanics all come together to create a truly memorable experience, despite some minor frustrations.

This War of Mine has [b]parts[/b] of the winning formula but falls short on realism. Death is dime a dozen in video games but in TWoM: war crimes are committed, and you can commit a few yourself. TWoM stakes its claim on the ugly realities other games shy away from. 

Prostitution, Gangs, Addiction, Depression... hell, just plain ol' tiredness. Get too hungry or too sleepless and your characters start moving slow. Alcohol is present and properly valuable; good for cleaning wounds, trade, or just blowing off some steam. Some characters are addicted to cigarettes or coffee and they'll get cranky without them. If their mood gets bad enough they'll peace out forever. There's ambushes and raiders. Hatchets are good for chopping firewood... [i]or people[/i].

But why does it take [b]FOUR[/b] 2x4s to make a [i]hatchet[/i]? And [b]where are the damn [i]backpacks[/i]?[/b] There are no bicycles. The enemy APCs never come rolling in. Frankly, the answer to all the missing elements are probably: "the engine wouldn't handle it." It's sad. Not [i]Schindler's List[/i] or [i]Life is Beautiful[/i] sad. It's sad that the statement TWoM wanted to make is buried under the gameplay. This War of Mine's vision still feels fresh & relevant in light of 2024... but the immersion required to fully reveal it is lost in the frustration.

It has taken me a while to get the drive to fully complete this game; however, I believe this game has one of the best portrayals of serious real-life issues in game form. 

The stories, interactions, and messages behind this game are truly amazing, from the tiny interactions between civilians to major story points in things such as the DLCs. All of this highlights what civilians may and likely do experience during war. The game's ability to evoke emotions such as hope, despair, and intrigue with each unique interaction is a testament to the quality of its storytelling. The game is able to bring a sense of realism and humanity to what is often a very complex and challenging topic. This game is a prime example of how video games can be used as a powerful storytelling medium and can convey important messages to a wide audience. 

This is the sort of game where you need to simply sit down with a nice beverage, turn off all other forms of media, and just immerse yourself into the scenarios. The gameplay allows you to embrace the struggles and accomplishments of civilians during a time of war. Sometimes you will need to make difficult decisions that will have consequences, and at times, they may even get lucky and be blessed with positive outcomes. Initially, all of this is present when playing the game, and the allure is surely present. 

Unfortunately, this beautiful game has a couple of downsides, despite all this praise. The first downside would be that the scenarios just feel too darn long. I feel like this game could have had the option to speed up certain things but simply chose not to do so due to thematic reasons. I understand this decision; however, when playing through so many scenarios in order to 100% the game, I can only sit and watch people tinker with stuff for so long. The night portions of the game are engaging, but the day portions get fairly boring after a while, as once you finish a few playthroughs, you pretty much know how the game works and how to divert tasks in an efficient manner. 

Another downside is that getting achievements in this game is buggy at times. Sometimes I would need to reload the game entirely or simply get another achievement in order to unlock an achievement that didn't unlock properly. This only happened on around 3-4 occasions, but it is still an annoying thing to experience.

Overall, I believe the gameplay in this game is lacking for the long playtime required to 100% the game. However, the whole concept behind this game is amazing and thought-provoking. I don't think this game may be the best for achievement hunters, but I think that anyone who doesn't care about that should give this game a try. I love what this game promotes, and I do not regret the hours I've put into this.

The creators probably took a risk by bringing such a depressing and sensitive subject into the world of video games. But considering the praise the game received upon release, it's nice to see so many people willing to think deeply and try new things. When it comes to wars, it probably won't change anything in the real world because the people who start them usually don't fight on the front lines or in the trenches. They don't have to rush to bomb shelters or risk losing their worldly possessions. It's also a safe bet they don't play games like this—or more likely, they don't play games at all—or else they'd have better things to do than ordering massacres of ordinary people. Regardless, sometimes it's better than nothing to shock society a little and try to spark a discussion, which this game has done quite successfully. Not to mention the studio's contributions to various charities.

As for the game itself, despite its simple mechanics and dark theme, it manages to be quite engaging. Of course, it's possible to limit yourself to a single playthrough, which might last just a few hours, and then uninstall the game, because in the long run, not much new is added to the content: there's no leveling, grinding, or linear progression to the final boss. What you do get, however, is a variety of playable characters, each with unique skills and personalities that either contribute to survival in the war zone or, conversely, make it impossible. Therefore, it's rather interesting to let the game itself "draw" your next gameplay: you don't know which map you'll get, which characters, or how hard the level will be—how many days you have to survive, how much loot is around, how many violent co-sufferers you'll encounter, or how harsh the winters will be. There's also the "My Story" option, which allows players to set all the parameters themselves. This is especially handy for unlocking any achievements you might have missed during regular gameplay. Finally, the game offers a Season Pass with three stories that focus on more than just survival, in contrast to the main game, where survival is the primary focus. They consist of three specific missions and perspectives, with only "The Last Broadcast" feeling a bit too slow for my taste (literally so, as one of the two main characters could not run due to an injury, and instead limped around).

In this game, there's no way to make the "only right" choices, and there's no such thing as a "win." There are only traumatized, starving, freezing survivors whose moral compasses have never been tested like this before—and, through them, the player's own. In some ways, I would compare this game to [i]Disco Elysium[/i] (which I also recently revisited, and more thoroughly than the first time). Though from a different genre, it also focuses more on the journey than a specific victorious finish and forces the player to think critically, often questioning their choices. Perhaps [i]Disco Elysium[/i] leaves more responsibility to the player, while [i]This War of Mine[/i] doesn't hesitate to rub the player's moral slip-ups under their nose, if they have, for some reason, or even purposefully, morally slipped.

All in all, good stuff.

I have played my fair share of games over the years, but I must say that "This War of Mine" is truly a standout title that left a deep impression on me.The game's premise of surviving a war-torn city as a civilian is a fresh and unique take on the survival genre. The graphics are visually striking and add to the somber and oppressive atmosphere of the game. The soundtrack is equally impressive, providing an emotional backdrop to the daily struggles of the characters.One of the most remarkable aspects of "This War of Mine" is the emphasis on the moral and ethical decisions that players are forced to make. Each decision has consequences, and the game's non-linear structure allows players to shape their own story and experience.The characters in the game are well-developed, and their backstories add depth and complexity to the game's narrative. I found myself genuinely invested in their well-being and survival, which made the game all the more immersive.Overall, "This War of Mine" is a powerful and thought-provoking game that tackles important themes such as survival, morality, and the human condition. It is a game that sticks with you long after you've finished playing, and I highly recommend it to anyone looking for a deep and emotionally resonant gaming experience.

I've played this game a few times on different platforms since it came out, and it's impressive for two reasons:

- It manages to have a message without beating you over the head with it. For instance, there isn't much (any?) discussion of WHY the war you're caught in is going on or who it involves. 

I don't think many modern devs or producers could resist the urge to inject politics into the game, but 11 Bit Studios managed to walk that line. 

- Underneath the message and the art style, there's actually a game there. And it's a pretty polished one with solid mechanics. 

That being said, if I could make a critique of the game, it's that the "game" aspects could have been so much more. Again, there's such a solid, polished foundation here that with some tweaking and added content, this could be the kind of game you play for hundreds of hours.

As it is, you can see pretty much everything there is to see in two playthroughs. And even the "new" stuff in the second run is just a few differences in locations and who populates them, along with the small changes provided by your characters and base layout. 

They did release story-centered DLCs, but I'd rather have gameplay-focused ones instead. The best stories are the small ones that you encounter around the map anyways, whether it's saving someone or seeing how different groups of people live. 

In short, a good game, but one that left a lot of untapped potential on the floor.

This War of Mine is without a doubt a thought-provoking work on the subject of war gaming. This has been reflected in the game awards it won and the positive feedback of countless players. This article based on Jenkins' theory of spatial storytelling (2004), analyzes the narrative enhancement that ambient narratives bring to TWoM in four aspects: Evoked narratives, Enacted narratives, Embedded narratives, and emergent narratives. Through TWoM, we can see the crucial part that environmental storytelling plays in gameplay, but at the same time, we also have to acknowledge that the survival aspect of the game's core gameplay gives each of these storylines its own context. Returning to the article's opening and Jenkins' initial intention for spatial storytelling (2004), TWoM also demonstrates to us how narrative and ludology corporate together in games as interactive media. Together they "induce Emotions not available in passive media. Guilt, pride, remorse, or zeal, to name a few, can be utilized to provide experiences exclusively found in interactive media." (Kwiatkowski, 2014, 699)

I commend 11-Bit Studios for making an attempt to portray the tragedy and uncertainty of war from the perspective of an ordinary civilian. You are not sent down into the trenches, nor tasked with sweeping corridors in search of enemy combatants; you hunt rats for food, collect rainwater, barter for items, dismantle furniture to survive winter. I like games that are down-to-earth and feature a believable storyline with matching gameplay mechanics to accompany it.⁣

Reading the game is now exhibited in schools and museums, I get the impression the message behind it takes precedence over the way it plays in the eyes of the average consumer. I understand This War of Mine helped raise money for both charities and, more recently, Ukraine's war efforts; however, real world politics continue to skew the players' perception of it. My review will point out its subpar designs without dwelling on the devs' political agendas.

Your characters spawn into one of two (non-DLC) shelters, the difference between which is purely cosmetic. This means you will constantly stare at, and to some extent customize, the same screen in every run you play. During the day you clear rubble, build workstations, barricade entrances, play music, listen to the news, rest, heal, feed, talk to other characters depending on their status. Every two in-game days neighbors and traders arrive at your doorstep, making the same propositions in the same order throughout each playthrough.

Other modes of play ("Stories") change the starting group composition, but not any of the above. This makes the experience repetitive. You cannot converse or gossip with neighbors the way you'd expect to do during wartime. You cannot interact with people you meet in raids, nor negotiate with those breaking into your home to steal resources during the night. If you elect to fast forward the day in order to get to this night section, which is the "gamey" part (explained shortly), you skip all events without notice - a significant blow to your reserves.

If you raid place X with its predefined loot, you will be able to build station Y, then Z later to ensure otherwise unobtainable victory. The gameplay thus becomes about memorizing what resource quota you need to meet in order to build which mandatory workstation first. You will not survive without a heater, gas stove, rainwater collector, two workshops, and either a herb garden or a rat trap. This is very formulaic and does not vary between the runs. There is little incentive to engage with other optional workstations, i.e. ones for making alcohol or tobacco.

The characters' expressions feel forced and unnatural, their photorealistic polaroid looks out of place considering the textbook-scribble aesthetic of the game. Their past is summarized in a single paragraph under some menu, making it hard to care about them. Neither characters nor locations are randomly generated, again hurting the replayability of the game. Losing a character can doom your party, since nobody else can carry as much, or fight, cook, heal just as well. Replacing them takes so long you're better off restarting the entire 9-hour run.

Barricading the shelter is a linear process, nothing that requires constant maintenance or upkeep. Clearing rubble is done on Day 1, and the day you finally get a hatchet to destroy the furniture littered around the house. There is no decision-making involved in doing this; none of the preexisting objects can be interacted with, they only exist to get in the way of your building. The build marker is freeform, but objects can only be placed on a hidden grid and at a certain distance from one another, and can't be moved after being placed down.

At night, you can send a person in to raid points of interest while the rest sleep or guard the shelter. For some inexplicable reason you're not allowed to scavenge during the day, which would have saved you trouble obtaining resources, as well as skipped downtime waiting for people to heal, bars to progress etc. It's also beyond me why you cannot send multiple people to scavenge for bigger hauls and better security; after all, the AI raiders are able to do so.

I don't know if the game was ever designed with PC players in mind, but the controls for it are absolutely dreadful. There are no keyboard shortcuts for anything - you cannot open menus, rotate through characters, control them, or choose their equipment using the keyboard. LMB, RMB and MMB all scroll the screen, with LMB making characters sneak, and double-clicking (or RMB / MMB) making them strafe, the latter randomly not working at times.

There are no keys to change between combat / scavenge stances. There is no setting to tell characters to get to places by any means necessary; they will simply stop in place if there's an obstacle in the way. It's not always clear which elements of the level are part of the background and which are tangible means to reach certain areas, let alone which path the AI will ultimately decide to take. You have to drag it by the nose to where you want it to go, otherwise it sprints through hallways meant to be snuck through and into the field of view of enemies.

Damage and health values are never made clear to the player, making stealth takedowns and melee unreliable. Enemies cannot be incapacitated, you either kill them or they kill you. After a takedown inevitably fails, you then cannot push through them to escape. You cannot back out of the situation either, as the entire stage is alerted to your presence. This is what usually kills your character; you're expected to flawlessly sneak through dangerous levels the game pushes you to explore in the lategame with faulty AI and awful character controls.

There are a slew of other bizarre design choices that make me question the devs' thought process making this. The gas stove cannot be upgraded or used to boil water if there's food on it. This food has to be eaten, it cannot be moved. Water is only used for crafting or barter, the characters never need to drink it. Characters cannot queue up to do the same action, and they cannot assist others in building and deconstruction. They often say nonsensical things, for example that they have tools to perform an action they don’t really have.

Not a single item - two-by-four, rock, pipe, rebar, metal rod - can be used as a weapon, beside a knife, or a specially-crafted crowbar and shovel. The knife requires [i]an entire metal workshop[/i] as well as [b]four weapon parts[/b] to craft. Characters return to the shelter depressed if they are forced to kill, but the mechanic quickly loses its merit as you set another character to talk to them or play music for 8 consecutive hours until the moodle disappears; no long-lasting effects that interfere with executive function and warrant a change in playstyle.

None of the characters can figure out how to temporarily barricade the front door for the night. They're apparently all certified electricians, carpenters, engineers; they can all lockpick doors, make the same stations, items, and products regardless of traits. However, they cannot move a single chair to make space for building without disassembling it. The passage of in-game time doesn't make any thematic sense; why does it take 20 minutes to descend a flight of stairs, and winter last only 10 days?

Every facet of this game is poorly thought out and implemented. Solutions to most problems are oddly specific and limited. There is little variety to the things you build, food you eat, resources you collect, and weapons you use. How can this be the purported "emotional experience" when everything is so clunky? A boring, buggy experience, hardly offering the expected gameplay and replayability value for a $20 title - with four DLCs revolving around the same dull stories and mechanics. This would have fared much better as a comic book or show.

These choices can affect your survivors each either negatively or positively.

This War of Mine ist ein einzigartiges und tiefgründiges Videospiel, das das Genre der Kriegssimulationen revolutioniert hat. Anstatt den Spieler als Teil einer kämpfenden Armee oder einer Eliteeinheit zu sehen, setzt This War of Mine auf die Perspektive von Zivilisten in einer vom Krieg zerstörten Stadt. Dieser Fokus auf diejenigen, die am Rand der Gesellschaft stehen und unter den Folgen eines Krieges am meisten leiden, ist eine erfrischende Abwechslung zu den meisten anderen Videospielen, die Krieg zum Thema haben.

Das Spiel beginnt damit, dass man eine Gruppe von Zivilisten zusammenstellen muss, die in einer schwer bewachten, befestigten Unterkunft überleben können. Es gibt keine Anleitung, und man muss selbst herausfinden, wie man Essen, Wasser und andere wichtige Ressourcen beschaffen kann. Aber man muss auch darauf achten, dass man seine eigene Sicherheit und die Sicherheit der Gruppe nicht gefährdet. Während des Spiels muss man Entscheidungen treffen, die das Schicksal der Gruppe beeinflussen können, z.B. wer essen darf, wer schlafen darf oder wer die Unterkunft gegen Plünderer verteidigen muss.

Dieser Aspekt des Spiels macht es zu einem einzigartigen Erlebnis, da es einem eine Vorstellung davon gibt, wie es ist, in einer Kriegssituation zu überleben. Die Entscheidungen, die man trifft, können lebensrettend oder lebensbedrohend sein, und man muss lernen, mit den Konsequenzen umzugehen.

Obwohl This War of Mine ein sehr ernstes und nachdenkliches Spiel ist, hat es auch seine humorvollen Momente. Zum Beispiel kann man versehentlich die ganze Gruppe mit verdorbener Nahrung vergiften oder versuchen, einen schwer bewaffneten Soldaten mit nichts als einem Brecheisen auszurauben. Aber der Humor des Spiels dient nicht dazu, die Ernsthaftigkeit des Themas herunterzuspielen, sondern um dem Spieler eine kurze Pause von der harten Realität zu gönnen.

Das Spiel ist nicht ohne Mängel. Einige der Mechaniken können unhandlich sein und das Spiel kann mitunter etwas repetitiv werden. Doch trotzdem bleibt This War of Mine ein herausragendes Videospiel, das den Spieler emotional berührt und zum Nachdenken anregt. Das Spiel vermittelt auf eine eindringliche Weise, dass Krieg keine Abenteuergeschichte ist, sondern eine Tragödie für diejenigen, die darin verwickelt sind.

This War of Mine ein Spiel, das lange in Erinnerung bleibt. Es ist ein Spiel, das den Spieler herausfordert, aber auch belohnt. Es ist ein Spiel, das den Spieler zum Lachen und zum Weinen bringt, und das ihm hilft, die Auswirkungen von Krieg auf die Zivilbevölkerung besser zu verstehen.

This War of Mine is a game that will stay with you long after you've finished playing. It's a survival game that puts you in the shoes of civilians trying to survive during a war. The game is based on the real-life events of the Siege of Sarajevo, which happened in Bosnia and Herzegovina during the early 1990s.

As a player, I was moved by the emotional journey of the characters. The game does an excellent job of portraying the difficulties and moral dilemmas faced by civilians during war. You have to make tough decisions about who to feed, who to help, and who to leave behind. It's a game that will challenge your values and make you question your own humanity.

What makes This War of Mine even more relevant is the ongoing war between Russia and Ukraine. The game serves as a reminder of the human cost of war and the devastating impact it has on ordinary people. It's a powerful reminder that war is not just about soldiers fighting on the frontlines, but about civilians who are caught in the crossfire and are struggling to survive.

In conclusion, This War of Mine is a powerful and emotional game that is not only entertaining but also thought-provoking. If you're looking for a game that will challenge your beliefs and leave a lasting impression, then this is the game for you.

If you've ever asked yourself what it's like to be caught in a crossfire, "This War of Mine" answers exactly that. In a shelter in disrepair somewhere, survivors are caught in a crossfire and have to manage what little resources they've got left to endure until a ceasefire. That's basically the whole premise of the game, sounds simple, right?

The survivors will have to be fed, to rest and to be satisfied, emotionally that is. Your shelter starts off with a workbench that allows you to craft different beds and furniture and a stove to heat up food. The thing is these things require materials, that are scattered around the nearby areas that are also ravaged by war. Once the unclaimed territory is swept clean off of food, meds and whatever you'll need to survive, you'll have to go to other settlements. You can either barter with those people or kill them and steal all they have. You may survive for a time by doing the latter but it would take a toll on the morale of your survivors, who will find that killing another man to eat is the worst thing that could happen to them. Needless to say that during Winter, you'll actually be pushed by the game to make that difficult morally-evil choice to be able to keep going. Of course, some armed thugs will frequently raid your own shelter, stealing your food and even wounding your survivors, who are going to then require bandages that you'll have to scavenge, steal or barter. 

Once you get the hang of the game, it's probably one of the best survival games out there. Albeit a bit repetitive a few campaigns in, there's still an element of randomness to it all. For instance, Anton may or may not kill himself after you murder an innocent old couple to steal their meds... In one of my walkthrough actually, Roman (another survivor), killed the same old couple by his hands (with fists) and when he was back in the shelter, he was like: "We had to do it, I'm not going to regret something that had to be done!"... Lol that was the first time this has ever happened to me, in literally seven playthroughs. The many random aspects of the game turn this survival game into a roguelike that is not be underestimated. I'll give it a [/b]7.5/10[/b] because of how repetitive successive campaigns tend to get. Other than that, it's a solid survival game that is to be played with an open mind.

I want to like this game, I really do, I'm a fan of Frostpunk by the same dev. The concept of This War of Mine is great, but there are important issues that prevent me from leaving a positive review in the end. Especially in the base game (+The Little Ones DLC). I do like the Stories DLCs quite a lot more, however (more on them at the end of the review).

1. There is no tutorial. And while outside of combat things are generally intuitive enough, you learn combat by seeing the words "(character) is dead" over and over. Maybe they died when you clicked on the backstab icon but the character didn't manage to backstab for one reason or another. Maybe you discovered that ranged weapons can't be used in melee range and that powerful shotgun of yours is now dead weight. Or maybe you put some distance from a guy in melee range in order to shoot him, but it turns out the game leaves you in melee mode when you do that and you're confused why you're getting gunned down and can't use your own gun. Perhaps it was another issue.
Either you accept that outcome or you hit alt+F4 and redo the last 10-15 minutes of gameplay because there are no manual saves and the game only saves at the start of each day (and combat can only happen at night).
Another issue with combat is that it can be hard to tell who's okay to kill and who isn't. Some soldiers are fair game, some aren't. Sometimes you'll be told there are enemies in an area, and you'll sneak up on one and kill him before realizing that's a non-hostile civilian (hard to tell from a distant 2.5D perspective!) - revealing yourself is the only way to tell if an enemy is hostile or not, but that leaves you extremely vulnerable as stealth kills are the only reliable (+ silent) form of kills against armed enemies. At one point you even get shot at by a civilian as soon as they see you, and in that situation defending yourself and killing the shooter will be considered "bad" murder and make your characters sad. So if you don't want the game to screw you over like that, you have to look up the given situation online.
The AI is buggy. I've had enemies walk past dead bodies of their comrades to inspect an open door that's supposed to be closed. "Guess it was nothing."

2. The game is easy and/or much longer than it needs to be. Early game can be challenging depending on your familiarity with the game and the starting scenario. But once you more or less know what you should be doing, you'll have pretty much nothing to do by day 14 - and a "run" typically lasts 30-40 days, with little in terms of options to speed things up. You'll be stuck, for ~4 hours of real time, with the routine of feeding your survivors and revisiting previously looted locations to grab things you didn't have the inventory space for last time.
The Little Ones DLC doesn't do nearly enough to make the game challenging. It adds children who only eat (somewhat less than adults) and play, and get sad easily. Unlike adults they also speak a lot, typically to no one in particular, which is pretty annoying as it is repetitive and their words don't carry any meaning, being mere idle chatter.

3. This is the worst part: the adult survivors don't have any bonds or interactions with each other beyond survival-related events. A child can have a bond with a given adult, but it doesn't do too much. The characters are placed in a world with a random selection of pre-designed levels and situations, and once you've experienced a given situation, it feels old the next time you encounter it, reducing replayability.


This War of Mine would work best as an actual story game instead, one with unique events that tie into each other rather than being stand-alone and disconnected like they are in the base game. Which brings me to the parts I enjoyed much more: the Stories DLCs.

There are 3 of them, and they get progressively longer and (imo) better. Even the first one is worthwhile, while the third one actually gets pretty epic. These stories don't fix the clunkiness of combat, but they do explain themselves better in terms of what you can do and what consequences it could have.

So I would recommend the Stories DLCs, yes, but not the base game.

“Not only that, but…

I am 32 years old.

My ex-wife and I have a daughter together, and we adopted our son together. Both are now 4 years old.

When we were going through our separation, I felt lost and unhappy. I was self-destructive. One day, I was so angry with everything spiraling out of control that I punched a concrete wall in a moment of overwhelming emotion. This resulted in breaking my fifth metacarpal in my right hand—the hand I worked with, played games with, and used to carry my children to bed—the hand I desperately needed to ensure I could continue providing.

Upon learning the severity of the self-inflicted damage, I became almost suicidal. Keep in mind that just a few months before this, I was the happiest man, with no history of depression or anxiety. I had never experienced anger outbursts, nor was I the type to break down and cry, but I was in a tough situation that truly prevented me from seeing the light on the other side.

With nothing better to do, I looked for a game I could play WITH ONE HAND while recovering. Somehow, I stumbled upon this game and read some of the comments. I decided it was worth a try... I must admit I didn't beat the game, nor did I play as much as some of you. In fact, I may have played this game for only a day or two. That being said, after doing so, I had a new joy and hope for life. I managed to leave behind the pain and suffering that had been thrust upon me. I could experience the joy and happiness of other people. I relaxed for 5 ♥♥♥♥ minutes listening to this music, long enough to realize that I would be okay.

After realizing this, I turned off the game and went back to work. My hand hurt a lot, but I was motivated. I stopped feeling so sorry for myself and became the father I needed to be at that moment, not the weak boy I was behaving like.

Today, I am close friends with the mother of my children. We don't fight, argue, or say hurtful things to each other. We are parents and friends.

Now I have 3 children. My third child is, wait, ALSO 4 YEARS OLD. The woman I am with was going through a very similar situation at the time of my separation, and we just unexpectedly stumbled into each other's lives. We have been dating for a year and are very happy together.

Moral of the story: you never know what life has in store for you, and if I had given up when all odds were against me, I wouldn't be where I am today. This silly little game helped me realize that.

Thank you.

Well, the hours played on record speak for themselves.

This game speaks to those, like I - who are scavengers and survivors at heart; which is essentially what this game is, set in a war torn city in Central/Eastern Europe.

What happens when the delicate logistical chains break down or are deliberately destroyed to subdue resistance in an urban setting?
This game pursues this question and logical conclusion very well in that you play characters who do what they must - even KILL - to survive.

Most of my criticisms are positive, in that I enjoy the simple gameplay, the graphics, the crafting, the time management and the game progression.

My negatives are that once a player understand the "beats and rhythm" of the game - it becomes rather simple.

For instance, in one scenario before the mandated end based on days played, I had built a little, internal empire wherein I was producing plenty of meat, vegetables, moonshine, alcohol and meds coupling this with the vast amount of weapons I had uh..."acquired," I truly desired unironically to be given the option to expand beyond my one shelter/abode into the neighborhood and manage the entire block - then be placed in ambiguous circumstance where I might become a gangster.

However, this is beyond the scope of the game, and its simplicity through strength to which I wrote earlier is the sign of an early game from an independent developer.
I agree - they kept it simple, strong, efficient and effective.

Yes, I agree with others who criticize the combat for its wonkiness; however, this is NOT a combat based game - it is a survival, sometimes stealth game.

Thus, after spending many hours playing through the base game, and then returning a year or two later to purchase ALL of the DLC (including the topically contemporary charity), I can say that I am satisfied with the game, despite its repetitive feeling towards the end once a player masters the game.

This game is brutal. You play as survivors living in a war zone. During day time you take care of your shelter, manage emotional and physical needs, and prepare for night time. 
During night time you scavenge, protect your home, sleep through illness or injury, and do your best to survive. The scavenging can be done safely, or not. You can definitely develop a play style, and swap things around depending on the run.

I'd compare it to Darkest Dungeon, to give context for the gritty and sometimes depressing gameplay. But in this title, you bond with your characters, you learn to like them as unique individuals, and overall the journey is quite intimate in that you will care a lot about your playthroughs. The characters have story to them, and react to the passing time and events uniquely.

This game does not add a filter to the grit of war; it aims to be pretty realistic. It's overall balanced, feels rewarding enough, and is one hell of a journey. You will die, and suffer a lot of consequences from your choices, and you will fail a lot, but the runs that go well make it feel.... not so bad. You get challenged in a way that feels possible to overcome. 

I think what appeals to me is the challenge, and learning more about the areas and characters. Every play through is different. The map changes, and you hand pick your crew. The characters you get to choose from have variety, the graphics are interesting, and the game is very replayable.

Just please be warned that if you have mental health issues or if you are a massive empath, this game could be too rough for you. Seriously.

I love the Last Broadcast one especially. It is just immersive. Every scenario is different, and the "stories" you can make during 'survival scenarios' are near endless. The little girl in the main story cries all the time, which is plausible but not something I want to hear every waking in-game minute. A very well made and stylish survival game about the brutality of war and how it effects the civilians who live in war zones. As supplies start to dwindle you need to go further afield into more risky areas, barter and trade with other survivors to ultimately survive. I highly recommend this game to anyone that's a fan of survival games.

War is never fun. In "This War Of Mine" this truth is presented to a player as a simulation. What does it take to stay alive in the fictional city of Pogoren?
This game is a totally different approach to the topic of war. Instead of fighting against enemy soldiers, a player has to fight  physically and on an emotional level to survive in a (post-)war setting. Through collecting and sometimes also stealing raw materials, food and other resources, the player has to craft items, get basic necessities (e.g. firewood and food), craft tradeable goods and make deals with some other survivors to stay alive. The change in seasons brings an additional challenge, since necessities vary from summer to winter.
By playing as different main characters, the player can set up a team with different perks, whose individual strengths help towards the goal. Also the stories and individual challenges of the characters add to different needs to survive. And if not, then death is always the result.
The game is not 3D but also does not need to be. It is perfect as it is. Together with suitable music and sounds in the background, the ambience is very well represented.
The DLCs add different stories, characters and settings. Strongly recommended.

This War of Mine is a game that creates an immense experience from a relatively minimal format. The game is an excellent example of the survival genre, with mechanics focused on making trade-offs and difficult choices to manage the needs (food, rest, warmth, health, mental state, and more) of a small group of civilians surviving amidst a city rapidly being rendered into  ruins by the constant bloodshed of war. Actually managing to survive is not expected, and it will require unending sacrifice and unfailing strategy to make it through the war. The art style is gritty, bleak, and almost apocalyptic, and the music is just as haunting. 

Several interviews from the designers lay out how This War of Mine was actually inspired by the stories of civilians who endured war, especially those who survived the 1992 Siege of Sarajevo. All of the game mechanics are meant to represent their experiences of these real people with as much depth and intensity as a video game can bring, and This War of Mine does just that very well. This War of Mine is a creative experiment in empathy and anthropology which revolutionizes how the interactivity of video games can be used to show the lives of real world people in ways that few other pieces of art can. I would recommend it to anyone that wants to explore what great things video games are capable of.

The game is too focused on making survival difficult to be a game that is fun to be playing for a certain amount of time. It seems to be more of a drama story with a gaming balance set a bit too much towards an exercise in futility resource management.

I didn't think I'd like this game as I tend to avoid games with real-life settings, but This War of Mine turned out to be quite addictive and interesting. 

Your goal is to survive until the ceasefire (or escape the country entirely) with as many people alive as you can.  When you're first starting this can be a daunting task since a lot of the challenge involves trial and error.  In time, you will eventually figure out how to efficiently scavenge by taking only the supplies you need the most for your immediate goals.

However, it's not enough to have plenty of supplies, since making bad moral choices can lead to shelter members leaving with a bunch of your stuff or committing suicide, which means you have to be careful not to make too many evil decisions in a row.

However, managing supplies and member moods gets a lot easier once you figure out how to stealth kill since the most well-stocked scavenging zones tend to have enemies you can kill without moral issues.  Once I figured this out I didn't have much trouble keeping everyone comfortable, happy and safe.  

There is a lot of replay value in this game because there many different characters to play and they all have different abilities.  If you're finding the game too easy, try playing with a group that has children or a group that has weak fighters.  There is even a solo scenario that I haven't tried yet but it looks interesting.  

Overall, this turned out to be a pretty great game.  The message it has is interesting and the mechanics are fun and addictive.  Frostpunk is pretty cool (pretty cool, get it? ha ha) too and it's also made by this developer.

This War of Mine brings a hard hitting view of war from the perspective of those most transformed, but often overlooked group of human beings during armed conflict: civilians. Manage the resources, risks, and psyche of your party in what is invariably a losing battle. Steal from those who can't defend themselves and your party will question their own morals and sink into depression. Give your resources to other characters in need and watch your own get sick and die from starvation. Kill others using whatever morally justified means you like and observe your character's humanity slip.

Ultimately, this is the kind of game that should be played by everyone that has touched an FPS and should be supported by the entire gaming community.

[h1] THIS WAR OF MINE REVIEW [/h1]

[b]This War of Mine is a survival-themed strategy game where we control survivors inside the shelter. The setting is a besieged city (fictional of course) of Pogoren, Graznavia. The main theme is to stay alive and survive until ceasefire (which in this case is the endgame).

During my first couple of hours and days playing through the game, I have no idea what to do and my longest days of survival is just 5-10 days since they all died in different circumstances, such as survivors being starving, depressed, killed during scavenging, left the shelter and even committed suicides. It took a while for me to get used to the mechanics and what your job as a caretaker for this survivors let's say.

THE GENERAL CONTEXT:[/b]

- There are different types of characters with different quirks and abilities that can be an advantage in your daily playthrough. It can be seen via clicking their biography or just in top of their names [i](Ex. Katia = Bargaining Skills, Pavle = Fast Runner, Bruno = Good Cook, etc.).[/i]

- Each characters have general character states, we call them [b]Moods, Sleep, Wounds/Injuries and Hunger[/b] but each characters have unique [b]Sympathy Levels.[/b] Characters that you play varies degree of Sympathy [i](ranging from Lowest to Highest).[/i] Characters also have [b]Addictions[/b] as their way of coping during the war. These mechanics affects the characters' morale, overall gameplay and also affects the endings.

- You can build [b]Workshops[/b] and [b]Household Items[/b] and there are plenty of them and they cost [b]Materials, Parts and Components[/b]. They are necessary since characters have their needs and how you provide it to them also affects their morale and daily activities.

- There are plenty of locations to visit or interact that have [b]Food, Weapons, Medicines, Materials, Parts and Components[/b] but take note of their overviews. These overviews are following; [b]The Amount of Loot, Their Potentials and Their Danger Levels[/b]. It's up to you how to navigate the area and your methods on how to deal with them.

- There are certain events that will affect your gameplay. The canon events include [b]Normal Days, Outbreak of Crimes and Winter Season/ Snow.[/b] There are also certain events such as [b]Shortages, Increased Fighting, Band Of Looters, Area Cut-off, Bombings, etc.[/b] It can be monitored by having a [b]Radio[/b] in your shelter since it provides updates depending on the radio stations and their broadcasts.

- There will be visitors and neighbors that will come to your shelter. They either [b]Ask for Something (Help, Favor, Food, Medicine), Offer a Deal, Share Food, Trade, and etc[/b]. The way you interact with them will also affect the morale and status of your characters. Combine all those mechanics and there you have it, you can come up with ideas on how to manage your shelter to survive the war.

[b]MY THOUGHTS:[/b]

It's quite tricky at first like I said earlier. I didn't knew about those certain mechanics and factors. It's like diving into the pool and you don't know how to swim. I failed a lot of playthroughs and seen my characters die like a human being on war, it does get me when some characters have concerns and are in pain or something troubling them. You can metaphorically say that you're the guardian and you're overseeing people during the war. You get frustrated, angry, quite shocked and disappointed when something happens to your character.

The more you play, the more you gain. Not only seeing your characters progress in longer days but you tend to understand the current situation they're in. You can also understand the character's character. You make better judgement and decisions and cope up with strategies and methods how to deal with the current situation and having plans throughout towards the endgame.

I recommend it to players who like simulation, strategy and survival games. It did give me a new experience in games and it's kinda relatable not just during war scenarios but in daily life problems. I also commend the developers of the games since they made a fundraiser and donated to the Ukrainian Red Cross Funds. Give the game a try, it's worth it. 👍

I assume This War of Mine is inspired by the Yugoslav civil wars in the 1990s, and it delivers a compelling narrative ride befitting that heavy inspiration. They chose the quote: "In modern war, you will die like a dog for no good reason" in the splash screen, which set the tone quite grim from the outset, but fortunately it doesn't descend into some sort of over the top emotionally manipulative nonsense. It delivers a nice mix of highs and lows and as a result keeps you pretty invested for the duration of your playthrough, free of any invitations toward ironic detachment that might be typical for a game that went too far taking itself too seriously.

In terms of game play it's very much of a base building type except what you're building up is not a big settlement or city but just an ordinary safe house of sorts within a residential building, filled with plucky characters in the midst of a devastating conflict. You send people out to forage for supplies hoping they return, occasionally meet external characters at the door to make a tough decision or two and for the most part experience a slice of the sort of indoor suburban claustrophobia that was daily life for millions of people sometimes for years at a time throughout various 20th century conflicts from Spain to WW2 to Yugoslavia. Over time you build up a little stability and become more capable of caring for your basic needs, and the game a primal satisfaction in building a sense of security in place of chaos.

If you are a power gamer, you might have trouble accepting the fact you have to accept trade offs in This War of Mine. I think that was a deliberate design choice. You probably can't take on that military-base single-handed: you'll likely just die. If you think you'll survive by making friends with everyone and playing the nice guy, the game does a good job illustrating how weakness can and will be taken advantage of during a crisis. Importantly, however, the game offers up just enough of the best of humanity that playing the total sociopath can also land you in trouble before too long. In hard times you have to take kindness where you can get it while still avoiding getting taken advantage of and I think it's a great effort that the devs captured the reality of that nuance to the social human experience during a crisis. 

What I'm trying to say here is that it captures the atmosphere of its subject matter in a fairly value free way (well, relatively speaking anyway) insofar as that upstanding ethics, dubious ethics and sociopathy are all rewarded and punished in their own way at different times such that no strong value judgement is hitting you in the face constantly via the gameplay itself. This variability to what sort of ethical strategy is value optimal does an excellent job of capturing the capricious reality of civilian life during the tragedy of armed conflict. The multidimensional nature of life and the social human experience is characterised well and I think that was necessary to make an experience like this engaging and authentic. 

I must admit I went into this title with fairly low expectations, but I was pleasantly surprised by how deftly its subject matter was handled. [h1]Overview[/h1]
This game is one game that show you a tiny portions of how country at wars to civilians feels like. Sadness, depression, hopeless, shame, tense, etc. But if you think this game is base management game like fallout shelter, sheltered, or anything similar, you're completely wrong. This game more like action survival game. You only control these max 4 characters and they can't function autonomously except sick. So more characters, more difficult lol.
[h1]Pros[/h1]
+ The graphics wan't bad, and i liked the B & W stile of it for immersion into every dark things i mentioned in Overview
+ The gameplay is smooth and responsive, no overused animations wasting time and awkward combat
+ The surviving winter is hard but not impossible as long as you unlock hatchet quickly
+ Weapons also quickly not that scarce as long as you can toy with AI that wielding guns in stealth and having saw blades
+ The story missions can be more harder than regular mission lol since you follow events that forced you to stay at base or skipping few hours (Especially 3rd episodes)
[h1]Cons[/h1]
- Food in this game is really punishing, they grow at long time, you can only harvest meat with rat trap on base and there is a limit to it to eventualy run out. And in stove you can mostly produce 2 foods, no options to increase it to 4 for 4 players. Wasting day time and bcs there's no autonomy, it's really hard to maintain 4 player that basically 1-2 of them had a moment doing nothing. Also canned food even you dont need to cook it can't function as meat or into helping ingredients to make food. Kinda nonsensical lol. Plus why require vegetable and meat to make 2 portion? Not just 2 meat or 2 vegetable only?
- The lack of autonomy making the 3rd story mission hardest for me since the museum large AF, and one male characters never really go to well and always stay sick, wasting drugs/medicines.
- The quest in 3rd episode is robbing your firewood that essentials in early missions, but if you interact with them over and over is really annoying.
- Stacking of items in this game is your main enemy, you can only stack 2 woods and it occupy most of your inventory, making you keep repeatedly going over and over just to gather woods wasting nights that you only used barely 2 hours of it
- Explorations only at night and it was short AF. Include the punishing limit of stacking, i tend to get bored visiting same place over and over.
- Melee weapons except knife is your tools, and because of its ultra fast durability wear down. Sometimes its hard to fight enemies in early game. Until you found gun and understand bullet management. So stealth is highly encouraged.
- I know this might be sensitive, but why "balkan country devs" economy always so unfair lol!! Is that dire there to actually profit items in game? This is my personal issues anyway. This game remind me so much to Withcer economy. Merchant tent to rob you anyway.
- The last thing is theres no interim save, if you regret killing NPC, crafting/upgrading workbench or placing counters in room. You must repeat that day and if you do so much thing at that day, you basically f*cked.
- Sadly the mod community somehow died out in 2020 while the game keep updated in 2022, many mods get outdated to helping you around these problems.
[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
The game is a good survival sidescroller adventure game, but after 10 hours playing it, you keep seeing the same places and scenario over and over and it tend to get you sick of it lol. So after completing one or two take a break. Maybe it freshen again later. Recommended? It's a good game but some things too punishing and unrealistic just to make our life harder lol,
I play it casually, it is hard to say that I enjoy it but it is definitely challenging and you will be surprised with the chapter conclusions. In my personal opinion it is worth the money.
