As you know, this is a game about being a civillian during war. You have to gather resources, defend your base, build new crafting stations and maybe even kill to survive. The soundtrack and atmosphere are absolutely stunning, the graphics, while imperfect, have a nice art style and the DLCs are all worth the price. 
    My main issue is the difficulty. While the game is hard during your first playthrough, the difficulty is mostly artificial and with enough experience you can easily survive anything, especially with the right survivors, after which the gameplay becomes tedious, since you can stay at your home, flood the local market with expensive stuff and buy everything you need from traders, who are almost everywhere. This results in you having to do challenge runs to make the game replayable.
    Another issue is that your survivors don't feel human after some time. Sure, they have backtsories, might get depressed and kill themselves if they experience too much, but during night, they will do anything you order them. Rob the local hospital? Yeah, sure. Kill a soldier? Ok, done. Kill an innocent civillian? Nvm, he's already dead. They don't react at all during night and after killing soldiers or thugs their only concern during day is that it was dangerous. Some are more empathetic than others, but is also reduced to a system that can be optimized. The only reason you differentiate them at all are their abilities, some of which are unreasonably strong and some severely underpowered. This removes a lot of immersion, further broken by some illogical things, like for example taking anything, even a single grain of coffee from the old couple's house will [spoiler]have them dead the next time you visit the location[/spoiler].
    Overall, a very solid and emotional game, but only for the first playthrough. After that it doesn't have much to offer, aside from the DLCs.

TWOM is hard for me to play, because it makes me feel the ugly heartache, loneliness and inescapable pain of war. In Real Life (RL) I am sitting in a warm, dry, lighted, & relatively safe home, cabinets full of food, four legged friend sleeping nearby, with family and friends around. May our hearts and minds connect back up, and end this madness in a way that is good for all people.

This War Of Mine is an emotional, intense, and challengeing experience as you observe and control the actions of various surviving civilians in the center of a war torn city.
The game itself is based on a pretty simple concept(survive and thrive) split into two rotating phases - day and night. During the day you make food, build new things, have your survivors interact with each other, and deal with ailments or wounds. Nighttime is where you decide wether you want to send out one of your survivors to scavenge, guard the shelter, or sleep. Typically scavenging is the most fruitful option, as it's your main source of many of the important resources needed to create your nescessities. It's also the most gameplay-rich part of the game as you have both a time-limit and an inventory limit to consider. You will sometimes, however, have to adapt to the situation you're in and either stay put, or take a risk and scavenge in a potentially dangerous location.
For me this is the greatest strength of the game. It's quite difficult, and it's VERY punishing if you make a mistake, while also being greatly rewarding if you do something right.
The graphic is a perfect fit to the game's spirit; the environments are diverse and not repetitive and while the music themes can be a bit repetitive they do create a very good atmosphere.
In all, if you like survival games for the sense of vulnerability and intensity they provide, if you appreciate rogue-like games, you will definitively love This War Of Mine.

First, the good.  If you're looking for a game with a gritty atmosphere that has crafting and survival elements, this is for you.  It's got a good story, good lore, real choices with real consequences, real survival and crafting strategy.  All good things.  

Now, why did I give it a thumbs down?  

Because I have a scoped rifle.  I love scoped rifles in other games, they're awesome.  As soon as I found out one was actually available in this game I spent hours trying to successfully get it.  In the hands of the NPCs, they play about as you'd expect - scoped rifle in a fire field pretty much means you're dead unless you've got really great cover options, speed, and a bit of luck.  

But when the PC has the scoped rifle, well then the rules change and you're some dumb kid fighting a Terminator... using a semi-automatic weapon, with no way to use the scope that makes the rifle logically deadly in other people's hands.  Take cover?  Doesn't really matter, the enemy has full auto fire or shotguns.  Surprise attack for bonus damage (say, like a SNIPER would)?  Nope.  You get to make one shot, then you die.

So yeah.  This game gets a thumbs down from me because the weapon that is the hardest to get is a deathtrap for you... but it's the hammer of god in the hands of the enemies.

The game has severe issues with both it's resource gathering, random RNG that will take them from you and making it drastically more difficult to gain resources within the second week (or when you are done looting the two safe areas). It encourages risk taking but then subsequently punishes any player who does with near uncurable wounds. From a purely mechanical perspective being a (based) psychopath is the optimal playstyle and largely trivializes the game. The devs try to counterbalance this by 1) having the character you control constantly (they never shut up) whine about what you did and 2) Giving you a bad ending if you're a (based) psycho. I found these measures to be ineffective since I never felt immersed in the world. You don't learn character's backstories organically (i.e. they don't talk like normal ppl you just click on a card and read a summary) nor do they have any endearing quirks. You act as a tardwrangler controlling a bunch of annoying tomodachi pets constantly whining about how war is bad and stuff man. Nobody is likeable so I always revert to being a (based) psycho. A smart game would maybe have had its characters become inured to this and have their dialogue change since they're becoming a sith lord. This game does no such thing. If you want anti-war themes Metal (autism) Gear has more profundity and still manages to be fun. If you want a survival management go play anyone of the million such games. This War of Mine falls flat in terms of being both anti-war and a fun game.

War of Mine has become a classic of its kind, a game one should be aware of when talking about a resource management de facto point-and-click survival game. Also a factor leading to my negative review was having the expectation that this game truly is something special. People tend to like this game because of its atmosphere, the dilemmas it puts you in, questioning your moral compass, and this is enough for many people. However, I feel like in terms of atmosphere, or rather immersion (since they're [b]really[/b] trying to enforce this serious, yet realistic, dark vibe), they have kinda failed when one takes time to look through the disguise and at the gameplay at hand. Following things are more or less present in all games of this kind in a way or another, so you feel at home if you like them:

> You have to filter rain water with stuff you found in a pile of debris because rain is apparently dirty, giving you rectal-turbo-tuberculosis (I wish, there'd at least be an option to use it with a downside) - even going so far that you have to waste resources on filtering it when watering plants... yes, plants...
> You live in a broken house with redundant wooden furniture but still have to spend a night gathering firewood in different buildings because you don't have -...a hatchet? Remember, people die because of this. It's not the game setting's circumstances that defeated you, it's the game. Doesn't matter if there's a big wooden fence around your house.
> Bandits steal your stuff but you don't get their loot when defeating them - on maps, they also have infinite ammo until you loot them but else would've surprised me.
> Lockpicks break after one use, minor issue because it's a classic.
> Game doesn't give you instructions, two weeks had passed before I figured out that sprinting was a thing...
> Only one person can scavenge at night, rest is just getting stabbed and digesting or something, I don't know.
> Doesn't matter how long you're scavenging, always the same malus on Tired stat.
Note that much of this is only an issue because they're trying to set the atmopheric and immersive bar high. You just keep getting reminded that's it's a stat juggling game with the wrong meat on the bone. It's thus not much different than other games of its kind.

Now, I do not like the average resource management survival game because I like having some "reason to care" around me that's not simply balancing stat meters because it's what the game tells me to do. Resource usage just doesn't seem to rhyme with reason. Without me being able to dive into the world that is This War of Mine, the atmosphere as the advertised selling point of this game, the reason to play, is diminishing.

It is not unlikely that you will like or even love the game. Also not unlikely that you drop it after playing it once or twice.
I'm not judging you if you still like the game, for me it's just "one of these". It is not worse than other games of its kind, it's just that I didn't get what the trailer, the game told me I'd experience.

This game does a very good job of setting the mood and bringing you into the war-torn city aesthetic. Things are bleak, miserable, and everyday is a struggle. Getting ahead means stealing or hurting someone else, but when it comes down to it, what other options do you have? You are fighting for your survival but also struggling with the morality of what you're forced to do. You manage a group of characters and they all have their own strength, vices, and personalities. 

As far as gameplay, it's not very engaging and generally a slog. The base management mechanic is needlessly open-ended and could easily be simplified with a cleaner interface (although this would maybe remove some of the impact of the bleakness of the game). The exploration is interesting but very janky/unclear in terms of visibility and interaction, which makes this already unforgiving game even more unforgiving. A full play-through takes way too long - my first and only complete run probably took 3-4 hours and I spent the last 10 or so days sleeping through the day and guarding at night since I had amassed plenty of supplies and just needed to wait until the war ended, and there was no benefit to leaving.

I'd recommend playing this game for 1-2 hours just to experience the aesthetic and feel the bleakness of the world that's been built, but in terms of gameplay, it's hardly notable and not worth the time. I've decided to change my review from negative to positive since I think it's a unique and worthwhile experience; I was just a bit disappointed at the weak gameplay.

This War of Mine is one of those unforgettable indie games that people who are into the survival genre, doesn’t matter whether it is zombies or fallout, simply MUST HAVE in their collection. In fact, I daresay anyone who is into war games needs to have played this to experience the other side – no, not the opposing army’s, but the civilian side. Because so few war games ever bother to address *their* war as well – one for food, shelter and daily survival.

In This War of Mine, you take on the role of a handful of civilians who have banded together as residents of a bombed out multi-story apartment building to survive the war that has befallen their city of Pogoren, capital of the fictional republic of Graznavia, where vyseni rebels have taken control and seek to re-establish the former nation of Vysena, but find themselves surrounded by the Grazi army with all escape and supply route out of the city cut off by the military. As fighting and shelling is relentless during the day, only the night offers a chance for the besieged to leave their shelters and scavenge for supplies. Only one person at a time leaves the building each night to loot an increasing number of locations in the city that pop up on the map as the days pass. The other survivors guard the house until dawn, or sleep.

This game is therefore divided into a day mode and a night mode. During the day (6 AM to 8 PM equals about 7 in-game minutes), there are various things you can do in your building. Most important of which are to create specific work stations devoted to one particular thing, e.g. home improvement or tool manufacture. These allow you to access their build menus and then create further things in your building. From building additional furniture like stools to sit on, beds to sleep in, stoves to cook raw food into meals, radios to listen to the latest developments (weather, fighting, the rise and fall of prices for valuable commodities in the black market) and heaters to keep warm during winter, to reinforcing the shelter by boarding up the windows to lessen your chance of getting wounded by burglars and robbed of valuable resources.

As the game progresses, you will need to upgrade your stations so that you can build more complex work stations, like a place to collect rainwater, or brew moonshine, or catch mice, or grow herbs and vegetables, or another place to create medicine or roll those herbs into cigarettes that you can then trade in the black market for other supplies you need.

Meanwhile, the survivor you send out to loot each night has a fixed number of inventory slots he can fill upto a certain amount of one specific type of looted item as he combs the location for valuables. Every tool he takes with him occupies one such slot, but helps him out on that map. E.g. since your looter is on a timer (9 PM to 5 AM), a shovel will help him quickly dig through piles of rubble, a crowbar to (noisily) force doors and locks open, single-use lockpicks to do this quietly, or, unlike knives, the axe as a multi-purpose tool to chop down furniture into wood he can collect later – or people. 

Be warned through, that this game has a built in moral system – robbing or killing civilians will bring down the morale of all your survivors, down to the point of depression and even suicide. And getting hurt in combat requires expensive bandages to allow for the wounds to heal. So it is best to avoid it. The game therefore also has a nice stealth mechanism incorporated into it – you can hide in dark alleys to let potential enemies pass you. And should you get caught, the AI will generally warn you to leave, and if you comply, you can avoid confrontation. The AI is also smart enough to remember previous encounters (at least on the same night) so if you get caught a second time, they won’t be so forgiving. Running out of resources though will mean desperation can set in – and drive you to increasingly dire encounters with those who guard their valuables dearly.


DLC

This game has two separate DLCs which consist of The Little Ones and the Season Pass that contains three storydriven episodes (which you can  also buy individually). The DLCs also adds new locations to the game, although these locations have been made available for free even for people who don’t have the DLCs, in the form of the Final Cut update. 

The Little Ones adds additional characters in the form of children: survivors with initially very limited tasking abilities (such as shoveling snow, fetching a bottle of moonshine that has finished brewing or herbs that have finished growing) but with an aptitude for learning most household tasks grownups do, if the adults are willing to take the extra time to teach them. However, children have to play to be happy, and they will get sad quickly if they don’t. Each shelter initially starts with just one “game” that only the child can interact with, and doing so will make it play that game for 1 hour. You have the child construct additional games in the shelter, and playing 3 different games a day will lift the child’s sadness. When winter sets in, the buildable snowman outside that is pretty useless for adults serves as an additional game station for children once it is completed. 

Father’s Promise is the first of the three story driven DLCs and introduces you to the children mechanic, although not really, as it is heavily scripted and mostly involves the dad in a city-wide goose chase as he hunts for clues leading to the abduction of his child.

The Last Broadcast is a far more interesting DLC because for the first time in the game it introduces a disabled character, who is on crutches and can only hobble around and not even go downstairs. However, he has a caring wife who goes out each night to scavenge and brings back supplies and news for him to broadcast as a radio host. This story presents you with choices you have to make throughout the episode that have consequences: do you use your power as a radio broadcaster to “join” in the war and help rebels against the army? Or point civilians toward looting army supplies? Or fail to warn rebels of an impending army attack? 

Fading Embers is perhaps the most ambitious and expansive of all three story driven episodes as it is heavily focused on narration and even involves the survivors changing shelters to the largest shelter ever – an entire museum full of priceless historic artifacts that need to be secured while the war is raging on outside. But as winter sets in and wood starts running out, which priceless piece of history will you incinerate to survive for one more night? And to whom will you turn to, in order to save the rest of the collection from destruction?

Overall, this game is a gripping experience with a steep learning curve, and as you familiarize yourself with the city of Pogoren, and learn which things to build first, which locations to loot first, and which ones to avoid, over time you will transform from a starving, broken soul to a successful survivor even neighbors can depend on. Highly recommended!

A game loosely based on the conflict in Donbass between the Ukrainian government and the Peoples Republics of Donetsk and Lugansk.

It covers the hardships and struggles of civilians living in war zones without presenting an excessive amount of bias on the "government" and "rebel" forces that are featured in the game. An argument could be made that the incidents of torture that occur by the soldiers but not the rebels could be anti-east bias and the roles would most likely be reversed if the game had taken place in a NATO aligned country.

In terms of actual game play they had a good balance of resource management, stealth, character development, with the opportunity for action and combat if that's the route you choose to go. The game is pretty replayable and the DLC stories offer some nice finite structure while keeping all the things that made the game good.

Great new style of game (for me) in my favorite genre, post-apoc. It was really interesting how it felt a lot like an interactive story/comic than a traditional first/third person style. Might've even made it more compelling for me.

We are talking about good people in the middle of war. They wont steal because they know the consequences of getting their own things stolen. They wont murder because they are in a bad situation exactly because of other people do it. And you cant be on a shelter with a murderer, or with a thieve. 
You cant lie, because thats not an option when you are seeking to survive and depend on the people that lives with you.

I think the game portaits perfectly the whole "being a civilian surviving in a city at war" picture. Random good people shoved together in a ruined house, because the option is a bullet in the head. All trying to keep alive while staying sane and healthy. You had a normal life 2 months ago, but now you dont have a choice.

When you are at war, you dont have much to get distracted. You dont have much to keep you from OVERTHINKING. All you think about is the war. And the thougth of stealing from someone as miserable as you can break your soul if you dont find a way to forget about it.

This game tries to show the other side of the those war games where you are the hero that brings death to your enemies without thinking twice, sometimes without even looking at your victim's face. This is a game about normal people, about emotions, about struggling to avoid death while surrounded by it. This is a game about suffering. 

To be in the situation where "You're starving. The kid is sick, and you have no meds", and you are facing the impossible choice, is exactly why you want to play this game. Do you become the vilain and steal, or even murder your neighbor? Someone who could have been your friend a couple of weeks ago? If you cant think of another option, then you will do it "because you have to"? 
The alternative is your own suffering and misery, so you have to decide. What do you choose? Will you become the monster who survives or the monster who let the kid die?

This is war.

Sorry, but after spending a good amount of time, I cannot recommend this game. At first, I was actually finding this game to be pretty good, but then the massive flaws starts showing up and really dragged this game down way too much.
1) The game is buggy. I found a good number of items disappearing from scavanging spots I dropped my stuff off when I find something I need more of during revisits, especially when I come back in the very next day and there are no NPCs in said area.  
2) Melee combat does not work whatsoever. Even if you have a good melee weapon and need to take out an enemy, almost all the time you try to engage in melee combat, the enemy will almost always be the one to successfully attack your character. Especially in parts where there is no hiding spots and/or if you ran out of ammo and need to resort to melee combat. 
3) The cover is pretty awkward at times. If you step out of cover, you have to move around before you can get back into the same cover. Getting back into the same spot from where you exit doesn't work. Tried it a couple of times during a lot of my failed attempts (mostly due how awful the melee combat is), and never worked. It gets pretty bad when you sneak attack and kill an enemy, and sometimes that triggers the others to come up after you, and trying to get back into cover like this will take a bit more time, when time is sometimes what you don't have. 
4) The game is way too slow. There is no speed up option to make the day go any faster, meaning you have to wait forever for the clock to run out as you wait for whoever that is working on something to get their job finished. It gets even worse if you have to restart the same day with a lot of things you have to redo again, mainly cause of failed attempts, meaning you have to wait for the game to drag on even longer just so you can wait for the night and whatnot.

A good game that will make you feel sad. It's nice to have games like this that talk about the horrors of war from the perspective of the civilians that have to live through it. The game is held back by some of it's more frustrating aspects.

The downsides:

1. It really needs a save function. When runs in this game take as long as they do, its beyond frustrating to get cheesed into a bad situation because of a miss-click or something. Possibly a bookmark function every five days? Ten days?

2. The UI for combat is kinda clunky. If you're going to have a clunky combat interface then you probably shouldn't also have perma-death. Add to this the deadliness of bandits and the unforgiving spirals of injury/illness/robbery/death that are easy to start and you can see why the game should probably either be shorter or have a save function. 

3. Runs get kind of boring after a while. While nowhere near as boring as Frost Punk, a game that is supposed to be about the horrors of war shouldn't be this dull towards the end game. There should be some middle ground between death spiral and watching the paint dry.

4. Some of the random events come across as extremely arbitrary. Being unable to give children canned food is NOT the same thing as telling them "no, I will not give you canned food," but the mechanics of the game make it such and thus give your team morale penalties. Additionally, if children are going to ask for canned food you should probably be able to substitute with cooked meals. It's beyond frustrating to have cooked meals sitting on the stove ready to go only to have the game decide that you're inability to specifically give canned food results in children dying, which results in your team members getting depressed and hanging themselves, effectively ending a run ten days into it and wasting hours of time. 

I wanted to like this game more than I do, and I want it to be better than it is. But it isn't. So sadly a game that tries to be about the horrors of war just sort of ends up being about the horrors of bad game design.

This one is a very soft yes as I am really on the fence about it. The artwork and styling is gorgeous. The characters are interesting. The game mechanics are somewhat difficult to learn. The premise is original. And it actually becomes pretty fun once you know what you're doing. Save for a small number of very annoying problems, I'd absolutely recommend this game.

Let's start with the time efficiency problem. Suppose you have your characters working on something in the shelter. You want to complete that task and then start the next one? Sit there and wait and watch them work as there is no fast-forward option. You have only the "End Day" button. The game would be unplayable without this. But even still, it's a frustrating waste of time to sit around waiting. This complaint matters a lot more once you've learned the game and want to play through all the scenarios quickly, especially if you don't have much time to game. There is simply too much time wasted waiting around staring at your monitor.

Speaking of the "End Day" button, it's conveniently located next to the "our stuff" button. Mis-click? Too bad, it doesn't ask for confirmation. Close the game, re-load, and re-do the whole day.

Also annoying is that there is no built-in game save feature. I know they didn't want the player to defeat the RNG and simply re-roll when something happens that they don't like. I appreciate that as I like playing games the way they were meant to be played - bad things happen and you have to deal with them. But, back to the efficiency point. I'd love the feature to simply save the game at any point and return to it at that point instead of being forced to play through the whole in-game day and night. Also, it could allow you to have a few different games in parallel.

Final critical points. 1) Can't change keybinds and M1 and M2 do the same action. Why on earth wouldn't you split these up??? Can't say how many times I've tried panning the camera with M2 only to accidentally move a character to the wrong place. 2) Character pathing. "I don't know how to get there." What? But you know how to run to the exit across the whole map! Also, you were just there! Also, when you do know how to get there, why are you running into the locked door instead of going around?

These complaints are from the perspective of someone who doesn't have that much time to play games. So when I do, I don't want to spend a lot of time waiting around. I actually really liked this game but these few problems almost made me not recommend it.

I have only played this game 11 hours or so, but I have to say that it is one of the most unusual gaming experiences I've ever had. It is extremely bleak, difficult, dark, and engaging.  The reason I have not played it more is that I lose a lot. I'm crap at this game, and I don't want to go read a guide about it, because I'm still intrigued about learning the game. 

So why haven't I played more often? When you lose, you have not just died yourself like in most games, but your whole group has died. One. By. One. It is just brutal to lose this game. The developers have truly created not only an atmosphere (which is noteworthy, detailed and lit with artistic sensibility), but you get character development and story beats that are absorbing and emotionally affecting. It is highly stylized realism. I cannot say enough about these elements of the game. Simply brilliant.

The mechanics and game play are excellent. everything works, and there are no boring chores. Crafting makes sense, and it is not simple. The levels of realism in the game do not make it boring or plodding.  Things happen at a perfect pace.  The various missions and the map are intriguing and varied, so there is never a sense that they have re-purposed a previous level or model. Excellent craftsmanship, all around.

I had no technical problems in the game. Everything worked as expected, and the visuals are great, but do not seem to burden a system set up for gaming (mine is modest, not top of the line). [h1]Gameplay[/h1]
[b]6/10[/b]

This War of Mine presented a survival simulation of citizens who were stuck in the middle of a civil war in a city called Pagoren. Players take control of one or more characters, each with their own attributes. The game difficulty depends on the composition of your party, you can choose a default composition from the game or create your custom group. The game can be quite challenging at first but once you're introduced to all the elements, it becomes a boring repetition. Is it worth the money though? Yes, you can clear your first playthrough in under 4 hours and I played for 56 hours before uninstalling the game.

[h1]Story[/h1]
[b]5/10[/b]

You get to piece information together figuring out what is happening in this world, it's not a mindblowing mystery, just common tragedy humankind repeated over centuries. The characters have their own background/lore/personality which gives life to the decision you make, some get sad when you kill, some just shrug it off.

[h1]Social[/h1]
[b]-/10[/b]

No co-op or any multiplayer feature.

[h1]Graphics[/h1]
[b]6/10[/b]

The graphic styles and designs are spot on with the setting of the game, it adds a layer to the aesthetic and immerses the world, even more, painting the torn city of the bitterness that is war. The use of pencil sketch style and the almost monochrome color made everything so much better. It's a small but smart addition.

[h1]Audio[/h1]
[b]6/10[/b]

The game's music and sound effects were pleasant but nothing to write home about. Throughout my gameplay, I did not experience any disconnection or sounds that don't belong to an object or action.

This War of Mine is a great game that tells the story of survivors, mere civilians, caught in somebody else's war and just trying to survive. This is a simple survival/crafting game that keeps on giving even after you have mastered it.

Much has already been said by others about the mechanics of the game so, while I will touch a little bit on that topic, I will mostly focus on the storytelling.

To start with: the stories in the game leave a bit to be desired. All the characters are stock, with stock storylines. However, when I first opened the game up, I was still amazed at THIS story, the story that I was playing through!

When people say that decisions matter in a game, they usually are referring to branching storylines, but in TWoM, there is only one storyline - the one you are playing. (In fact, until the DLC, there wasn't even any alternate win-conditions! You just had to survive until the end of each group's story.)

So, when I say "choices matter" in this game, I mean your day-to-day, moment-to-moment choices have an impact on the experiences of your survivors. Do you help your neighbors or let them die for lack of resources? Do you help the hoodlums looting abandoned buildings or let them go their way? How will your characters feel about those choices? Will they be content with their humanitarian efforts, or will they become depressed because they are callously adding to the devastation around them? (Each choice can sometimes lead you down a path, also; if you make a shady choice, you may be asked to make even shadier choices, until eventually you realize that you are no longer the Good Guy.)

Whenever you do/not do a humane deed, you will suffer a morale bonus/penalty, so if you are looking for a game without consequences, this one isn't it. This one preaches at you that you must be a good person.

The mechanics are stupid-easy; use your left mouse to go places and do things, use your right mouse button to go and do faster. Collect, build, produce, trade. Survive. Win. At first, until I understood how the game worked, survival was somewhat challenging; now? Not so much.

On the other hand, the entire game is constantly busy telling you, "War is bad, mmkay?" And, about the time that I could play the game with my eyes closed, I realized something else: I knew exactly which people to help (because they would return the favor,) and which to leave behind (because they either wouldn't help me back, or they wouldn't penalize me for not helping.) I knew which tools to take to which locations to maximize my looting time. I knew how to optimize my trades. I knew how to create a comfortable economy, and how to make the right weapons, and which weapons to sell and which to use. I knew when to be peaceful for maximum benefit and when it was okay to kill. I also knew how to get my spirits up after I had done so. I knew how to ignore This War of Mine.

The final treat in this game is the realization that I have become inured to This War of Mine, and while I still return to the game over and over, I have become desensitized to the human suffering that exists all around me in the game. I took this gaming experience and tried to look at the Real World through its lens, and now I am faced with a choice in the Real World: Do I become desensitized and cynical, or do I keep trying to help the people around me with the little bit that I have been blessed with?

Even though I (arguably) have mastered this game, it is still preaching to me and teaching me things I need to think about.

Even though I felt like I already knew everything in the game from watching streamers play it back around 2015 for hours on end, it still felt very satisfying to buy and play it myself now years later. It was nostalgic and that gave it value yes, but what's really meaningful in this game is not the content to explore but the feeling and emotions there are to it. 

You don't control a bunch of fighters, but just normal people trying to survive while war rages on. You cook, sleep, keep your shelter up, and get ready for the night by day. If you have time you might want to try playing the guitar or build a snowman to keep the spirits up. By night you choose one character to go out and scavenge with and hope that you prepared the others so that they are able to defend your home from bandits. 

If it gets too cold you'll get sick and die, if you get hit you'll bleed and die, if you don't have food you'll starve and die, if you don't sleep enough you'll get weak and die, and if one character does poorly others will get stressed and unhappy. 

The game is not perfect and it doesn't have super deep mechanics, but everything there is works very well together. There is a danger to a game like this to have too much stuff to do, making it confusing for a starter. But I don't feel like This War of Mine has that problem. There could be more to it though, but it's definitely not too little either. Even though I knew most of the maps and characters by heart I still spent +25 hours playing just the core game and having fun right after buying it.

There is Stories (DLC) that I didn't even touch yet (even though I bought it too), which I feel can only make the game better with the extra play value it offers. Even if the stories would turn out to be a weak addition, the core game is good enough alone to be well worth buying This War of Mine.

I'm really on the fence about this, and if this was a question of stars rather than the binary yes/no I would probably still give it six or seven. But I just cannot recommend it. 

It is actually a solid game. You search for resources in a great variety of detailed and unique settings, and use those to build up your home in a way that'll help you survive the war. There's a lot of freedom in how you do this, and a lot of flexibility. That's great.

The art style is really fitting, and very tasteful. It's grim without being dark, it's busy without being cluttered, and it's simple without being dull. Honestly, presentation is 10/10. 

But where it falls down, for me, is when the game starts to punish you for playing in a way that is seen as immoral. Here's how it works:
You have a shelter, three adults and a kid. You're starving. The kid is sick, and you have no meds. All the safe places have been picked clean, and you're faced with a choice: You can go and risk scavenging in an extremely dangerous area where there's a good chance you'll die way before you find food or meds. You can go and try to rob a few thugs and probably get your ♥♥♥♥ wrecked in the process, or you can sneak into a rich house and steal some of their ♥♥♥♥. Guess which choice the game punishes?

Yup, stealing. A minority of characters are OK with it, but the majority will get sad and eventually depressed if you steal or murder, which makes them sleep badly, refuse to work, or just leave one night. This is annoying for a few reasons:

-NPC's are always more important than the more moral PCs. Doesn't matter how tough things are, stealing is never OK, and boy does the game shove this down your throat with little speech boxes appearing every two minutes where the guy is ruminating on how terrible your choice was. 'Did we really need to steal from those poor people?' YES, the kid is seriously ill and we have no food. YES we needed to steal. Next time we'll just eat your sanctimonious ass. 

-The aforementioned sadness mechanic. There are a whole list of things that can increase PC sadness, but very little that can decrease it. Being well fed and warm isnt enough to make your guys 'content', they also need to be helping other people every couple of days. Meanwhile, steal one can of meat and WHAT HAVE WE BECOME??

-Finally, why is my guy always going back to the shelter in the morning and just telling everyone that he brained some crazy old guy with a crowbar to steal his meds? He went out alone, he came back alone with a bag of goodies. At least give me the option to lie to the other folk and maybe avoid the sadness.

So that's why I can't recommend this game; they want you to play a game set in a besieged, war torn city in the depths of winter, with a collection of people who have had their families and homes torn apart, but they want you to retain the moral standards of a wealthy, church going suburban American family. Thou shalt not kill, thou shalt not steal, thou shalt not play this game any way that would upset the developers. 

Oh and if someone dies because you didn't steal those meds, guess what? Everyone gets depressed anyway. ♥♥♥♥♥♥...
I can understand not having a tutorial in certain games, but This War of Mine I could not even find any resource in the game to tell me what the controls are, which feels more lazy than atmospheric

If we can classify a game as “important”, this is definitely one of them.

A great survival perspective from a civilian’s POV, in a besieged city during a civil war, where your choices will impact their lives drastically. Will you hold on to your humanitarian values and help those in need or pursue survival at all costs, facing its’ horrors and moral implications? There aren’t right answers. Wrong things don’t happen to good or bad people, they happen to people who did the wrong thing at the wrong time. Even if you think you’re getting the hang of things and actually have supplies and food, the game reminds you that war and its cruelty will get you no matter how much you plan or organize. It can and will break your soul to the point where, even if survival is possible, it’s not wanted anymore.

I found myself emotionally exhausted after finishing each game, which I see as an incredible achievement from the developers. Your play through will stay with you even after you’ve turned off the game hours ago, as survival is of upmost importance and seeing your characters not make it is heartbreaking. The way their faces look so real and their eyes close when they pass away is gut wrenching, as we see them as real people who we failed.

The Little Ones DLC adds to the challenge as children are now involved. They won’t naturally know how to do most things and you can teach them while also spending time playing with them, since their happiness and spirit also affect the rest of the team. It’s a constant battle to maintain the little innocence they have left while living in an active war zone, their memories and thoughts being of better times in the past.

The stunning artwork and soundtrack lift this game to another level, as despair isn’t only conveyed by your actions but also through the existing atmosphere. A low saturated world where happiness feels like a foreign thought, listening to depressing and revenge anthems whilst trying to live just another day.

Immense replayability with different scenarios, characters and traits. Simple game mechanics for any type of player. High recommendation for its loud meaningful message.

I have been deployed in hostile fire zones, peacekeeper missions, and relief work from Africa to former Yugoslavia and no matter what,  in all of those situations, there are occasional moments laughter and fun. Without a doubt, 'This War of Mine' has had the most impact on me out of any other game I own on Steam. As someone who lives in a generally peaceful country without the worry of an invasion or other armed conflict, many of us sometimes take our idyllic lives for granted, when many people throughout the world live in a conflict zone daily, trying to live a normal life, raising a family, or simply attempting to live to see the next day.

'This War of Mine' screws with your emotions and feelings like no other. You must make incredibly complicated and influential moral decisions that can make or break your band of survivors. Do you have pity on the defenseless elderly couple and accept their pleas to not take their medications or do you accept their sacrifice for the child that you have waiting back at home with a fever? Do you let some of your band starve for multiple days while those who are in better shape go out at night to find vital supplies and provisions? Do you help the two children who come to your door looking for food to help their mother or do you keep that food for your own friends?

This game can either be incredibly rewarding or incredibly depressing. It is your decision to decide which, through gameplay and survival. While the game may seem simple in the beginning, don't let that deceive you. It will most likely take multiple playthroughs until you successfully survive the conflict.

The combat system is a bit clunky, the inventory feels a bit complex, and occasionally you find a bug, but that isn't the point. The point is to educate the player on the horrors and challenges of war, and that is exactly what this game does. I cannot recommend any product on Steam more than I do 'This War of Mine.'

Fabulous stuff -- this game will be timeless, classic and evergreen.

This War of Mine is definitely mentally prepping me for the upcoming apocalypse of 2021. Learning to eat once every 2-3 days, this game has enabled me to be strict to my diet and ive lost like 30 pounds just working out and appreciating life. W fallout games i had a weird habbit of picking up bobby pins on the street from collecting them so much, and with this war of mine ive learned to become a prepper. the way the world is going w lockdowns and such, i truly feel like this game will help people mentally get ready for the inevitable societal collapse.

This is a game that shows you the truth about all those war-gaming games. Where you shoot all your problems away.

Reality is, sadly, a lot different. Survival demands hardship, sacrifices and harsh choices. Where not everyone you know and love will survive, and you are the one making the call.

Story:
An unknown state is in turmoil. The rebellion started only recently but was promt attacked by the government which then surrounded a small area of a noname city. Many residents have left the area  but your protagonist and his/her team accidantly bumped into it's core finding themselves right in the middle of war. They try to survive the siege and scavenge, steal or buy food, guns and cigarettes. Sometimes they manage to sneak out of the warzone  to steal in a safe area but then suddenly choose to go back to their base to make it even less dilapidated than it was before. They make no efforts to contact the rebellions but sometimes visit their neighbors mostly to steal from them. They have no interest to establish  a provisional government neither they want to join some. Actually there is no functional government - despite the rebellion of course - but the protagonists rather like to live in anarchy like most part of the inhabitans. 

I hope you see my point now. There is basically no rational plot in this game. That's why I wrote lightly humoristic about the given story. As a matter of fact the game provides you with some multiple endings which give you a couple of sentences like "your protagonist survived but lived a horrible life after it" or "your protagonist survived wrote a book and was given the nobel piece prize". Despite these texts there is practically no dialogue or story elaboration during the whole playthrough. This game is 98% pure gameplay.

Character presentation is pretty terse with a couple of sentences about their background story and their preferences (e.g. Mr. X likes coffee or likes cigarettes. Before the war he was a doctor, a scientist or reporter). No personal difficulties regarding their life nor their attitude towards the war is given. You also need to consider that every character knows how to build a heater, a moonshine still, an electric vegetable garden with a heater lamp and last but not least guns and bulletproof vests. ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ why can't they just build a tank to drive out of town?  Oh right they want to be anarchists.

If you think the setting is any better I have to disappoint you. The whole setting is about the war. You don't know why this war started nor do you know the name of the city you live in. Further you have no contact to the rebells who participate in this war and cannot change anything about the state of politics during the isolation.

Alltogether this game is a bit of fun for those of you who really like to grind a lot. The gameplay and atmosphere are just fine as they are. Sneaking and not get caught makes pretty much fun but when fighting opponents hand to hand it gets to the point of ridiculousness where enemies can make 360° no scope headshots from close range while you try to knife them multiple times in the back.

As gaming has developed into an art form, many have tried to use games to portray harrowing concepts like the trauma of war. This War of Mine is without a doubt the best of the bunch, and I would argue potentially one of the best games ever made. Every element of the game is carefully designed to portray the stressful reality of a civilian during wartime while remaining a compelling survival game in it's own right.

[list]
[*] Beautiful muted artwork and piercing sound effects provides a spooky atmosphere
[*] Live one day at a time trying to gather as much food and resources to make it to the next day
[*] Play as weak civilians who must sneak around and avoid danger - no running and gunning, exploring is slow and tense. 
[*] Face countless moral dilemmas - would you steal from an elderly couple if you were starving? Would you share your resources with other survivors that might die without your help?
[*] Keep playing for as long as possible as resources dwindle and stress builds, with no idea when the war will end and if you will be able to make it all the way
[/list]

Where to begin...

Firstly, this is an incredible game. It's certainly not what I would call light-hearted entertainment, but that's sort of the point; the reality is that war isn't fun. Too many games take the position of the battle-hardened soldier, those who know what they're doing, who have been trained by an elite-squad, and who follow a linear objective to defeat the enemy at all costs. In TWOM there is no "winning", there's only surviving. And doing that means more than picking up a weapon. You start off with a group of civilian survivors; ordinary people, cooks, artists, housewives, children, and try to survive as long as you can; just over 30+ days until the war ends.

TWOM isn't just another click-and-collect survival game, either. It challenges you on a moral and ethical level. With one of your survivors starving and sick, do you send out another, a timid middle-aged schoolteacher, to rob that elderly couple down the street for their last morsels of food and medication, knowing full-well it means their death? Or do you try your chances at looting the bombed hospital that's struggling to keep patients alive with minimal staff and limited resources, all while under the watchful eye of shell-shocked soldiers who won't hesitate to shoot you if you give them cause?

Admittedly it's been a while since I've started this game up again - simply because it's a game you can binge on (as I did) but then need to step back from for a while and catch your breath. It's deep and often times dark because your choices really do matter. All action -and- inaction has consequences. If you wait for help to come, you'll die. There's limited supplies in your home base that doesn't re-spawn (unless you craft new items), so they will eventually run out. Other people will raid your home if you don't secure it and have other survivors with you awake and alert enough to keep watch all night. Take new survivors in and risk low morale with cut rations, or send them away and risk the anxiety that follows. Temperatures will plummet and winter will kill. Starvation will kill. Sickness will kill. Boredom leads to addiction which left untended can kill. The repercussions of difficult choices will kill. If you're not careful, survivors can become depressed and will take their own lives. Keeping them alive is a balancing act that's certainly not impossible. With some careful planning and resource management your survivors can even see out the war in relative comfort, make a profit, and even flourish.

I know this sounds like a bleak game, and in a way it is. But there's far more to it than that. TWOM is one of those rare games that made me as a player question what I would do if faced with the same predicament. It made me think then, and still makes me think now years later, offering a glimpse into a reality many face but hopefully I never, ever experience. Above all else it gives you a fresh perspective into the other side of war so often glossed over by popular culture. As it should - it was based on real life war survivor experiences.

Stylistically the graphics resemble that of a comic with a flat background of destroyed buildings and a littered landscape, and mocap-figures moving seamlessly amongst the levels. It's a click-to-move/do game with pre-set locations to visit, hide, run to, attack, craft/interact, or steal from. The action icons are pretty self-explanatory, and the objectives like the interface is pretty basic and easy to understand. It's not a confusing game to get a handle on, nor is it bogged down with endless help-tips that ruin the immersion. It will however feel like a grind to some who are looking for more edge-of-your-seat game play. You absolutely can arm yourself to the teeth if you find the right weapons and ammo and go in guns blazing to every and all situations - but mentally your survivors probably won't last too long. 

Reading up on your survivors stats will help you play to their individual strengths and weaknesses. Their various backgrounds and dialog will pull at your heartstrings. The music and sound effects are IMHO both brilliant and haunting. The constant noise of distant gunfire and flicker of burning fires keep you on edge, but there's oddly also a kind of peacefulness to it too. Once you find your flow it can at times be a relaxing game, especially when it comes to crafting in your once-secure abode. But then as night falls and you step outside the tension ramps again. The anxiety of the unknown lay ahead, and that's where the real challenge begins...

Adding children with a DLC was a genius touch; it added yet another level of tension with young survivors needing help, but having their own skills and traumas, and a limited capacity to help compared to the adult survivors. Taking kids in or sending them away can make or break your survivors' morale. (Its also worth noting that in the many hours I played this game I didn't actually see any of the children "die", so if that's a concern maybe that allays your fears a bit - even if it does fly in the face of facts that tragically kids are often a casualty of war). You don't really need any DLC to get a full experience with this game - it stands up well enough on its own.

If you've read this far you can probably guess I thoroughly recommend this game, but that said it won't be for everyone. If you want a classic-style shooter, TWOM isn't for you. If you want a survival game where your choices actually matter, TWOM will be right up your alley. It's easy to get into and hard to let go of, both while you play and emotionally long after. Few games have that kind of power. Personally, I think everyone should play this game at least once just to get a different (real) perspective on the effects of both violence and war.

This War of Mine is an intimate survival/management experience that aims to highlight the horrors of war and the toll it takes on the non-combatants still struggling in the war zone, and on all accounts it succeeds. The message is clear, and This War of Mine succeeds in addressing it's themes while managing to avoid the excessive praise/shame that often comes with making choices in games that attempt to portray similar issues. The game avoids taking a stance on which combatants are "good" and which are "bad", and manages to do so without resorting to an "enlightened centrist" take. This works to great effect, as the focus is put solely on the civilians you control and their fight for survival.

The game plays very similar to Fallout Shelter (and actually predates it by about a year), with the player controlling a handful of characters and managing their wellbeing inside a small base. The characters all have a variety of needs, most notably food, but the majority are abstracted out in some way. For instance, all characters need to stay warm. There is no "heat" meter though, just an increased chance that the character will become sick. Similarly, there is no sickness bar, just a word or two to indicate severity on the character card. In order to manage all these needs, you'll need to gather supplies by scavenging, trading, or stealing. Unless you're lucky enough to have a trader come to your door, each of these options pose a risk as you will need to journey out to another location in the city during the night to look for opportunities to gain supplies. This is no "one-click to search location" exploration either, you must physically control the character as they scavenge and navigate the hazards of each location. Some of these locations are benign, but you'll quickly exhaust their resources and be forced to move to some of the more dangerous areas. Perhaps one of the best choices here by the developers was to make sure that there are no renewable resources. There are certainly trading strategies to emulate something akin to a steady supply, but you will always need to find something to exchange for those items. This creates an atmosphere of desperation throughout, as you will almost certainly run out of a vital resources and be forced to make hard decisions. All of this adds together to create a tense survival management game with an excellent gameplay loop, and enough randomization to allow for multiple playthroughs.

[b]This War of Mine is an altogether excellent experience, successfully blending a satisfying and challenging core loop with an emergent narrative about the oft-forgotten victims of war[/b]. Ultimately, the message you choose to take from This War of Mine is entirely your own, but the choices you make during your journey are undeniably yours.

As a big fan of brutal survival atmospheric resource management games, this game appears to have a lot of potential. In this game, one wrong move can cripple your entire play through, which is exhilarating and scary. However, it feels absolutely terrible when your run gets crippled from unclear mechanics. I can't express how many times I have lost a playthrough simply because I did not understand a mechanic or my options were very unclear. I do understand that it is possible to reference encounters, scenarios, or mechanics outside of the game online to understand what will actually happen, but that doesn't feel like it is my game then and I am simply following a recipe for my actions where I know the consequences.

It short, the game lacks clarity and satisfying control in a game where every choice is vital. To start, the atmosphere of the game is great. Gunshots and sounds of fighting are heard in the background, constantly reminding where you are. 

Graphics is very minimalistic,but it gets the point across quickly. Although the game is 2D the developers still managed to pull off a 3D environment where people interact with the world around them. 

Gameplay is basic and direct, but requires some practice to get the gist of it. Eg. Click on stove to cook or click on heater to add fuel.

It is the small things that makes this game great, even down to the littlest details. There are too many to list down,the developers had so many opportunities to get the easy way out but they choose not to. If you are a person who likes to take time to take with everything then you are in for a treat.

Such as if you steal someone's meds or food while scavenging and remain undetected, you can hear(or see his text bubble) him being confused about why his stuff is gone before realising that someone has crowbar'd his way into his house. Opening doors would get people to check as they were closed before and pointing a gun or holding a weapon would get everyone to tell you to put it down.etc etc

This game of course is not perfect and has some flaws that should be looked into:

1. Lack of tutorial or teaching the player of the controls.

The game throws you into the gameplay with almost nothing that properly teaches you the basics. Although this might be symbolic or some sorts as you are a person who is trying to survive a civil war and is confused and scared.

2.Lack of a proper save function.

The only way to "save" your progress is when a new day starts and then you quit. This saves it but it resets the entire RNG of the entire new day. This can be exploited to reset the day to your liking( if you dont want to get raided keep leaving the game via the top right button and continue the day again and again until you are safe, this takes a lot of time to pull off so dont lose hope)

If everyone dies then you lose everything, just like in war. Guess this is also symbolic too.

Overall, this game is for patient people as lots of times are spent recovering from brutal scavenging missions where you raid deserted soldiers and bandits, or armed civilians if you are desperate enough to fight for their supplies.

This War of Mine is not exactly a new release, and I'd seen it pop up on my feed a thousand times before I finally bit the bullet (much like Marko would come to...), and boy am I glad I did. 

If, like me, you looked at the stills and thought, 'meh, looks a bit drab', then I can almost guarantee you will be wrong. The gameplay is a scavenge and craft combo, something that is quite popular these days. The scavenging is done at night and in the day you use the materials you gathered the eve before to upgrade your house. Sounds simple? Well it's bloody challenging. Sneaking around abandon buildings to find the 4 tins of food you need to keep yourself and your friends alive is genuinely anxiety inducing! 

Day 1: Piece of cake. Enter house, scavenge, come home. 

Day 2: Parts are harder to come by than I expected. Better grab more.

Day 3: Where is all the food! 

Day 4: Oh this place is bound to have food. I'll just waltz up to that there fridge and... Did someone just shotgun Marko in the back of the head? 

Day 5: These guys really miss Marko!

Day 6: Perhaps I'll try somewhere easier. That house should be abandoned. Oh, just a couple of grandparents. Sorry, sir, I just need some things. Sir, out of the way please. Sir, I'm warning you! 

Day 7: Pavel falls into depression following an unscheduled double homicide...

This War of Mine is a 2D game that takes a unique approach to the theme of war. Instead of playing as a soldier on the frontlines, you experience the harsh reality of surviving as a civilian during wartime. Your goal is to gather materials for building and maintaining your shelter, find food to keep everyone alive, and acquire weapons to protect yourself.

The management aspect is well-designed, with a small group of people under your care. Each character has their own backstory, and towards the end of the game, those who survive will share their personal reflections on what they went through.

The game immerses you in the tough, emotional moments of being a helpless civilian, forcing you to make difficult choices to endure until the end of the war. It’s a deeply engaging blend of survival and strategy, and I highly recommend it to anyone looking for a war-themed game with a different, more human perspective.

This War of Mine is a survival side scroller where the player incarnates civilians in a worn-torn Eastern European setting. The game has two settings: a day time in your refuge and a night time where you scavange around. The game is Polish, so expect to feel miserable. The universe is inspired in the dreaful Siege of Sarajevo, from 2 April 1992 to 29 February 1996 (3 years, 10 months, 3 weeks and 3 days), and the game even has a sniper alley such as in Sarajevo. This game has a good idea with an okay execution. The Hungarian soundtrack is immersive but the tone is sometimes too "in the face" and the overall "gaming economy" is always on a descending spiral, where you always run out of resources.

You start the game by picking your survivors and the game settings (such as places to scavenge). You need to keep improving your home, and sometimes people knock on your door with different problems for you to solve. The player constantly needs to scavenge resources in order to survive, going out at night to find more resources in a situation of continuous misery. You use the resources for cooking and building furniture, such as beds. Sleeping on the floor doesn't get your survivors well rested, so this is your top priority when the game starts. You need to find ingredients and prepare food, so pick a character that is a good cook so you get the highest satisfaction for your meager resources.

During the night runs the player meets soldiers, bandits and civilians, having a random set of events and responses. The NPCs can be willing to trade with you, or they can be hostile. Some civilians might need help and you have the option of helping them, risking your own neck by doing so.

The soldiers can be evil, as in one of the first missions a soldier tries to rape a girl in a supermarket, or indifferent, exchanging resources with you. Those interactions are mostly random in a per game system, thus increasing replayability. The combat is very finicky, with your character not always doing what you ordered him to do; something unpleasant in life-or-death situations.

Albeit the game claims to be amoral, you get punished for bad deeds, with the survivors suffering from depression by killing inoccent people or stealing; and the player is also encouraged to help the civilians you find along the way. Sometimes you can do this by stealth and others by brute force. This game is no Spec Ops: The Line but at least it doesn't lecture you about how war is bad or anything like that, but I feel like the "war economy" in This War of Mine is always a calculation of zero sum, progressively getting worse as long as you go on. It's not a terrible game but I wouldn't pick it to a casual play when having free time.

A deeply heartfelt and poignant game, This War of Mine is an exercise in empathy. Far more than just a survival management sim, it shines a light on an aspect of warfare rarely seen in video games: that of the civilians caught in the crossfire. It's a must play for anyone and everyone.

This game is a somber reality check that is here to remind you that in every war, there are people who are just trying to survive. When you play a shooter such as "Call of Duty", you don't put much thought into the civilians or the damage to buildings around you...just kill the enemy by any means and go to the next mission. This game is about just looking for food, water, medical supplies, staying hopeful for tomorrow, and keeping a shelter secure while the city you lived gets destroyed by a war. There are other survivors who need help and looters that come in the night for your little supplies. Hard choices must be made when supplies run low, who will risk their life to gather supplies and how to get them. This game is worth every penny, and keep it mindful in your head next time you watch the cool action movie or game where a apartment building gets blown up or set on fire. That what the game is for, to remind you of the third perspective of a country at war...the people who are not fighting.

Hauntingly bleak, but beautiful in the message that this game portrays.  In trying to keep your survivors alive, please be patient with yourself if you fail the first few playthroughs of this game. War isn't glorious; it's depressing, it's dark, and it's a test of human dignity and perseverance in the face of grim odds.  I HIGHLY recommend playing through this game blind (without any walkthroughs/guides/tips and tricks), because you will grieve when your survivors succumb to illness, freeze to a sudden chill, or get shot down just for stealing some canned foods.  But also, the flip side is true.  You will appreciate more intimately the moment when you finally make simple improvements, whether if your survivor was able to overcome his/her depression and brokenness, whether you were able to rejoice in extending precious supplies to children knocking at your door, and whether you were able to keep goodwill and love for your fellow neighbor alive when death reaped both the evil and good equally.  This is one of my most favorite games in the 25+ years of gaming I've enjoyed.

This War of Mine is a survival game set in Pogoren, the war-torn capital city of the fictional country of Graznia. You begin the scenario with a group of survivors, civilians caught in the crossfire of a war between the government and the rebels. You have to guide the survivors through the war, trying to keep everyone alive and happy.

Gameplay is split into two phases, daytime and nighttime. During the daytime, you take care of your survivors' needs and improve their shelter. At nighttime, you decide if your survivors will sleep or guard the shelter, and if you want to you can send one out to scavenge for supplies. You'll have to make some tough decisions as the game goes on: who gets the food and medicine when supplies are scarce, what to prioritize in improving your shelter, whether or not to help other needy folk when the opportunity presents itself. 

Survival is really difficult the first few times you pay the game, when you don't know what your survivors' strengths are and you don't know what buildings are especially important. However, after playing through it a few times, you'll get a good sense of what is important to build, what you're likely to find in each location, and how to protect against the threats you'll face.

Aside from the DLC episodes the game doesn't really tell a direct story, but the information you can get from the game gives you a sense of a really well-built and interesting world. You get a sense of what Pogoren and many of the characters were like before the war, as well as a sense of what the two fighting sides are like and the tone they take towards civilians. A huge theme of the game is civilian losses in war, and you see a lot of that too. Good people getting hurt or having to fight each other for scraps, property damage and destruction of culture, and the dehumanization of others in times of desperation. While it isn't always a pleasant game, the themes are very well-told, and they make the lighter, happier moments you can get all the nicer by contrast.

There are a couple of things about the game that I'm not a huge fan of. I've found a lot of bugs in the game, not enough to be unplayable, and they definitely don't show up in every session, but often enough that they've been realy noticible. I'm also not a huge fan of the combat system. I've found it to be somewhat confusing and difficult, especially the first few times I played when I suddenly found myself in an unexpected combat situation. However, neither of those made the game unplayable or too much less enjoyable.

Overall, This War of Mine is a very enjoyable gaming experience. It has a couple of minor flaws, but those are easily overshadowed by everything else in the game, which is excellent. I don't normally enjoy survival games, but I found this one to be very good. 9/10

This game provided me with a unique experience upon my first playthrough because, though I had played survival games before, I did not have to face the consequences of my characters actions. This War of Mine pits your survival skills against the desperate feel of a war-torn country, all the while balancing your characters health and mental suffering. Characters are a big element of the game and they will respond to events according to their personality traits. Further, characters each bring their own strengths and weaknesses to the table. Once you play through the game a few times, you will start to know which characters you love, and those you hate.

What's great about the game is that it gives you (until you play some of the harder scenarios) the option of being good survivors or bad survivors meaning you can either collect and obtain the foods and necessities you need without resorting to violence or you can become an outright bandit (I usually choose the ladder because I am sadistic like that haha). However, beware, the consequences of being a morally upright survivor has its pitfalls, for instance, its much harder to come across large stores of goods for your characters to live a comfortable existence during their time in the dilapidated war-torn city the game takes place in. That being said, there are weaknesses in taking the bandit route in that its much more hazardous and is mentally draining on many of your characters.

All-in-all, I loved the realism of This War of Mine and it is a very decent survival game. So if you like survival and are ready to face the harsh realities of war, try this game out because it will most likely tickle your fancy.

A very impressive and atmospheric game. It's not just a surviving game, but a war novel. My character was killed by bandits while looting for supplies and well, there is no second chance to replay the moment. It's the war.

Would I recommend this game?  --  YES!

Why? 

CONCEPT
Well, the concept is still a rare one in the gaming world. Showing the other side of war - the one of the civilians - the victims of aggression - is an important one, because as badass and cool usual war games might let someone feel himself, they are far away from the truth of war.

VISUALS - SOUND - ATMOSPHERE
The Artworks are beautiful (to me) and accelerate the immersion into the overall atmosphere. It's a fine line between creating a visual style that also characterizes the despair and tristesse of war without being repellent to the player. The devs did a really good job on that.
If you haven't done so, I recommend trying out the other visual mode ("Settings" -> "Pencil effect" -> "Soft" or "Sketchy") 

MUSIC
It's good enough to not having own songs played in the background yet also not at the league of AAA-Games. I dig the guitar songs (if the character can play it of course)

GAMEPLAY
While the interface being pretty simplistic the gameplay demands a certain task management and planning ahead (especially in the harder modes). It has a certain learning curve (which is extensive enough to be constantly learning for 30+ hours till you've "cracked the game"). Once it's reached though, the game has not very much new to offer, except trying out new strategies. Which is fine by me, replay value is still very high.

MAP
The Locations are manifold in style and encounters. While they're new to you it really is an adventure to getting to know the different encounter and loot possibilities. 
The map has quite some locations but after a few dozen hours of gameplay you've seen it all, know it all. That's one of the little downsides of the game in terms of long-term-playability. If the devs would decide to publish a Location DLC I'd happily and instantly would invest in it. (Yeah I know they stopped development)

SOCIAL ENGAGEMENT
11 bit studios proves, that being a profit oriented company and active engagement in social improvement doesn't exclude each other, but pair rather well. A certain amount of the profits for "This War Of Mine" and all DLC's has always been and always will be transferred to organizations that help children in areas of war.
If you want to contribute further you can buy the Art-DLC. It contains art regarding war and peace from artists around the globe which will be depicted ingame. 100% of the DLC-Profit goes to charity.

DEVS and PUBLISHER
I've got this game since quite a while (since before the first DLCs) and 11bit is a cool bunch of People. Their communication with the community is nice. The Prices of the games and DLCs are fair. They live social responsibility by heart. They had free major updates and content extensions. I never had that EA- or Paradox-Feeling with them. Here you got a team that is worth supporting.

DLCs
The DLCs are okay. Nice addition and good new content. I've played them once or twice (The Story-DLC), but mostly stick to the main game with some mods.
The best DLC to me is the "Little Ones" one. Having children in the house makes a huge impact and difference and the DLC adds tremendously to the gaming experience.

MODDING COMMUNITY
There was/is an active and productive community. Workshop is full of Mods, Skins, Items, Stories, Characters.
If the game starts to feel a bit repetitive, I recommend browsing a bit through the workshop content.
Whether you want the game to be more or less vanilla, add more items and crafting complexity or just want to play with custom characters (I know that there is even a John Cena Character downloadable, but I gotta admit, I haven't seen it yet),  the workshop got you!

CONCLUSION
If you like 2D-Style games, point and click, survival, looting, crafting, micro management, drawn visuals, dark atmosphere, emotional and ethical choices, many modding possibilities, devs that stick to creating good games rather than scamming their customers, then this is a must have game for you.

Combat is an absolute joke (Snuck up on a thug with my athlete character, knifed him from behind while he was completely unaware, and it only took half his health. I completely understand the limits if your carrying just timber, but when I'm completely out of space from carrying scrap/teddy bears/tobacco/meds each items small stack is just ridiculous.
