From [url=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spacewar!]Spacewar![/url] to the latest batch of FPS and RTS games, war is without a doubt the most popular topic for games. This War of Mine by 11 bit studios is probably the most honest and least naive game about war ever made. A survival simulation about civilians in a fictional war-ravaged Eastern European country, it begins with a quote by Ernest Hemingway: “In modern war… you will die like a dog for no good reason.”

The initial campaign gives the player control over three characters: Katia, Pavle and Bruno. They found each other through tragic circumstances and decided to stick together, moving into one of the few remaining houses to mount their fight for survival. Each character has a trait, and some have addictions, which help them excel at certain roles in the game. Katia, a former reporter, is skilled at bargaining, but also a coffee drinker; Bruno, a former TV chef, is a good cook, but also a smoker. Pavle is a former athlete, and therefore a fast runner, without addictions.

After looting the house bare and collecting the materials, you’ll have enough to craft the essentials: beds, a stove, a rainwater collector. Crafting materials range from wood and scrap components to electric parts and weapon parts. Some resources are more scarce than others. You can use the general workshop to build other household items such as a heater or a garden, as well as a metal workshop for looting equipment and weapons. Some of these stations can be upgraded to optimise resource consumption.

Gameplay consists of the usual mix of base-building, resource management and scavenging that is familiar to the survival game genre. There’s nothing original or even perfected here, and the UI could definitely use some improvements. What makes This War of Mine stand apart, however, is not the gameplay, but rather the way it makes you care about the characters, and the bleak — oppressively grim, even — atmosphere as you explore the map to scavenge during nighttime. At times This War of Mine feels like the original isometric Fallout games in terms of tone and ambiance, though with less character interaction and gallows humour.

There are tests of character throughout the game where you must decide whether you will help other people in need as your characters struggle with hunger, sickness, depression, cold. In my first playthrough, Katia was terminally ill at one point, and finding medicine was almost impossible. I could have just let her die. It would mean one less mouth to feed after all, but I just couldn’t do it. I made Pavle steal from an elderly couple so he could get the medicine Katia needed, which in turn sent Pavle on a spiral of depression and guilt for stealing from helpless people.

The characters often talk to themselves as they walk around the house, and even though it’s just a simple AI performing logical operations under the hood, you still end up caring for the characters in ways that defy logic. You can only see a photograph of their faces in the HUD (and sometimes they blink), but apart from that there’s nothing else to help you relate to them. The animation is great as they walk or perform various actions, but you can’t zoom in enough to see their faces, so all that’s left is their occasional comments and complaints. It’s a testament to skilled writing that you come to care about them enough to sacrifice resources, trading for the things they need.

Seeing the characters make it through sickness or injury and return to health actually gave me relief as I kept playing, making hard choices and concessions, finding ways to cope with the scarcity of resources. I had wanted to build an alcohol distiller to make moonshine from sugar and water, which I could then use as trade currency, but I was never able to because I kept sacrificing the necessary resources to help my characters.

Each character has a journal, which you can access when you click on their “Bio” section, where they talk about recent events and the choices they made, while also telling bits of their life story. This is nothing particularly remarkable, but put together with everything else it somehow all coalesces into characters that feel real, that you care about. If you don’t, all that is left is the slow and tedious grind of looting and managing resources, which is less appealing. That’s why This War of Mine is an honest game about war. There is nothing worthwhile about war and survival without people you care about.

The ending to each campaign will vary according to your decisions and actions for each of the characters. The variations are a bit simplistic, based mostly on whether the character has killed or stolen, regardless of whom they killed or stole from, and whether they helped others who needed help. It fails to take into account that the characters might have stolen or killed only to help their companions, which is not as heinous as simply stealing or killing for mere profit. Even stealing from people who are hostile and attack on sight nets bad karma, which somehow results in completely unrelated consequences. While it does make sense to punish you when you steal from helpless people, the game could have explored some grey areas, mitigating the negative effects of stealing from bandits or militiamen who abuse their power, with more consequences for your actions in-game rather than just in the endings.

Once the initial campaign is finished, you unlock a few other characters with different traits and addictions that add more variety to playthroughs. Each character has their own backstory and personality, reacting differently to events and actions. Depending on the set of characters you choose, the war will begin at different stages, and the duration can be shorter or longer, with random events such as an increased military presence.  This adds quite a bit of replay value to the game, and that’s not even including the DLCs. The base game is more than worth the full price at $19.99, and the DLCs are modestly priced, especially the War Child DLC at $0.99, which was developed for the War Child organisation to which all proceeds are donated, even to this day.

Compared to similar base-building and resource management games, This War of Mine is definitely still compelling, but not outstanding in its gameplay. It’s not supposed to be a fun game, necessarily, but there is a fascination in making through each day with every character alive and well. The soothing, quiet desperation of the soundtrack and the bleak, black-and-white art make for a unique aesthetic. The mature ambiance and character development give it a depth that is sorely lacking in most survival games.

There is an ancient saying: “Dulce bellum inexpertis.” War is fascinating to those who have no experience of it, and war games are fascinating because most of us have never experienced war. This War of Mine is fascinating, even as it shows that war is hell and there is nothing special or heroic about making hard decisions to survive.

I just stood on a piece of glass in the middle of my kitchen, and it went straight through the arch of my foot, and I had to pull it out. Blood spills whenever I walk. The experience reminded me of this game- not to put on bandages, or question why this particular shard of glass was so unconveniently poised- because This War of Mine is, and adverts itself to be, the game where no amount of skill, carefulness or experience can truly save you from the fate of those living through a brutal civil war. Sure, you can press alt and tab, and close the game before it saves the death of one of your characters. But that’s not what 11 Bit Studios wants you to do. It even recommends you to wear a headphone before playing the game to enhance the experience.

This said about the purpose of the game, and the harshness of its system at times, anti-war propaganda isn’t its only good point. In fact, whilst it’s evidently what it aims to do, in some points in the gameplay, you’ll forget your morality, or what you’d normally do in a moral situation, and steal from a pacifist older couple, raid a hospital aiming to aid those in need, and deny children knocking on your door for medicine. Because you have to.

Beyond some people just being bastards and not caring about the ethics of video game mannerisms, there’s also the connection the player gets to the characters in their control which in turn controls the player. You generally start with three characters (out of twelve), with the chance of recruiting more, all of whom have a realistic background and a broody expression on their models’ faces.  It’s surprising how easy it is to sympathise with them because of those real, human faces, especially when some of them have attractive ones.

The sound is primitive at times, however, this does set the mood quite well, and so does the music. The art style is pleasant (and adaptable between a sketchy/solid style) and moody. There’s enough personalisation/adaptability to interest someone with multiple hours in the game so that, even if you can generally evade harmful situations, you can increase the time it takes to win the game (about 40 days on normal mode), for example, or change what characters you begin with. The repeatability is high, and This War of Mine is one of those games that you can experience in all of its depravity in full screen, with no music or television on in the background, or windowed, whilst watching other things. 

There are few people whom I wouldn’t recommend this game to. Its main downside would be pacing. Although winter is harder than summer, and the bandits get more vicious at points, the pace of the game remains relatively slow. Otherwise, and especially for people who prefer a more realistic experience, This War of Mine is a good one to have in your library.

This War of Mine is demanding survival and resource-management game concerning a city under siege. It explores the aspect of the war from the perspective of the most vulnerable group, the civilian. While the simplicity of its premise might seem dull for many, I was a few who adore this piece of work. Mainly it's because of where I'm from, but partly because 11 Bits Studios is also known for amazing games such as Anomaly: Warzone Earth and Frostpunk. The expectation was high, and the result wasn't disappointing.

As a civilian in This War of Mine, you'll have to survive in a warzone before a ceasefire. You will have to scavage for resources across the city, from abandoned areas or other survivors, often with force. Trade in the black market, avoiding soldiers and bandits. The goal is crystal clear: Survive.

So what's make it stand out from the usual 2D survival game with a touch of war? The answer is This War of Mine provided a powerful depiction of civilian life in wartime. Aside from the essentials, items like cigarettes, alcohol, and coffee exist and are in high demand on the black market. People cherish a beverage like coffee for that sweet caffeine. People treasured cigarettes whenever the stress of war creeps up from within their minds. It reminds us that conflicts affect people emotionally rather than physically, and at the end of the day, these characters are commoners, not soldiers or heroes in FPS games.

The problem is that gameplay becomes repetitious over time as players repeatedly scavage and fight days after another. It gets worst once players have a good understanding of the underlying systems in place. At that point, the challenge is non-existence.

For me, I've been looking for a game like this for ages. Unlike other titles where the mission is to save the world, this portrays the reality of war. You'll face complicated and challenging decisions as you're forcing to steal and kill people for resources. One mistake can cost your character's life.

Barge into a room full of survivors from another survivor group all huddled up together. Say ♥♥♥♥ under my breath knowing I’m a dead duck. Random guy comes up to me and tells me to leave. I fear he’s armed and going to shank me. Pull out a knife in self defence. He doesn’t mean no harm and only wants to talk, or so I think. Slowly slowly walks closer to me. Don’t know what to do. He creeps closer. I panic and accidentally stab and kill him. His brother hears the commotion and runs from the other room. Finds his brother dead next to me and starts crying, asking me why I did this. Stand there helpless asking myself what have I just done. Drop knife, turn around and run all the way home.

It’s weird that in a video game while controlling a character, I killed a guy in a video game game, and yet, what I did sorta haunted me. It made me want to turn the game off so I could take back what I had just done in a virtual world. Made me want to just sit and think about it for a minute. No game has ever done this before this well, captured this feeling of war, desperation, regret and survival where you are left questioning your own morality and wishing you didn’t have to do what you just did. Most games make you kill over a hundred goobers throwing ammo at you like candy but they never make the enemies feel like real people or make you question the price of taking a life.

This game is about war, but not in the common sense of being a soldier, but a group of civilians just trying to survive. (As the description says) I really feel it is truly unique. Personally, I have not felt such a high level of immersion in a war game before.  You are forced to choose whether you want to do something immoral or risking not surviving the next day. You think, "sure I could steal from this old couple pretty easily" but then you discover his wife is badly injured, making you feel bad about thinking about stealing from someone so helpless. 

Your survivors will react to both positive and negative actions, affecting their mood accordingly. Your survivors will tell stories and reveal things about their life, wondering what has happened to family and friends. Different survivors excel at different things and some may have addictions to coffee and tobacco while others don't. There also are notes left around in buildings, telling parts of other people's stories. Some of these are intriguing and others are tell of the murders, beatings and hostage taking.

How you choose to survive and whether you keep your moral rules or throw them out the window will directly affect how the game ends.

I very highly reccomend this game, even if you normally don't play war games and especially when it is on sale. (I only buy on sales though TBH) The new perspectives you get are well worth the price.

This War Of Mine has been a long time favorite "survival" game of mine since it came out (survival in the sense that your main goal is to not die, of course). It's unforgiving, challenging, and sometimes downright depressing, and that's what makes it so truly awesome. It highlights the power and struggle of surviving in a war environment as an innocent bystander, and how no matter your choices, nobody is truly a winner when a ceasefire is declared. 

From harsh winter conditions to thinly divided materials, from raiders to corrupt military officials, This War Of Mine will keep you on your toes even on the easiest of difficulties. The atmosphere, the pre-made characters (and the ability to create your own), the ability to adjust the difficulty of the game (and what CAUSES the difficulty), and the reality of it all truly makes this game stand out in it's genre. Better yet, it's still being updated and has recently received the "Stories" optional DLC (which is amazing, as well, and I can confidently say it's worth the purchase for the season pass after only one has been released).

My only wish would be that character relationships would be deepened. I don't necessarily mean "romance", I would just love to have a bit more of an interactive element between my survivors, such as arguments due to differing personalities or some being more nurturing in general than others.

In general, yeah, I seriously recommend this game. It's amazing.

I played this game for free and I ended up buying it on sale because it was so addictive. 
This game is great and deserves a full thumbs up, but at the same time I personally thought that some things could be improved. 

First what is good: the idea is unique, the message of the game is an important one and it's a game that makes you think a lot, and it has replay value thanks to different characters with different abilities and the possibility to create groups with various characters. The atmosphere is great, the design is awesome, the music is perfect. 
You might feel discouraged at first as the game doesn't have any tutorial, but please give this game a try, as you will learn with time what works and what doesn't, and you would be missing a great experience by skipping this game. 
I also liked that there are different ways to play this game. You can rob and/or kill people, or decide to try and build a self-sufficient refuge and keep your hands clean - while the second option is more difficult, I believe it can be done (currently trying and on day 20ish but I will probably die soon, will do better next time!)

Then, what is mixed:
the game tends to get boring around day 20 or so (that's where I am now). At that point everything is scarce, and all you can do is look for food and fuel to barely scrape by. There's nothing to scavenge for, no new locations to explore - obviously that's what war is like and it can be considered part of the game's message, but it makes me want to quit the game and start a new one because I'm bored. You can try and get a 100% items clearance of all locations, but if you don't want to kill and rob people that's also impossible. The good thing is that you can switch teams and start again, but you will lose your progress. 
The scenarios are also too different sometimes in terms of difficulty. For example, getting the Garage location grants you a very important tool quite easily, but when you're without the Garage it's much harder to get this item, and this makes a lot of difference later in the game. Obviously that can also be a message (life is not fair!) but this is a game, not real life (where I don't get to reset the day if I suddenly die!). 

Finally, what is not so good: I would really like to be able to have different savings for different groups of characters. As I mentioned before, since the game became quite boring for me around Day 20, having different savings would have allowed me to alternatively play different scenarios, avoiding the boredom. I also wish the game would save after the day AND after the night, not only after the night. 
Also a very small thing, in the Italian translation there's an absence of distinction between masculine and feminine in the "X is back" sentence at the end of the night. It probably can't be helped, but the translation is otherwise perfect so that bothered me a bit when playing. 

Overall this is a very good game, so if you're undecided about buying it, go ahead! You won't regret it. The only problem might be that you can't stop playing. I would 100% recommend it to anyone who is in International Relations / War Studies or just has an interest in these topics, as the game makes you reflect on the impact of war on civilians. Also recommended for people like me who don't like stealth or killing in games, as you *can* complete the game without hurting anyone or sneaking around too much, even though it's hard.

My friend bought me this game yesterday with the note "You need to play this game." And I can honestly say yes, yes I did.

This game is one of a select few that I would call an experience. We see the war from our angle here in first-world countries, where we are "liberating" or "providing our support." But rarely do we truly see the civilian side of things.

And that's where "This War of Mine" comes into play.

Here, we're greeted with an unforgiving party of 2 to 4 members. And almost instantly, your situation is dire. You must scrounge from your building to gather enough resources to get a head start on day 1, lest you make no progress. Within a few moments, I realized night had already fallen, bringing me to the scavenging portion of the game.

Everything has weight: do you steal from these people and cause them to potentially die, or starve to death yourself? As you go along, listening to the radio, you hear how bad it's getting elsewhere, and gradually it begins to take a toll on your playthrough. Dilemma upon dilemma: make a bed, or get fuel for the heater? Trade for water, or save the jewelry for something better?

I can honestly say no other game has made me feel such a wide range of emotions, ranging from anger to sadness to joy. My only complaint is that there is no tutorial, but in real life, would there be a tutorial on how to survive? Therefore, that is not a complaint, per se, as much as a heads-up: this game is Fallout Shelter: Dark Souls Edition.

This is a great game which had the potential to be something truly special.  It starts off strong and I was immediately hooked. It's based in the bosnian/serbian civil war (i assume) and has a compelling story with a few really gritty moments if you have to kill people to steal medicine for your sick housemate or whatever. I found it touching and poignant. 

Sadly I played it for a free weekend and I'm already 'done' with it.  I would have gladly paid for the game if it had more content and more things to do but sadly I have seen it all already.

Unfortunately after playing ~2 full games I feel I have basically seen everything there is to see.  Despite the randomness there is not a lot that is new and after say 1-2 weeks in game you fall into the same routine:

scavenge components
build filters
get water
cook/make moonshine
get timber
build something
repeat

Alternatively, if you're having a bad game, it can get extremely frustrating where you get stuck spending all your timber on fuel and you can't get components to build stuff cos you need timber and if you haven't got timber people get sick and die etc. 

The main stories are designed (imo) so that you will never/rarely be able to build all that you want, which makes it challenging, but the limited number of locations, lack of 'late game' stuff and inability to 'level up' in anyway killed the longevity.  

There is a lot of busywork like scanning items over and over every night for 40 nights, not my idea of fun. Being able to 'scan' the items and then 'auto scavenge' them (e.g. via a menu, not actually visiting the site and walking around) would be extremely useful in areas where there are no people or where you have cleared it out already.

I love the concept but I'm not willing to pay more for the 'stories' DLC which just has more of the same, essentially.  I will be back in a heartbeat if they announce a War of Mine 2, e.g. with a full campaign or a zombie campaign (that would be amazing). I will also be checking out the developer's other game with great interest.  I give it a recommended - it's a fantastic game - but ultimately it doesn't have a lot of longevity so I would suggest getting it on sale.

This War of Mine is a unique game where you play a group of survivors that will hopefully survive long enough to make it out of the war alive. There's a lot of crafting, trading and scavenging for materials. The core idea is to keep your characters fed, warm, happy and safe by all means possible until the end.

The game has two major components which repeat - day and night. During the day you craft, rest, cook food, trade and perhaps have a chance to help a neighbour. During the night you visit other places to clear them out of everything worth having, stealthily or by force. Engaging in battle is very risky if you're not well equipped.

There will be moments when you will feel guilty or unable to do something even though the characters portrayed aren't real. Would you rob an elderly couple blind just to survive a few more days? The dialogue in this game is powerful. You can be a pacifist, only use violence against thugs or mercilessly kill everyone (and make your characters sad).

This game does have a steep learning curve. You will most likely fail your first tries. But have a look at the guides - they are helpful in revealing how you should be playing the game. Make food traps, board up your house (upgrade the crafting bench!) and don't eat everything as soon as you get it! The characters can go hungry a few days with no problem. There's also a chance that they can cure their wounds/sicknesses by just resting in a bed.

All in all, I recommend this, but be prepared to exert a bit of patience with learning the game.

Wow!  This is one addictive survival management game.  After trying out the free trial, I can't seem to put it down.  I practically almost burn my weekend just playing the game.

The game focuses on managing your resources wisely amongst your fellow survivors, while scavenging for scarce resources with a very small backpack.  In other management type games, you normally build to grow and build your empire or whatnot.  Ultimately, you feel great over time on the growth of your city.  This is the not the case here.  In this game, you build to survive.  As the days go by, you are more depressed when you lose more than you gain.  In other words, if you can’t manage properly, you and your fellow survivors will meet a sad end.

In my first playthrough, I tried focusing on building what I believe was important and started scavenging on areas that are safer first for the first several days.  This was my first mistake.  I didn’t know what was important until several game-days later.  When small problems arise, I tried to remedy them as soon as possible.  This was my second mistake.  I tried buying off items that I needed at the moment and sold off items that aren’t needed at the moment.  This was also a mistake.  After going through great difficulties trying to solve one problem, such as food shortages, another big one arises, such as illness or wounds.  Over time, locations become inaccessible due to war or weather conditions.  All I’m left with is places I’ve already searched.  Converting items just to create any type of medicine is difficult because resources are lacking.  Eventually, it became a roller coaster ride of emotion when you end up losing the people in your group due to illness, starvation or wounds.  There is nothing that can be done other than a miracle or just watch them slowly die.  I did fight right to the end despite how hopeless it seems.  In the end, I did manage to make it a day before presumably the final day before everyone died.

In my second playthough, I am more prepared.  I maximized as much as I can everyday: going to places where there lots of needed resources; allocating food and medicine only when desperately needed; focusing on what needs to be upgraded first; paying attention to bartering, buying more for less, selling in-demand items that are unneeded; taking risk at high danger areas with an assault rifle and taking out baddies.  In the end, I felt like I was ahead of the danger and stocked properly.  I managed to finish what my first playthrough couldn’t.

In all honesty, even though it felt good to complete game, my first playthrough was the most realistic.  Going through the emotion of keeping everyone alive, knowing that your best efforts wasn’t good enough was real and engaging.  My second playthrough is more of a dream because I knew what to do ahead of time.  If you only had one shot, how will you manage to keep the group of survivors alive before the war ends?  That was the beauty of playing this game the first time around.

Highly recommended.

So I grabbed this during the free weekend because I was bored and am always interested in checking out different games.  I normally play FPS type games as well as single player games with good story.  [i]This War of Mine[/i] is a quaint little title that offers a whole new outlook on videogames for myself as someone that doesn't stray very far from his comfort zone of "shoot 'em up destroy everything" genre.  I originally planned on just giving this a quick look, but ended up playing 4 straight hours without any realization of the passing time.  Instantly purchased afterwards.

The mood that the game sets right off the bat is somber, somewhat depressing, as you control a 3 person group, each with a special skill set to help you survive in the war ravaged city that you live in.  There is a gentleman that is a proficient cook, a master scavenger, and a marathon runner that runs faster than normal.  You will have to use strategy when assigning certain characters to different actions to be the most efficient.  There is looting and crafting, but not like your typical survival/horror game.  That being said, I only have about 4 hours in the game at time of this review (on a different account; have to start a new game on this account) but the ambiance and basic functions of the game were extremely appealing to me as I was looking for a game that I could play when I felt like there was nothing else to play.  The GFX are pretty neat and IMO unique, never having played a game with pencil drawing type art.  It was definitely refreshing and I think helped play a part in the sad mood that this game sets.

All in all, from a casual gamer just looking to add a little variety to their library, this game is definitely worth a pickup, especially if it is on sale (currently $5.99 for the weekend.)

NOTE FOR CONTROLLER USERS:  There is controller support for this game, but it doesn't allow you to be able to use the loot function properly (or I just haven't put enough time into making it work correctly?).  I ended up switching to mouse for a more point-and-click experience, which totally was not a deal breaker for me.

I read the reviews, I saw the trailer, I got excited - ready for something new, intelligent, and emotionally provocative.

The developers, and in large part the players, seem to have lauded the very real struggle through this battleground for being just that. So thank god I got to play this piece of ♥♥♥♥ in a free window without having to buy it, because if I bought it - even at the largely discounted price - I would be upset, as opposed to just staunchly dissapointed.

This game is challenging, in the way that farmville is challenging - there are a many goals to reach, and they all take a fair amount of effort and understanding to achieve. However, for a game that popularly stands on its realism, the obsenely nonsensicle technical difficulties completely obliterated my immersion experience.

Are you the kind of person that spends 5 minutes dillegently studying all exploration opportunity summaries to make the best choice? Too bad, the RNG will select a scenario upon arrival that amounts to either letting you walk through the doors to loot freely - or ostensibly shut you out of the level - trespassing punishable by death.

Get locked out of the level? Have fun watching the upper left screen clock mete out minutes as slowly and steadily as Total Shogun's seige timer - except without the opportunity speed up - until you've spent 20 real life minutes daydreaming through all of the basic tactical options you can't adopt by virtue of only being able to walk/run left or right, then painfully relinquish the night you waited all damn day for. For real, you'd think a game that puts such ornate emphasis on extra-room sensory information and the 12 items in your backpack would allow you to engineer some sort of diversion - or at the very least render an effect on your surroundings beyond unlocking doors - but no, all you have to look forward to are vicarious fantasies of throwing an empty can to distract the dumb as ♥♥♥♥ NPCs. Finally, if you manage to farm your way through this insanity, you're rewarded with martial might to reduce all of these "challenges" to ♥♥♥♥♥ and giggles.

And the recipies..... it takes roughly the same amount of wood to build a shovel, as it does to build a workshop. Nuff said.

Want to move your stove? Ironically, despite this being the one crafting game that lacks adhesives, your placed equipment is less mobile than an SUV in quicksand.

This War of Mine rainwater collectors collect rainwater independent of rain, so you're gonna havta forestall skipping the otherwise barren day, for that handful of precious water units.

And god help you if you have an improper ratio of part units marked with gears to part units makred with vague circuitry...

Oh! And you can't save!

All of this alien, arbitrary ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ - that kills off a character per incorrect response - and you can't save.

I heartily encourage others who feel the same way to speak up, because this game continues to absorb undue credit for being different, while the only notable exception to this game seems to be its unworkable set of rules.

I'm sure I'll get a lot of disapproval for this review but I played it while it was free this time around, and I was having a lot of fun at first. Scavenge for food, meds, gear, upgrade your base, have your people stand guard, sleep, or leave for the night to find materials. It was working out really well at first, until I started reaching dangerous areas. I'd like to preface this with the fact that I restarted after having a survivor die once, believing I just performed the combat incorrectly or something since my weapon did little to no damage while the person I was raiding killed me in two swipes of a knife.

I can't for the life of me understand how you're supposed to kill someone without getting a gun. Without having past experience, you don't know how strong weapons are, or if your gun will one shot a soldier or end up getting you killed. And even if you're lucky and manage to kill someone who isn't a bandit or soldier (even thought they might attack you first), the mechanics that revolve around the sadness and depression caused by killing or stealing are just annoying. You NEED food because the game's RNG doesn't want to give you more than 3 food scraps a night? Well sorry because you're going to have to steal from that elderly couple and now your characters will constantly moan about how awful they are every 10 seconds for the next few days. 

In a real scenario, I would go there, realize that the only option would be to steal and kill their mood, and immediately leave to go somewhere else. But once you go somewhere, even if you leave instantly, your night is over. You have no room for error and the only way to know about the specific ways each individual place works is through experience. That means that if you go somewhere on day 7 that you haven't gone before because you need to or else your characters will starve, if it turns out you actually can't get anything good from it then you lose. Have fun restarting, because you either have to deal with that or look up areas on the wiki.

Example: I needed food, had raided every "food" labelled area that had popped up so far, and the garage was the only one left. The description says I might be able to sneak in and take goods if I don't have anything to trade them, so I send in my scavenger and quickly realize there is absolutely no way to sneak in because of the randomly generated level. There is a single entrance guarded by this guy who wants to trade with me but won't let me in. Now if I had known that, I would have maybe tried going to the supermarket or something that had a danger warning even though I didn't have a solid weapon yet but I didn't, solely because I hadn't seen the area before. So instead of running back to grab medicine to trade with the man, I had to head home and skip to the morning. Why? It took absolutely no time to get there, and I left withing an in game hour. Why am I not allowed to go back and grab what I need and take maybe 3 hours to do so or some other penalty?

On a subsequent run, I went to the supermarket, realizing I needed as much food as possible and my RNG pool was awful meaning I had no valuables drop and I needed the others for crafting. So even the rare trader that shows up would only have a few pieces of food and the loot I had gotten the night before now went into trading for food instead of being able to actually progress by building more barricades or upgrading my metalworks. When I got to the supermarket, the literal first door I came to had a man behind it with a woman, and he was basically harassing her. Seeing as I had no other option, I opened the door to have my character IMMEDIATELY die to his assauilt rifle before I could even turn to run. 

Now during these 15 days of playtime over two runs, I had never encountered another survivor so once I only had two left because one died, I pretty much ran out of options. Have one sleep and one scavenge? Well then we get raided and lose our food. Have one guard and the other sleep? Well now I can't find any new resources. Have one scavenge and the other guard? Now neither of them have any sleep and I have to spend half of the next day sitting there doing absolutely nothing while they sleep for however long they want to.

The food system is just obnoxious. I undertsnad why it's there and it makes sense that your characters get hungry every night. But if because of the random loot pools I only get 3 pieces of meat from an entire place that says it has "Large amounts of food", I really don't understand how I'm supposed to keep going on. It makes you feel like you have to get food every single night, so you never have an opportunity to scavenge places without food drops. And why can't you have two people scavenge in one night? That would solve the problem because then you'd run the risk of being raided with one person at home, either sleeping or guarding and being exhausted the next day. But nope, you have to have everyone stay at home except that one scavenger.

The stacks are so small when looting that you have to leave around 80% of what you find whenever you go scavenging. The wood and scraps that you need? Maybe 20 of each. But in that case you need to take two trips and have to waste a night bringing back half of that and food, meaning the next night there is no more food there and you're going to have to starve them just to upgrade that workshop or something.

Now I'm sure I'm going to get a lot of hate surrounding the fact that "I'm not good" or whatever by people with 150 hours in the game, but that's the issue. If this game revolves around trial and error until you understand the mechanics, then why is the permadeath so destructive? Again, not a single survivor ever came to the house to join us so I was stuck with three people until one of them died leaving two which can't run it by themselves very well. There are absolutely no tutorials which I'm fine with, but when I get so heavily penalized for not knowing what I'm doing when a tutorial could have cleared it up, that just pisses me off. After three hours of playing I just couldn't restart again, it felt like a lost effort once I hit any area that had even the "Cautious" warning.

TL;DR:
I'm sure a lot of people can end up loving this game and put over a hundred hours into it, but when it comes down to it, the food and combat systems, as well as the spastic RNG absolutely ruined the game for me.

5-6 hours played

Pros:
Provides enough of a challenge to make your party's plight significant without being overwhelming.

No save scumming, you have live with your choices which is appropriate for the style/atmosphere.

Atmospheric. Successful art style.

Cons:
You cannot choose when to save: it only auto-saves at the start of each new day. This is very frustrating if you want to stop because you'll lose your progress.

Related: the pacing is dictated by the clock which means at times you literally have to wait for a character to complete a long action with nothing to do but watch a circle fill up and no way to fast forward.

No plot. From the description I thought there would be more of a story. There are little events, and your choices do have consequences, but you are forced to react to the game instead of the other way around. Also, in nearly 6 hours of play, I can think of maybe 4 plot events, each of which only occur for a moment.

The description also states that you don't play as a soldier. Maybe I just got lucky, but I was able to kill a rifle toting guy using just a shovel, taking very little damage myself. I then used his rifle to kill the other two enemies. Now all my characters have a gun, which drastically increases the power of my party. I understand the point isn't to win the war, but I don't feel like a civilian now.

Conclusion: I wouldn't choose to buy it for $20, but I can see why some people like it. I do remember playing a free Android game with nearly identical gameplay...

This game has alot of fun aspects, the setting is very different and thought provoking. You have alot of options for playstyles, you can get by just scavenging, crafting, trading and getting into minimal fights. There's alot of variety to the characters and locations, offering alot of replayability.

Combat is not too fastpaced or too slow and the game achieves alot, even despite how simple the game engine and controls are.

There are a few annoying RNG based mechanics that impact gameplay to much imo., like the events on each daybreak. It's not uncommon for characters to leave the shelter, even if they are only just sad and hungry. 

Some times sickness and wounds get worse even though the character is fed and resting. A bad chain of events like characters fighting, arguing or sleeping badly at night, can easily end your game in a few turns of the day. 

These random events also makes stealing from innocents a very risky strategy, even with the least symphathetic characters. As soon as a few of your characters become sad, you risk getting railroaded by RNG events.  

On the other hand it takes a very long time or a huge amount of resources to recover from sadness and depression.

It's very tempting to save scum and restart the day when dwellers leave the shelter or start a downward spiral of depression that could take up to 10-15 days to recover from or effectively end your game.

I don't think these events should be removed entirely, but they can often impact the game too much.

I normally wait awhile before I review a game, just so I can return to it and see if my opinions have changed. This War of Mine is consistently rated high for me. I bought it on a whim, years ago, and it remains one of my favorite to this day and I play it for a few hours from time to time. 

You play a group of survivors in a war torn country that has to do everything it takes to survive. Nobody is a big hero, and there's no glorious victory or defeat. You're average folk who have to make some hard, life altering decisions to just survive. It's impossible to have a solid play through of the game where you don't sit in agony over a single decision, because you know someone isn't going to make it, or you might have to steal from other folk, or turn down some neighbors in need of assistance. The list goes on and you have to choose between others or taking care of your own. 

As far as the gameplay goes, it's a unique yet solid take on platforming. I am generally not one to play platformers, but this one has a lot of depth with the multiple floors, looting options, hiding, etc. Audio is top notch. The UI can be a tad clunky at first as you get the hang of it, but you'll figure out the best way to navigate it quickly.

There is a custom campaign option, where you can set specific parameters in the game, create your own survivors, or load some in with the workshop. This helps add to the replayability of the game, as you can have custom campaigns and play them the way you desire. 

All in all, really solid, fun game that you can dump some surprisingly long hours into. Especially when the whole game is new to you, it is really easy to get caught up in the experience.

This is a surpsingly addictive game and I would recommend it to nearly anyone.

This is a sobering look, subtlety told through the eyes of civilian survivors caught up in a war they did not want. 
You control a handful of people banding together just trying to survive. These you are given a house that needs repair as well as some supplies in which you must build equipment and tools to further your survival. At night you elect one of the group members to carefully hunt for supplies in other locations near by.

If Katia screws up trying to steal some food from other survivors and was caught and shot dead the rest of the house feels this and mourns which effects other aspects of the game. Coming back to this game, I feel like I need to update my review as initially it wasn't received well. Well, I say that is if I'm some famous reviewer for this game, but I don't think it's sat well with me how much I bashed this game. That won't change however, so suck it.

In terms of story, this game is supposed to mimic that of a group of survivors in a besieged city during a war. The development team is Polish so I would assume it is supposed to resemble one of the many eastern-european wars that have occurred over the years. Most recently with the invasion of Ukraine by Russia, this game may have had an uptick in attention as it has become relevant again recently, and I think this game does a good job of creating an experience of being survivors in a city affected by war.

The gameplay is extremely simple and, unfortunately, suffers from extreme ludonarrative dissonance. I went on and on about the combat before and I do still think it's one of the most important parts of the game to discuss but I'll try and summarise everything into bite-size paragraphs.

The gameplay is split up into two phases, day and night. 

Day consists of interacting with visitors(accepting tasks, trading, recruiting new survivors), building/upgrading your utilities, and maintaining the health of your survivors. The day segment realistically has very little to it and once you understand what utilities, upgrades, and equipment is worth it and what isn't. Once you get a basic setup going, the day segment turns into an awkward waiting phase in-between the actual combat, and it gets very boring quickly.

Night consists of scavenging and combat. Scavenging is at the whim of RNG, but this is due to the game seemingly generating available loot either on the first visit to a map, or when you first search a container. Loot can range from getting just a few items, or get many items, so it gets frustrating when you loot a lot but get nothing out of it. 

The combat is where this game falls flat. The majority of your fighting will be either stealth  or with guns / melee weapons. The latter is *awful* because of how the combat works. You press a button popup to attack, but I've had plenty of times where I would be stunlocked as you have just about 1 second to react and press the button to attack, and if you don't you get hurt instead. The stunlocking leads me to always avoid fighting and simply stealth kills enemies as enemies do tend to conveniently conveyor belt past hiding locations. Guns are very deadly in this game, so if you get the first shot off you tend to win, as you can also stunlock other enemies. At least it's fair, some-what.

Intermission : I need to point out that this game truly isn't difficult. The difficulty mostly comes from what you loot and how much loot the game graces you with. That and...

The mood mechanic. It sucks and it contributes to the overall issue with this game. Other reviews have said it better than I could but I'll try to explain. The sadness mechanic consists of being Conte, sad, depressed, and broken. There is overall more negative factors than positive that affect mood in this game, so maintaining mood is one of the most difficult parts of this game. Especially because almost all 'bad' things you can do in this game tend to reduce the mood significantly faster than positives.

I think this boils down to the fact that this game was made as an informative "experience" and not made to be a game to be won. I've seen many comments and reviews that suggest negative reviews are "missing the point" but I disagree. I agree that this game is developed as an experience but I disagree that people are missing the point. This game is, at the end of the day, a game and should be reviewed as such. If the game is bad and unbalanced(which I think overall it is), then I'd argue that it detracts from the experience the story provides. It's the developer's just to make the game fun to play otherwise, what the hell is the point?

I think the experience is fantastic but the gameplay itself isn't really that fun to play. It's not even a particularly difficult game. It takes a couple playthroughs at most to figure out the optimal way to play, and further playthroughs play the same. I genuinely feel that this game is gruelling and cruel and simulates what it *may* feel like for some in a war-torn world, but the game detracts from it because it just simply isn't fun. 

It's unfortunate but this game fails to deliver adequate gameplay in exchange for an experience that has been mislabelled as "punishing on purpose" and "realistic, a truly depressing and gruelling experience". I can only assume these comments come from people that don't play difficult games very often or regularly play video games at all, and forget that a game does have to actually be fun regardless of the message it's trying to deliver.

Initially, I was a bit turned off by this game, as all of the reviews (even the good ones) called it depressing, and I just wasn’t in the mood to be bummed out.  When I finally picked it up, I just didn’t get that vibe.  The stories can be sad, and the lore you experience can be melancholy, but the game itself is still about overcoming challenges and hardship.  And I think that message is what made this game addicting for me.

The atmosphere and sound design are incredibly immersive.  There’s tension everywhere, and even a friendly knock on the door can be terrifying.  This is when you know a game has pulled you in and demonstrated just how helpless you are.  The art style portrays the hard times and difficult environment, but it is also so beautifully done.  It’s hard to not admire it sometimes, even when everyone is struggling.  The characters also have interesting back stories, and you even learn to care about some of them. Some.

One of my only complaints is that once I beat the game, I felt like I learned the “formula” needed to be successful in this game.  There were also only so many places to explore, and very little changed about them.  This meant you knew what to expect every play through.  This dropped the replayability a lot for me, and it also killed a bit of the magic I first had when I initially played.  

My other complaint is that I think ALL of the characters are too sensitive about the same things.  I can understand some not wanting to steal to survive, but it negatively affects almost EVERYONE.  For example, some replayability could come from treating situations differently.  Maybe I want to try stealing to survive, or defending myself with weapons while scavenging (meaning, I could potentially kill someone).  Well, I can’t, because every character will take each of those actions so negatively, they’ll most likely kill themselves if I play this way.  This sort of mechanic felt a bit shallow to me.  Maybe not shallow, but I felt like the devs definitely want you to play it their way.

Even though I have those complaints, I cannot overstate how much I recommend this game.  It’s beautifully done, and there’s nothing else out there quite like it.  Trust me, I’ve checked when I needed to scratch that itch.  Thanks to the devs for a great game!

This game is one I have enjoyed playing and continue to enjoy. It's one of the few games that can, successfully, have a meaningful and real-life'plot' while still being genuinely enjoyable. 

The premise is truly evocative and makes you think on issues that, as a westerner, i often do not think of: the plight of those stuck/trapped in cities and countries struck by war, civil unrest or even civil war. This is not something I personally have ever thought of so I found this game interesting and enjoyable to play.

This game is thought-provoking, you are struck with moral decisions that have consequences, for instance one  member of my group committed suicide after I had him kill a son and father to gain their food and other resources. This had knock-on affects for the rest of my group brining their morale down as well, resulting in them all being depressed, not wanting to scavenge and eventually starving to death. If you get into this situation with no alcohol or cigarettes then you may drive yourself into a corner like I did. You can invite other survivors to join your group, so a loss doesn't necessarily mean you've irreversibly screwed up, just a minor/major setback in your groups' continued survival.

The gameplay is smooth and I have had virtually no problems, dying is not hard but you won't die in a few hits either. The threats are very real and you have to be careful when scavenging, I really like how they convey the fear of the unknown to the player and you really understand how difficult and scary it can be to live in this sort of situation.

There are political overtones in this game so do be warned, they are not too bad, but it leans heavily on open-borders and the 'refugee' (migrant) crisis, in this case the eastern European migrants. This was reinforced and I think stated far more explicitly in the DLC Little  Ones. This was however, done in a way that I, as a conservative female Brit, did not find offensive or put me off the game. It made it very interesting and you can see that the creators truly care about this issue and made an entire game dedicated on educating and telling people the stories of some of these people.
I find that very commendable.

After a year-long hiatus on this game and numerous others, I finally got around to resetting my computer entirely and now have reinstalled the game. Jesus Christ I couldn't have done it fast enough. Simply starting this game and being greeted by its hauntingly beautiful soundtrack is utterly spellbinding.  

Drawing inspiration from the Bosnian War and its numerous battles, The Siege of Sarajevo in particular, This War of Mine utilises real stories and events from survivors of the Bosnian War to paint a vivid picture. In This War of Mine you control a group of survivors that are thrust into an unknown warzone, the point of the anonymity aids the game in relaying the fact that a conflict like this can and will be happening somewhere in the world. This group must fight, scavenge and survive until the conflict is resolved, weapons and tools are rarity, food and water more so.  

Every decision you make, you make for the group, and if you wish for the pack to survive, you best make the right ones. Constantly hammering you with ACTUALLY impactful adaptions to the gameplay and ACTUALLY punishing you for stupid or "necessary" mistakes or judgements. Enter buildings at your own risk, steal from those less fortunate or outright kill others and become as mad as the world around you, the choice and freedom of your decisions will reverberate through the community and your other housemates however. 

The soundtrack is as I've previously said, hauntingly beautiful, taking inspiration from games like the Metro series, it's sweeping and yet at times so focused on minor details. Such as the winds providing an almost breeze-like effect, the lone guitar providing something that can hook the player in and can feel solidarity to. Other times the music shifts to a much darker tone, leaving open to anxious thoughts and allowing panic and fear to enter your once resolute mind. In short, Piotr Musial has done a gorgeous job and provided something that could hold a flame to composers such as Alexy Omelchukand, Keiichi Okabe and Austin Wintory 

The gameplay and UI are simplistic, taking away any unnecessary filler information that could distract you from completing your tasks. Your tasks for the day are easy; stay home, build and shore up whatever defences you can, maintain the wellbeing of your household and keep warm. Simple as. However, when night comes, so do the monsters who hide in plain sight. Opting to either keep all your occupants home and safe, or risking the night is a harsh but easy one, risking a bullet to the head certainly keeps the house fed after all. So, with whatever tools that can be found or made and hopefully some protection, the scavenger can get to work. This is where a majority of your thinking skills come in handy, figuring out who to hit. Do you go for the hospital where medicine and clean water are in surplus, but you're ultimately stealing from those far worse off than you, or do you steal from the elderly couple whose house has remained untouched, but your very presence strikes fear into their hearts. Especially when they catch you stealing from them.  Again, completely up to you, but for every ill deed there comes a reckoning. 

Scrolling past some of the other user reviews it's easy to be disheartened or even scoff at seeing the fifth review calling it "depressing" or seeing some diva whine about the how emotionally scarred they are after playing this game. But the funny thing is, they're true, at least partially. This game IS depressing, it's heart wrenching, punishing and judging. But that's exactly the point. No longer are you John Generic, US Marine and world champion crayon eater who saves the day by shooting anything dressed in red and has the words EVIL ductaped to its head. You are a human being, flawed, complicated and up a very large creek called ♥♥♥♥. This War of Mine isn't meant to be another story about John Generic saving the world, it's about you, and the choices you make to save the house that is your world.  

This is a sobering game. These events have happened, will happen and will continue to happen. War is an unending cycle, it's something humanity is good at and let's face it, people don't like to stop when they've realised their potential. However, instead of picking up the controller or opening up GTA: V to have some 11-year-old tell you about his sexual conquests whilst he blasts you from three kilometres away. Buy this game and attempt to live as a stable house whilst the ever-present fear of failure, madness and death breathe down your neck. Suffer, and witness what it's like to be one of people caught in John Generic's crossfire.

Challenging - Can't just blast everything in sight and upgrade to bigger guns if you have a problem. Characters might need food, sleep, heat, safety, bandages or drugs - some are emmotionally and morally fragile. Some make better use of the limited resources you have.  Some are better at negotiation. It is very much a strategy game where you make choices about who you will help and who you will let suffer for the greater good of your 'household'. Inevetiably due to the limited resources most characters suffer to some degree most of the time during a game.

You 'win' when the war is declared as over but this is not a fixed point in time or a particular glorious feeling. It is more like "Thank god! - Thought I'd nearly lost those fragile wimps!" rather than a "Yes! - Totally mastered that survvial thing."  But sometimes "Why so soon? - I was just getting started!"

I think the developers have actually conveyed that feeling of hopelessness and unfairness during a war (within the context and emotional bounds of a safely played game that is!). It's a bit scary and depressing but can also be challenging. It can go from "I'm sailing through this" to "Oops! - What happened" pretty quick.

In summary: Primarily a strategy game where your strategy is backed up with your point and click ability about what resources you get. A suprisingly good game when you get into it. I am really glad I bought it.

This War of Mine is one of the very few games that makes death carry weight. In many video games, killing someone is just overcoming an obstacle; that is not the case in This War of Mine. Bandits are usually nameless, faceless, evil carriers of loot. However, in this game, it's possible they're just another person struggling to survive. Killing them for their food is as good or evil as them killing you for yours. The scarcity of goods and resources make you take things you normally would avoid into actual consideration. Maybe you do need to steal from others. You don't always have the option of strolling into any random location and securing food for the entire house. It's a struggle. You make sacrifices. And that's part of what makes it a very engaging game.

On gameplay and mechanics: 
This War of Mine suffers from a few gameplay issues. The "End Day" button should have been replaced with a "The Sims" style fast-forward button. There's often too much you have to do to make use of skipping ahead all at once. Enjoying the ambience and the soundtrack while watching your characters sleep is nice at first, but it gets old very quickly.

Left mouse, middle mouse, and right mouse all perform the same action. I instinctively use middle mouse to drag the camera around, but if you click without dragging, it will order a move command on that character. It's very frustrating to have your character move to a location while they're supposed to be sleeping because you tried to move the camera. The ability to disable commands on middle mouse click would be a huge quality of life improvement.

On the topic of replayability: 
With a few additions by the developers, I feel you could get much more mileage out of this game. Beating the game with different groups of civilians sounds like a nice challenge on paper, but things get extremely repetitive when your shelter remains the same. The two current shelters are too similar. You end up putting your furniture in the same spots every run. If each group got their own unique shelter to use, I would be excited to play every group. After two successful runs, I don't know if I can play another simply because of this. A small shelter, like the Shelled Cottage location, fits the solo and two-person groups perfectly. You would have to manage your space carefully, as you wouldn't have room for much furniture.

The ability to add custom civilians is great, but being able to build custom shelters out of pre-made rooms would add so much more replayability.

This is an immersive game that illustrates an often-overlooked side of war within gaming. As a civilian you try to stay away from violence but in the warzone, it will come looking for you. The challenge of this game is the choices that are and that aren’t presented to the player. A few quests involve neighbours needing help and wanderers looking for supplies. But most of the time it is you trying to improve the situation of your shelter. All is well as you loot buildings for wood and adhesive to make a workshop or a comfortable chair. But you will probably face multiple occasions where you desperately need to find food or medicine to keep one or more survivors from dying. Often in these scenarios you will lack anything to trade for expensive medicine and there are no more empty buildings up for grabs. If no more supplies will be given or can be found, then it must be taken. You decide whether stealing, threatening or murdering is worth the need that you have. The game however does not force you to take a stand on a certain moral question at any time, it only tells you to do something or perish. Often you will have to choose the least bad option to survive which could be sending a sleep depraved person with a high fever into the warzone as your best chance to find food for the next day. The DLC The Little Ones will introduce children to the game and will add a new spectrum of emotion to the gameplay, which is very recommended. 

The game is a dark illustration of human nature. But it also brings out the very best of it with kindness, cooperation, love and hope. 10/10, no doubt about it.

The game executes its concept well - that's the one thing I did not expect from a simple indie game like this one. You play as a group of survivors living their lives avoiding the war while facing the brunt of the impact on society. By day you sort out what resources you have and make use of them, by night you go out to scavenge or rest. The soundtrack for this game is gorgeous, the background music at home just helps you feel welcome and safe; during scavenge missions you can feel the intensity in a hostile area or otherwise in empty areas you feel melancholy. 

I played this game for a few hours the first time around and actually found this process so mundane and simple, even boring. And then I realized I had been playing this for a few hours - the game gets you hooked on managing your survivors. Days can pass by extremely fast in the game and your survivors need time to rest before you can get anything done if you've sent them out during the night. Each day becomes a struggle of trying to get things done before nightfall and giving your survivors things to do or rest. Then comes the night and unless you're well stocked for the next day, you have to send a survivor out and risk their lives to bring back valuable resources. Some locations have enemies which make scavenging a dangerous endeavour and injured survivors become a pain to care for, even worse dead survivors destroy the morale and cognition of your remaining ones.

The game however does have a trait I don't like too much: the scavenge inventory. Without the use of mods that improve item stacking, scavenging areas is a massive pain. Every location in this game has so much loot that taking it all in as little tries as possible is a chore. I understand this is to help move the game along and give you incentive to return to an area multiple times to continue picking out what you need. However, some items have a very bad stack to scavenge ratio. Most notably are the wood planks, of which two will take up a whole inventory slot out of 10 (on an average survivor) while many items give out a generous amount of planks. [b]HOWEVER[/b], thankfully due to the availability of Steam Workshop mods, this problem is easily remedied and not detrimental to the fun I've had in this game. The game also comes with an option to customize your survivors (to an extent) and allows for endless roleplay potential if you're into that sort of thing.

Definitely worth your money. Sort of like the game Fallout Shelter, but more in-depth, and more realistic.

[h2]Who Lives, Who Dies, Who Tells Your Story[/h2]

[h3]Who Lives[/h3]
Unlike most war games that glorify victory and heroism, This War of Mine shifts the focus to the civilians caught in the crossfire. As a player, you control a group of survivors hiding in a crumbling shelter, scavenging for food and medicine at night while avoiding snipers during the day. The scarcity of resources and the weight of moral dilemmas make every decision feel like walking on a knife's edge. There are no heroic moments here, only relentless struggle and compromise.

[h3]Who Dies[/h3]
When supplies run low, do you steal from others or risk venturing into more dangerous areas? When a companion falls ill and medicine is scarce, do you save them or keep the cure for yourself? There are no right answers, only harsh consequences. Most of the time, survival is a zero-sum game. You might save a few, but more often, you’re left watching helplessly as one by one, your companions succumb to hunger, injury, or despair.

[h3]Who Tells Your Story[/h3]
The endings are rarely happy. Even if you manage to survive, the cost is often unbearable. Scattered radio broadcasts and forgotten diaries serve as makeshift epitaphs for those who didn’t make it. When the war is over, will anyone remember the ordinary people who suffered, or will their stories fade into obscurity, untold and unheard?

[h1]Intro:[/h1]
In This war of Mine, you control a ragtag group of survivors surving an all out catastrophic war. No one can get in, and no one can get out. Trying to do fancy shenagians will have you either pinned to a wall by rebel gangs, arrested by the military or made into a punching bag. Or you know ... die. 


[b]I will warn you[/b], while this game does not look outright scary, the things that will happen to your survivors and the other NPCs of this game will at times horrify you, scare you and maybe just maybe teach you about how privelleged you are to sit comfortably in front of your computer safe and sound. I speak this from experience as this game will throw hardship after hardship at you, which if you aren't emotionally sound will end up breaking you.


[h1]Story 10/10 [/h1]
Your main goal is to survive in this mess, with as bad as a starting condition as you'll ever realise. Even the easiest options still leave you on your toes. The game is as much as a challenge as it is a lesson to the hardships udnergone by the people who are in this condition everyday for years. Pinned down, down on thier luck, no one to cry out for and no one to even to hear a word.

Thankfully the game gives you a trio of pre-set citizens each with their own unique quirks, backstory and progressing storyline. Did I forget to mention that these guys still have to smoke and do drugs just to remain sane (not sure how the latter works but it just is). 

You manage a broken home, randomly generated with meager suppleis that you must scurry to find fast or the second-third night WILL kill you.  You build stuff to survive the days, months and soon years (if you picked endless) , such as builiding various workshops, lights, stoves, beds , chairs and everything in between. Not to forget that keeping your survivors sane is a big thing as well as keeping them healthy and well rested. You then prowl the night at various locations that you progressively discover as the game progresses. The story of your characters come out from these actions in their little bio tab on their pictures, and you will learn to love or hate your own survivors as well as learn their strengths ( the selfish one doesn't gets motivated easily and murders by other chars will matter less to them for example).

Throughout your struggle, and I will admit you WILL struggle the entire length of the game, not once does the game give you respite other than your survivors aiding each other physcologcially ( which can also be your guys screaming in pain and agony as everything falls around you) . This will always be a double edge sword for you, and the Little Ones DLC will only add to your hope OR agony. 

The game will move you in the most subtle ways imaginable and trust me that this game is more of a reminder of the horrors and sometimes valiancy of the civilians of war. 

This game will teach you that there are no enemies, just men, women, children trying to return to their normal lives. Some break, some steal, some give, but most importantly the all want out from this hell. The decisions you make in this game will include these people, but are you willing to push away or lend a hand all for the sake of seeing tomorrow?



[h1] Gameplay 9/10 [/h1] 
The gameplay is hard, you build and manage your shelter by day and scavenge for resources by night. You will have to endlessly manage your survivors as time progresses. the one who went scavenging will grow tired and you must trade for another to go out, even if he/she is very poor at it. Simialr to games like BEHOLDER and PAPER'S PLEASE, certain events will happen while on either stage. You might hear an alleged rape attempt while pillaging an abondoned (or so you thought) house. You might find kids asking you to help their mother (Little Ones DLC). Or your friendly-ish neighbourhood trader may come and visit. 

You start out with near nothing,and must work with what you get from clearing out your home to survive the next comming days before you can really start progressing as the supplies you obtain from night scavenging pull you through better. Note: keeping stuff outside your home may ahve better odds than keeping it at home as night raids are a thing (which require yet another survivor standing duty, so really only one guy gets to sleep). These odds soon leave your survivors very broekn and tired, and you may have to take risks and leaving your home wide open to raids in order to ensure their survival (which mind you may gimp yous eriously later on as raids tend to steal everything you have). This makes for a game that is ever changing, you must continuously adapt, take risks often and choose between gimping yourself to save someone or letting them die so you one less mouth to feed. It's all really haunting if you reach deeper into it and the accompanying chats your survivoors will make will make you doubt how you are really managing the situation at hand. It's appropriately tough, just like the real thing and if you have the guts to stomach through, you will be rewarded with the sweet hand of saving people from this hell. 

The game leaves you to decide how your morals are, and whether you choose your humanity or your life. Maybe listening to the radio's jazz station may soften up the mood a bit.

The game does tend to become a bit repetitive after a while but it never has a dull moment.


[h1] Atmosphere 10/10 [/h1]
Hands down, the best atmosphere I've ever seen in a game. the visuals are so well designed , the sleepy music captures just how fragile the situation is, the occasional gunshot from afar, the omnious whimpering during scavenging and the best of all. The music dies when something big is happening, fully putting you in a sudden situation at hand. Never had the decision to bash a guy's head been more nerve-wracking. This game is more like a war memorial to all those innocent civilians than an actual game for how well it mimics the real thing. I applaud the developers, so so much for this aspect alone. The responses of the poor citizens you're looting from and the hellish thing some rebels say ... just makes it all too real. 

[h1] Overall Verdict 10/10 [/h1]
Pain and Angush turned Courage and Survival against all odds make This War of Mine truly a gem of a game but the real decisiveness of this game lies in it's strength in putting the player at odds with their own morals, seeing how dire a war is, and utterly breaking you over decisions that can't be reset.Seeing your survivors rise up or become the villians is all up to you, as long as you get to live for a few more days.

 The game is more of a testament of the atrocities of war than anything really, and the sheer nerve-wracking situations you'll be put in will make it more than worth it even at it's original price. I highly-recommend this game, it is truly ONE OF A KIND.

War is raging all over the city. You direct a group of survivors to hopefully make it through the upcoming hazards. 

TWoM is a really great strategic survival game. Beginning may be difficult, as you learn the game. Everything is trial and error, every action seems to have it's consequences. Try to remind yourself about it when you point a gun at a harmless old couple, just because you need some food. 

Game is full of troublesome moments - from sickness, through managing your puppets diet, up until general resource shortage during winter. You'll also be fighting off other people that try to steal your precious stuff, especially during the criminal outbreak. 

Mechanics wise the game is really good. The further you get, the more hectic it gets, the more stuff to do and choices to make there are. One weak point is that if you know what you're doing, you can make yourself completely self sufficient and independent from all external food, medical and whatever else sources. It makes the game slightly boring after that point, but it's only a really small con. This War of Mine takes you in it's grasp and doesn't want to let you out. "Just one more day and I'll turn it off", "Just one more scavenging action", "I'll wait for a trader and then go to sleep". Game gives you constant challenges and isn't really holding itself back on throwing logs under your feet, which makes the gameplay incredibly consistent, engaging and fun. 

Graphics wise TWoM excells in it's kind. Not because of very detailed, well polished 3D explosions and character detail, but because of the unique art style. It's done really well - ruined buildings, people acting differently  depending on their state, nighttime during scavenging, the tiny details here and there. It makes this title really immersive and easy to pick up for any postapo and survival fans out there.

Would I recommend it? Hell yes. It's a great title to just sit there in your headphones and forget about the whole world. Just...just survive.
