~The last two days of my first playthrough~

It had been a run of bad luck. The food had run out four days ago, the medicine even longer. Pavle, the best runner of the group had set out in search of something to eat - anything to eat. During the night, combing through the ruins of a once proud city he came across a frail old man in what used to be his home asking for medicine for his son. The old man tells Pavle his son is very sick, bed-ridden for days. He'd be willing to trade any food for any medication Pavle can provide - he won't however, consider anyting else. 

Another dead end then? Pavle's face drops as he says goodbye and turns to walk away. Then it occurs to him... the old man appears unarmed. Surely he would struggle to defend himself? Once he's past him, a sickly son inside would hardly pose a threat either! Besides, didn't his friends back home need the food more..?

For a brief moment, Pavle forgoes humanitarian thought and decides killing the elderly neighbour is necessary, tightening the grip on the kitchen knife hidden in his coat pocket. But before he can act, hunger relents... and makes way for shame. Pavle opens his mouth to say something, but there were no words - nothing to articulate the regret he felt for what had nearly been. Disgusted with himself at having considered such evil, he hurriedly leaves to head back towards the shelter.

On his way back out however, something caught his eye - something buried beneath the rubble of a war-torn hotel. Beneath the shattered brick, and broken timber lay a kitchen unit, a perfect-intact unit. Pavle scrambled to open the cupboards, now possessed by the desperation of hunger and his starving friends at home waiting for him. Yes!! Inside there were stacks of unopened tin cans, enough to last a week or more! 

Pavle filled his rucksack to the top and leant back into the rubble almost as if it were a warm bath. There was nothing funny about this war of his - but for some reason all he could do was laugh, laughter of relief - at how insane this situation was. Before the war he was a footballer, yet today he was scraping through rubble, dodging shells and snipers - as well as trading with the homeless. 

As Pavle stood to leave, ready to bring the good news back to his friends, two figures stepped out of the shadows cast by the ransacked hotel. Without saying a word, a flash of steel in the moonlight from one of the figures plunged itself into Pavle's chest, while another came from behind. As Pavle fell to his knees he slowly raised his head to speak, tears forming around his eyes - but before the words came out - to beg - to let them know his friends were starving - a stranger stood over him, and the killing blow was dealt.

Back at the shelter next morning, things had gone from bad to worse. Early that morning, looters had paid a visit to Katia and Bruno whilst they slept. Everything they had, was gone - taken by thieves and cowards. Bruno had been grievously injured and was unable to leave his bed in the basement, whilst Katia's wounds barely allowed her to get to the chair they had placed by the ruined porch. As she sat down in that familiar place, she realised there was nothing left inside. Nothing in her to hold on to for hope. Pavle was dead, that she was certain of - and with no food or medicine, nor any way to aquire some - all that was left was to wait. 

Wait... for hunger or sickness to cast over them the cold shadow of death.

While other games encourage you to play 'survival of the fittest', 'get the bad guy', 'regret nothing', 'rule at the top', and other game play mechanics; TWoM takes a knew approach. While yes the player still has the choice of pillaging, murdering, and serving themselves there can be serious consequences. The player and characters can actually suffer from cruel acts adding a large slice of reality to the game. Whats more, TWoM offers more pacifistic routs like helping neighbors, donating supplies, taking in survivors, surviving with and even surviving with minimal to no hostile moves on the players part. As with hostile choices, the player/characters will still live with the consequences positive or negative. This adds a bit a realism, joy, guilt, remorse, and a huge amount of perspective. 

Of course with any game there are bugs, problems, and features that the community may or may not want to see implemented. Luckily the dev team is very talented, amazing, and thoughtful of their fans. Thank-you to everyone at 11 Bit Studio's! You guys are truely awesome! :D

[b]My review for This War of Mine[/b]

  
I've just finished This War of Mine and I must admit I was a little sceptical of a Sims-like approach to a war game, that said, when I saw my partner playing it and I was instantly hooked and bought it that very night.  

Whilst a combat-element is certainly there, this 2.5D side-scroller game revolves around keeping your small group of survivors as content as possible whilst attempting to avoid death, starvation, sickness, wounds and depression. It's so brutal losing your characters (the few you start with is all you get per game) that when you actually find yourself faced with a dangerous situation you are often much better off sneaking around and stealing what you need to avoid combat in the early stages.  

  
The game works in a two-part day and night cycle, during the day, you are at your base where you can craft, build and attend to your survivors needs via a fantastic progressive-crafting system used for supplies, food, weapons, even items like beds, rat-traps and water-collectors. Then during the night, you can set survivors to sleep or guard the base whilst you send an individual survivor out to one of the many different areas to scavenge for food, weapons, ammo, building components, medical supplies or other valuable items. 
  
[b]The Pros;[/b]
[list]
    [*]Nice visual style and relaxing but suitable music throughout 

  [*]A good choice of different interesting characters, all with their own perks and story 

  [*]A progressive building system within your main house/base 

  [*]Short day by day autosave so you could jump in for a quick game 

  [*]Highlights others sides to war often not seen in gaming 

  [*]It actually has a finish - when the war is over! 
[/list]
  
[b]The Cons;[/b]

[list]
    [*]I personally had a few issues using a controller but no issues with keyboard and mouse 

[*]No choice of base/house to start with 

[*]Some more involvement with other survivors would have been nice, even running missions alongside groups of survivors 
[/list]
  
[b]Conclusion;[/b]

This War of Mine is a dark and harsh game. Killing people makes your teams sad, depressed or even broken in spirit. Stealing from old people so that you can finally have a proper meal after days without may foresake those folks to death by starvation. Getting in a fight with the wrong person may end up leaving you with one less survivor making the strain harder on everyone else.  

Gritty but damn fantastic, a very well-designed game and I'm very excited to try out the DLC.

While the game isn't too original of a concept (It's essentially one of those ant farm style colony management games) its story and message are actually rather powerful. Essentially, it's a war game that takes a new point of view on war. Rather than playing as the soldiers and fighting the battles mentioned throughout your session, you play as a group of civilians. Lost, homeless, and broken with only the most basic of survival necessities. It's a rather eye opening experience on how games tend to take on the topic of war. While Battlefield, Call of Duty, and all those other FPS titles tend to glorify it, making the explosions big and the action constant, This War of Mine takes a much more human approach. You start with two or three 'survivors' of the war (Depending on who you choose to play with, you can have up to four) and start out with a bare minimum supply of food and medicine.

You would typically spend the first day clearing out debris, opening doors, and finding anything you can within your 'base' while you get your bearings. The first night would typically start with relatively safe areas to scavenge for supplies and, if you're really lucky, may even have someone to trade with. Anyway, every night you spend scavenging has a chance to bring long lasting damage to your crew's moral. If you decide to rob someone, kill another person (Even in self defense) or decide to let two civilians fight it out, resulting in the death of an innocent person, your crew will regret that decision for a long while. This regret, if left unchecked, can eventually turn into depression which can, eventually, end in suicide. The suicide will then make your crew even sadder, and so on and so forth. As a mechanic, however, sadness actually lowers the productivity of your survivors, as they lose motivation.

As for story, most of it is rather up front and basic. You're in a city under seige and you're trying to survive until a cease fire is called so that civilians can evacuate. If you read notes, graffiti, and your characters' bios (Which update at certain intervals) you can find out more about the game's plot and the life your characters had before and during the war. You'll find abandoned notes from other civilians about how snipers had just killed their best friend while scavenging, or how a school had to go under lockdown due to rising tensions in the neighborhood. Your characters will also comment on each area you enter upon their initial arrival, giving a little bit of context as to what the area used to be like.

A few flaws I've noticed, though, is that combat is a bit confusing to newer players, at least in my experience. You start nightly scavenging runs in 'scavenge' mode. A mode that doesn't let you fight until you enter 'combat' mode by clicking your weapon's icon on the side of your screen. I believe you're then supposed to click who you wish to attack, but I haven't been able to do so succesfully since most combat has been largely in the enemy's favour. Another small flaw, in the case of gameplay, is that some items are able to stack while others, which would be able to stack within reason, cannot do so in a reasonable manner or at all. For instance, you can have two planks of wood per inventory slot, but, you can't carry more than four units of 'parts' per slot despite them being a good bit smaller than a plank of wood. While this is obviously meant to make gameplay more difficult and force players to prioritize certain supplies over others, it's a bit annoying that you have to make an annoyingly large amount of trips to pick up items that, really, should be able to fit in your inventory based on the game's logic.

The game is definitely a challenge early on and supplies tend to be rather rare throughout the entire game but, and there's always a but, it gets kind of easy in the later game if you plan properly. If you prioritize barricading and weapons, you'll be almost immune to raids and you'll be able to kind of brute force your way through hostile areas, assuming you're able to bring a gun and plenty of ammo (Which are both relatively hard to obtain early on). If you plan well ahead of time, you'll also be able to get through the winter section of the game with ease, assuming nothing goes wrong. Essentially, the game can be a cake walk for experienced players which kind of takes away the fun after a while. Newer players, however, may really enjoy the challenge of this game for a while. The decisions you have to make, and the time frame to make them in, may ultimately spell your doom if you make a choice before you're prepared for its consequences.

Overall, a solid game with a powerful message. I'd suggest it to anyone who wants a new take on war in video games.

This War of Mine scores on both sides of the spectrum. It's an honest depiction of the horrors of war as seen from the perspectives of innocent but affected bystanders. It's also a good survival game relying on tactics and resource management. The first aspect alone makes at least one playthrough worthwhile just for the experience.

It's entirely possible to survive without ever resorting to violence. As the days go by, it's getting harder and harder to scavenge for usable items though. The game's difficulty depends on the number of people in a group and a little bit on what predispositions, strengths and vices they have. Areas with cautious or hostile people, nightly raids on the shelter and cold temperatures with snowfall pose additional problems to the already heavy situation. Hardship and loss are to be expected and there's almost no way around it. 

The gameplay revolves around a rudimentary crafting system, scavenging for resources at night and tending to the inhabitant's needs by day. The mechanics are reasonable and well balanced, so long as there are no bugs that may lead to inexplicable circumstances. It's troublesome encountering even minor bugs as they can easily spoil a run, but at least they're rare and the autosave function reliably solves any problems.

The overall aesthetic bears a ruined vibe with rough pencil lines, realistic and unadorned animations and gritty, cold and almost monochrome colours. Real life portraits give the character's stories a face that promotes empathy and provides a more personal form of involvement for the player. On a mechanical level, there are characters with traits that are more advantageous to the group, at least in this situation, than other characters. The portraits, however, show the people behind the sprites seen on screen and ideally suggest equal importance as human beings.

There are only a few but good ambient music tracks. Especially the acoustic guitar tracks, which are played by the characters after repairing a guitar ingame, add immensely to the atmosphere similar to the S.T.A.L.K.E.R. games. The guitar is supposed to brighten the mood of the inhabitants but really, it's there to offer respite for the player.

Without a doubt This War of Mine is a valuable and ever relevant display of how war impacts the civilian population and more precisely the fate of an individual. All the while still being an enjoyable game with flawed but essentially solid survival mechanics.

Final Review: This War of Mine is over six years old and a classic by now. I am not sure what I could add or take away from some of the reviews here. This War of Mine is a survival-themed strategy game where the player controls a group of civilian survivors in a makeshift shelter in the besieged, war-torn fictional city of Pogoren, Graznavia. The main goal of the game is to survive the war with the tools and materials the player can gather with the characters they control. Most of the characters under the player's control have no military background or any kind of survival experience, and will require constant intervention by the player to stay alive. That simple. It had different effects on the entire family when we tried it. 
PROS
Lesson: if you love survival games and teaching your kids the reality of war in a game without blood and gore. Then War of Mine may just be a great try to you
Game play: It can be very addicting and has a day to day satisfaction in accomplishing tasks development.
Simple: Clear, clean and straight forward. There is a total of 12 playable character that can be played.
Theme: It is dark and musty in its presentation that fits its theme. 
Smart: Daughter, loved it to a point. She enjoyed the stories. Son, enjoyed the strategic day to day tactics. The game has meaning which many games do not. It does not insult your intelligence and children can learn some lessons in its game play. Realism does not mean disgusting game play. 
CONS
Ironman: Though the lack of save at any time hurts, especially when a bad tactic can lead to death can frustrate many. Especially the young, since my daughter was upset that she had to stop only the morning of a day. 
Controls: My son’s biggest issue was too much mouse control during confrontations that hurt actual tactic times. The lack of Controller support hurts the speed of switching between tactics. That may frustrate players. Mouse is fine, but clunky in maneuvering in player tactics. This may change, slight con. 
Grind: A little too much repetition and not enough tactical or gameplay choices. The Upgrade unit system does force you to plan specifically and just drags out the day to day gameplay of War of mine.
Gear: Lack of Backpack upgrading can frustrate even the best planned raids. Game should not count defensive or offensive weaponry or equipment. They should have been more literal in this translation. For example, Helmet or Vest if you’re wearing it should not take up a pack slot or gun and ammunition. We understood a shovel or other units taking up space. The bad allocation design of storage can frustrate players unnecessarily. Pick one, be realistic or not. 
Depth: The game does not go beyond the initial game template. This game also is hurt by the flat development of its presentation. Better graphics, engine and presentations. For example, first person view or effects hurt its overall game play. It lacked depth. 
OVERALL: War of mine is not going to change the world in gaming, but has some great pluses, will keep you occupied, and teach survival can both teach and be fun. All of us enjoyed the overall presentation of a game that tried something different. We rewarded the passion of the developers here. I would preview the game in VIDEO in the discussion section to see if the game play is for you. It does have an expansion, but does not offer much more than a different story perspective from survivors. The game is easy to execute and play and there are online wonderful tutorials to help. My advice to the developers is go beyond the initial idea. Adding more choices and better tactics to a survival game will enhance game play and give players reasons to come back. The mood and atmosphere of this game simply is quite overwhelming.

Set in the fictional location of Pogoren, Graznavia, a group of survivors are trying to live through the rage and damage war can cause, battling hunger, illness, and bandits in order to pull through. In order to gain resources they must scavenge many locations or trade with the occasional traveling trader.

This is arguably the most grim and bleek game I have ever played. Instead of living the "glory" of war being on the frontline going 10 and 1 for kills, this game has a riveting change of perspective. Living as survivors, dealing with wounds, having to build improvements to shelter, among many other things make this game truly haunting. 

The atmosphere, sound design, and graphic design make this game just plain depressing. Dark colors, the sounds of war in the background, and very somber music play almost all the time. Also this game may test your humanity as there are some rather appalling decisions that must be made in certain parts of the game that can affect the survivor's morale.

The characterization isn't super heavy, but you truly get the sense that these are just people. Sad, worried and scared they may not see the next morning, whatever they are thinking you will see very well. 

The point-and-click gameplay may sound a little lacking, but the scavenging mechanic is pretty interesting, and it truly feels like a stealthy-type game having to avoid threats and potential killers.

Overall, this is a truly difficult and riveting game to play. It feels like the end is near after supplies start to dwindle and medication is lacking, and at that point you feel like giving up. I have to force myself to finish a game before restarting in order to get full effect and practice of this game. Nonetheless, I would recommend giving this game a try so long as you are willing to get a feeling of unease when playing it.

A game that's different to most others in the best possible way. Making you think with decisions that could benefit or cripple you in time.

Even though This War only gives you just a few options to customise how you want to start, it doesn't give you so little to choose that each new game feels like a total repeat of the last one. To help, selected DLC will give you more choice of characters and/or stories. 
Using characters to their individual strengths is important. But a big part of the gameplay requires you to manage basic resources, ensuring they are replenished as quickly as they are consumed. In addition to this, you will need to gather items to help construct equipment which will potentially make life slightly better in some way. The main challenge, whilst doing these things, comes not only in the limited amount of things you can carry whilst scavenging or looting, but also keeping an eye on the time, or you could struggle even more.

Your characters will also feel the morale pressures of the decisions you make. This is most evident if your character takes another persons life or steals from others needing these items as much as you do.

Overall, This War of Mine is fairly slow in pace and will not be one for people craving explosive action, but it delivers a thinking persons game through its unique characters, atmosphere and varied amount of in-game choices that decide how your characters will survive the hells of war.

The game gets you to control a few civilians trying to survive a war in a city called Porogen, a city now where Soldiers, Rebels and Civilians are in a constant battle in order to stay alive, some will be helpful, others won't, some will ask for your help, others will help you, so on. When you start a game, you have to wait an unknown amount of days till the war ends (it's random unless you created a  custom story), you'll have to create furniture, workbenches and other items to help you survive, you will need to scavenge for supplies each night (you can stay inside if you want to) and ration food in order to get to the end of the war.

Soon, you'll come across random events and have to loot more dangerous areas, making the game harder as you go on, so you will need to use your supplies wisely in those times. Once you have made it to the end of the war, the game ends, in the ending screen you will see the epilogue of all the characters you have met, their endings will depend on how well you survive so remember to try and make the right decisions to keep them alive and happy.

That's the game in short, it's a great game and you should definitely try it out, it doesn't cost that much and the DLC that comes with the game is also very good, including the War Child DLC in where you donate money to children living in cities and towns affected by war.

I give the game 9/10, it does have it's flaws at times, but it is certainly a game that I will always remember.

In terms of subject matter This War Of Mine is really good at what it does. However the never ending grimness does come at some cost. The game is relentlessly depressing and often boring, and not by accident but by pure intention. Your situation is essentially hopeless and that’s exactly the point the game is trying to make, but that makes it difficult to keep you engaged over the long term.

It doesnt help that the combat and stealth mechanics are awful. The AI can hear you and see you from a mile away making the dangerous missions all the more terrible. You dont have much room to hide and your characters speed is that of a drunk Walrus. Nor can you control how stealthy or quiet you are as there is no mode or mechanic to compensate for stealth. So you will slowly be pushing your controller while you sit in agonizing boredom and frustration. 

All in all its a fun little survival game but dont expect it to hold your attention to the end because you will either quit out of boredom, frustration or just beign too damn easy.

Its not 'enjoyable' per say, but it is a rewarding and satisfying experience to well, experience.

All of this making you feel part of it with the gameplay - nothing in the veins of a massive RPG that spans hundreds of hours with a great climax at the end of a tale but... the story of a father making it out of a war with their daugther, the war reporter that got stuck inside the war, just your average fellah' having to cope with surviving and knowing that danger is everywhere and not a single day can be spared!... even tho', you have to spare some days to just simply not go insane.

It difficult to explain what this 'game' can do because its a game, but also not. Its a piece of art, but one that you experience... and its also something you wish to experience, but never in a million years ever want anything near like this happen to you!

Many people have already talked about the more emotional side of this game, and I think many of their thoughts ring true. While I wouldn't go so far as some reviewers in saying this was an "emotionally difficult" game to play, I would say that it gives perspective and makes you think in ways that games usually don't. That's valuable in itself.

I think what a lot of people don't mention though is that beyond all the weighty themes, the gameplay itself is solid. It plays well, it's challenging without being overly punishing, it surprises you and keeps you on your toes, there's a definite and satisfying sense of progression. It has the quirks you would expect of a small indie title - the controls don't always work as you want them to for example, especially during combat - but they remain as quirks rather than frustrating bugs or flaws. I know others have mentioned bugs in the game, but my impression is they aren't common or game breaking as I have yet to encounter one.

I also appreciate that there is in fact an end to the game. Many games with similar approaches as this one feel content to let the game simply go on and on without end, and while that may be fine for some it's never been something I've enjoyed. I want to feel like there's a goal to the game, an end point where it all wraps up, and this game provides that.

I've really enjoyed this game thus far after putting close to 20 hours in, which was a complete playthrough and a few aborted attempts, and I can see myself putting in another playthrough or two before I decide to move on. With the full price of this game being so affordable, and sales being even cheaper, I would definitely recommend it for anyone who enjoys games with elements of base-building, strategy/stealth, and unique atmosphere.

Update: a couple weeks later and I've put in much more time than I originally expected. I've pretty much maxed out my interest in this game at this point, but it hooked me for even longer than I thought. A great game at any price, and an easy decision with the very low price of admission.

Each day in this game is a struggle, your survivors are often injured, sick or hungry and supplies to mend this ailments are few and far in between; you often have to choose who gets a meal today, who gets bandages, who gets medicine, etc. This game is full of incredibly hard decisions that expand beyond deciding who gets to eat as well; often people may come to your door begging for help, supplies or shelter and you must decide if you help them or not. While yes, donating some supplies may earn favor with them, you may never see this survivor ever again and if you deny them the supplies, this often weighs heavy on your group's minds and consciences. You often find yourself in situations when scavenging where you make tough calls as well... Say one member of group is starving or injured, sometimes you can trade for these supplies- or you can steal and retain all of your supplies; often if you steal, you may find yourself in situations where you must decide to flee and risk injury and damaging relationships, or you can kill and preserve yourself and supplies... As you can imagine this would also shake up your group and the survivor who did the deed.
This game really does give an insight into war that we all need to see that war is hell, not a glamorized, epic adventure full of explosions....
In short, "This War of Mine" is a true masterpiece that everyone should play and truly shows the impact war has on people.

This War of Mine is a 2D plat forming game with some rogue like elements. In which the player is put into 3rd person perspective and is given control over a band of civilians trying to survive in an abandoned building. The game play and mechanics are simple yet solid, with a primary focus on resource management as the player searches for food, water, medicine, weapons and building materials to try and improve their groups situation. However, what really makes the game is the setting. Be aware this game is not for the faint of heart. The premise of the game is your little band of survivors are civilians living in the nation’s capital that by circumstance got caught up in the middle of a brutal civil war, and 11-bit Studios  handles this phenomenally. Several of my friends are veterans, and after I had them test the game for themselves their responses were a bit surprising.  Of all the thousands of main stream war games on the market, they said that This War of Mine was one of the ones that came the closest to showing the bleak reality of what life in a war zone was really like. Your enemies are not infected zombies, soulless terminators, or even elite super soldiers. They are just people; you all are just people, all just trying to survive another day. This game is real, it’s depressing, it’s raw, and it’s quite frankly hard to play. I’m a 6ft 300lb macho man, and there are moments while playing through the Little Ones DLC, that I was fighting the urge to cry. And despite being an indie 3rd person perspective side-scroller, This War of Mine captures life in war better than COD ever has.

The simple graphics belie what an intense, meaningful game this is. Unlike most games where you're the hero winning the war, here you're just a normal person trying to survive. The choices you make are much more meaningful: do I rob this elderly couple so I can eat? Do I give a stranger my last bandages because they say someone's in trouble? Do I share my food with a homless beggar? This game explores the morality of how you act in a game - kill too many people, and your characters will become depressed and stop doing anything. Help others out, and they'll become happy - but at the expense of your possessions. There is action while scavenging at night to keep the game exciting too, and while it may not be overly intense, it manages to check all the boxes for what you'd want in a game. 

What's also great is how much the developers care about the game. Aside from donating some of the profits to helping kids affected by war, they also keep adding new content to the game, even after three years. There are plenty of games that take your money and run, but you can tell these developers actually put their heart into the game. The story and the passion makes the game special, especially in this era where so many games offer nothing more than shoot-em-up explosion fests.

When we hear of a war video game, we associate it almost immediately with first-person-shooters storming through enemy camps, making headshots, avatars dashing through firing lines of bullets and curses. We think of strategic battles where each death is seen from afar, eagleview, distancing and trivial. We glorify the destruction we hail upon our enemies and we raise our flag as we dancing from a captured checkpoint. This War Of Mine turned that around, letting us peek at the conflict through our shattered windows and broken walls, letting us hear the grenades exploding miles away but each one getting louder, hitting closer to our fragile mortal hearts as we crawl under our dimly lit basement, in a blanket, trying to sleep time away till the day we can see the sun again.

When I bought This War Of Mine from Steam, I was looking for some entertainment for a Saturday night. I did not find any. The game was dark, bleak and brutal, with each decision leads to a gut-wrenching consequence, leaving me breathless, depressed and teary. I quit the game after 3 hours of trying to maintain my group of survivor unsuccessfully, with two died from gunshots and one from suicide. I felt something in me just broke and I left the game untouched for a few months. I ate little that night. 

One hot summer night I opened the game after a long day at work. The game remains the same, but something in me started to take it in. Something slowly guided my hand through the emotional journey of these characters, each with a name, a story, a heart-breaking dream, and very, very few chances of living it. This War of Mine delivered a gut-wrenching ride through a fictional with very real stakes, in a way that has never been delivered before.

This War Of Mine is a 2D-survival-strategy platform video game from Poland game company 11 bit studio. The game sets in a fictional Eastern Europe country being torn apart by war and undergoing a siege, inspired by the 1992–96 Siege of Sarajevo during the Bosnian War. Main characters take roles of civilians living in the warzone instead of soldiers, giving an entirely different perspective of war to the players. Survivors refrain from going out in the day and only scavenge food, medicines and tools at night to avoid snipers. Players are given a group of survivor, consisted of randomly selected members, each with a different background, specialty, personality and purpose. Players guide them through daily activities like cooking, building tools, growing plants and filtering water, while making hard decisions like food, medicine and resting ration. However, the toughest decisions are at night when players have to decide scavenging location and interaction with habitants within that area. Characters encounter from morally ambiguous bandits, desperate doctors, homeless people to the military. There is no good nor bad decision: each choice comes with a consequence that would benefit one group over another. Once during the toughest winter days of my survival group, I had one member visiting a hospital to trade with doctors all of our medicine for a three-day food amounts. Another time, the cheerleader of my group got shot from stealing from a group of woman bandits. In order to escape, I had to fought her way out while killing two in the process. Burden by guilt and injuries, the cheerleader died one night, tumbling my group into a circle of depression and sickness that eventually prevented us from fighting any longer. While obstacles are ruthless and brutal, with each new member comes a pair of helping hand and a mouth to feed, the worst moments of the game come when the survival of my own group is leveled with the morality of our decisions, or when in a moment of panic, there seemed to be no choice at all. I mistaken a someone’s wife for a bandit because she was pointing her gun at my most precious member caring medicine for someone at home. As she felt to the floor, her armed husband arrived at the scene. He kneeled down and started crying. He no longer care for my characters’ intruding presence. He is broken and so was my character.

A rare game in which the choices generally arise out of the mechanics organically rather than having a thinly disguised decision tree. Do I take a gun when going scavenging? If I hear people do I shoot or hide? Who gets the food? While the game can be played entirely pragmatically, I've found that it's particularly hard to take some actions that would certainly benefit my party. I've often encountered dilemmas such as whether my desperate need for medicine is worth stealing from an elderly couple. The "nice" thing is that it impacts the game mechanics as well; the person doing the looting might get depressed from the action, impacting their mechanical usefulness.

Overall, the game is well-designed and has you consider a great number of different (terribly disheartening) variables in each playthrough while giving you the freedom to be as kind or as ruthless as you would like without overly heavy-handed doses of morality.

I have spent so much time trying to complete all the scenarios for this game, as well as playing my own custom campaigns. This is a game that will tug at your heart strings, it will make you nervous and make you fret about your characters and the wisdom of your decision to have them go in that abandoned building with soldiers camped out in it. Ive felt the drop in my stomach when the kids appear at your shelter in need of a can of food and you have none to give them. It is a game that wants to teach you about the horrors of war, but its not a documentary and its not preachy. Its genius is teaching you by having you live the experience, you have to accept that this is just the way things are. You arent going to be a hero saving a city being torn apart from the inside by war, you are a vulnerable powerless citizen leading other citizens in a daily quest just for survival. 11 Bit Studios is clearly devoted to this game, 3 years on from its release and the game is still receiving updates and dlc. This is a game that is hard to move on from, you think you have done everything and then something happens to draw you back. Whether you just get an urge to go back and play another again or the game receives a new addition that you are jumping for the chance to test out and see for yourself.

I highly suggest this game, for whatever price (I got it on sale, but if I knew what it was about, I'd consider the full price).
By the way, it is still very fun without the DLC. This game ought to be the model for how DLC should be implemented.

"I think this quote from a US Serie tells a lot about war, and the feeling that I get, when I played the game.

Hawkeye: War isn't Hell. War is war, and Hell is Hell. And of the two, war is a lot worse.

To me, this game depicted what the consequences of war will do to bystanders stuck in the middle of it. 

The game starts by having random people (2-4) grouped together in the same broken house that act as their shelter. 

Gameplay
Gameplay revolving around how they will get food, medicine, and basic needs during the war for certain period of time and preparing themselves for winter. Daytime is curfew for them, so they had to scavenge everything that they need during nighttime. Risking everything including their life while scavenging for needs while the others had to keep watch of their shelter from outside disturbance.

The characters are different for each everyone of them, and they also had different set of skills. Everything takes into accounts, your action, your ability and inability to do things will effect your characters.

Lots of places to go for needs. Lots of precaution and preparation should be make before going outside. Interaction when someone go to scavenge at night are really beautiful, saddening, reflecting the war itself. 

This game also offer us to create our own story, which or what character to make/choose and and where the places should be available to us when we go scavenging. The difficulty also can be choose. But i strongly suggest you to play the main story first.

Should i get it or not?

For me, you should, this game combine a masterful music, arts and gameplay. The positive reviews from other gamers really showed that. If this game is not your cup of tea, refund it before 2 hours. But i believe, you will get hooked.

This War of Mine is a survival game that places you in a besieged city. Your goal is to surive the horrors of war: the scarcity of food, medicine and heat (during winter). You need to expand your base, a dangerous assignment for you need to venture out of the safety of your base. Bandits and soldiers alike will try and kill you during these scavenges, desperate survivors will try and raid your base. They will be succesvol if you are not carefull.

The game has nice mechanics, pushing you to find those extra resources. The more you learn about your group, the more it hurts when they suddenly get ambushed, or you make that fatal misclick. Overal its a good game that, I suppose, represents the struggles of civilians who are caught in a war. This is pure survival strategy with only a general storyline. Keeping your people healthy, energized, content, and productive is the name of the game. Seemingly minor decisions can impact their moods and snowball the stability of the group if unchecked. It's stressful in a super addictive way.

The music has this grand cinematic feel to it. There are no words for how much I love the scavenging song.

This War of Mine makes you feel like you're actually in a war. The music is very mute, helping you not be too afraid, but really making it feel like you're depressed, like the people you control.

Visuals are minimalistic yet great, dialogue never seems forced, and everything in the game is really great.

I don't even like dark and edgy kind of games, but this one I really enjoy. 8.75/10.

In this survival game you control a group of civilian survivors during wartime. During the day, your survivors have to stay inside the shelter because of possible sniper fire. This allows you to maintain their hunger, sleep, illnesses and wounds. At night you have to decide which of your survivors gets to sleep at night, which of them has to guard the place and which of them will be tonight's scavenger. Sometimes locations become inaccessible, and you end up having to choose locations you haven't visited before. At these locations you may just find loot that you can use, but sometimes you will also find other NPCs to trade with, or a group of armed thugs that will simply shoot you on sight. Sometimes you will find harmless people that put you up to the decision of stealing items from them that they need to survive, or to survive another day without food. Sometimes you are put up to the decision to kill someone, or to be killed instead. These choices have a short-term and a long-term impact on your characters. In the short-term, your characters may get depressed, and so may you, and in the long-term it determines the ending of the game you will get after the war ends.

This strategy survival game is like none other as it lets you experience the civilian survival during wartime and as it lets you reflect on the (un)ethical choices you have to take to survive. I'd certainly recommend you to try this out.

On the surface, this game appears to offer a space for the player to make their own moral decisions given a difficult situation. However, every player-controllable character in the game has their own thoughts and feelings about everything and the player is punished for making decisions which are in conflict with them.

This is taken from the store page:
“Make life-and-death decisions driven by your conscience. Try to protect everybody from your shelter or sacrifice some of them for longer-term survival. During war, there are no good or bad decisions; there is only survival. The sooner you realize that, the better.“

The game does not play out this way. You’ll be continuously guilted for deviating from the game’s own rules of morality and your group will become depressed and hard to control.

Also, the range of decisions available to you is extremely limited. So far, every encounter I’ve had with a “hostile” npc results in one of us dying or severely wounded no matter what (unless I run from them). Here’s an example: In one area, I peeked though a door to see there was a soldier sitting in the room. I knew he was armed with a handgun, but I was armed with an assault rifle. He wasn't in a defensive stance, so I open the door and point my weapon at him, thinking this will trigger some kind of stand off, but he just stands up, pulls out his gun, and shoots me. So I put three rounds in him, he stumbles for a second and I stop shooting. He recovers, takes aim for about a second, then shoots me again, so I put three more in him and he dies. And somehow, having been shot twice (with no body armor), I’m only slightly wounded…

To me, there’s a mismatch between the actual core gameplay and what is being marketed. And without interesting and ambiguous moral conflict, the survival aspects by themselves are grindy and uncompelling. Definitely disappointed.

Play this game. And then stop when the sadness crushes your soul. Your crew is just trying to survive and you start out raiding abandoned building for supplies. Then those buildings have been picked clean and you move on to occupied buildings. People can trade with you so bring some stuff along. You will always be on the losing end of deals and you will definitely feel it. In my own story, many of the buildings become inaccessible due to fighting and I ended up having to rob a house to make sure the crew could eat for a day. Then a hospital for meds and food to eat for another day. And then I quit. The next step would have been shanking strangers for supplies. Yes, it's just a video game and I shouldn't care about pixels dying really but this is the genius of the game.

You actually care about the crew. Sure, it's purely a stats game. This character is sad, tired, hungry, exhausted, but that member of the crew needs to stay alive, especially if they have a useful skill. Skilled scavenger has a bigger backpack. Good cook makes prepared meals cheaper. The cloud hanging over everyone's head is that you never know what you will come away with from a nightly scavenging run. Sure, the description of the scavenge site might say "lots of food" but guess what? The door at the very beginning of the building is blocked on the other side. I didn't have enough material to build a prybar or a sawblade so time to just go home. No gains at all and the crew starves for a day.

You are really watching death in slow motion. You can't stop it, only suspend it. You can have knives and guns but they won't get you through that rubble-blocked hallway. You can have a shovel but it won't help you against the thug with that AK-47.

So in the end I went from a scavenger to a blatant thief and, frankly, I wasn't able to go further. Your crew is a generally decent bunch and there were hard repercussions for stealing from a kindly old couple hiding out in their home or robbing a hospital for meds which would ensure death for some of the patients.

If you are a generally decent person this game will hit home hard. How far are you willing to go? From scavenger to thief to outright murderer? Sure, you can do all of those things without feeling anything for the crew or any other character in the game. But some of it will make you feel like a truly awful human being and that turns back around on the genius of this system.

Not politicizing this game is hard. When you watch the dismal treatment of middle-eastern refugees, the shouts of "Go back where you came from", "This War of Mine" shows you where that is. It is violent, uncertain, and makes anyone in that situation decide how far they will go to survive even if it makes you a murderer for that last can of beans. This war of mine quickly became my most and least favourite game. It achieves this oxymoronic status through strong storytelling, a linear, but flexible upgrade path, and the challenge of emphathising with a ragtag group of people holed up in a random, damaged house in the outskirts of the capital. The second- least favourite- happens at two opposed emotional poles: feeling, deeply, the hopeless and random depression and uncertainty that an armed and prolonged conflict at your doorstep brings with it; followed by the realisation that a gamified, pragmatic approach to the situation is not uncalled for, rendering all the empathy you have developped towards the characters not meaningless, rather very calloused and cynical. 

Days pass- you try to keep sane amidst the screams, the shells, the gunfire that has transformed your familiar city from a place you know into a place that is unknowable, ever in flux and deadly. Moments of solace in the strumming of a guitar, the crackly radio, a hot meal that does not consist entirely of rat. You know what you have stolen, how much effort went into avoiding faces attached to your loot, and how your mates reacted when you came home with the vital food and medicine. The life you once knew has been reduced to a series of compromises to stay alive. You have killed a raider in self-defence. You relish the opportunities you are given to pretend that there is a semblance of kindness amidst the rubble and blood. 

The moment of identification with the protagonists goes beyond the initial armchair empathy with the sprites on your screen. As the game progresses, it ekes out the players limits, as they reflect the actions they are playing out, going from scavenging to theft, to finding ways to prevent either by equipping your home as well as possible, to helping others. 

The challenge then, is to find that spot between heartlessness and natural kindness. And to survive the night. Bullets help.

The story is that there is different characters you might start out with, and different places you may be able to access. This is a civilian experience of war. That is to say, [b]an experience of a precarious civil situation[/b] aggravated by the daily dilemmas between - on the one hand - satisfying your own (future) material needs or - on the other hand - risking your means of (future) survival (for example, next week's guaranteed provisions) in order to answer the other's needs; and between - from one point of view - usurping the other's means of living (so you may live) or - from the other point of view - finding yourself without the basic means to keep living... along with a base building and management gameplay.
Since in our daily lives we're not very much willing to share our today's (or next day's) meal and that we live under the menace of being usurped of it by the ones who live precarious lives, one could say that it might not be so distant the analogy of this game with our daily lives.

This is an unbelievably powerful game that I think everyone should play. It is a harrowing survival game that relies on difficult decision-making, personal choices, and desperate survival. It is worth multiple playthroughs, as the characters and circumstances change, giving you different stories and forcing you to adopt different strategies. Both the artstyle and the music are stunning, haunting, and truly elevate the gameplay. 

There are games that you will play in your life that will never leave you, that you stay awake into the early morning playing because you can't save and quit, that you dream about day and night, that will break your heart in more ways than one, that will tell you a story that becomes a part of you. What irrevocably changed me was the fact that this game is based on real events. To me (as cheesy as it sounds) this is more than just a game. This is a small and distant window into a world that exists today and into too many lives that have and are still lived.

I can safely say that this game changed my life and will stay with me forever.

To me, This War of Mine (twom) is an ok game. It's not good, great, awesome or a masterpiece, it's ok. The main problem I have with the game is that it feels unfinished, I'll get to that in a moment.

To explain twom, picture the base building aspects of games like XCom or Sheltered, combined with scavenging for supplies which you use to help craft items and workshops to continue building your base. The game is primarily a base builder and second a scavenger/stealth/2d shooter. The scavenging is pretty fun, you get to hear some stories with npc's, trade medicine to a family who has a sick dad which will then give you more of the items you need for building your base. But most of the good stories are told when you're building your base.

Your characters have morals, agendas, needs and emotions. Some are addicted to tobacco and you need to grow homegrown indoor tobacco crops and harvest them to roll cigarettes for them or making moonshine to satisfy an alcohol addiction. You'll encounter a moral dilemma like stealing food and supplies from the lonely old couple so your characters can survive another day, but then some of your characters feel sad for doing so and may even leave you because your decisions don't align with what they would've done.

The plot behind the game is you're at war, you're not actively in the military, but you're a group of citizens living in a damaged house and meet tons of interesting people thorughout your time there. Some of the things that you'd picture could happen during a war, like theft, violence and possibly r@pe, can happen. It's really engaging and sad at the same time.

Besides that story telling part of the game, which is great. You grow to love your characters, you take care of them, live this part of their lives with them. You want them to live so much, you'll do whatever you can to get the resources they need to survive, better their lives, all while making sure it aligns with what they would do.

Now why I feel this game is ok and unfinished. The scavenging part of the game is too easy once you get a gun. But that's not as big of a deal as you'd expect, because scavenging is still fun with a gun. The main issue is when scavenging you never know exactly what items and in how many quantities of that item you should gather to take back home. If they let you review your recipes & home base inventory when scavenging and some how let you craft a backpack, it'd be a good, possibly great game. Sheltered at least lets you craft backpacks. NEO Scav lets you use plastic bags. twom gives you nothing.

To make your home base better, all that matters is having more inventory space when scavenging and knowing which items you should get and which you should leave behind. You also would like to know which location you should scavenge, but can't remember what you left at a certain location the last time you visited it, so I wrote a list. That paper list turned into a spreadsheet. The spreadsheet kept track of what items were where, what items I needed to make which recipes worked so well, I was building things at my homebase that would've taken about 3 days in 1 day. It worked so well, I would stare at numbers in a spreadsheet just as much time as playing the d*m game. This lowered the chance that I would need to steal from the lonely old couple and have one of my characters leave me.

The way to get more inventory space is to make sure somebody has the scavenger trait, there aren't that many. So in the pre-built group of characters, there's only a few to choose. If you can't get somebody good at scavenging in your team, pick another team. Or you could just scavenge for valuables and trade those valuables to the trader and hope he has the items you need to survive. That latter option is too passive imho. I'm no longer making decisions in the game, I'm dependent on rng to bring the items I need to my doorstep every 1.5 hours of the game. Plus there's little need for scavenging valuables once you can produce them yourself.

Problem for me at least, that creating a simple spreadsheet that lists what is in your home base so you know what you need to pickup at night works so well, it should be in the game! Making, updating, and maintaining that spreadsheet is part of the game for me. It became a game mechanic that the devs didn't intend on creating, but it was created out of necessety because I consider, twom, an unfinished game.

Did you know twom on mobile is almost an identical port? Who plays games on their phone for 40minutes at a time? That's how long you have to play twom before you can save the game.

Wow. Seriously, *wow*. I bought this game on a friend's recommendation years ago but just got around to playing it. I was expecting some stealthy sneaky game where you just tried to escape the city. I was certainly not expecting a game where you try to hole up in a busted house while fighting for survival, helping or rejecting the needy, outlasting the winter, and bartering everything you can.

The game's three strongest points are its decisions, its aesthetic/atmosphere, and its hidden mechanics.

1) The game presents you with many choices that you will have to make. The most frequent is the stressful task of figuring out what to scavenge and bring home and what to leave behind for the next visit, which runs the risk of losing it to other scavengers. However, you will also face choices to help neighbors, divide meager resources as best you can, and just how far you are willing to go to survive.

Unlike in many games, which present many superficial, ultimately irrelevant and meaningless choices to provide the illusion of a reactive story, these decisions actually matter. Your grateful neighbors may come back to help you; giving your only set of bandages to one survivor may leave another bedridden for days or even kill them; resorting to theft and murder to get resources can drive your survivors to kill themselves out of guilt. The game's relative simplicity allowed the developers to focus on making each decision count. 

2) "This War of Mine" does a splendid job of depressing you beyond belief with every aspect of the game. The smog-colored sepia daytime lighting in your house and the bleak, dark loneliness that pervades the scavenging areas combine with the survivors' desperate thoughts and sad stories to constantly reinforce just how precarious your situation is and how absolutely devastating this war is.

It also is a chilling reminder that this game shows only the barest shade of the boundless misery and suffering that people endure in war.

3) Normally, I would spit on games that hide many of their mechanics, but "This War of Mine" is beautiful in its simplicity, and this beauty would be marred if the game simply came out and laid itself bare for you from the get-go. Unless you use a guide, you have to discover what the various crafting tables and tools do, explore sites for yourself, figure out your survivors' strengths and weaknesses, and deal with unexpected consequences. The game lets you know, for example, if your survivors are growing sad or depressed; it does not tell you that morally repugnant actions can burden your people with so much guilt that they run away or hang themselves. 

The game's major flaw is that it becomes relatively predictable, though it remains rather difficult since one or two bad nights can derail an otherwise perfect playthrough. Still, this is not a game you're going to sink hundreds of hours into. Since it is not expensive though, that is not really a problem. 

Overall, "This War of Mine" is simply an excellent, excellent game that hits all of the right notes. Its developers clearly had a solid vision of what they wanted to do and managed to achieve it without burdening the game with unnecessary fluff and frilly mechanics. I highly recommend it to almost anyone.

10 hours in review: I hate this game.

I am a completionist. I mostly play RPGs and strategy games. I like to win, so my gaming style primarily involves achieving goals, expanding my powerbase, meeting my targets, improving my strength, all of which to end in a smashing victory.

This War of Mine offers very little and frequently none of these things. The gameplay is inherently simple. You have a few survivors in a badly damaged house. During the day they can do simple tasks, like building furniture, patching a hole in the wall or something else to help you survive, cooking meals, distilling hooch, or resting from nightly activities. During the night one person can go out to scavenge for badly needed supplies, while the rest sleeps (hopefully in a bed) or stands guard, hoping you won't get raided during the night.

Rather than adding and expanding, the game constantly offers straightforward but difficult choices. Does the scavenger bring home raw materials today so somebody can patch a hole in the wall, or does he bring medication in case somebody gets sick or wounded? Do I risk life and limb to steal from armed bandits or inflict myself with moral guilt stealing from the defenseless elderly? Do I give my last piece of food to the wounded guy who has to stand guard tonight or to the sick man on the bed? Do I trade away my last bandages while nobody's wounded so we can all eat tomorrow? There's no do-overs either so I am stuck with my choices. Beyond just restarting the entire story of course.

This is what makes This War of Mine so damn good.

Every day in the game, it's one bad choice or another, all for the sake of staving off immediate disaster. For one more day. For the sake of survival. For the hope that things will be a little bit better tomorrow, if only you can get through the problems right now. Can you survive without resorting to theft? If you can't, who do you steal from, how much do you risk in the process? What about murder, when does that get justified by survival?

If as a player you do not get upset by stealing or murdering for the sake of your group of survivors, then your survivors will. They get sad and depressed, even suicidal, from committing atrocities. Morale is an important part of the game, and the horrorific actions you commit to in the name of surviving are as relevant as the ones that are inflicted upon you. Maybe even moreso.

Because war is horrible and this glimpse of what living in a warzone is like, just so. It is atrocious. It is insecure. It comes with the realization that while this game has plenty abstractions, these stories are real. There are people who have lived through this. Who are trying to live through it in the world today. Who probably will be trying to live through it in the future.

Who only want to survive. Just one more day. Maybe tomorrow will be better.

[b] TL:DR; [/b] This is a very well crafted, down-to-earth gaming experience with great atmosphere and exciting (and sometimes depressing) highs and lows. Your experience here will be finite, but it's still certainly worth a buy.


If you've ever played Don't Starve (or other survival games) before, some of the mechanics of this game will be familiar to you. You can create a lot of different things, however your supplies are limited, so you'll have to guess at which things might be the most important and learn from experience. This really works well for the game in your first or second playthrough because it forces you to make tough decisions... Your food supply is low. Your survivors are starving. You ask yourself if you have anything to trade for food... Would you trade away your store of life-saving medicine to buy a tin or two of meat? How about the firearms you've crafted to protect yourself? Would you kill an innocent person just to survive for a precious few more days? These are some of the questions you will have to ask yourself, and it is this part of the game that is probably the most memorable and unique for me.

This is the kind of game that is quite easy to become immersed in, especially in your first couple of playthroughs.  The music, the drab, monotone color palette, the sound effects - everything is just done and presented very well. 

To me - and this feels like the really important bit - it doesn't feel like the game is just telling you a story - like so many other games would do - but rather like you are writing your own. It's the story of your survivors, and it's completely up to you as to what kind of story that will be. As the days went on in my game, I found myself getting attached to Marko, Bruno, and Pavle. I felt guilt on the days I couldn't feed them all, and uplifted on those precious occasions when I found a can or two of meat to share amongst them whilst scavenging. Then Marko was shot and killed - and it felt genuinely horrible and I wanted revenge. So I had revenge! Pavle gunned down the murderer and his parents too, and took their supplies - a lot of wood, scrap, food, and other necessities - home. But it was small comfort for Pavle and Bruno; they had lost their friend, and Pavle's hands would be forever stained with blood. Perhaps he would be next to die in the neverending search for supplies just to go on living. In that run, being quite new to the game, scavenging became a bloodsport and killing a necessity for life. It was honestly unreal. I found myself justifying murder! Soon, I was no better than the other bandits and criminals that were raiding my shelter for supplies. No game has ever made me feel like that - about making hard decisions to get from one day to the next. I was so happy in a later run when I could just feed everyone enough to keep them going, and when I had the spare resources to make a guitar and an armchair to bring my survivors some small comforts.

However, it should be stated that the experience is most certainly finite. Once you figure out the optimal way to do things, you will find that the game falls flat. When everything is in abundance, there are no difficult decisions to make and that core element of the game that makes it so appealing is suddenly gone. It is not an 'if' but a 'when'. It's a bit of a shame too because at this point, the game has gotten so easy that I don't even want to see it through to the ending. It would have been nice if the gameplay went beyond 'figure out the correct build path through trial and error and then you will pretty much never lose'. My playtime says ~50 hours, but I left it open, paused, and in the background over a few nights so 20 hours is more accurate.

That said, This War of Mine certainly delivers - and it delivers something truly unique and fascinating over a good 15-20 hours of gameplay. For these reasons, it is definitely worth a buy in this humble reviewer's opinion.

[h1]Noteworthy info[/h1]
[list]
[*] Crafting is a major component in this game. If you don't enjoy crafting, beware.
[*] You're supposed to survive through the war. It is not expected you do this on your first playthrough. You're expected to uncover the game mechanics as you play and fail, and improve in later playthroughs.
[/list]

[h1]Good[/h1]
[list]
[*] Dark, gloomy, adult atmosphere.
[*] Nice symbolic graphics.
[*] Difficult decisions.
[*] High replayability. There are many available characters, and you have only a few of them in a single playthrough. There are also many devices/equipment to build, different strategies to survive, many locations to visit.
[*] Multiplatform.
[*] Available DRM-free.
[/list]

[h1]Bad[/h1]
[list]
[*] Save system. Can't make a manual save, the game saves automatically on end of each day (~15 min of play). [b]Can't[/b] save when leaving the game - you have to replay the last 15 mins again. Developers probably don't have kids or any other immediate responsibilities.
[*] The game glitches out when alt-tabbing out of it and back again. The support forum is filled with reports, yet devs don't seem to intend to fix this.
[*] No way to speed up daytime activities. Wastes your time horribly.
[*] A single run (surviving the war with a set of characters) takes a long time, easily 8 hours. That would not be a problem, if you could save properly. But since you can't, you feel reluctant to experiment and try new approaches. If they failed horribly, it could destroy your whole run, and since you aren't able to load a previous save, it would waste a lot of your time (you'd have to repeat all of that basic starting stuff again). So you don't experiment, but rather read instructions on game wikis. That takes a lot of "figuring things out" joy away. I don't object to night time, it's fun. But daytime is a chore that artificially extend the play time (see point above) and should've been done differently (not that time consuming).
[*] No tutorial.
[*] Missing keyboard shortcuts. Everything has to be driven by mouse.
[/list]

[spoiler]The first few times around, it's an absolute eye-opening masterpiece. Even though individual character development is rather non-existent, the morally challenging choices and the feeling of unity the game throws your way is incredible. The scavenging mechanic is challenging and hits the nail on the head. The tension the game creates with its time mechanic during both day and night is great and builds up even further if you can't escape the scavenging area before dawn, since you never know if your precious survivor will survive the unrelenting sniper fire during the day time. Coming back from looting run can be either a massive relief or a huge dissapointment depending on whether you can get raided or not. And the first time you hold a gun in your hands... You feel like a god who can do anything. And once you use that (fire)power for wrong purposes, on purpose or not, it feels like you actually committed murder. You feel like you've taken the life of a fellow man trying to survive, just like you. This was the first time a game has made me feel genuine guilt for what i did to an NPC, and in a way, it was very eye-opening.

However, the more the game goes on, it starts to feel more like a strategy game than an unique experience. Depression, sadness and hunger become mere status effects. The micromanaging gets sort of annoying at times and the game sadly loses it's uniqueness. Although i'm not sure how long i expected the game to keep it's emotional side. You might be able to enjoy it for longer if you go into it a bit less optimistic than I did (and believe me when i say that i waited for the sale I got this in for several months)[/spoiler]

Overall, the game offers a very unique experience at the start and devolves into a strategy game heavy on micromanagement later on. If the game goes on sale and you want to experince the horrors of what happens behind the scenes of other war games, I urge you to give it a go.

Walk into a hospital. A soldier tells you to behave yourself, so you violently chop up the chair he’s currently sitting on for firewood, then sell it back to the nearest doctor. Then you go home and build a guitar using only wood, gears, and a broken guitar. 

I really like what this War of Mine is trying to do, but I’m not a fan of the execution. The game centers around resource management and crafting in the style of civilians trapped in a city under siege. As you fight to survive, you’ll have to build beds, make alcohol, gather firewood, and scrounge the ruined cities. 

Characters are well developed through their updating bios, Bruno especially. The game has a striking somber tone and grey scale art style which is especially wonderful to see during the winter scenarios. However, I think the most tragic thing about the game is the pacing. A typical story lasts 45 in game days. That’s a long time when there's only a maximum of 24 scavengable locations and most of those will be inaccessible at any given time due to either a raging battle or snow. 

The war in This War of Mine doesn't actually effect the game that much. Sure, there are locations guarded by soldiers. Sure, you can hear shells in the ambience. But bandits and snow are a far greater threat than anything the military in this game has to offer. Shells will never hit your house and break your defenses. Battles will never occur outside your shelter. Rebel fighters will never hold you up at gunpoint for supplies as all attacks on your shelter happen off screen. Without some context to ground the player in the setting of an ongoing civil war, the game might as well be set immediatley after a nuclear apocalypse because the ongoing battle on its own has no meaning. This War of Mine isn't your war at all.

The point is that once you get past the game’s unique premise, there’s not a lot to do. Once you have your essentials and are generating some tradable items, you can skip most of your time in the shelter. The difficulty curve is initially a sharp climb because you don’t know what to expect. Once you know what locations need what item and which items are the most useful, the difficulty curve hits freefall at terminal velocity. The result is that you have everything you need to survive and trade with around Day 20 and then have nothing to do for the remaining 25 days. Once I realized this, I decided to raid army strongholds just for fun. 

I wish I had more to say, but overwhelmingly I was just bored. Returning from scavenging was always the same. Send tired people to bed, feed someone, make moonshine, see if trader will show up, skip to night, repeat. The scavenging can throw a few curveballs with enemies and a tiny inventory, but that just wasn’t enough to keep me engaged. I appreciate what this game is trying to do and the message it sends, but as a game I think it falls short.

Strong game design is about short term goals and long term goals. ExamIple from Monopoly: My long term goal is to make other players bankrupt. To do that, I'm going to buy this property at all costs. 
This War of Mine asks you to make your own short term goal (what supplies you need) and also your long term goal (finishing the game). The game provides no hints about when its ending is coming or how to achieve it until the late game. This leaves players stranded around the half way point as they have no overarching task to complete. All you can do is wait and continue to amass a dragon's ♥♥♥♥ of supplies. This uncomfortable lull makes the game feel like a cheap mobile app rather than a cohesive interactive experience. There's another way to complete the game, but it requires sufficient planning (or luck) and it's locked on a timer. There's nothing to hold you until the ending and when it happens it's incredibly underwhelming. 

Edit: After finishing the game with all my survivors still alive, I think I know why I got bored. Too much water. It's such a simple thing, but it's true. With 2 rain water collectors, you can collect 16 water per day for the price of 12 scrap. That water is then used to make alcohol, grow food, or grow meds and tobacco, all of which are trading staples. You can collect 16 gallons of rain water in 12 hours when its not even raining outside. You don't even need to boil or otherwise sanatize your water. I never took water from scav locations because I had near unlimited amounts of it. By the end of the game, I was trading 25 gallons of water for 30+ pieces of scrap, to make more water, to make more alcohol. I didn't need anything because if I ever ran low on food (I didn't) I could just trade more water for food. Water is, in my opinion, the single most overpowered resource in the entire game. 

What's underpowered, undervalued (to new players), and underavailible is electronic components. You don't know how much you need until you already upgrade your workbenches, which is punishing to new players. There seems to be a finite number of this resource, but they're not especially important unless your entire strategy is to make your own cigs, food, and medicene.

Final thought: The inventory system also doesn't make a lot of sense to me, even for a video game. 15 cigs take up the same backpack space as 2 wooden planks or 4 piles of scrap? 15 cigs take up the same space as 20 bullets? Do you, player, really believe that? The limiting of these small objects doesn't make me weigh the pros and cons of cigs vs wood, it just tells me "buy it from the merchant instead." As a result, you can ignore luxuries entirely until your house has become the local brewery.  It's even worse since there are three different types of cigs and different types don't stack in the same inventory slot. So if you have 1 tobacco cig, 1 quality roll-up, and 1 roll-up you're using the same inventory space as 6 wood planks OR 12 pieces of scrap. All of this points to the conclusion that inventory should have been based on weight instead of slot, because otherwise players have no need to weigh the pros and cons, there is always a definite right answer. Not all characters want luxuries and there's no penalty for not getting people thier coffee or cigs so I rewarded my survivors with cigs and coffee because, again, I had nothing else to do. I was bored.

This War Of Mine puts you in charge of a group of survivors in a city. You control every character as you manage things like scavenging, fighting, bartering, crafting, and doing things around your shelter. Your choices matter, and you get epilogues at the end of each game, regarding all your characters, as well as recap of major events that happened.

This is not a game that forces you to be good. This game doesn't force you to be anything, but you'll find yourself compelled to donate bandages to a hospital, or to give medicine to kids...or, as your survivors starve, to murder an innocent elderly couple and steal their food to save your own. You can play a pure good or pure evil run, but you'll find it increasingly hard to stick to either path, and probably end up somewhere in the middle.

This is not a game where good is arbitrarily rewarded more than evil. Evil is by far the most "comfortable" run for your survivors, because other than moral penalties and some risks of death, stealing is a lot more lucrative than scavenging. A lot of games make good the more rewarding choice in-game, with rewards that are literally better, so it's no question as to what side a player chooses. Given that evil is the side with better rewards in This War Of Mine, resisting the temptation to take the easy way and rob to get what you want is hard than it would be in another game.


The game includes:

- Stealth

- Fighting

- Trading

- Crafting

- Loot management

- Survival game stuff

- Sim game stuff

- Time management

It's a lot like Oregon Trail...if Oregon Trail didn't have a wagon but instead, a house in a city devastated by war that stood in the city...as the city fell apart around the house.

You can customize your game or do a preset campaign. There's an active Steam Workshop and it's easy to use and well integrated into the game. If you find the game too hard, there are lots of mods that make the game very, very easy.

This game is the epitome of "just one more level". In this case, it's "just one more day/night"...both in game nights and IRL nights...
