I have to admit I never reached the end of the playthrough but I think I got a pretty good feel of how the game evolves. The binary recommendation system of steam doesn't give you a lot of choice, but please note that [b]not recommended[/b] means what it says. It doesn't mean I hated the game and had no enjoyable moments with it at all. It just means that I wouldn't go to my friends and say "go buy this game, it's so awesome!"

[h1]The Good:[/h1]
[list]
[*] Cool setting with realistic execution
[*] Art/Graphics are interesting
[*] The atmosphere is delivered successfully
[/list]
At first you get a very distinctive [i]wow-effect[/i] when playing the game. It kind of combines stealth with those point and click adventures you played back in the early 90s but merges a fighting system into it that actually works pretty well. The developers have thought about what they are doing and executed a solid system that at first seems unintuitive (everything is done with mouse-clicking although you have to react fast at times) but works quite flawlessly in the end.
The art is set in a place between the graphics of Deadlight and Limbo. Colors are scarce and everything is rather dark and depressing, as it should be. The different locations are giving you a feel of dread and desperation which works quite well most of the time. Some are chosen a certain way that lets you just hear the name [spoiler](e.g. the warehouse)[/spoiler] and you immediately know that this is probably one of the more dangerous places (but very rewarding if survived).
Which brings me to the atmosphere of the game. It delivers. You are in a warzone and it's supposed to be brutal and unforgiving. You have to make tough choices that might influence or even ruin the lives of others in order to survive yourself. The ambient sounds with the graphics work very well to achieve that and the different locations you can visit are chosen in a way that can touch you on a surprisingly emotional base.


[h1]The Bad:[/h1]
[list]
[*] The difficulty makes you rage-quit and can basically destroy your savegame
[*] No character creation, only male starting characters
[*] Some aspects are so misplaced that it kills any suspension of disbelieve (e.g. crafting and scavenging)
[/list]
Decisions are hard and you never know how they will pan out. One decision can end someone's life and that's exactly what the game does. But in the end it is a game. I want to go back and reload it if it doesn't work out. You might argue that this would ruin the game's aim. Hard decisions are only hard if you can't go back to fix it and you might be right. But the game's playtime is far to extended to really say "I'll do it correctly next time when I caught up the six hours of this playthrough." Some people would probably feel my wish for saving and going back game-breaking and I can understand that but this is how I felt.
The other issue with the game was for me that you are given some very unlikable male characters with a incredibly bland and discouraging backstory. When one of those characters was dying I felt completely disconnected; not because the war is so bad and turns you into a sociopath but because the characters was only a pawn in my game and it actually would have been easier without him (he survived in the end, though). If I just could create my own characters they would've had a different backstory that happens in my head, that makes me feel a lot more emotionally bound to the characters. But instead you are stuck with what you get, let your character be uninteresting, completely replacable and a white male (as happens with many, many games nowadays).
What put me off the most were some of the weird and nonsensical choices the developers made. For example the crafting system is so [i]gamistic[/i] that it totally ruined the experience for me. You get your workbench and then you need to upgrade it with some insane amounts of loot to build new or improved other tables that help you out. Speaking of loot: Your characters have an arbitrary number of inventory slots, just like you remember from your 90's point and click adventures. Those slots are filled with one kind of item. Some stack, some don't. And they stack in different amounts. So you can end up with carrying 20 wooden planks and 4 pieces of scrap metal (which is not nearly enough to do even the first upgrade of your workbench) but you can't go home with a rifle, a pistol, ammo for both, and a roll of toilet paper because that takes more slots. So, the logical thought here for me was "I don't have enough inventory slots, so lets take more people out for scavenging." But, of course, that is also not possible. You can't have a team of two in one scavenging zone and no, you cannot send out two teams to scavenge at different spots in the city. Also, in the end it turned out that those hard choices you make did not matter at all. I robbed someone [spoiler](an old couple in a house in the north, they begged and cried for me to stop when I entered -- I didn't even have a weapon with me)[/spoiler] of all their food and when I came back a week later they were still very much alive [spoiler](their front door was still open and they were at the exact same spots, screaming)[/spoiler]. I encountered a few more issues like that during my playtime with the game but I think you got the idea.

[h1]So, I think...[/h1]
... the game is a nice idea and has some very strong points in its execution but also some issues that finally made me not like the game. It is supposed to be super atmospheric but at pretty much every turn you make you will find yourself confronted with those small things that rip you out of your immersion and throw you back in a state that makes you question the game's mechanics all the time. And this spoiled my experience with [i]This War of Mine.[/i] Add the characters that were unlikeable and hollow in the first place and you lost me. Many people think differently about the game. Maybe they don't get put off by those small details like I did or they are totally fine with it. So please read a bunch of other reviews to get a better idea wether the game is worth the money for you. I just know it wasn't worth it for me.

I know that many who have played this game will disagree with me when I say that this game is limited in scope and in  challenge.  Yes, there is a horrors of war, that turn decent human beings into less than human beings.   Aside from the political message... war is bad, the game lacks depth and is limited.  

There is the survival aspect of the game, scavanging for food and materials.  Making makeshift tools and building things to aid in survival. Even that is limited.  Trade and bartering is limited.  

Social interaction is also a limitation in the game.  There is almost no interaction between the main charcters, what interaction there is very scripted and repetitive.  There is no interaction with secondary characters, although that opportunity is there if the developers wish to explore that option.

The game is indeed thought provoking without a doubt, but that does not always make a game good.  I do recommend the game for the social content, there is merit in the game on that. I not recommend the game if you are looking for playability and depth.

I do not regret buying the game, I only wish there was a bit more substance to the game.

This game... I LOVE and HATE this game!!! Its survival in a way most don't think about it: sure, fight the elements, fight the enemies-but wait, fight your own conscience? Yes. In this game, your biggest enemy is YOU: not in game you, REAL you. 

This game, after the first time i played through ONE of the stories, had my nerves frayed SO badly, I NEVER wanted to touch it again... but at the same time, it captivated me so thoroughly that i REALLY wanted to play through the next story, and COULD NOT put it down! (although I did force myself to take breaks when I was obviously too nerve-fried to make objective decisions).

Its terrible in a way that it makes you FEEL! And OH how you'll feel the first time a Character dies, because it WILL happen at least once, but at the same time, its WONDERFUL because is captures you, it binds you to your characters as if you were there, you WANT to survive the war with a passion. But the Strongest feels of all, are the ones you'll have to face from other people. 

Guys with guns and prisoners? Bad. Obviously that's not a hard moral choice. But... lets say you visit the little old cottage where an elderly couple lives... but just barely... they don't attack, as a matter of fact, they directly ASK if you're with the bandits, and BEG you not to take what little they have... but wait... they have bandages and medicine, and your favorite character is at home, severely wounded/sick and dieing? Sure, the couple don't need the building supplies or maybe gears you may come across... but... the old man begs you not to take his wives medication, she's not well... and they might not have enough food to last the winter, even if you DON'T take any of it... now what? Who's good? Bad? In a bad spot that you can choose wither or not to take advantage of? Or leave them alone? Or help in some cases?

Are the people who hoard their food and water bad? Or protecting their families safety? Are the people raiding your base doing so out of malice? Or desperation like you might have done the night before? or the one soon to come?

All in all, if you don't mind frayed nerves, and long nights, at the payout of GREAT satisfaction and peace of mind, then I BEG you, give this game a high priority: you wont regret it.

I found this game really beautiful and gripping. It shows us the true horrors of war and what people have to go through during these times. The game is also quite hard and requires a lot of planning and patience.

The Good Things:
-Non-Linear Storyline. There are many different stories to pick (After you finish the first one) and many different scenarios to witness in the many different places you can visit. If you are angered by a soldier who is going to rape a woman you can change it's outcome!, If you are worried about some kids with a sick mother who is about to die you can change her fate! The survivors reveal their story over time and comment on actions of other survivors.

-Realistic Combat. Except for the bullets and stealth, the combat is very realistic. Players don't have more health over enemies (Unless you're playing as Boris or Roman), and killing is not always the option because some enemies will surrender.

-Realistic Simulation.
There is no Easy, Normal, or Hard, there is only Realism. When the tempertures drop, people can get sick. When crime is on the rise, the group will suffer a lot of raids. When survivors are depressed, the group falls apart.

-Different ways to play.
Players don't always have to steal food. They could trade for it or even grow their own. Players don't always have to use stealth kill enemies, with enough bullets and body armor they could rush in and shoot everyone.

-Beautiful Graphics.
The graphics perfectly captures a war zone and contributes alot to the atmosphere. By the looks of it 
the game seems to take place around eastern europe during the 1990s.

-Shows us what war really is.
This game is a big ♥♥♥♥ you to people who support wars or even play the so called "Game of the Year" Call of Duty or similar. It shows us that the Military will do anything for "Glory" and will abuse
their power for their own desires.

The Bad Things:
-You are only able to have one save. It autosaves after every night and it prevents you from making backups saves or restarting a day incase you make a mistake.

-Food is extremely scarce and limited. There are only 4 types of food: Vegetables, Raw Meat, Canned Food, and Cooked Meals. There is no existance of Rice, Fish, Bread, or other foods which are commonly found in many places. Some places, like the Military Outpost, Have a lot of food but not enough to keep a group of 4 well fed for a week.

--Water is kind of useless. Nobody drinks water, only Coffee and Alcohol. Water is only used for in making Moonshine, and Cooking Food.

My Score for this game is: 9/10. Many of the bad things were not that bad but some tweaks should be implemented. Overall the game is really great for an Indie game and it's worth your money!

This game has a lot going for it its art style is absoutly stunning and rather compliments the hopeless depression that the characters of the story are constantly battling. Built from what first appears a very simple survival sim you'll quickly learn this game is anything but. Finding yourself making incredible choices both on missions and in the hub of your house. Should i let my best friend die just so there's enough supplies for everyone?, Do i rob this elderly couple knowing that the lack of supplies may lead to their death?, Do i save a father's life for the risk of my own?, Do i stop the raping of a woman and risk my life or let it happen so i can gather supplies for the people i live with. 

This War of Mine is a fantastic game for just getting you into those situations and the drama it causes. Its no save's also means your desicions cannot be reversed so you must think carefully about your actions. The crafting system is also quite intellegent as well as how you protect your base. You may spend all night grabbing a magnitude of supplies only to come back in the morning and find everyone wounded and half your supplies gone. 

However if there is anything to critic it would be the lack of adjustments. Simliar games i've played to this have usually included an option to boost resources or make hours shorter/longer and extend/reduce seasons.

I love This War of Mine, even though it bums me the hell out.

Its premise revolves around civilians surviving in a fictional war-torn country. You start out with three characters all residing in a shelled out house, which you can switch between with the "Tab" key. Each member has their own peculiarities (some smoke, drink coffee, etc) and skills (better at sneaking, scavenging, better at cooking). You give orders to them based on context bubbles that hover over interactive objects in the world (open doors, eat, cook, sleep, take meds, dig through rubble, attack, etc). When you first start out, you need to scavenge what is in the building to survive. Food, water, and parts. Parts can be used for a variety of purposes, from making beds so your guys can get a better sleep, to chairs, to workshops so you can craft crowbars to force yourself past locked doors, to shovels to help move debri faster, to cooking stoves, water purifiers, the ability to board up windows to lessen the chance of looters, etc etc. That's a VERY small list of what's possible, but to give you an idea.

This is basically what the game revolves around: resource gathering and crafting. There are two phases to the game: daytime and nighttime. Day's are about 10-15 minutes long, nights about 5. During the day you're at your house, building stuff to help in dealing with hunger (building a stove, a trap to catch rats, a water purifier, etc), shelter (boarding up windows, setting up traps to stop intruders, making beds, chairs, etc), comfort to make your guys content (making guitars, radio, a moonshine distillery, etc), and tools that will help outside during the night segments (knives, lockpicks, crowbars, guns). You let your guys sleep, eat, and do things to keep their spirits in check. You require a diversity of resources to accomplish all of this, and once your place has been ransacked in the first few days it's necessary to venture out at dark to scavenge for supplies to be able to live another day.

To get an idea of the gameplay at night, think Mark of the Ninja, though it's much slower paced. You make sound in whatever you do which is indicated as a visible ring that pulsates outwards, which also allows you to hear what's nearby, indicated by a red ring. Venturing out in a warzone is all kinds of unpredictable, and you'll never be sure of what you'll find. You're limited in inventory (some members can carry more). You can take stuff from your place out into the field, such as meds for those in need, crowbars and guns for weapons, lockpicking to reduce the noise of getting through a locked door, but doing so risks using up one of your slots that could bring back much needed loot for the next day. You'll meet people who are in need, who are suffering the hell of war at the mercy of the unmerciful, those who mind their own business, and those who are not all that friendly to say the least. Your job is to get as much resources as you can be any means necessary to sustain your crew.

The Mood:
Once I started playing, I could not put this game down.  Its a heavy game.  It sets the mood perfectly and there's never a moment that you're waiting for something.  You are always in need, on edge, and nervous about how bad its going to get trying to obtain that next thing.  Your characters may have a very difficult time with a lot of situations, so its not really about how you feel about what you're doing, its about how the people in the story feel about whats happening.  Killing or stealing from the innocent will have long lasting effects on the person committing the actions, as well as the rest of the group once they hear what happened.  Some characters will need to smoke to keep their sanity, others will drink coffee.  Sometimes when something terrible happens you may need to use some survivors to comfort the others.  Perhaps you want to build a guitar for a group member that can play and lift everyone's spirits.  Maybe build a radio that has some contact to the outside world.  The crafting system is very deep and intuitive and all survivors have some special trait about them.  Everything has an emotional impact and it grows an attachment to the characters more so than I wouldhave imagined.

The Combat:
The combat in this game mechanically is nothing special.  You select what you want your survivor to wield when they're out scavenging.  Based on what you're wielding, you will get different options.  For example, if you have a gun out your guy will take aim at anyone in range and it will display you a icon to fire.  If you're hiding or behind someone you'll get an icon to attempt a backstab attack.  None of this is particularly innovative or interesting, however there's one BIG difference compared to a lot of games.
If you engage in a fight with someone else and they take a hit or you take a hit, often times, both parties sort of freak out and try to leave because nobody wants to die needlesly.  You're rarely just going to areas to kill bad guys and then take their loot, it plays out a lot more humanly (is that a word?) than that.  I was in a situation where i was looting and some people didn't like where I was doing that.  One came at me with a knife and he made me bleed, I hit him with a hatchet and he seemed to immediately just want to run away.  Neither of us wanted to fight any more really, just take as little loss as possible because medicine and bandages are hard to come by for everyone. 
TLDR: Combat isn't about killing the other guy, its about surprising and damaging them to the point that they run away, unless the situation really calls for some cold blooded murder.

Replayability:
I'm pretty sure I marathoned a 15 hour single playthrough.  Now thats only one playthrough with 1 group of survivors, of the 6 total starting groups.  You have different endings for each character based on how bad things got and how close you were to not making it at the end.  The war ends at some random time based on your group, you have to listen to the radio to know when its coming.  The locations that you're able to travel through progressively widen as you play the game, and even though the locations on the map are the same, the layouts and the scenarios that happen at these locations vary each playthrough.  There is a lot of randomization to keep things fresh.  Loot, trader visit frequency, some variation in scenarios at all locations, if other survivors come to visit your shelter, you get the idea.  I'm definitely looking forward to my next playthrough with a different group of survivors.

In This War of Mine, players control a small group of civilians as they try to survive during a civil war, in the fictional city of Pogoren. Its a really unique experience, emotional and brutal.

Gameplay is split into two sections: day and night. During the day, your survivors are at home. You need to keep an eye on any negative status effects - when they're hungry, give them some food, if they're sick, give them medicine, bandage their wounds and make sure they sleep when tired. You can build equipment such as a stove to cook food, a workshop to craft tools and weapons, rain collectors and filters to get clean water, traps to catch small animals to eat, beds to sleep in, a furnace for heat. And you can craft valuable trade items like cigarettes and booze.

During the night, you can select one survivor to scavenge local buildings for supplies, while the others either sleep, or guard your home from bandits. There are lots of areas to visit around the city, and you'll encounter some tricky situations. There are only a couple of completely abandoned areas where you're free to take everything without consequence. Sometimes friendly people will trade with you, but if you don't have anything valuable, would you steal from them instead? Would you murder innocents and take their stuff so your own people can survive? Some areas are occupied by dangerous bandits, who will attack you on sight - but if you're desperate, you might have to risk it.

The combat system, like the rest of the gameplay, is managed through a point and click interface. Left click to walk to a location, right click to run, left click icons to interact with an object or person. I found the combat to be very hard, but I think that is probably by design. Our survivors aren't trained soldiers, and powerful guns are rare and expensive. So far I've tried to avoid combat as much as possible. There's no reloading or respawning, so death is permanent.

There are several scenarios to play through, where you'll start with between one and four survivors, and sometimes another will ask to join your group. Even that can be a tough choice - an extra pair of hands can be useful but its another mouth to feed. Each survivor has their own story and some of them have a special skill. For example Katja can get better value in trades, Bruno spends less resources when cooking and Arica can sneak quietly.

Its the kind of game where you'll generate your own stories. I thought my second attempt was looking good, until we got several days of snow. I couldn't keep the house warm enough, so Bruno froze to death overnight. Realising that every meal would cost me more resources, I started to take risks in the dangerous areas. Arica stealth killed two bandits but a third one shot her dead. Katja went to the same place the next night, figuring one more bandit would be easy enough. Turns out there was more than one and they shot her dead as well. Now alone, and very desperate, I had Pavle murder an old couple and steal all their food, but the next day he was depressed, wouldn't eat anything, and overnight he committed suicide. Game over. But its failures like that which made my next, successful run feel so good. 

TWOM is a fantastic game and I thoroughly recommend it as a full price purchase.

Bleak and uncompromising, this game will quickly put your morals to the test as you're beset with the harsh realities suffered by the victims of war. My first play lasted just 7 days, I was faced with rape (didn't come out well in that one), desperation, and starvation, and learned the lesson that survivor or soldier, not everyone can always be the hero (or villain) they want to be.

As you struggle daily to eat, drink, sleep, and bargain your way to survive only until the next day, you'll soon realise that war can find the worst and best in people. Sometimes you'll be able to take the moral high ground, but this could well put you on a quick path to misery, death, and failure. As right and wrong become blurred, you'll gradually find what it takes to survive through determination and swift action. As the days drag on you'll need to feed, rest, and keep your survivors content with a meagre glimmer of hope. Meanwhile, the night can bring opportunity and reward, but also danger, emptiness, and despair.

This War of Mine is a thoughtful insight to the often neglected aspects of war (at least when it comes to gaming). While the days can sometimes be a bit tedious as you have to carefully tailor how you manage each of your survivors needs, the nights bring the thrills and edge-of-seat gameplay that teases you along and keeps hope alive.

While the game itself is enjoyably challenging, in a simple but wonderfully sketched 2D world, a lot of the gameplay seems dependent on chance. My experience of the drop rate of 'Parts' was abysmal (none found after turn 10 or so despite many locations saying “huge amount of parts”, such that building anything became nigh on impossible until Franko (the regular and oft needed trader) arrived. Chance aspects aside, this game is really good, and pretty addictive, but has not inspired me to play again (yet). Not because it's bad, but because it does such a good job at making you feel depressed and ultimately relieved by the hardships of survival, that you don't really want to go through it again (much like IRL I would imagine).

I rate this game between 8.0 and 8.5/10 because the difficulty is, in part, fabricated by unbalancing the characters' emotions.  If civilians really reacted this way in a siege (i.e. degenerating from sad to depressed to broken so easily), they'd die by the millions weekly rather than pulling through, even after many months, as they so often bravely do.  

It's difficult to suspend disbelief this far because real conditions in war zones are so gravely distressing; e.g. having game characters deteriorate for lack of cigarettes was contrived to create more tasks, but it doesn't say much for humanity's priorities in a crisis.

So, even though This War of Mine is an intensely stirring social commentary on the horrors of war, and well worth buying if you enjoy survival games, there's room for improvement should the developers decide to upgrade it.

This game, as several reviews state, is unlike any other. 

It's a dark, horrible environment that you play in, with tough decisions to be made.  Some will save your group but make them depressed, others will use precious resources but cheer your group up, and some may get you killed.

I will state now that I haven't made it past day 14, I usually get to that stage (with various group lineups) and decide to take a chance at a 'dangerous' scavenge and always find myself dead fairly quick.  I know I should delay the 'dangerouss until I have better gear and resources but I always start to panic at 2 weeks heh.

What it does show me is that this isn't a game you can rush.  Everything is slow and careful, some nights (later in the game) with no scavenging but scouting instead (if you have the right group set up).  You need to plan in advance your resources, both food and workshop.

The graphics are very atmospheric, adding to the darkness and grittiness of the game.  It's black, white and grey,  No other colours, so don't expect a pretty game.

You start off with a few set group choices, and often in the game other characters will appear asking to join you.  There are plenty of guides on Steam that explain each characters pros and cons, and I really recommend reading them.  Some you will want to be cruel and turn away.

And that leads to, in my mind, the one bad thing about the game.  The characters and their skills.  Some skills are still unknown, others aren't obvious, some are just generally useless.  All of which leads to a set 4-5 chars you want in your group.  Every guide states the same.  I've tried it my own way and found that yup, the longest I've lasted is with at least 2 of those 4-5.  It's the same chars over and over again, which gets dull and boring.  It would be nice to mix it up, perhaps chars with 2 main skills each, allowing cross-over and use of the other 'useless' chars in the game.  

Please note, by useless I mean long-term use.  Each has a skill which could be useful if the game was easier and you could support 6-8 chars easily.  You can't.  The most you can generally support AND survive the 40 days is 4 chars.  So you have to be brutal and choose only the most useful out of all 12 chars.  It just so happens it's the same 4-5 chars every time :-(

However, if you ignore that one con, the rest of the game is amazing and addictive.  Hours pass by without you realising it, as you concentrate on your group so much, and what you need next, then it's just one more scavenge so I can make item xxx then I'll log out, but you make xxx then realise you need to make item yyy so it's just another quick scavenge...

When you get to approx day 10-11, it opens up new group set-ups on the main menu.

This War of Mine is one of the few games that I actually read the 'bunff', in this case the character's and their stories.  I read each and look forward to learning more about them.  Each story seems dark (as with everything in the game) and sad, and gives a terrible perspective about what it is really like to survive in such a situation.  I have yet to finish them, but there are guides on Steam that tell every character's story.  Personally, I want to wait until I've earnt it.

However, I do recommend reading some of the guides on how to survive.  Don't just read one, but several, as each gives different advice, some work for some people and some for others.  After trying and testing, I've found I do bits from all of them.  I did try doing it without reading the guides to start with and never made it past day 5.  After reading the guides, I found out where I was going wrong and it made a huge difference.

So to end.  This game is definately worth the money.  It seems to be well supported by its developer.  It's a dark, gritty and brutal game, and that works.

RATING
8/10

The game is very good. Exellent music, reasonably deep gameplay (think State of Decay), brilliant art style, lots of replay value, and provides a good challenge. I'm glad I bought it, and it's one of my favourite games that I've played in a while. 

The only "bad" part about the game is the combat, which is very unforgiving. You may go 20 in-game days without entering combat even once, and then you may get cornered by a gang of armed thugs and your favorite character dies in literally 2 seconds due to no fault of your own. The combat is simply not balanced properly, and feels like an afterthought from the developers. You never really have a feeling that you can safely attack or avoid someone, because chances are 5 other enemies will swarm you immediately and you will just die. What makes combat even worse is that you have to switch from 'Scavenge' mode to 'Combat' mode, which is just a really clumsy/clunky/un-intuitive method of engaging in combat, especially when your character can die in 2 seconds if you don't switch to Combat mode fast enough. It's actually a really really BAD part of an otherwise excellent game. 

The presentation of the game is very good, although I feel like some corners were cut in production, specifically the lack of variety in the music, lack of voiceovers, and lack of a real storyline. 

Music = 8/10, great, but hardly any variety. Sounded like there was only 1 or 2 tracks in the entire game, although they never felt repetitive. 
Sound = 8/10, great, felt very realistic and gritty, however there is a lack of voiceovers, which feels a bit meh.
Combat = 3/10, unforgiving, clunky, not really that fun or satisfying. Glaringly bad. 
Scavenging/Crafting = 9/10, excellent, the best part of the game
Art = 10/10, amazing, fresh art style with solid graphics and animations.
Overall = 8.7 out of 10. Would have been nearly perfect if the combat was better and if there was slightly higher production value. Worth playing for sure.

This War of Mine. What to say about it? It is a game that we needed to come out. You are /not/ a specially trained  super soldier, a guts-n-glory stoked battle master, a heartless mercenary - you are none of these things. You are responsible for guiding the actions of a group of civilians caught in the middle of a civil war. They want no part in the war between the rebels and the government, they just want to survive.

Sure, there's crafting, and exploring, and even a bit of combat. But those aren't the focus of the game. They aren't the main reason. The main goal. Survival is the goal. Remember, these are not faceless people that you steal from, they used to be your neighbors or friends. That bandit that you had to kill? The survivors will feel remorse for their actions.

The best outcome for the game is to survive the war and have as many of the survivors alive as possible, in as good a mental state as you can maintain. That is the trick - while you can kill and steal your way to survival, how will you live with yourself afterwards?

This War of Mine is a game focused on the other side of war, not the soldiers, but the normal people that find themselves caught in a war torn city. It uses this setting to frame the survival gameplay in some interesting yet flawed ways. 

I'll talk about the progression of a single game. This War of Mine is not a story driven game or level based game, it's a try to survive game and either succeed or fail, then if you're up to it try again. The game cycles through a predictable gameplay loop with differing objectives at each step. 

First, you'll start in your safe zone, a dilapidated building, and here is where you build things you'll need in the coming days or meet the needs of your group of people. You can have multiple people that you control at this stage, each with a small backstory of who they were before the war. These people will grow tired, sick, sad, and hungry and you'll have to handle their needs when they arise or negative things will happen like death and depression. 

The next phase of the game loop happens when night comes. When night comes you'll have to plan how you want to spend it. You decide who will go out scavenging for items and who will stay back at the house. The people that stay at the house can be given direction on whether they should guard or sleep. If they guard they'll be more tired the next day and might have to sleep the whole day through.

Once your night plan is setup the final phase of the game loop occurs: you scavenge with the character you chose to scavenge with. The gameplay is 2D sidescrolling at this point and you'll have to find various things to loot. You'll only be able to hold a small number of things depending on who you chose to take scavenging so even if a location you choose to scavenge has hundreds of supplies you might only be able to take a fraction of that meaning you'll have to spend multiple days trying to take it all back to your house. Some locations that you go to will be dangerous and you'll have to sneak past. If you're seen stealing then you'll be attacked and you'll have to run away. Combat is almost non existent because it will most likely lead to death. The only exception is stealth attacks which can only be performed from pre-decided dark hallways that you can jump out of if someone happens to walk past it.

Once you're done scavenging you return back to the house with the goods you've scavenged and the different characters all will adjust accordingly to the passing day. If they were guarding all night they'll be tired, the character you scavenged with will be tired and maybe wounded if they got hit, everyone will get a little more hungry, someone might get sick if it was too cold, some will get sad if anything bad happens, or people that lost all hope might kill themselves or abandon the group. You'll have to handle each of these situations in different ways: prepare food to best combat hunger or eat raw food to help it a little bit, talk with depressed members to try to cheer them up, add things to the house that make it feel more normal to raise spirits like radios or soft furniture, apply bandaged or medicine to the sick and wounded.

It all sounds very easy, and it would be, but the difficulty arises when you find just how rare some of the stuff you need is. Food and medicine is hard to find. Your members will begin to get hungrier and hungrier and you might not be able to do anything about it. A slight sickness might lead to death because you can't find medicine. All of the above will continue to make people sad to the point that they might not even want to move (broken = won't listen to any of your commands). At that point your group is as good as dead because you won't be able to guard your house and raiders will steal any small things you do have or come in and kill you.

The problem I have with the game is that there is only one way to play. You have to be a nice guy otherwise your group will start to get depressed and broken. You have to get all types of items instead of focusing on one type because any death or sickness in the group will lead to a snow ball effect of everyone just becoming depressed and broken. There is no variation to the way you have to play this game. Killing people is out of the question because everyone in your group can't handle it and ends up killing themselves over it. One thing I think should be changed is after killing someone everyone shouldn't respond to it. Once you kill someone during scavenging it is telepathically told to the entire group that you killed them and they all get depressed and want to die. I should be able to carry the burden as a single person, the person that scavenged. Another thing that shows that you have to play the game in this very strictly defined way is that if you do happen to kill someone that had a firearm in clear sight, it cannot be looted, it just disappears.

The game tries to incite emotional responses with the content, but it turns out to actually be quite comedic when a single person getting sick puts everyone into a paralysis induced depression to the point that they don't even care themselves to live and end up hanging themselves over it. 

The game makes numerous illogical jumps like this to hit home its message of the effect of war on normal people. Everyone in the game supposedly has their own backstory, their own personality, but they are all as soft hearted as mickey mouse. Couldn't a few actual survivors make it into the mix? I get the message, but it is executed in a bad illogical way.

Subsequent playthroughs change slightly since each time you lose you can start up again with a new base group of survivors and they start in a different locations. Since all the survivors basically act the same this has no real gameplay implications other than a different number of mouths to feed. The new locations offer more or less space to build things, and in some scenarios you may start out in winter which can make it more difficult.

This War of Mine is an artificially hard game to beat (survive max number of days) if you try to play it outside of the narrow vision how it should be played. The game can still be enjoyed without ever beating it though just to see some of the outcomes that can occur. Unfortunately, the more you play the more you notice the flaws in the game design; flaws that I think take away from, rather than improve upon (which is the reason I can imagine they were introduced), the primary objective of the game to tell the story of the non-soldiers of war. 

I do recommend the game overall because I did enjoy my time playing it, but don't expect a hardcore survival game or a game with a deep story. It's a very simple game from a gameplay standpoint that tries to convey its message in clunky and illogical ways which end up hurting the believability of the situations and changing the tone of the game entirely from what is intended to farcical.

Wow, just wow. This is an absolutely beautiful game. No game has ever impacted me as much as this one has, despite how minimalistic it may seem at first. But it is this minimalism that makes it so much more powerful and therefore have a greater impact. Most war games nowadays just show the "glory" of war - whether it be shooters or strategy games where you must crush all opposition. The games in which the civilian toll of war is explored are few and far between. Even strategy games where you besiege a city or planet to force the population to surrender gloss over the civilian toll. Probably the most notable instance of civilians being involved in a conflict game would be *that* level in Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2. But even then, This War of Mine is completely unique in that you are controlling the civilians. While you may encounter combatants from either side, you don't participate in the conflict at all, you just try your best to survive on the peripheries of the unmentioned Civil War tearing the city and its population apart.

This is a very meaningful game in ways unlike most others. War is Hell, and no game demonstrates this as well as this one does. There are many conflicts in the world right now, and civilian casualties are a very real, and very sad part of this reality. Having a keen interest in military history, and knowing just how destructive city sieges are/were, let alone the bombing raids on cities, this game really does strike home just how terrible war is. The hard choices that civilians must make in order to survive in such situations is a really important part of this game, and truly one of the standouts. Just like in the real world, there is no black and white, just a whole lot of greys. You are unlikely to make it out of this game feeling like a champion; there are terrible decisions to make one after the other. The decisions you must make, and the consequences of these decisions, are incredible, and I needed to take a break after some of these decisions. No spoilers here, but you may feel like a disgusting monster, or a hero, and well... will either decision even affect the survival of your own group?

The playable characters, though with Eastern European names due to the geographical setting, all have excellent back stories and personalities which actually influence how they may react. Some characters may be more or less willing to do certain things, and certain actions will either positively or negatively your group's morale. Being caught on combatants aren't the only hazards, however, starvation, dehydration, and depression can be, and are real killers in This War of Mine. Depression is particularly well handled in this game, given the tough choices you must make, and the effect that these choices will have on your group. Special mention owing to the difficult nature of depression and other mental illnesses.

The graphics and sound may not be complex, but they convey the themes of the game excellently. For the game's theme, the simple 2d side view of the game works better than something which would be provided by either a first-person or third-person perspective. The 2d nature of the game allows you to better encapsulate what it is all about, from building your shelter to scavenging for supplies. The audio is also brilliant, with a haunting soundtrack punctuated by the sounds of combat in the distance.

Meaningful and excellent in a way that few games are, I cannot recommend this game enough.

This is a game that was widely reviewed as a 'must play' and a 'gamechanger' because it puts you on the other side of war. Despite enjoying my playthrough (s, I lost quite a few times before surviving to the end) I didn't at all see how this was a moral or introspective game at all. What i will say is that the game makes you regret a choice to steal from a kind family or kill others to keep your own group alive, but the only consequence is a sad character which can be salvaged by having another character talk to them for a little while. I won't go as far as to say you don't care about killing people, but it is largely as inconsequential as killing in other games. You end up strategizing to keep your characters from being bothered by your orders rather than feeling guilty about them yourself.

That being said, I liked the game. It looked good, it had a really sad feel to it in the artwork and the music, and even in success you are pointed back to what you had to do to get there. The gameplay itself was unlike anything I had played before, but wasn't revolutionary to the point that this is a selling-point.

The game is not worth the money. If it is on sale, by all means try it on, it is a new type of experience. I had two huge problems with it that keep it from being worth the price. 

-first, as I mentioned above, the game is really sold as a moral dilemma type game, where you sacrifice ease for doing the right thing, etc. It isn't that. If you want to challenge yourself by all means walk the high road, but there is not connection with any of the characters, especially the ones you are in control of. There is a little bit of background for each reavealed as the game progresses, but they all have repeated, generic lines, without voice acting, that occasionally play and do little to make them endearing, or even disliked which can be a connecting point.

-Lastly, and the main reason i can't reccomend is that the second I actually finished the game, I was done with it. There was absolutley no replay value at all. I don't want to sound hypocritical, because as you can see I put some serious time into this. I have often heard said about games that they can be addicting without being fun, and I never really bought it. This game is that. I had to survive, I had to win, but once I won I really wondered why the hell i bothered to do all that, I didn't even enjoy the ride.

A game that relies heavily on consequences. Nay, is composed of said consequences. The moral and ethical decisions one has to make in the game to survive the devastation of a civil war, it can be heart-clenching (or brutally amusing depending on what kind of "person" you are).

Should you steal medicine for a terminally ill survivor from a defenseless elderly couple or conduct an honest trade at the the shelled hospital?

Should you risk your survivor's life to save an unknown girl searching for food for her family from the wrath of a drunk (and armed!) soldier or leave them be and scavenge the area in relative safety?

I LOVE survival games and this is probably the best I have ever played!!  

MOST survival games consist of gathering resources, fighting off what ever the hostile mob is for that particular game, and finally achieving self-sustainability which makes gathering materials far less necessary.  At that point, most survival games become boring and pointless.  TWoM is NOT your typical survival game. 

 Every single day is a struggle.  Self-sustainabilty, while not impossible, is EXTREMELY difficult to achieve.  The decisions that you have to make in order to make it to the end of the war are often tough, gut-wrenching calls in which there truly ARE no good answers (i.e. trading medicine for food and allowing a sick survivor to die so that the other survivors can eat...which in turn causes the other survivors to become depressed and refuse to even defend the shelter from bandits who come in that night to steal all the food you traded for.)

Some of the scenarios are less difficult than others.  Some of the scenarios are down right brutal.  All of the scenarios are challenging.

If you are looking for another CoD FPS remake, this game is not for you.  If you are looking for a gritty, immersive, survival experience where every decision is important and every mistake potentially critical, then look no further.

Primary Objective: Survive.
Secondary Objective: Preserve your humanity along the way.

You control a group of civilians trying to survive in an urban warzone. They have different talents (or lack of talents) and differing tolerances of morally questionable actions you may elect to take in order to survive (such as killing and stealing).

The survivors must take care of their basic needs and protect their shelter. Supplies run out and each night a member of the group must go out scavenging for materials, food and goods for barter. 
The game plays out as a 2D survival management sim; during daytime you'll manage your resources, trade and improve the shelter. During the night the game is a 2D stealth-action game: You search for useful supplies while avoiding or possibly killing enemies. Combat is determined by RNG, but heavily influenced by equipment and player timing. The game is hard, offering little help to the newbie and your first playthrough will probably go poorly. Doing better the next time is a great appeal of this game. In later playthroughs you can play as a different group of survivors and possibly start the game during the winter season (which changes the game economy in favour of fuel for heating).
You can only save upon exiting (essentially always iron-man mode) and death is permanent. This makes your choices and priorities much more relevant and engaging.

Will you risk getting shot by the soldiers or will you prey on those weaker than you, taking their supplies by force? You can imagine your own little stories about the survivors as you decide their actions.

Ever enjoyed Survival, sidescrollers and tactical natures to a game but never found one with all three within it?

Your feels will eventually be struck in parts of the game. Not because of the game itself with any sort story line, but the decisions you do within it and the outcome of them. [h1][b][u]Game play[/u][/b][/h1]
This War of Mine focuses and portrays as more of a Survival game than a military game, although there are firearms within the game, its main aim is to make you scavange for supplies in order to keep all of your survivors healthy, fed, warm and most importantly, alive.
The game itself is rather slow at the start, as there isn't much for you to explore and on the first day its more of a point and click Rubbel Remover Simulator 2015. However eventually the game will pick up pace and that is when you really will be getting into it. Although its slow at the start, don't let this cause you to have second thoughts about buying the game, with the slow start it allows you to get one step ahead of the game by placing down beds, heaters, stoves ect. as you're removing the rubble and ranksacking the place.
The scavanging side of the game is pretty simple, you have two options, Live or Die. When out scavanging some areas may be hostile and some may be neutral, so you have to be aware of the NPCs that may or may not be there.
When scavanging, you're most likely going to want to stay alive, so if you find yourself in a hostile environment without a knife or character that can 1 shot instant kill them, you're better of trying to hide and stay in a Stealth mode.
This War of Mine makes you be afraid to die, as dying not only effects you by having 1 less playable character, it also lowers moral within the rest of your crew. The same goes for Firefights with Guns and fist fights, this game is brutal and will kill you within 2/3 bullets from hostile NPC if you're not well equipped or have an escape plan.

[h1][b][u]Looks and Feels[/u][/b][/h1]
This War of Mine has a very interesting colour pallet to it and style of art. The majority of colours you will see are cold colours, such as; Blue, Black, Grey, however the odd Orange/yellow and white is thrown in there also.
This game is supposed to feel dark and make you feel like you're actually apart of the war, in sence the game does achieve that, however I wouldn't quite say that its because of the gameplay itself, the colour pallet and the style of art which is in the game ties it together and creates this Dark atmosphere.

[h1][b][u]Replayability[/u][/b][/h1]
Although the game doesn't seem to have much Replayability to it, it somewhat does.
Reason for this is due to the ammount of differant character sets that are available to start of with, upon that you also have 2 Differant households to randomly start in and a differant Scavanger map with random quick time events. I'd say this game has at least a Replayability of 3/4 Untill you've actually seen everything within the game.
On record I've put in a good 28hours of play and still am playing now due to not even I have seen everything within the game and I'd say it'd be at least a solid 35+hours in game time untill you have seen everything!

This is one of the most depressing games i've ever played but that's not a criticism.It's what makes this a brilliant game. You control a group of civilians who are holed up in a house in a war-torn city. During the day the gameplay is focused aroud the house where you can make your characters eat (if you have any food) and carry out upgrades or improvements on the house like building a stove or a cooker.

At night you need to decide who get to sleep, who stays on guard and who goes out to scavenge. The scavenging is done by picking a location in the city and then your transported to that location where you can guide your character through it looking for supplies like food or medicine. You only have limited space so this mines having to prioritize.Do you need to take more medicine or will you sacrifice some to bring back more food for example. The scavenging can be made more dangerous with some locations having hostile armed npcs who will kill you if they catch you.

What this game does brilliantly is the moral decisions it throws at you? For example in one of my playthroughs i went to scavenge from a quiet house. As i entered the house a man appeared and shouted at me. I stabbed and killed him as i thought he might attack me. I then had to kill his wife who i was worried might run and fetch help. The situations like these that the game throughs up are harrowing and can even badly affect the characters who get depressed when they kill someone. It really captures the bleakness and desperation of being trapped in a warzone.

As for the look of the game it's got a sort of bleak look which really adds to the atmosphere as does the music. It's also an easy game to get into as it's got a quite simple point and click control scheme.

The Good:
- Really captures the misery and desperation of trying to survive in a warzone.
- The game will really test your morals and does so better than most games
-Each playthrough is always different so has a fair bit of replay value

The Bad:
- Scavenging can be a bit tedious at times

Overall this is a great game that highlights the horror of war better than most games i've ever played. 8/10

Here's my summarised verdict on the game. 

It's incredibly immersive and forces you to make such difficult decisions which will ultimately 
challenge your very morals, all for the sake of survival. Representing this game within a dystopian world ingulfed in the horrors of war has truely opened up a whole new perspective. The message that the game is trying to represent about the impact of war torn countries upon its citizens is truely fascinating. 

Overall, 'This War of Mine' is a game that deserves much praise for not only it's representation but primarly its immersive gameplay.

On the whole this game is not enjoyable in the traditional sense.  It's not a fun game, it's not action packed, it's not instantly rewarding, and it's not fast paced, nor is it supposed to be.
What it is instead is gripping, suspenseful, and internally rewarding.  It is extremely difficult, and every decision you make will trickle down to other decisions in the future.  Do you eat today, or do you stockpile fuel for the cold weather coming up ?  Will you steal from the elderly couple down the road and ultimately condemn them to death just to feed yourself?  Are you prepared to allow one of your survivors to die to better insure the survival of the others, or will you waste medical supplies and sleepless nights trying against all odds to nurse a friend back to health?  Will you murder in cold blood for a piece of raw food?

These are decisions you have to make, and each one no matter how small can mean not only the difference between life and death but affect the emotional and psychological stability of your survivors.

Not only is the gameplay and strategy riviting, but the artistic style, RTS like controls, and musical score all together paint a portrait of a dismal life of despair and heartache with limited options and no end in sight.

Should you get this game?  Yes!  Definitely!  When was the last time you had a video game make you sit back in your chair, sip on your beverage, and look around and appreciate the home you have and the life you are living?  For me, it was just a few hours ago, and it was this game...

Having played this game for over 40 hours, I can say that I was hooked right from the get-go. This game deserves a 10/10. The game puts you into the role of survivors holed up in a house, where you will be living/sleeping/eating and surviving in. 

Everyday is split into a "day" portion and an "night" portion. During the day, you will be crafting things such as metal workshops, a stove or a herbal garden. If your characters are hungry, you will need to feed them in order for their condition to not worsen. In the earlier parts of the game, material and food collection is crucial. 

At night, you select one of your characters to scavenge another building in the area while the rest of the characters guards the house or sleeps through the night. Each character has their own "special" abilities, such as having more backpack slots to store items that you have found in the buildings, or being a good cook. Once you have filled up your slots, you return to your home for the next day. 

As you progress through the game, some buildings have thugs that reside inside and may attack you on sight, and if your character is killed, the game still continues on.

Some things to consider:

Each player has their own statuses and addictions. These may be changed as the game progresses.

The statuses include emotional ones (sad/content/depressed) and condition based ones(hungry/sick/injured)

I just finished my first playthrough of the game, and I can say that it was well worth the money, and I am not someone who buys many games these days.

There's no tutorial, but the games mechanics are simple, which means you fumble around trying to get everything together for the first few days as your initial supplies dwindle.  I soon got used to perpetual hunger, and was satisfied as long as my band of survivors was not starving as I tried to figure out how to navigate the city's wartime economy of barter and scavenging.  

I get the feeling that if you know the city well enough after some playthroughs, and as long as the game doesnt start you in winter (which means you may forsake building vital security improvements to your shelter and focus on building heaters and stoves to melt snow and keep you warm) then a player could learn how to optimise their economy very quickly.  The problems come when you make mistakes (see the story below) or when you get very unlucky (which happens a lot) then the risks of death become very high.  You also come across people who need your help, for example a starving hobo in an old building who needs food bad, and if you don't have it, by the time you spend a day or two getting back to help him, you find him starved to death, so it's inevitable that you will see people suffer.

I desperately tried to keep all of my ragtag band alive through the war, and failed when, due to a misunderstanding at the hospital, I lost poor Boris.  Boris ate a burst from a rebel soldier's assault rifle when, after making one of them mad, he couldn't leave the building fast enough for them due to his injured leg.  Eventually they got tired of shouting curses at him and hitting them with their gun butts and shot him.   Somehow he survived and crawled halfway across the city to the house.  When it became clear that he would die of his wounds unless he recieved some real treatment, Katia, who was the most cheerful of the group, ran into the house of an elderly couple that lived across town and raided their medicine cabinet for bandages and medicine while the poor husband and wife begged her to stop.  Katia only took what she needed: two packs of bandages and a bottle of antibiotic pills, but for days after felt depressed by what she'd done while boris hovered on the brink of death.  Then the bandits came in the night.  And though we had some weapons, boris suffered a minor wound while in his bed, and died.  My heartbreaking robbery of the old couple had been pointless.  The rest of the group lost all hope after that, but somehow we pulled through.   

Boris had been the strongest, and could carry the most back from dangerous forays scavenging the ruins, but then my group met Marco, a former firefighter, and although I almost turned him away because we had no food to feed him, much less ourselves, he quickly proved his worth.  With Marco's help we managed to scavenge enough supplies to keep from starving.  We also had more people to spare to help our neighbors, and even save a few lives when we were out scavenging before relief finally reached the city.  If that little story doesn't convince you that this game can be very engrossing, then this is not for you.  For me it's a great and wonderful adventure into human suffering that is more engaging than many games where the war is from a soldier's perspective.  8.75/10

This War of Mine is an excellent concept buried under a plethora of bad gameplay elements. 

I'll start right off the bat with my first "nitpick," which I've put in quotation marks because of just how bad this concept is: Every single character, regardless of background, upbringing, etc. has the skills and the knowledge required to build complicated appliances that, more often than not, at least require a few weeks, if not months of training in order to even learn how to MAINTAIN. It's a huge stretch to say that a single person studying music understands how to distill moonshine, build an oven, and construct firearms. They do all of this perfectly; the guns themselves don't have any individual stats, unlike Rimworld (a game which I find quite similar in terms of having colonists/survivors that all work in tandem to survive in a harsh environment), which features pawns who are oftentimes only good at a few things but are able to learn new skills as they develop.

This game is long enough to have developing skills and could have at least had a system where people learn how to build more complex things with experience, for example after building X amount of furniture. It's not a perfect system, but it makes more sense than having a news reporter essentially do the same level and quality of work that an HVAC technician can do.

This isn't even the main problem with the game. The biggest problem is that the gameplay is EXTREMELY unpolished. Combat feels terrible and clunky and is very hard to learn given how rare it is in this game, and getting into a fight is VERY punishing if you do not kill your target instantly. A lot of the combat mechanics like cover, hiding, etc. completely fall apart when you are fighting more than one opponent, as most of the time you will be overpowered very easily. Furthermore, NPC aggression is also quite stupid in this game. NPCs will more often than not get angry at you for running towards them or getting too close, but by the time they give you their warning dialogue they will likely turn hostile and try to kill you. It's just stupid and makes this game feel way more unpolished than a game this simple should be. If it weren't for the bad combat and the janky controls (because believe me, this game feels really jank even outside of combat), I would have likely recommended this..

Part two of the gameplay issue features my second critique: The game is way too ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ easy. It's the same thing every time. Houses barely differ if at all (I never noticed them being different), you usually get enough resources to make every single station besides the garden, herb bench, and the distillery (these three are barely helpful by the way), and the way the game scales is very anticlimactic. More often than not the game will get progressively harder but then take a huge nosedive in difficulty in the last 10 days. I find this game so easy that I often spend most days making my guys eat food and then sleeping because of how overly abundant most resources are. Of course, it depends on how much risk you're willing to take, but more often than not you can easily win most fights simply by shooting bandits with the shotgun.

The game's scaling is off and it's very hard to actually find yourself in a desperate situation in this game, mostly because it's very easy to bail yourself out of most situations. Sure, stealing is wrong, I get that, but it's often too easy to do (in some areas) and the rewards far exceed the punishment. If I were the devs I'd make the final few days REALLY hard, just as a "final push." Most of my experiences had the final few days be very easy which is very underwhelming and BORING to play through.

That's the main problem this game has. It's not challenging and it doesn't respect your time very well, nor does it allow you to do anything interesting with the micro system this game has. Queuing up tasks or creating bills for your characters to do would make this game far more interesting and dynamic. Unfortunately a lot of the time spent in the house will involve you sitting there and watching. This is the same for items like the shovel. Most of the time you won't need it. Most of the time when you see bars or a locked door it will do nothing but create a sticky note in your head that reminds you to check it out later. All the impediments in this game just serve to slow you down or delay you, thus wasting your time. It doesn't provide a challenge. There's no RISK in making lockpicks, saws, etc. because the resources to make them are cheap and found practically everywhere. There's no reason to invest all your resources into anything other than basic weapons (the assault rifle is horrible and the shotgun is the best weapon in the game), reliably ways of acquiring food, and medicine to heal your units. All of the advanced stuff really doesn't do anything when all it takes to guard your home is a handgun and a few bullets which you will find everywhere.

Killing people is way too easy in this game and most gunfights make no sense. Somebody shot at my unit 10 times and they were only "wounded." I'm pretty sure if I shot someone 10 times they'd either be dead or on the brink of death. Meanwhile I can kill people instantly with a single bullet using a pump action shotgun.

I don't have anything to say about the design of this game other than it's beautiful. Artstyle is cool, I like the polaroid style for the characters, and I love the music and the themes behind this game. It aged very well for me given that I appreciate the mature and realistic themes far more, it's just that the gameplay really hurts this game.

This game still holds a tiny place in my tiny heart because I like the themes and concept behind the game. The core gameplay is good but it needs so much work. I wish it was a lot harder or had difficulty settings. I want to STRUGGLE to survive, and I want the last few days of the game to feel like a huge desperate push where I must do everything in my power to see it through. Instead my colonists are living better than I am in my luxury apartment on the East Coast. This War of Mine is one of the most emotional, grim games I've ever played. There were many moments in this game where I felt absolutley terrible for the things I had to do to survive. WARNING: this is not a happy game in any stretch of the imagination. This is a game about war, and war is hell. Sure there are a couple mildly happy moments in the game, but overhall it's very grim. This War of Mine is a game based on the Seige of Sarajevo that lasted 1,425 days and it is known to be the largest seige of a city in history. You play as a group of civilians trying to survive in a fictional beseiged city called Pogoren. You must deal with starvation, lack of medical supplies, scavangers trying to raid your supplies, and the emotional state of the survivors.

  One of the best things about this game is the fact that I couldn't reload a previous save to undo a horrible thing I've done, the game only auto saves after every night of scavenging and override's the previous save. This makes it more emmotionally gripping and nail-biting since it makes my decisions perminant and that it made me try even harder to not die. And it's not easy, trust me. There are multiple points in the game where I had little resources and my survivors were either starving, depressed, exausted, freezing, or all of the above. All of the abbandoned buildings were either stripped clean of supplies or didn't have the resources that the survivors needed to, well, survive.  There were only 2 options: raid another shelter for supplies or die. I had to rob and/or kill (mostly) innocents for their supplies in order to survive. It's not a walk in the park either, it will be emotionally heavy for both the player (unless they're a psychopath or a sociopath) and their survivors. The one who got to raid and kill the innocents for food and supplies will suffer from severe psychological trauma. And the player will have to deal with that.

   And due to the trend I've seen when people who review this game tell a story from their experience from the game, I'm going to do that too. 
There was one day where my survivors were starving, some wounded and/or exausted. They had little resources, their options were limited. They had no choice but to attack another Shelter full of people. Marko, an expert scavenger, couldn't go because he was emmotionally broken from all the people he had to kill in order to survive. Bruno seemed to be the only one capable to go and steal from another shelter, so he was sent to steal supplies from another shelter while Pavle was to gaurd the shelter from looters during the night. When Bruno reached the place, he looked through the peephole and saw a gaurd. He waited when the gaurd wasn't looking. Bruno then equiped his knife and then stabbed the gaurd in the back. This didn't insta-kill him though, so Bruno had to stab him a second time. Bruno then looted the gaurd's corpse and found a shotgun with some ammo. This caused some noise however, and caused a woman to come down from the stairs. The woman was crying out: "Oh god! Herald, no! No, this can't be happening!" and sat down next to the dead gaurd while sobbing. Bruno couldn't think striaght, he thought it was best to shoot the woman and put her out of her misery. The gunshot alerted two gaurds nearby, they came down and saw the two dead bodies of their comarads. They yelled out "Murderer!" to Bruno and tried to kill him. Bruno killed the two soldiers but was severely wounded. As he looted their corpses as well as the nearby area with no gaurds, he was soaking in the fact that he just murdered innocent people for food. 
I felt like crap after doing that, there are many moments like these that the player will encounter during their playthrough. It's depressing but in a good way, if that makes any sense. 

But the game isn't perfect, the survivors will sometimes say obvious things like "this shovel is doing well." while they're  digging it. And the controls can be annoying at times, I've accidentally closed doors when I was trying to get through them multiple times in the game.  It runs pretty smoothly on my pc, and I haven't noticed any bugs sp far. 

But the game's flaws hardly take away from the experience. This is by far my game of the year. I give This War of Mine a 10/10. I highly recomend it if you're sick of war games from the point of view from a soldiers perspective and glorifying violence.

This War of Mine is an excellent survival game that shows off a different aspect of war. You are not a health-regenerating god with the skill to shoot enemies in the head with a pistol from 100m away. No. You control a group of survivors that are facing the hardships of war: having to scavenge for supplies, fend off bandits, beat the chill of the winter, etc. And trust me, it is HARD!

The controls are simple: click here to walk, click there to search through some trash, click on that guy to punch them, etc. And it is well done too as I never felt like that controls were inadequate or dodgy, so props to the developers on that one. The gameplay is simple too (there seems to be no tutorial, but after 5mins of playing you will surely figure out what you're doing): build up your base with furniture, create weapons, manage your survivors health and hunger, trade with other survivors that approach your shelter, and more, throughout the day. When night comes around, you get to decide who sleeps, who guards (or have no one guard, which is risky due to the possibility of being raided), and who goes out on a scavenging run (e.g. search an abandoned house for materials, or go all out into a military outpost looking for food or medical supplies).

The soft pencil aesthetic is very pleasing too over the top of the 2.5D look of the game. The music and sounds are all well-done too, although the variety of music on the radio is limited (probably due to the war, which is justifiable). The different characters you meet along the way all have their own bio, which changes depending on how they're feeling (e.g. if they have just killed 3 people on the last-night's raid, they may be feeling quite depressed about it). Because of all these factors and the fact that the war could last only 30 days or over 40 days, the potential for replayibility is high.

If you're interested in seeing the side of war that most modern-military shooters don't often portray these days and want to play a rather difficult survival/management game, then definitely pick up This War of Mine. It is truly brilliant!

Enjoy! :D

This War of Mine is an emotionally distressing experience every gamer must play at some point in their lives. Though stylized and simplistic on the surface, it pulls no punches in its gut-wrenchingly realistic depiction of survival amid the unforgiving chaos of war. Inspired by the personal account of a survivor of the 90's Balkan War told on a survivalist forum, the development team clearly did their source material justice. "The War is Over." That's the phrase that pops up when you survive the war, and frankly after playing this game that's all the satisfaction you will ever need. 

This game is indie. It's not funny, it's not known for its fighting mechanics, but it sends a message that can be summed up in three words "war is bad." But of course we already know that right? 9 out of 10 people you ask will probably say that war is bad. They might say support our troops, let the conflict in the middle east end, or hold a moment of silence as a sign of respect. But talk is cheap, actions are what define a person. 

By actions are what define a person I am not suggesting a call to action that every single one of us quit our dayjobs or schooling to go rally and achieve world peace. What I am asking is that you experience a very accurate simulation of what war is truly like, because after this game trust me, you will have a whole new understanding of what war is. Playing this game won't suddenly make you relate to the horrors that the REAL victims of war have seen. But it will make you feel like a human being and if you do it right, you will get some strong emotions in the mix too.

If you do get this game, I suggest you try to play it as realistically as possible and as humanly as possible. What I mean by that is that you keep in your mind that these are real people you are controlling, because eventually there will come a point in the game where you will simply forget that. Everytime your character helps someone, you will feel happy. Everytime you turn away a neighbor asking for help you will feel bad. You will see things in the game that you are powerless to stop. Your morals will be questioned all the way until you either survive or perish. Will you steal from an elderly couple? Will you stand up from those who are being abused even if it means putting yourself in danger? Will you barter with the very people who are responsible for raping, looting, and taking advantage of ordinary citizens like you? You won't know who you really are until you play this game, until you realize that the game is sad for a reason, until you realize that all of the things that happen in this game could and have happened to other people in real life.

You know war is bad. Now experience it for yourself.

TL:DR I was feeling inspired and emotional. War is bad. Get this game if you have a heart and want to learn at the same time that you have some fun. :)

I feel like this is somewhat of a sleeper game that flew under the radar for a lot of people and for that reason I am writing a review. This War of Mine puts you in the shoes of a civilian with one simple goal: survive! You and a few survivors (usually between three and five from a roster of about ten or twelve) are put in a house and need to do whatever you can to survive. During the day you can scavenge around your house or build upgardes such as weapons, stove, animal traps, rain catchers, beds and even a guitar. 
During the night time you must pick one person to venture out into one of the locations where supplies must be scavenged. Early in the game you only need a lockpick or two to search for cigarettes, food, and building supplies. Yet as you start to exhuast supplies you must venture into areas where other people are living, usually armed and dangerous. It becomes a balancing act by ensuring the survival of your group and trying to navigate the tough moral implications of you stealing supplies from other or in extreme situations killing them.
It is a tough game and you must be prepared for members of your group to suffer quite a bit as the strain of trying to live in a warzone takes its toll. It is a visceral and somewhat brutal take on a facet of war that is seldom explored. It is definitely worth a try to see if you can last in This War of Mine.
